Google Classroom

The assessment and feedback loop, using features every teacher already has. · 4 sub-tools · 21 examples

Availability. Rubrics, comment bank, private comments, learning goals and five originality-report assignments per class: every Workspace for Education edition. Creating student groups, unlimited originality reports with school matches, interactive YouTube questions, practice sets and teacher class analytics: Education Plus or the Teaching and Learning add-on on the teacher's account. Admins must turn on YouTube as an additional service, enable school matches and add teachers to the verified-teacher group for sharing. No under-18 restriction stated. LAET's edition is not recorded here.

Assignments with rubrics, comment bank and private comments

Attach a scored or unscored rubric to an assignment, grade against it in the grading tool, reuse or export it, and tag it with learning goals for per-goal analytics. Store reusable feedback in a personal comment bank, annotate any file type in place, and leave private comments students can reply to.

Options. Up to 50 criteria and 10 levels each, ordered ascending or descending; reuse from any class; export to Sheets, import only Classroom-exported sheets; up to 10 learning goals per assignment, with UK standard sets available since May 2026. Comment bank: type # for the five most-used comments or keyword search, paste a list, edit or delete. Private comments take text, audio, video or screen recordings (five minutes on Education Plus, per the help page).

Constraints. Rubrics cannot be edited or deleted once grading starts. Private comments cannot be edited or deleted after posting and co-teachers also see them (community thread). Comment bank is per teacher account with no built-in sharing or export. Gemini rubric generation, file or photo conversion (June 2026) and feedback suggestions are AI features needing Plus or Teaching and Learning.

1Make students score their own essay on your rubricStudents self-score a timed OCR essay against the same four-criterion, six-level rubric you will use, then compare. The gap between their level and yours becomes the week's teaching point.English Literature9ModificationPCK4610Medium effort

A* lever Mark-scheme literacy: A* answers judge themselves against AO2 and AO3 criteria while being written, so evaluation is deliberate rather than accidental.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build one rubric in the assignment: AO1, AO2, AO3 and expression, six levels ordered descending, wording lifted verbatim from the OCR mark scheme.
  2. Tag the assignment with two learning goals, for example sustained critical judgement and integrated textual detail, so per-goal analytics accumulate across the term.
  3. Reuse that rubric from this class for every essay, and export it to Sheets once so levels are comparable week to week.
  4. In the instructions require each student to post their own four levels, with reasons, as a private comment before turning in.
  5. Grade against the same rubric, then reply in the private comment thread naming only the criterion where their self-score was most optimistic.
Student workflow
  1. Write the essay in the lesson under exam timing, with the rubric out of sight.
  2. Open the rubric, choose your level for each criterion and justify one choice in a private comment.
  3. Read my reply, then rewrite only the paragraph carrying the criterion we disagreed on.
Copy and paste
Before you turn in, open the rubric and post a private comment in exactly this form: AO1 level __ because...; AO2 level __ because...; AO3 level __ because...; Expression level __ because.... Use the rubric's own wording, not your own paraphrase. End by naming the one criterion you are least certain about. I will mark against the same rubric and reply only about the criterion where our levels differ most. Your rewrite this week is that single paragraph, not the whole essay.
The three routes
A → A*

Give no rubric wording in advance: they must retrieve the descriptors from memory, then check. Reply only about the top two levels, where formulaic evaluation hides. Ask them to name the phrase that would have lifted level five to level six.

B → A*

Pre-teach the rubric line by line with a full-mark exemplar beside it, then have them self-score. Focus replies on AO3, since B-grade answers describe interpretations rather than evaluating them. Repeat the same criterion for three consecutive weeks before moving on.

C → A*

Self-score on two criteria only, AO1 and AO2, with a printed one-page version of those rows. Accept a level plus a quoted phrase, not a full reason. Add the third criterion once their level matches yours twice in a row.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyslexia, supply the rubric as a numbered list with one descriptor per line and accept the self-score as an audio private comment rather than typed text.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The rubric, in the mark scheme's own words, is the model of what a top-band answer must contain.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The gap between self-score and teacher score is a direct check on mark-scheme understanding, not on content.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Reusing one rubric and its learning goals every week makes the same criteria cumulatively reviewed.
SAMR · Modification

The task is redesigned: self-assessment against the live grading rubric, with a tracked disagreement, becomes the assessed activity rather than an optional extra.

TPACK · PCK

Subject-specific mark-scheme knowledge drives it; the rubric tool only carries descriptors the teacher already understands and must translate for students.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: self-calibration against mark-scheme criteria is the A-to-A* discriminator. Evidence 3: feedback plus metacognition and self-regulation. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, no marginal cost. Cost and risk 1: rubric building takes time and cannot be edited once grading starts.

EEF feedback and metacognition and self-regulation strands, both high impact at low cost.

Research: Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong

Success measure Within eight weeks, student self-scores sit within one level of the teacher's on three criteria out of four.

2Codify twelve precision slips into a reusable comment bankA comment bank of the twelve accuracy errors that cost A-level mathematicians the last ten per cent of marks, plus weekly rubric export to Sheets, turns scattered marking into one reteach list.Mathematics8AugmentationPCK1610Low effort

A* lever Accuracy under time on multi-step questions: the A* is lost to units, premature rounding and unjustified steps, not to missing knowledge.

Board Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9MA0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Mathematics,…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste the twelve comments below into your comment bank in one go, each naming the error and the fix in the same sentence pattern.
  2. Attach a four-criterion rubric, method, accuracy, justification and presentation, scored nought to three, to every weekly Section B paper.
  3. Mark by typing hash and a keyword to pull the matching comment, so an identical slip always receives identical wording.
  4. Export the rubric to Sheets each Friday, sort by the accuracy column, and pick Monday's ten-minute reteach from the two commonest codes.
  5. Add one new comment a fortnight only when a thirteenth error appears twice, keeping the bank small enough to search by memory.
Student workflow
  1. Attempt the two hardest paper questions under timing, showing every step.
  2. Copy each coded comment into a personal error log with the question reference.
  3. Redo only the flagged step, not the whole question, and resubmit for a second look.
Copy and paste
Paste into your comment bank, one per line. Units missing or wrong on the final line, state them. Rounded before the final answer, carry exact values. Step unjustified, quote the rule used. Variable used before it was defined. Sign lost expanding brackets. Limits not substituted into the definite integral. Domain ignored when cancelling. Diagram unlabelled, so the method is unreadable. Answer never checked against the modelling context. Radians and degrees mixed. Inequality not reversed on multiplying by a negative. Method correct, answer transcribed wrongly, check the copy.
The three routes
A → A*

Withhold the code and write only the line number: they must diagnose which of the twelve applies. Restrict the diet to the final two questions of each paper, where the A* marks sit, and time them at examiner pace.

B → A*

Give the code plus a worked example of the fix from your bank, then fade the worked example after three clean weeks. Mark whole topics rather than single papers, so gaps in older content surface alongside precision slips.

C → A*

Use only four of the twelve codes to begin with, all foundational: units, signs, rounding, undefined variables. Pair each with a short algebra drill at ninety per cent success before the exam question. Add codes one at a time.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, keep feedback to the two highest-frequency codes per script and colour the error log by code, so the pattern is visible without rereading every comment.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. The error log is reread at the start of each lesson, so last week's precision slips are retrieved before new work.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Resubmitting only the flagged step checks whether the fix is understood, not whether the question can be redone.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The Friday Sheets export makes the commonest codes the agenda for Monday's cumulative review.
SAMR · Augmentation

Marking is the same task. The bank makes wording consistent and the Sheets export aggregates it, but nothing about the mathematics students do has changed.

TPACK · PCK

The twelve codes are subject-specific misconception knowledge; the bank is only a faster way of delivering what an experienced marker already says.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: precision on the hardest items is the A-to-A* margin in maths. Evidence 2: feedback is strong, though the mechanism is largely efficiency. Dose 2: every weekly paper, whole class. Cost and risk 1: building and triaging the bank and export takes teacher time.

EEF feedback strand; specific, actionable feedback outperforms grades alone.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate

3Replace margin notes with recorded private-comment feedbackFor a student whose handwriting effort crowds out thinking, feedback arrives as a recorded private comment that talks through the argument, so the analytical demand stays and the decoding load falls.SEND: dyspraxia affecting written output in History7AugmentationTPK458Medium effort

A* lever Sustained analytical judgement in Edexcel essays: the reasoning is modelled aloud, so effort goes into the argument rather than into reading dense marginalia.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Attach the same three-criterion rubric, AO1 knowledge, AO2 analysis and AO3 interpretations, to the essay for the whole class, unaltered in demand.
  2. Record a private comment of up to five minutes on Education Plus (check availability) reading one paragraph aloud and naming what the judgement lacks.
  3. Add one short written private comment listing the two rubric criteria to act on, so there is text to work from as well.
  4. Reuse the same rubric next essay and compare the two criterion levels side by side in the grading tool.
Student workflow
  1. Listen to the recording twice and note the two criteria named.
  2. Rewrite the judgement paragraph, typed or dictated, on the same essay question.
  3. Reply in the private comment thread stating which criterion you targeted and how.
Copy and paste
Script for your recording, about four minutes. I am reading your third paragraph aloud so you can hear where the argument turns. Stop. That is description, not judgement. On the rubric this is AO2 level three, not level five, because the evidence is listed rather than weighed. Here is the same sentence with a judgement in front of it. Your task is one paragraph: rewrite this one, keep the same question, and tell me in a reply which rubric criterion you were targeting.
The three routes
A → A*

Record at examiner pace and comment only on the final judgement paragraph, where an A becomes an A*. Ask for a spoken thirty-second defence of the judgement as the reply, so evaluation is rehearsed before it is written.

B → A*

Record a full-mark paragraph first, then their own, so the contrast is audible. Name one AO3 historian interpretation to bring in each week. Keep the written comment to two rubric criteria until both levels hold for a month.

C → A*

Record in ninety-second segments, one rubric criterion per segment, with a pause for them to write the fix. Supply a paragraph frame in the Doc, removed once two essays reach the middle band unaided.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: allow the rewrite as a voice-typed draft in the attached Doc and grade the argument only, marking spelling and punctuation in a separate later pass.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. Reading a full-mark paragraph aloud models the sound of a judgement, which written annotation cannot convey.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. Recorded talk-through scaffolds the analysis while the transcription barrier is bypassed, leaving the cognitive demand intact.
  • 5 Guide student practice. The single-paragraph rewrite is guided practice on the named criterion rather than a whole redraft.
SAMR · Augmentation

Verbal feedback already existed in tutorials. Recording makes it replayable, asynchronous and attached to the work, but the essay task itself is unchanged.

TPACK · TPK

The move is a feedback-modality change that would work in any subject; the history content is unaffected by the technology choice.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 2: targets judgement quality, an A* discriminator, but for one student at a time. Evidence 3: feedback plus oral rehearsal of reasoning. Dose 1: individual, not whole class. Cost and risk 1: recording time and the permanence of private comments.

EEF feedback strand; verbal feedback is effective when specific and acted on.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Worked examples, fading and the e… Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate

4Deep-mark one rubric criterion each week and rotate itEvery 16-mark answer gets all five rubric levels, but only one criterion gets comments, and that criterion rotates. Students meet AO3 elaboration as a fortnight's single focus rather than as one line among twelve.Psychology6AugmentationPCK4610Low effort

A* lever Elaborated AO3 evaluation carried through to a consequence for the theory, which is what separates the top band in AQA's 16-mark extended responses.

Board Psychology, AQA (7182 - AQA A-level Psychology (first teaching 2015)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build one five-criterion rubric for 16-mark answers: knowledge, application, evaluation, elaboration to a consequence, and research-methods accuracy, with four levels each.
  2. Fix the wording before the first grading run, because a rubric cannot be edited or deleted once grading has started.
  3. Each week award all five levels but write comments on one criterion only, named in the instructions, and rotate weekly.
  4. Pull the comments from your bank by keyword so the same elaboration prompt is worded identically every time it is used.
  5. Tag the assignment with an elaboration learning goal so per-goal analytics show whether the rotation is moving that criterion.
Student workflow
  1. Read the week's named criterion before writing, and mark up where in your answer you intend to meet it.
  2. Rewrite only the paragraph the comments address, extending the evaluation to a consequence for the theory.
  3. Keep a running list of the five criteria and your last level on each.
Copy and paste
This week I comment on elaboration only. You will still receive a level on all five criteria. For elaboration, a point is not finished when the criticism is stated; it is finished when you say what follows for the theory. Take your weakest evaluation paragraph, add two sentences beginning 'this matters because' and 'so the theory must', and repost it. Name the study or figure that licenses the claim. Next week the commented criterion is research-methods accuracy, so keep your working and your statistical reasoning visible.
The three routes
A → A*

Rotate fastest here: elaboration one week, research-methods accuracy the next, since these students already meet knowledge and application. Comment only on the second half of each evaluation paragraph, where a competent criticism stops short of a consequence, and require the rewrite in timed conditions.

B → A*

Hold the rotation on evaluation for a month, because the pattern is description where evaluation is required. Supply two full-mark elaboration paragraphs as models, then fade to a single sentence stem, then to the criterion wording alone. Check the per-goal analytics monthly.

C → A*

Start on knowledge accuracy, not evaluation: comment only on whether the study, procedure and figures are correctly recalled, so the success rate is high. Introduce the evaluation criterion in the spring term, with a paragraph frame supplied, and rotate only once the frame is no longer used.

SEND adaptation. A student with ADHD benefits most from the single named criterion: put it in the assignment title as well, so the week's one focus is visible without opening the rubric.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. Comments on one criterion can quote a full-mark version of that criterion, which twelve scattered notes never leave room for.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The rewrite of a single paragraph shows whether the criterion was understood, before the next assessment.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Rotation brings every criterion back monthly, so no criterion is commented on once and then forgotten.
SAMR · Augmentation

The rubric and comments are the same marking, made narrower and repeatable by the reusable rubric and the comment bank; the assessment task itself is unchanged.

TPACK · PCK

Choosing elaboration to a consequence as the criterion worth a fortnight comes from knowing where AQA Psychology candidates plateau; the platform only holds the wording steady.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: it targets the AO3 discriminator, but through marking focus rather than extra practice. Evidence 2: feedback is strong; narrowing its volume is an inference. Dose 1: each criterion returns only monthly. Low cost and risk 1: a rubric cannot be edited once grading starts.

EEF feedback review: feedback works when it is specific, acted on and not overwhelming in volume.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate

Risks No pupil data leaves Classroom and no AI is involved. The risk is a rubric fixed too early, since it cannot be edited after grading begins; draft the five criteria on paper with a colleague first.

Success measure Per-goal analytics show the elaboration criterion rising a level for most of the class within six weeks.

5Withhold the French translation mark until the repair closesFive comment-bank codes name the error families that cost AQA French marks. The mark is withheld until the student reposts each sentence corrected, with the rule stated, in the private comment thread.French6AugmentationPCK5610Medium effort

A* lever Accuracy of complex structures under pressure: the AQA translation into French and the essay are decided by subjunctive triggers, tense sequence, agreement and pronoun placement.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste the five codes below into your comment bank, each naming the error family and the rule, not the correction.
  2. Attach a four-criterion rubric to every translation and essay: complex structures, verb accuracy, idiom and register, and coherence of argument.
  3. Mark by typing hash and the code keyword, then post one private comment: repair these three sentences and name the rule for each.
  4. Release the rubric levels only after the student replies in the thread, remembering that private comments cannot be edited once posted.
  5. Reuse the same rubric weekly and retire a code once it appears in nobody's work for a fortnight.
Student workflow
  1. Read the coded comments and rewrite only the three flagged sentences, in French, in the private comment thread.
  2. State the rule you broke for each one, in your own words.
  3. Redeploy the same structure in next week's essay and flag it yourself for checking.
Copy and paste
SUBJ: the trigger demands a subjunctive here; name the trigger, then reconjugate. SEQ: your tense sequence breaks after the reporting verb; state which tense the main clause forces. AGR: agreement with the preceding direct object or the subject is missing; say which word governs it. PRON: pronoun order or placement is wrong; write the order rule out. REG: this is spoken register in a written essay; give the written equivalent. Repair the three sentences I have coded, in French, in this thread, naming the rule for each. Marks follow your reply.
The three routes
A → A*

Knowledge is secure, so cap the codes at two per script and spend the thread on idiom and register: ask for a more precise alternative to a correct but plain construction, then require it in the next timed essay under exam conditions.

B → A*

Coverage is patchy, so run the loop on one error family a fortnight across the whole class, starting with the subjunctive. Add a five-sentence retrieval drill on that family every Monday until the code stops appearing in anybody's translation.

C → A*

Foundations first: mark only verb accuracy and agreement for the first term, with a model correction supplied beside each code so the success rate stays high. Withdraw the supplied model once two consecutive scripts need no repair, then add the remaining codes one at a time.

SEND adaptation. For a student with a language impairment or slow processing, record the coded comments as audio in French and English so the rule is heard as well as read; the repair demand is unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 6 Check for understanding. The student must state the rule, so the thread shows whether the correction was understood or merely copied.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Repair happens with the teacher's code as the only prompt, then the structure is redeployed unaided next week.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The same five codes recur weekly, so each error family is revisited until it disappears from the class's work.

TPACK · PCK

Dose 1: the reply thread is one student at a time. Low cost and risk 0: weekly replies cost real time and posted comments cannot be edited.

EEF feedback review: feedback that requires a response and is acted on is the strongest strand.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong

Student groups and assigning work to individuals

Create named groups of students on the People tab (for example, an A* target set or an essay-structure support set) and assign any classwork item to one or more groups, or to individually ticked students, so one lesson can carry a stretch essay for some and a scaffolded version for others without students seeing the grouping.

Options. Groups tab inside the Assign to picker; up to 75 groups per class and 100 members per group; a student may sit in several groups or none; a targeted assignment reaches at most 100 students; membership is captured when the assignment is saved, scheduled or posted, so later edits do not change earlier assignments. Any teacher on the class can assign to existing groups.

Constraints. Creating, renaming and deleting groups needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning on that teacher's account; others may only assign to existing groups. No admin control. Editing members on mobile is unsupported. Group names and members are hidden from students, but a differently titled assignment can still reveal the differentiation.

1Rotate a moderation ring through four hidden groups weeklyFour hidden groups rotate each week: every group marks another group's anonymised set-work analysis against the Eduqas mark scheme, so students learn what perceptive means by having to award it.Music9ModificationTPACK346Medium effort

A* lever Harmonic and stylistic analysis with accurate terminology: applying the mark scheme to someone else's writing exposes what the top band actually requires.

Board Music, AQA (7272 (AQA A-level Music)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create four groups on the People tab named neutrally, Ring A to Ring D (creating groups needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Collect last week's set-work analysis, remove all names yourself, and attach one anonymised response plus the relevant mark-scheme extract to each group's assignment.
  3. Post the same titled assignment four times, once per group, rotating which response each ring receives, since membership is captured when you post.
  4. Grade the moderation, not the original: score whether the level awarded is defensible and whether the terminology in the justification is accurate.
  5. Publish the correct level and the examiner's reasoning to the whole class the next lesson, before anyone rewrites.
Student workflow
  1. Award a level to the anonymised response and quote the mark-scheme phrase that justifies it.
  2. Name one harmonic or stylistic term the response should have used, and where.
  3. Use that same term accurately in your own next set-work analysis.
Copy and paste
You are the examiner this week. Read the anonymised response attached. Award a level for each mark-scheme strand and, for each one, quote the exact phrase from the mark scheme that justifies your level. Then do two things. First, name one harmonic or stylistic term this response needed and the bar or passage where it belonged. Second, write the single sentence you would add to move it up one level. You are marking the writing, not the music. Do not guess who wrote it.
The three routes
A → A*

Give them responses sitting on a band boundary, where the judgement is genuinely contestable, and require them to argue the higher level down as well as up. Then apply the same boundary test to their own last analysis.

B → A*

Give a clear top-band response and a clear middle-band one together, so the contrast teaches the descriptor. Require the missing terminology to be named from a supplied glossary, then withdraw the glossary after three weeks.

C → A*

Moderate one strand only, with the mark-scheme extract cut to three lines and two model justifications shown first. Success rate matters more than range: keep going until their awarded level matches the teacher's twice.

SEND adaptation. For a student with autism who finds inferred criteria hard, supply the mark-scheme strand as an explicit checklist of observable features, keeping the analytical demand of the judgement identical.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every student must answer the examiner's question, which level and why, rather than only the confident few.
  • 4 Provide models. Another student's real response, plus the published level, gives a worked model of the descriptor in use.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The awarded level is a visible check on whether the criteria are understood, not just read.
SAMR · Modification

The task becomes moderation rather than production, and invisible weekly rotation of who marks whom is what makes it sustainable and anonymous.

TPACK · TPACK

Mark-scheme knowledge, peer assessment and invisible targeted distribution genuinely fuse; remove any one and the weekly moderation ring collapses.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: mark-scheme literacy and terminology precision are the A* discriminators in Music. Evidence 3: peer tutoring and feedback are strong at KS5. Dose 2: weekly, whole class. Cost and risk 1: anonymising work each week is teacher time.

EEF peer tutoring and feedback strands; both strong at secondary and post-16.

Research: Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong Exemplar deconstruction and makin… Moderate

Risks You must strip names before attaching work, since group names are hidden but authorship is not. Never label a group by ability. No AI, so no hallucination risk; the offloading risk is nil because students do the judging.

Success measure Awarded levels agree with the teacher's within one band for most students, and glossary terms appear unprompted in their own analyses.

2Split the class into three groups by diagnosed errorA Monday diagnostic sorts the class into three hidden groups, unfamiliar-context transfer, multi-step accuracy and definitions, and Wednesday's follow-up sends each group different questions on the same topic.Physics8AugmentationPCK679Medium effort

A* lever Application to unfamiliar contexts and multi-step accuracy in AQA Paper 3, where the final band of marks is won or lost.

Board Physics, OCR Physics A (H556) (H556 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Physics A (spe…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Mark Monday's six-question diagnostic, then create three groups on the People tab named Set One, Set Two and Set Three (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Post one assignment with the same title, for example capacitance follow-up, three times, once to each group, so the title never signals the grouping.
  3. Attach different questions per group: unfamiliar-context transfer items, multi-step calculations with significant-figure traps, or definition and derivation drill.
  4. Give every group the same final extension question, so the class still shares one common reference point in discussion.
  5. Rebuild the groups every fortnight from the latest diagnostic, because membership is fixed at the moment each assignment is posted.
Student workflow
  1. Sit the six-question diagnostic cold, with no notes and no calculator page.
  2. Complete the follow-up questions you are set, writing the reasoning chain in full.
  3. Attempt the shared extension question and compare your approach with a partner's.
Copy and paste
Diagnostic instructions to paste. Six questions, twenty minutes, closed book. One definition, two standard calculations, two multi-step calculations, one question set in a context you have not met. Do not skip the unfamiliar one; an outline of the reasoning earns more than a blank. For every calculation write the equation first, then substitute, then state units and significant figures. I will use these six answers only to decide which follow-up questions you get on Wednesday. This is not a test grade and it will not go in your report.
The three routes
A → A*

Their set is unfamiliar-context transfer only, with the stem rewritten into an unseen scenario each fortnight and no equation list. Mark for the reasoning chain, not the answer, and time them at examiner pace.

B → A*

Their set mixes retrieval across earlier topics with the current one, so the diagnostic covers the whole specification rather than the last fortnight. Provide a worked example alongside the first multi-step question, faded on the second.

C → A*

Their set begins with the definitions and the single-step calculation that the multi-step items depend on, at a high success rate. Add one multi-step item per fortnight and keep the equation sheet visible until spring.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, extend the diagnostic to thirty minutes and cut it to four questions, keeping the unfamiliar-context item, so the demand is unchanged but the pace is not the test.
Rosenshine
  • 6 Check for understanding. The diagnostic is a check that decides teaching, not a grade, so it is read for error type rather than score.
  • 9 Independent practice. Each group practises independently on the error type actually diagnosed rather than on a shared average.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Targeting questions by diagnosed error keeps each group working at a productive success rate.

Differentiated worksheets predate the tool. What is new is invisible targeting and zero distribution cost, a functional improvement to the same task.

TPACK · PCK

The value lies in knowing which three physics error types matter; the grouping feature only delivers work the teacher already knows how to choose.

A* lever Planning under time: A* answers reach a judgement because the structure was decided before writing, not discovered while writing.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create two groups on the People tab named Route One and Route Two (creating groups needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Write one source question and two attachments: a blank plan grid, and the same grid with topic sentences and a judgement stem supplied.
  3. Post the assignment twice under the same title, one attachment per group, with the same due date and marks.
  4. Move students between routes each fortnight and retire the framed version for anyone who reached the top band twice unaided.
Student workflow
  1. Plan the answer on your grid in ten minutes before writing anything else.
  2. Write the essay from the plan, under timing, without changing the structure midway.
  3. Mark your own judgement paragraph against the plan you wrote and note any drift.
Copy and paste
Ten minutes on the plan before you write a word. For each source, one line on provenance, one on the argument it makes, and one on how far it can be trusted for this question. Then write your judgement in a single sentence at the bottom of the grid, before the essay exists. Your essay must reach that judgement, and each paragraph must be the reason the plan says it is. If the essay ends somewhere else, that is the drift I want you to identify afterwards.
The three routes
A → A*

Blank grid, eight minutes, and a judgement sentence written before any source is reread. Feedback is only on whether the essay reached the planned judgement without drift, which is where an A loses the A*.

B → A*

Supplied topic sentences only, with the judgement left blank, so the missing skill is practised in isolation. Repeat the same question type weekly until the judgement appears without prompting, then remove the topic sentences.

C → A*

Full frame including the judgement stem and two provenance sentence starters, plus a worked plan for one source shown first. Withdraw one element a fortnight over a term, keeping the same essay demand throughout.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyspraxia, accept the plan grid as a typed or voice-typed list rather than a handwritten grid, and allow the ten planning minutes to sit outside the writing time.

4Make four groups own the four AQA Spanish themesFour hidden groups each own one AQA theme for a half-term, building the class's question bank and idiom list for it. Ownership rotates, so every student eventually fields questions on all four.Spanish6AugmentationPCK3910Medium effort

A* lever Spontaneity in the AQA speaking test: unpredictable follow-up questions are survivable only when high-utility idiom and theme vocabulary are automatic rather than memorised as a script.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create four groups on the People tab named Equipo Uno to Equipo Cuatro, one per AQA theme (creating groups needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Post the same-titled assignment four times, once per group, each carrying that group's theme: society, artistic culture, multiculturalism, or historical and political developments.
  3. Ask each group for twenty unpredictable follow-up questions in Spanish on their theme, plus ten idioms nobody would find in a textbook chapter.
  4. Check every question and idiom for accuracy yourself before publishing the four banks to the whole class, because errors circulate fast.
  5. Rotate theme ownership each half-term, and use the other groups' banks as the unseen questions in your speaking practice.
Student workflow
  1. Research your theme in Spanish sources and write twenty questions a teacher could not predict.
  2. Answer another group's questions aloud, unseen, with no notes and no preparation time.
  3. Log the idioms you reached for and the ones you could not.
Copy and paste
Your group owns one theme this half-term. Produce twenty follow-up questions in Spanish that an examiner might ask after a candidate's prepared answer, and that a candidate could not have rehearsed: ask for an opinion, a comparison, a concession and a prediction, not for facts. Then list ten idioms or complex structures a strong candidate would use on this theme, with the situation each one fits. Nothing translated from English. Every question must be answerable in ninety seconds by someone who has thought about the theme rather than memorised a script.
The three routes
A → A*

These students have range but rehearse. Require questions that force a concession or a prediction, and hold the answering session unseen with no notes, so the structures have to be retrieved under pressure rather than recited from a prepared paragraph.

B → A*

Coverage is the problem: one theme is strong and three are thin. Keep ownership but require every student to answer all four banks each half-term, ten questions a week, so the whole specification is retrieved rather than one comfortable theme.

C → A*

Reduce to ten questions and five idioms, supplied in a sentence frame the group completes rather than invents. Let them see the questions a day before answering for the first term, then withdraw the notice, then withdraw the frames.

SEND adaptation. A student with social anxiety or autism can answer on their own group's theme first, with the question order given in advance, so the unpredictability sits in the content rather than the setting.
Rosenshine

  • 9 Independent practice. Answering another group's unseen questions with no notes is the independent practice the speaking test actually requires.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Rotating ownership brings every theme back, so no theme is prepared once and then abandoned.

Proximity 3: spontaneity and range of idiom decide the speaking mark. Evidence 2: collaborative and peer-led preparation is promising rather than proven. Dose 1: ownership rotates only each half-term. Low cost and risk 0: four parallel briefs need checking, and creating groups needs Plus.

EEF: peer tutoring and collaborative learning are promising at KS5; retrieval and spaced practice underpin the rotation.

A* lever Data-skills questions and statistical tests in OCR Geography, where the marks come from choosing the test, reading the significance and reaching a substantiated judgement.

Board Geography, OCR (H481 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Geography (fir…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Write the data-skills question once, then prepare two attachments: the original figures, and the same data as an accessible table with a described transect.
  2. In the Assign to picker, tick individual students rather than the whole class for the accessible version, keeping the title and marks identical.
  3. Keep the same rubric and the same Spearman's rank calculation; change only how the data is represented, never what must be concluded from it.
  4. Check the table reads correctly with a screen reader before posting, since a merged cell or an image of a table defeats the purpose.
  5. Ask the student each half-term which representations work, and keep a standing note so later assignments are built accessible first.
Student workflow
  1. Choose and justify the statistical test from the table, as everyone else does from the figures.
  2. Calculate the coefficient, state the significance level and write the judgement with place detail.
  3. Tell the teacher which parts of the alternative format slowed you down.
Copy and paste
Use Table 3 to answer. Choose the statistical test that suits these two variables and justify the choice in one sentence. Calculate the coefficient, state the critical value you are testing against and the significance level you reach. Then write a judgement of no more than 200 words on whether the relationship supports the model, naming the place, the figures and one limitation of the data. The table carries exactly the same values as the printed figure; marks and criteria are unchanged.
The three routes
A → A*

Give the accessible version with no extra time and add the synoptic step: connect the physical data to a human-strand consequence in the judgement. The access change removes a reading barrier; it must not remove the evaluation of the model's limits.

B → A*

Add a worked example of the same test on different data as a second attachment, then withdraw it after two uses. Comment on whether the critical value and significance statement are correct before commenting on the judgement, because that is where these marks are lost.

C → A*

Break the question into three assignments: read the table and describe the pattern, then run the test with the formula supplied, then write the judgement from a two-sentence frame. Keep the accessible format throughout so the only thing increasing is the demand.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: for a student with dyspraxia in the same class, accept the judgement typed against the pre-formatted table, so drawing an accurate scatter graph is not a prerequisite for the analysis.

  • 6 Check for understanding. The half-term conversation about format checks the adaptation itself, not only the geography.

Originality reports

When switched on for an assignment, compares each submitted Google Doc, Slides or Word file against web pages and books and flags matching passages with source links; with admin-enabled school matches it also compares against the school's repository of past submissions. Students can run their own report before submitting, which teaches quotation and citation.

Options. Toggle per assignment at creation; students get 3 self-checks before turning in; teacher report appears on submission; files up to 2MB; 24 languages including English; flagged passages link to sources; reports viewable for 45 days, then must be rerun. Plus or Teaching and Learning: unlimited assignments plus school matches. Fundamentals: 5 assignments per class.

Constraints. Detects textual overlap only; it does not identify AI-generated text or close paraphrase, so it is a prompt for a conversation, not a verdict. School matches are off by default and need an admin. Only Docs, Slides and Word files are checked. The 45-day window means evidence must be captured promptly.

1Make students classify every flagged passage before submittingStudents run their own originality report on an AQA Philosophy essay and must classify each flagged passage as quotation, paraphrase needing attribution, or their own reasoning, then fix it.Philosophy9ModificationTPACK369Low effort

A* lever Reconstructing and evaluating arguments: an A* answer shows clearly where the philosopher's reasoning ends and the candidate's own evaluation begins.

Board Philosophy and Religion (Religious Studies), Edexcel (Pearson) (9RS0 — Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Religious St…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Switch originality reports on when creating the essay assignment; students then get three self-checks of their own Doc before turning in.
  2. Add a rubric criterion called ownership of argument, so attribution is scored as philosophical practice rather than policed as a rule.
  3. In the instructions require a table at the end of the Doc classifying every flagged passage into one of three categories with a one-line reason.
  4. Read the teacher report on submission and capture anything needing a conversation, because reports expire after forty-five days and must be rerun.
  5. Hold a two-minute conversation, not an accusation, wherever a flag and the rubric criterion disagree.
Student workflow
  1. Run a self-check, read every flagged passage and decide what it actually is.
  2. Rewrite unattributed paraphrase as your own reconstruction, citing the philosopher by name and work.
  3. Submit with the classification table, then defend one flag you think is wrong in a private comment.
Copy and paste
Run your originality report before you turn in. You have three self-checks. At the end of your Doc add a table with three columns: the flagged phrase, its category, and one line of reasoning. Categories are direct quotation with citation, paraphrase that needs attribution, and my own reasoning wrongly matched. Fix every row in the middle category by either citing the source or rewriting the reconstruction in your own terms. Then tell me in a private comment which single flag you believe the report got wrong, and why.
The three routes
A → A*

Set a question where the standard objection is widely published, so their evaluation must be visibly theirs. Score ownership of argument on whether the reply to the objection is original reasoning rather than a rehearsed textbook line.

B → A*

Require the reconstruction to be written in premise and conclusion form before prose, so the borrowed phrasing has nowhere to hide. Model one full classification table yourself, then fade the model over three essays.

C → A*

Two flagged passages only, with a worked example of each category supplied. Teach citation as a sentence pattern first, at a high success rate, and build to the full table across a term rather than a fortnight.

SEND adaptation. For a student with a visual impairment, check the report with the flagged passages copied into a high-contrast, screen-reader-friendly list, since report highlighting alone may not be accessible.
Rosenshine

  • 9 Independent practice. The self-check loop is independent practice in attribution, completed before the teacher ever sees the essay.

2Run self-checks on every NEA section as submittedEach NEA section is submitted as a Doc with an originality self-check, so borrowed algorithm descriptions surface early, the JCQ declaration is honest, and the student's own design reasoning is what gets marked.Computer Science7AugmentationPCK69Low effort

Board Computer Science, OCR (H446 - OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Computer Science, specif…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create four assignments, one per NEA section, each with originality reports switched on (Fundamentals allows five per class, Plus is unlimited).
  2. Ask your admin whether school matches against past submissions are enabled, since they are off by default (check availability).
  3. Keep Docs under two megabytes by linking code to the student's repository instead of pasting listings into the write-up.
  4. Where overlap is flagged, hold a five-minute viva: ask the student to explain the algorithm's time complexity aloud without notes.
  5. Record the viva outcome in your own notes, not in a private comment, and complete the JCQ authentication on that basis.
Student workflow
  1. Self-check each section before submitting and cite any standard algorithm you adapted.
  2. Rewrite any flagged description as a justification of why you chose it here.
  3. Explain your complexity analysis aloud in the viva without reading from the write-up.
Copy and paste
Before you submit this NEA section, run the originality self-check and fix what it finds. If a passage matches a textbook or website, you have two honest options. Cite it and then add a sentence explaining why that approach suits your problem. Or delete it and write the reasoning yourself. Standard algorithms may be used and cited; the marks come from your justification, not from the description. Be ready to explain your complexity analysis aloud without notes. Nothing generated by AI may be submitted as your own work.
The three routes
A → A*

Require a comparative justification: two viable data structures, their complexities, and why one was chosen for this problem. The viva probes the rejected option, which is where an A candidate stops thinking.

B → A*

Require a completed table of complexity for every named algorithm before the prose is written, so gaps in theory surface in autumn rather than in spring. Model one full justification paragraph and fade it across sections.

C → A*

One section at a time with an agreed structure and weekly checkpoints. Start from a single clearly justified design decision written at a high success rate, then stage the remaining sections across two years.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, break each section into three dated checkpoint assignments with its own self-check, so the write-up never becomes one large undated deadline.
Rosenshine

  • 9 Independent practice. Section-by-section self-checking is independent practice in citing sources and justifying choices.

Board Art & Design (Art, Craft and Design), Pearson Edexcel (9AD0 (Advanced GCE in Art and Design - Art, Craft and Desig…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Set the contextual study as a Doc assignment with originality reports on, separate from the visual portfolio submission.
  2. Require every image discussed to carry a full caption and source, so attribution habits cover images as well as text.
  3. On submission, read the report and ask the student to rewrite any flagged sentence as a claim about their own work's development.
  4. Capture the report outcome within the forty-five-day window, because it must otherwise be rerun before sign-off.
Student workflow
  1. Self-check the study and read each flagged sentence aloud to hear whose voice it is.
  2. Rewrite flagged sentences as a link between the artist's decision and your own.
  3. Add the source for every borrowed phrase you decide to keep as a quotation.
Copy and paste
Run the self-check on your contextual study. For every flagged sentence, ask one question: is this the gallery talking, or me? If it is the gallery, either quote it properly with a source or rewrite it as a sentence about your own work, naming the decision it changed. Every image needs a caption with artist, title, date and where you found it. Your marks come from what you did with the influence, not from describing the artist. Keep AI out of the writing entirely.
The three routes
A → A*

Require every contextual claim to be tied to a specific page in their own sketchbook, so the study evidences a journey rather than admiration. Flags become prompts to sharpen the link, not merely to reword.

B → A*

Supply a sentence pattern for linking artist decision to own decision, and require five such links before wider prose. Review one flagged sentence together each week until the pattern is habitual, then withdraw it.

C → A*

Begin with two artists and four linked sentences only, with a worked example of a rewritten flagged sentence. Build the study in short dated instalments across the year rather than as a single late document.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyslexia, allow the study to be drafted by voice typing and assess the critical argument separately from spelling, keeping the same requirement for sourced captions.

Board Drama (AQA option - board not confirmed by LAET), AQA (7262 (AQA A-level Drama and Theatre)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Set the review as a Doc assignment with originality reports switched on, so students get three self-checks before turning in.
  2. In the instructions, require every claim about a moment to carry the time, the position on stage and what the audience did.
  3. Tell students plainly what the report can and cannot do: it finds matching text on the web, not paraphrase and not AI use.
  4. On submission, ask for each flagged phrase to be rewritten as an observation, in the student's own theatrical vocabulary, before it is marked.
  5. Capture the report within forty-five days, since it expires and must otherwise be rerun.
Student workflow
  1. Run a self-check, then rewrite any phrase that a critic wrote before you did.
  2. Replace each with a moment you saw, timed and placed on stage.
  3. Name the design element and its effect on you, in precise theatrical terms.
Copy and paste
Before you submit, run the originality check on your review. For every flagged phrase, ask yourself one question: could I have written this without having been in the room? If the answer is yes, delete it. Replace it with a moment: where on stage, how long it lasted, what the lighting or sound did, and what the audience around you did. Use the vocabulary of the director, the performer and the designer, not the vocabulary of a review. Attribution is still required where you genuinely quote a critic.
The three routes
A → A*

These students rarely copy; they generalise. Use the report to catch the two or three stock critical phrases, then demand a sustained directorial reading: every observation must serve one argument about the production's intention, held across the whole review.

B → A*

Overlap here usually means notes taken from reviews rather than from the performance. Teach the note-taking routine first: ten timed moments recorded in the interval and immediately afterwards, then written up with the reviews closed and the report run on the draft.

C → A*

Start with one moment, not a whole review: 200 words on a single lighting state, with a sentence frame naming effect and intention. Run the self-check on that paragraph so the routine is learned cheaply, then build to two moments, then to the full review.

SEND adaptation. A student with autism may record superb factual detail but find the audience-response claim guesswork; accept observed behaviour rather than inferred feeling, and keep the analytical demand on effect and intention.

Board Politics, Pearson Edexcel (9PL0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Politics (Is…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Set the essay as a Doc assignment with originality reports on; Fundamentals allows five per class, Plus is unlimited.
  2. Require a two-column examples table at the end: the example, and the month in which it happened.
  3. Ask students to open every matched source the report links and record its publication date in that table.
  4. Ask your admin whether school matches against past submissions are enabled, since they are off by default (check availability).
  5. Mark the essay only after any example older than twelve months is replaced, and keep the table as the evidence.
Student workflow
  1. Run a self-check and open each matched source the report links.
  2. Record its date, then replace any example whose source predates this academic year.
  3. Rewrite the replacement in your own words, tied to the judgement it supports.
Copy and paste
Run the originality check before you submit. Open every source the report links and write its publication date into your examples table. If the source is a revision website, replace the example: revision sites are where everybody's examples come from, and an examiner has read them all. If the source is a news article older than this academic year, ask whether anything has happened since that strengthens or undermines your point. Then rewrite the example in your own words, in one sentence, and say what it proves about the institution's significance.
The three routes
A → A*

Their examples are accurate but shared with the whole cohort. Require one example per essay that no matched source contains, drawn from a named committee report or judgment they have read, and used comparatively against the United States.

B → A*

Overlap tends to be whole explanatory sentences about how an institution works. Set a weekly current-affairs retrieval task so there is a stock of dated examples to draw on, and require two per paragraph before the essay is written, not after.

C → A*

Do the audit on one paragraph, with the examples table already half filled in and two acceptable sources named. The aim for a term is the routine of dating a source, not a full essay of current examples; extend once the routine is automatic.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, cap the audit at three examples and put the table inside the assignment itself, so the check is a short bounded task rather than an open-ended one.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From the Resources tab, choose a publicly available examiner walkthrough of a top-band essay and insert questions at four timestamps (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Make each stop a multiple-choice question: which band does this paragraph reach, and which assessment objective is carrying it?
  3. Add one open question immediately before the examiner's verdict: what will the examiner say is missing here?
  4. Assign it with a due date and marks, then read the insights dashboard to find the paragraph students most over-rated.
  5. Open the next lesson by reteaching that paragraph's discriminator, using the class's own wrong answers as the starting point.
Student workflow
  1. Answer each paused question before playback continues, rewatching the segment if you were wrong.
  2. Write your prediction of the examiner's verdict before you hear it.
  3. Apply that discriminator to one paragraph of your own most recent essay.
Copy and paste
At each pause you will be asked two things: which band this paragraph reaches, and which assessment objective is doing the work. Commit to an answer before you play on, even when you are unsure; a guess you then correct teaches more than a pause. Before the examiner gives the verdict you will be asked what is missing. Write it in the examiner's language, not yours. Afterwards, find the paragraph in your own last essay that has the same weakness and rewrite it.
The three routes
A → A*

Use a top-band essay with one weak paragraph and ask them to find it unprompted. The open question is why this is band five rather than band six, which is the A-to-A* judgement in miniature.

B → A*

Use a walkthrough contrasting a middle-band and a top-band answer on the same question, with a stop at every paragraph. Focus the multiple-choice options on AO3, where B-grade answers describe rather than evaluate.

C → A*

Cut to a five-minute segment with two stops and two options each, so the success rate stays high. Supply the band descriptors on screen beside the video, withdrawn once predictions match the examiner twice.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, keep the clip under six minutes with a stop every ninety seconds, so attention is renewed by a required response rather than sustained passively.

Board Biology, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Biology 7402 (components 7402/1, 7402/2, 7402/3…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Resources, pick a filmed version of the required practical and insert a question at each procedural decision (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning; YouTube enabled).
  2. Make each stop multiple-choice on the decision itself, for example which variable must be controlled here and why, so it autogrades with instant feedback.
  3. Add one open question at the end: name the single largest source of uncertainty and how you would reduce it.
  4. Use the insights dashboard to find the decision the class got wrong, and rehearse that decision at the bench before the real practical.
  5. Reassign the same activity a fortnight later as cumulative review, since the questions and insights persist under Resources.
Student workflow
  1. Justify each procedural decision before playback reveals what the demonstrator did.
  2. Correct your wrong answers by rewatching that segment, not by asking a neighbour.
  3. Write the uncertainty analysis before the practical, then revise it afterwards.
Copy and paste
At every pause, decide what you would do and why, before you see what they did. Answer in the form: the decision, the variable it controls, and what would go wrong if you ignored it. At the end, name the single largest source of uncertainty in this method and one realistic change that would reduce it. Bring your answers to the bench. During the practical, note any decision the video made that you would now make differently, and say why in one sentence.
The three routes
A → A*

Add stops on the decisions the video makes silently, and require a quantified uncertainty estimate with correct units and significant figures. The open question asks how they would redesign the method for a different organism.

B → A*

Stop at every named variable and require the control, the reason and the consequence in full, building the vocabulary of experimental design. Reassign the same activity monthly until answers stop needing the rewatch.

C → A*

Two or three stops on the most fundamental decisions only, with three plausible options each so the success rate stays high. Supply a sentence frame for the justification and remove it after a term.

SEND adaptation. For a student with autism who finds unannounced changes difficult, share the stop timestamps in advance so the pauses are expected and the practical sequence is predictable.

Board Chemistry, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Chemistry 7405 (components 7405/1, 7405/2, 7405…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Resources, choose a mechanism explanation video and insert one question after each step of the mechanism (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning; YouTube enabled).
  2. Make every question multiple-choice on the step just shown, so instant validation tells the student to rewatch that segment rather than the whole video.
  3. Set no time limit and assign the activity as preparation, so the lesson itself is spent on unfamiliar-context application, not on transcription.
  4. Check the insights dashboard for the step this student rewatched most, and use it as the first question in the next lesson.
Student workflow

  2. Write the mechanism from memory once, after the video, without pausing.
  3. Bring the one step you rewatched most to the start of the lesson.
Copy and paste
Work through this at your own pace and rewatch any segment as often as you like; there is no time limit and no penalty for a wrong first answer. After each step, answer the question about that step only. When the video ends, close it and draw the whole mechanism from memory in one go, with curly arrows and lone pairs. Bring that drawing and the name of the step you replayed most to the lesson. We will start there, on an unfamiliar substrate.
The three routes
A → A*

After the untimed activity, set the same mechanism on an unfamiliar substrate under exam timing, so processing support in preparation is paired with full-pace performance where the marks are actually won. Ask for the reagent and conditions as well as the arrows.

B → A*

Add a question on the definition behind each step, so terminology gaps surface alongside the mechanism itself. Reassign the activity monthly across the whole specification rather than only the current topic, and require the mechanism written from memory each time.

C → A*

Cover one step per activity, with two options per question and the curly-arrow convention shown on screen. Build to the full mechanism over a fortnight, keeping the success rate high throughout.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: allow the from-memory mechanism to be drawn on paper and photographed into the assignment, so drawing tools never become the barrier being measured.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Resources, build one activity a week from a short francophone news clip: Paris, Marseille, Québec, Dakar (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Keep the topic constant across the series so vocabulary is held steady and only accent and speed vary.
  3. Write the multiple-choice questions in French at three levels: gist, a precise figure or date, and an inference about the speaker's stance.
  4. End each activity with one open question in French: which word or sound defeated you, and why?
  5. Compare the insights dashboards across the series to see whether the class's weakness is lexical, phonological or speed.
Student workflow
  1. Answer the gist question before rewinding anything, then work through the detail questions.
  2. Name, in French, the word or sound you could not catch.
  3. Add that word to your own list and listen for it next week.
Copy and paste
Question finale, en français. Quel mot ou quel son n'avez-vous pas réussi à identifier, et pourquoi ? Choisissez une raison et expliquez-la en deux phrases : je ne connaissais pas le mot ; je connaissais le mot mais je ne l'ai pas reconnu à l'oral ; le débit était trop rapide pour moi. Ajoutez ce mot à votre liste personnelle. La semaine prochaine, le sujet reste le même et seul l'accent change, donc écoutez bien ce mot-là.
The three routes
A → A*

Use unscripted speech: interviews with overlapping speakers and hesitation, not read bulletins. Make the inference question the scored one, since these students already get gist and detail, and require the answer before any rewind, so speed is trained rather than avoided.

B → A*

Pre-teach ten words from the clip as a retrieval starter, then run the activity, so failure is phonological rather than lexical and the diagnosis is clean. Reassign the same activity a fortnight later and compare the two sets of insights.

C → A*

Use forty-second clips with a transcript attached to the assignment, and let students listen once before reading it and once after. Remove the transcript in the spring term, then lengthen the clips. The point is a weekly listening habit at natural speed, however short.

SEND adaptation. For a student with an auditory processing difficulty, allow unlimited replays and keep the same clip for two weeks; the demand stays natural-speed French, but the number of exposures is theirs to choose.

5Harvest four-link chains from a paused data-response clipA commentary on a data extract is paused at the point where the chain of reasoning must continue. Every student types their four links, and the anonymised responses become the next lesson's marking exercise.Economics4ModificationTPACK346High effort

A* lever Chains of reasoning at least four links long, and evaluation that weighs magnitude, time frame and elasticity rather than listing however points.

Board Economics, AQA (board not confirmed by LAET - AQA form) (7136 - AQA A-level Economics (spec version 1.3, 29 June 202…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Resources, choose a video on a current data extract and insert an open question at the moment the second link is reached (needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning).
  2. Word it as a demand, not a question: write the remaining links, naming the direction and the size of each effect.
  3. Add two autograded multiple-choice questions later in the clip on which diagram the chain requires and which axis moves.
  4. Copy six anonymised open responses into the next lesson's slide, removing every name yourself first (how open responses are reported is unconfirmed; check availability).
  5. Have the class rank the six chains and say which breaks first, then reveal your own ranking and reasoning.
Student workflow
  1. Type your four links at the pause, before the commentary continues.
  2. Next lesson, rank six anonymous chains and name the link that fails in each.
  3. Rewrite your own chain, adding magnitude and time frame to the weakest link.
Copy and paste
Stop here. Write the rest of the chain, one link per line, from the change in the extract to the final effect on the market. Each line must name a direction and a size: not 'costs rise' but 'costs rise by roughly the tariff, around four per cent'. Then add one line beginning 'this depends on', naming the elasticity or the time frame that decides how big the effect is. Four links minimum. You will not see anyone else's answer until next lesson, when you will mark six of them anonymously.
The three routes
A → A*

Their chains reach four links but stop at direction. Score only the depends-on line, and require magnitude with a figure from the extract. Use the ranking exercise to argue about which of two defensible chains an examiner would reward, and why.

B → A*

Chains break at the second link. Supply the first two links in the question itself and require the last two, then fade to one supplied link, then none. Run the ranking exercise weekly, because judging six chains teaches the structure faster than writing one.

C → A*

Start with two links and a diagram already drawn, and mark only whether each direction is right. Add the magnitude requirement after half term and the depends-on line after Christmas. Keep the ranking exercise, but with three chains, one of which is plainly wrong.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, give the chain as numbered boxes and let them dictate the links; the thinking is the sequence, not the typing, and the pause already removes time pressure.
Rosenshine

  • 3 Ask questions. The pause forces every student to commit a chain before the commentary supplies one.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Open responses at one timestamp show exactly which link the class cannot build.

The task changes: every student's reasoning is captured at the same moment, and the class's own chains, not a textbook exemplar, become the material they mark.

EEF: peer assessment and metacognition at KS5; examiner reports on chains that stop at two links.

6Hunt the unjustified line in a worked-solution videoA worked solution on video is checkpointed so pupils must name, at each stop, the justification the presenter skipped. Proof marks lost to assertion become visible before pupils write their own proofs.Further Mathematics7ModificationPCK346Medium effort

A* lever Proof and rigorous justification carry marks fluent candidates lose by asserting; spotting an unwarranted line in someone else's solution is how that eye is trained.

Board Further Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9FM0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Further Math…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Menu > Resources > New video activity, paste a YouTube worked solution of an induction or de Moivre proof, and watch it through once yourself.
  2. Insert an open-ended question at every line that is asserted rather than argued: what licenses this line, and which theorem's conditions must hold?
  3. Add two multiple-choice checkpoints where the presenter's step is genuinely sound, so pupils cannot simply flag everything; those two autograde.
  4. Assign it, then read Review work > Class insights per question to find the warrant the class cannot supply, and reteach exactly that next lesson.
Student workflow
  1. At each stop, write what makes the next line legal, naming the theorem, condition or definition, before playback continues.
  2. Where the step is sound, say so and say why; flagging everything scores nothing.
  3. Rewrite your own last proof so that every line carries the warrant you have just had to name.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description: 'This video's solution reaches the right answer. That is not what you are marking. At each stop, write one sentence naming what makes the next line legal: the theorem used, the condition that must hold, or the definition applied. If the step is fully justified, say so and name the justification. Two stops are on sound steps, so flagging everything scores nothing. Bring the one stop you could not answer to the lesson, and be ready to say what you would need to know to answer it.'
The three routes
A → A*

Use a proof whose route is correct but whose induction step uses the hypothesis without ever stating it. Stops are silent: no options, no hints. Pupils must also name the mark the scheme would withhold, which is the discrimination the last two marks rest on.

B → A*

Use a shorter video on one technique, with the first two stops offering three candidate justifications to choose between before the open questions start. Run one activity a week on the same topic family, so hence, therefore, and if and only if become routine vocabulary.

C → A*

Use a two-minute clip with four stops, each offering the justification as a choice of three with instant validation, so success is high, and rewatching is unlimited. Open-ended stops arrive one at a time, once the class is choosing correctly without help.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed the pause-and-rewatch structure already removes the pace penalty; also accept the warrant typed in note form, since the mark is for the reasoning, not the sentence.
Rosenshine

  • 3 Ask questions. A question at every asserted step demands a warrant from every pupil, not from the two who volunteer.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Class insights show, per question, which justification the class cannot supply, before any proof is written.

The video will not continue until each pupil has committed a justification, turning passive watching into thirty simultaneous responses; the task itself, not just its delivery, is redesigned.

Google Forms

Auto-marked checks whose value is what happens after the answer. · 3 sub-tools · 17 examples

Availability. Quiz mode, branching, validation, Classroom grade import and locked mode: every Education edition, no add-on, no age limit; locked mode needs managed Chromebooks. Gemini in Forms (Help me create, quiz generation, suggest questions, response summaries): Education Plus or the Teaching and Learning add-on, users aged 18 and over only, with 'smart features and personalization' and the Gemini service switched on in the Admin console. Theme percentages listed only for Google AI Pro for Education; Education Plus unconfirmed.

Auto-marked quizzes with per-answer feedback

Turns a form into a quiz with an answer key, points per question and feedback attached to each answer, so pupils see an explanation, model answer or YouTube clip the moment they submit. Scores can be held back for manual review and released with per-response comments; Classroom imports the marks.

Options. Settings > 'Make this a quiz'; auto-marks short answer, multiple choice, checkboxes, dropdown and both grids; 'Default quiz point value'; 'Add answer feedback' (text or YouTube video) per answer; 'Release grades: Immediately after each submission' or 'Later, after manual review'; respondent settings for missed questions, correct answers and point values; collect email addresses to add individual feedback; response validation (number, text, length, regular expression, select at least/at most) with custom error text; Classroom 'Grade importing' and 'Locked mode'.

Constraints. Short-answer auto-marking matches listed answers only, so list every accepted spelling; paragraph, linear scale and rating questions need manual marks. Grade import needs the quiz as sole attachment, email collection, one response, same domain, and overwrites existing marks. Locked mode works only on managed Chromebooks. Hyperlinks inside feedback: unconfirmed (help page names text and YouTube).

1Build misconception distractors with mark-scheme answer feedbackEvery wrong option in a moles and titration quiz is a real examiner-report error, and its feedback quotes the mark-scheme line the student missed, so precision slips are named and corrected the same lesson.Science (Chemistry)9AugmentationPCK3610Medium effort

A* lever Multi-step calculation accuracy with correct units and significant figures, the last ten to fifteen per cent of marks separating A from A*.

Board Chemistry, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Chemistry 7405 (components 7405/1, 7405/2, 7405…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Take the three commonest errors for this topic from the 2024 and 2025 examiner reports; write one distractor per error in each multiple-choice item.
  2. Settings > Make this a quiz; set default quiz point value to one; enter the answer key and add answer feedback text to every option, right and wrong.
  3. Write each wrong-answer feedback as the mark-scheme line plus the corrective step: 'M2 needs moles = cv/1000; you used cubic centimetres, not cubic decimetres'.
  4. Set Release grades immediately after each submission, show missed questions and correct answers, then attach the quiz in Classroom with grade importing on.
  5. Read the question-level response chart and reteach only the distractor that attracted most of the class.
Student workflow
  1. Commit to one option before reading anything, then read the feedback for that option in full.
  2. Copy the mark-scheme line from any wrong-answer feedback into your error log, then redo the calculation unaided.
  3. Re-sit the same quiz forty-eight hours later and compare the two scores.
Copy and paste
Paste into each wrong-answer feedback box, editing the bracketed parts: 'Not yet. The mark scheme awards M[n] for [the exact step], so the examiner wants [expected working]. Your answer suggests you [named misconception, for example used cubic centimetres rather than cubic decimetres]. Redo that step, give the answer to [3] significant figures with the unit, and log this as error [code].' Keep correct-answer feedback too: 'Correct. The mark scheme also requires the unit and 3 significant figures; check you gave both.'
The three routes
A → A*

Use only the hardest items, where distractors are precision slips: wrong significant figures, missing unit, an unrounded intermediate value carried forward. Release grades immediately, allow no second attempt, and put twelve minutes on the clock so calibration and checking routines are tested under time.

B → A*

Cover the whole topic in two shorter quizzes a week so gaps are found systematically rather than guessed at. Include one fully worked example as answer feedback for each item, and follow the quiz with a faded worked example the student completes before the re-sit.

C → A*

Split into three five-question quizzes on the underlying algebra and unit conversion first, aiming for eighty per cent success before any compound item appears. Feedback carries the whole worked step, not only the mark-scheme line, and the same quiz is re-sat weekly until secure.
