Teacher workflow
  1. Build eight past-paper items as short answer, listing every accepted form of each answer in the key, including 'pi/3', 'π/3' and the decimal.
  2. After each item add a linear scale question, one to five, labelled 'guessed' to 'certain', worth zero points and set to required.
  3. Settings > Make this a quiz; set Release grades to 'Later, after manual review'; collect email addresses so individual comments can be added.
  4. Sort the response sheet into four quadrants (right and confident, right and unsure, wrong and confident, wrong and unsure) and plan from the wrong-and-confident column.
  5. Release grades with a one-line comment naming the student's dominant quadrant and the checking routine to use next.
Student workflow
  1. Answer, then rate your confidence honestly before any score appears; a dishonest rating costs you the diagnosis.
  2. When grades are released, list every wrong-and-confident item and write the checking step that would have caught it.
  3. Apply that checking step in the next timed set and record whether it caught anything.
Copy and paste
Confidence question after every item: 'How confident are you that your answer is fully correct, method and accuracy? 1 = I guessed, 3 = I think so, 5 = I would bet the marks on it. Be honest; this is not marked.' Release comment template: 'Your pattern is [wrong but confident] on [named topic], so the error is in your method, not your nerve. Your checking routine this fortnight: [substitute back / check units / estimate the size of the answer first]. Bring the evidence Friday.'
The three routes
A → A*

Use only the last two questions of past papers, where confident errors cluster on unfamiliar contexts and modelling. Track the wrong-and-confident count as the headline number and set a personal target of zero across three consecutive sets before moving to full-paper timing.

B → A*

Mix retrieval items from earlier topics with current ones, so slow recall shows up as low confidence on content that should be secure. Pair each low-confidence-but-correct item with a spaced re-test to build fluency, and model the full-mark method for every wrong item.

C → A*

Keep items at a level where success is around eighty per cent, so ratings are informative rather than uniformly low. Teach the rating scale explicitly first, then apply it to foundation algebra where the misconceptions sit, repeating the same eight items weekly.

SEND adaptation. A student with ADHD may rate confidence impulsively; require a written one-clause reason beside each rating on paper, which slows the judgement without reducing the mathematical demand.

Teacher workflow
  1. Take ten sentences from past AQA Paper 2 translation tasks, each carrying one high-utility structure: subjunctive trigger, preterite against imperfect, pronoun placement, ser against estar.
  2. Build each as a short answer question and list in the answer key every correct variant, including accented and unaccented typing and both valid word orders.
  3. Add response validation, regular expression 'contains', requiring the accented form where the accent is grammatical, with custom error 'Check your accents before you submit'.

Student workflow
  1. Translate each sentence without notes, typing accents, inside twelve minutes.
  2. Read the rule named in the feedback and write the whole sentence out correctly in your book.
  3. Retake the form on Friday, aiming for no repeated grammar error.
Copy and paste
Answer feedback template (paste and adapt): 'Not accepted. The rule: after 'es necesario que' Spanish needs the present subjunctive. Your version used the indicative, which is how the English sentence is built, not the Spanish one. Rewrite the whole sentence, not the one word, and say it aloud twice. A → A*

Use whole sentences carrying two structures each, with no word bank, timed at one minute a sentence. The target is zero accent or agreement slips across ten sentences, because at this level the marks go to precision rather than to knowledge.

B → A*

Keep one structure per sentence but cycle the same six structures weekly until recall is automatic. Add a second version of every item with different vocabulary, so the structure rather than the sentence is what is remembered. Mark the pattern of errors, not the total.

C → A*

Give the Spanish sentence with two gaps first, then the same sentence untouched in a later section, then the full translation three weeks on. Keep a visible reminder of the subjunctive triggers on screen until the success rate is consistently high.

Teacher workflow
  1. Build one multiple-choice grid whose rows are eight scenarios and whose columns are the statistical tests, then a second grid for level of measurement.
  2. Add three calculation items as short answer, listing accepted forms in the key, including 'p<0.05', 'p < 0.05' and the critical-value comparison.
  3. Add checkbox items offering six evaluation statements with response validation 'select at most two' and custom error 'Pick the two that change the conclusion'.
  4. Settings > Make this a quiz; add incorrect-answer feedback to each grid naming the design feature that dictates the test choice.

Student workflow
  1. Match every scenario to its test, then defend one match aloud to a partner.
  2. Choose at most two evaluations and be ready to say why the others are weaker.
  3. Rework any calculation you lost, showing the critical-value comparison in full.
Copy and paste
Checkbox item (paste and adapt): 'Below are six evaluation statements about this study's procedure. Select AT MOST TWO: the two that change what the study can claim, not the two that are easiest to remember. For each one you choose you must be able to finish the sentence 'and the consequence for the theory is...'. Marks here are for discrimination, not coverage.' Validation: select at most 2. Custom error: 'Pick the two that change the conclusion; a list of every criticism is a low-band answer.'
The three routes
A → A*

Use unfamiliar scenarios with two plausible tests and require the justification as a short answer marked by hand. The target is elaborated AO3: every evaluation carried through to a consequence for the theory in one sentence.

B → A*

Keep the grid but cycle the same eight scenario types weekly until test selection is automatic, and mark the calculation items separately so gaps in the mathematical content stay visible instead of being averaged away.

C → A*

Start with four scenarios and two tests, with the decision tree on screen. Build to the full grid across a term, and keep one calculation item every week so the mathematical content is never left to revision.

SEND adaptation. Grids scroll badly and can overload a student with a visual impairment: offer the same items as separate multiple-choice questions on request, at identical demand and tariff.

Teacher workflow
  1. In a quiz-mode Form, write ten short-answer items whose answers have one required exact form: a surd, a modulus-argument with argument in range, or exact matrix entries.
  2. Add response validation, Regular expression, Matches, to each item, with custom error text naming the required form, and list every accepted equivalent in the answer key.
  3. Attach answer feedback quoting the mark-scheme line that requires that form, and set Release grades to Later, after manual review.
  4. Assign through Classroom with grade importing, then read the responses for the items where the form, not the mathematics, failed.
  5. Each half-term add two items from the mock questions where exact form was lost, reusing the regular expressions you already have.
Student workflow
  1. Answer each item and, if the validation message appears, rewrite your answer in the form the mark scheme requires.
  2. Note the items you could do but could not write correctly; that list is your accuracy log.
  3. Redo the same quiz cold a week later on paper, without the validation messages to catch you.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description, and reuse the wording as each item's custom error text: 'Every answer here has one acceptable form, the form the Edexcel mark scheme requires. If the box turns red, your mathematics may be right and your form wrong: read the message and rewrite the answer exactly as the scheme would. Exact means exact: no decimals for surds, arguments in the range the question states, no rounding you were not asked for. Keep a list of items where only the form failed. That list, not your score, is what we teach from.'
The three routes
A → A*

Ten items, each in a different exact form, validation set tightly and no hint of the pattern anywhere in the question. Grades are held back and the follow-up is oral: the pupil states the form the scheme wants before they are allowed to read the feedback.

B → A*

Six items, one form a fortnight, with the required form named in the question text and the regular expression loose enough to accept equivalent orderings. The naming is removed from the question text once two consecutive sets run clean for that pupil.

C → A*

Four items with a worked example of the required form at the top of the section, generous validation and immediate grade release, so success is high. The worked example is withdrawn one form at a time, once the class stops needing it.

SEND adaptation. For dyspraxia affecting written output, typing the answers takes handwriting out of precision practice; let the working stay on paper unmarked, and allow extra time so the form, not the hand, is tested.

Branching sections (adaptive routing by answer)

Splits a form into sections and sends each pupil to a different section depending on their answer, so a wrong choice on a diagnostic question leads to a targeted hint or re-teach page while a correct choice skips ahead or submits. Works inside quiz mode, so points and feedback still apply.

Options. 'Add section' in the editor; on a Multiple choice or Dropdown question choose More > 'Go to section based on answer' and map each option to a section or to 'Submit form'; at the end of each section set 'After section N' to continue or jump elsewhere; combine with required questions, shuffled option order, images or embedded video in the remediation section, and answer feedback; preview as a respondent before publishing.

Constraints. Routing is offered only on Multiple choice and Dropdown, not Checkboxes, grids or scales; each jump depends on one question, not a combination; community threads report that editing a submitted response can clear answers in unvisited sections; Gemini 'Help me create' cannot yet build multi-section forms, so branches are added by hand.

Teacher workflow
  1. Write a short passage from the set text, then a multiple-choice question asking which reconstruction is the argument's actual structure.
  2. Add one section per wrong option naming the error (affirming the consequent, conflating necessary with sufficient), a worked reconstruction, and one re-test item.
  3. On the question choose More > 'Go to section based on answer' and map each wrong option to its own section and the correct option to the extension section.
  4. Set 'After section N' on each re-teach section to return to the re-test, and from there on to the extension section.
  5. Settings > Make this a quiz; write answer feedback in AO2 wording; preview as a respondent, since Gemini cannot build multi-section forms.
Student workflow
  1. Read the passage twice and choose the reconstruction you could defend, not the one that looks familiar.
  2. In your section, rewrite the argument as numbered premises and say which premise the objection attacks.
  3. In the extension section, state one objection and the strongest reply, then judge which survives and why.
Copy and paste
Extension section description (paste): 'You reconstructed the argument correctly, so now do the A* work. 1. Write the argument as numbered premises and a conclusion. 2. State the strongest objection to one named premise, attributing it to a philosopher on the specification. 3. Give the reply that defends that premise. 4. In two sentences, judge whether the objection or the reply is stronger, and name the criterion on which you judged. Use AO2 language: valid, sound, necessary, sufficient, question-begging.'
The three routes
A → A*

Skip the diagnostic and start every student in the extension section, where the demand is criterion-explicit judgement between an objection and its reply. Branch instead on which criterion they selected, routing each to a section that stress-tests that criterion against a counter-example.

B → A*

Run the full branching diagnostic weekly across the specification, because these gaps are topic-shaped rather than skill-shaped. Each re-teach section carries a complete worked reconstruction, faded to a half-completed one in the following week's form so the scaffold is withdrawn deliberately.

C → A*

Reduce to two options per diagnostic question so routing is reliable and the success rate stays high. Re-teach sections teach premise and conclusion identification alone for three weeks before any objection work, with the numbered-premise template visible on screen throughout.

SEND adaptation. A student with autism may find an unstated inference genuinely absent rather than obvious; make the enthymeme explicit in the re-teach section text and keep the evaluative judgement task completely intact.

Teacher workflow
  1. Build four sections: identify the complexity, justify it, choose between two structures, then an unfamiliar-context trade-off with no options offered.
  2. End each tier with one dropdown gate question; map the correct option to the next tier and every wrong option to that tier's worked-example section.
  3. In each worked-example section paste an annotated trace and one faded practice item, then route back to the gate question.
  4. Settings > Make this a quiz, points on gate questions only, release grades immediately, and shuffle option order so the gate cannot be guessed by position.
  5. Read which tier each student reached and group the class by tier for the next lesson's paired justification task.
Student workflow
  1. Write your reason for the gate answer before you click, so the justification exists independently of the option.
  2. If routed to a worked example, annotate the trace yourself and complete the faded item unaided.
  3. In tier four, write the trade-off in specification vocabulary: time against space, average against worst case.
Copy and paste
Tier four section description (paste and edit): 'No options this time. A logistics firm processes forty million parcel scans a day and must answer in under a second whether a given barcode has been seen today. Recommend one data structure. A → A*

Start at tier three and add a fifth tier from theory of computation, decidability or the halting problem, where the gate demands a written justification the teacher marks rather than an auto-marked option. Timing is tight and no worked examples are offered.

B → A*

Run all four tiers weekly across every data structure in the specification so coverage is systematic. Worked-example sections carry a full annotated trace, and the same ladder is repeated a fortnight later to check that the retention actually held.

C → A*

Rebuild tier one as counting operations inside a loop, reaching a high success rate before complexity notation appears at all. Keep the annotated trace on screen throughout the first half-term, then remove the trace and leave only the faded item.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyspraxia affecting written output, allow the tier four justification as a voice note transcribed into the short-answer box; the reasoning demand and the vocabulary requirement are unchanged.

Teacher workflow
  1. Split six multi-step Physics questions into six sections, one question per section, to cut the visual load of a full paper.
  2. Open each section with a dropdown offering 'worked example first', 'one hint', 'straight to the question', and route each choice to its own sub-section.
  3. Make every route converge on the identical question at the identical mark tariff, so the assessed demand never changes with the scaffold chosen.
  4. Settings > Make this a quiz, points on the questions only, and write answer feedback naming the physics step and the unit requirement.
  5. Review the dropdown log with the student every fortnight and agree one route to relinquish next.
Student workflow
  1. Before each question, choose the support you actually need and be honest about it.
  2. Attempt the question unaided after any scaffold, showing every step and the unit.
  3. At the end, name one question where you took more help than you needed.
Copy and paste
Section-opening dropdown text (paste): 'What do you need for this one? Choose honestly, because the question and the marks are identical whichever you pick. A) Show me a worked example of a similar question first. B) Give me one hint about the first step only. C) Straight to the question. This choice is not marked. It is data for you: across six weeks you should need A less often. Your teacher will review the pattern with you, not judge it.'
The three routes
A → A*

Offer only the hint and no-hint routes, with the hint costing nothing but always logged. The target is zero hints across a full synoptic set while accuracy, units and significant figures hold under genuine exam timing.

B → A*

Keep all three routes and add a fourth, 'show me the mark scheme after I answer'. Use the log to find the topics where the worked example is always chosen, and reteach those topics directly rather than only offering the scaffold.

C → A*

Default every student to the worked-example route for three weeks, then make it opt-in. Sections stay at one question with a formula prompt on screen, and the same six questions repeat weekly until the success rate is consistently high.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: put a progress marker such as 'question 3 of 6' in each section title and keep every section to one screen without scrolling, which cuts the task-switching cost for ADHD.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Write the opening dropdown as three defensible stances on a common research-project theme, each phrased in French as a candidate would state it.
  2. Give each stance its own section holding the counter-question an examiner would put to that stance, a paragraph answer box, and a second, harder counter.
  3. On the dropdown use More > 'Go to section based on answer' to map each stance to its section, then set 'After section' so branches converge on one defence.
  4. Add response validation, minimum three hundred characters, with error text 'A defence needs a reason and an example, so keep going in French'.
  5. Mark the paragraphs yourself against the Paper 3 criteria: Forms cannot auto-mark them, and the point is the argument, not a key.
Student workflow
  1. Choose the stance you would actually defend, not the easiest one.
  2. Answer each counter-question in French inside four minutes, with no notes or dictionary.
  3. Say your final defence aloud to a partner before you submit it in writing.
  4. Name the one structure you reached for and could not control.
Copy and paste
Opening dropdown (paste and adapt): 'Ta these sur ton projet: choisis celle que tu defendrais vraiment. A) Le progres est surtout politique. B) Le progres est surtout culturel. C) Il n'y a pas eu de progres reel.' Section text for branch A (paste): 'L'examinateur repond: mais les lois changent-elles les mentalites? Reponds en francais, en quatre minutes, sans notes: une raison, un exemple precis, une concession. Utilise au moins un subjonctif et un pronom relatif complexe. On note l'argument et la precision, pas la longueur.'
The three routes
A → A*

Add a third counter-question in every branch that attacks the student's own example, and require a subjunctive and a complex relative pronoun in the final defence. The aim is idiom chosen deliberately rather than memorised chunks reproduced under pressure.

B → A*

Head each branch with a bank of five structures and require three of them, so working memory goes to the argument. Remove the bank branch by branch across the term as recall of those structures becomes automatic.

C → A*

Offer two stances rather than three, print the counter-question in English underneath, and accept a hundred-word defence built from a sentence frame. Keep the same theme for a fortnight so subject knowledge is not the obstacle.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, split each counter-question into its own section and extend the timing; the French demand and the marking criteria stay identical.

Board Further Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9FM0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Further Math…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Take one eight-mark Edexcel Further Mathematics question and give each step its own section, so only one line of working is typed at a time.
  2. End each section with a dropdown of possible intermediate results, including the two commonest slips, and route every option to its own page.
  3. On each slip page name the error, give the correct intermediate value, and route straight on to the next step rather than back to the start.
  4. Settings > Make this a quiz with points on the final steps only, so one early slip cannot cost the whole question.
  5. Read which step each student lost and set the next lesson's practice on that step alone.
Student workflow
  1. Type only the result of each step, not the whole solution.
  2. If you are routed to a slip page, name the error before moving on.
  3. Finish the final steps from the corrected value, at full difficulty.
  4. Record the step you lost in your error log.
Copy and paste
Slip-page text (paste and adapt): 'That value comes from a real and common slip: you took the modulus before squaring, so the argument is right and the size is wrong. The correct intermediate value is r = 5. Write it down and carry on. The marks in this question sit in the last two steps, and you are still going to earn them. Log the slip in one line: what you did, what it should be, and how you will catch it next time.'
The three routes
A → A*

Remove the dropdown of possible intermediates and ask for the value as short answer, with every accepted form listed in the key. Route only on a wrong value, and time the whole question at exam rate.

B → A*

Keep the dropdowns and add a second question using the same technique in a different option module, so the method is recognised rather than the question remembered. Review the step-loss pattern with the student weekly.

C → A*

Reduce to four steps, head each section with a worked analogue, and repeat the same question shape weekly until the early steps are automatic before any tariff moves to the end.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: let the student photograph handwritten working into a separate Classroom assignment, so typing mathematical notation never becomes the skill being assessed.

Teacher workflow
  1. In Forms, Settings then Make this a quiz, then build one multiple-choice diagnostic question per skill: standard deviation, sign test, percentage change, ratio, graph reading.
  2. Add a section per skill; on each question use More then Go to section based on answer, mapping every wrong option to its own re-teach section.
  3. Write each re-teach section with the AQA Psychology wording and a worked example, then a second question on the same skill before returning to the main path.
  4. Add answer feedback to every option explaining why it is wrong; release grades immediately and preview as a respondent before publishing.
  5. Share the same form with the Psychology, Geography and Economics teachers so the same quantitative item appears in all four lessons.
Student workflow
  1. Answer each diagnostic question; if you are routed to a re-teach page, work the example yourself before answering the retest.
  2. Redo the form weekly until you reach the end without being routed aside.
  3. Use the same method names in your Psychology answers as the re-teach pages use.
Copy and paste
Re-teach: standard deviation. You chose an answer that treats the mean as the spread. Standard deviation measures how far scores sit from the mean, so a larger value means a more widely spread set of scores. In AQA Psychology this decides whether a summary statistic is appropriate: use the mean and standard deviation with interval data only. Worked example: for 4, 5, 9, 10 the mean is 7 and the standard deviation is about 2.9 using the n minus one divisor. Now answer the retest question below.
The three routes
A → A*

For the A-to-A* Psychology candidate, the routing only bites on the hardest items: choosing between a sign test and a chi-squared test from an unfamiliar scenario, or interpreting a standard deviation in a 16-mark evaluation. Add a timed section so accuracy holds under exam pace.

B → A*

For the B-to-A* Psychology candidate the gaps are systematic, so every skill gets its own diagnostic and re-teach branch and the whole form returns fortnightly. Each re-teach page carries a fully worked example first, faded to a partially worked one after three weeks.

C → A*

For the C-to-A* Psychology candidate, split the form into three short ones so a session is five questions, not twenty, and keep number work to one operation per question. Re-teach pages use the same worked example every week until it is automatic, and arithmetic is staged before interpretation.

SEND adaptation. For dyscalculia, keep one question per page, allow a calculator on every item, and put the formula on the re-teach page so the demand is interpretation, not recall.

Gemini in Forms (create quizzes from Drive files, summarise responses)

'Help me create' drafts a form or, since the July to August 2026 rollout, a complete quiz with answer keys and points from a prompt that references Docs, Slides or PDFs in Drive; 'Suggest questions' adds more. On the Responses tab Gemini summarises open-text answers into themes with counts and percentage charts.

Options. Desktop only. Prompt with the Drive file referenced plus specification point, mark-scheme focus, difficulty, number and type of questions (multiple choice, checkboxes, grids, short or long answer); preview, then edit and check the answer key. 'Suggest questions' appears once a form has two questions (two to four suggestions). 'Summarize responses' on text questions with 3 to 200 responses; 'Show theme percentages' best with 8 to 200; add or delete themes; 'Refresh with latest responses'; summaries are not saved.

Constraints. Needs Education Plus or the Teaching and Learning add-on (or Google AI Pro for Education), users 18 and over, and admin 'smart features' on. Summaries cover open-text questions only, never quiz responses, and stop above 200 responses. No multi-section forms; regenerating replaces the form with no undo. Suggest questions is English-only and ignores quiz settings.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload to Drive the 2025 examiner report, the mark-scheme extract and your own model paragraph as PDFs, with no pupil names anywhere in them.
  2. In a new form use 'Help me create', referencing those files, and ask for ten multiple-choice items on the errors the report names, with answer keys and points.
  3. Check every generated key against the mark scheme line by line and rewrite any item that tests recall rather than AO2 or AO3 judgement.
  4. Rewrite each answer feedback in mark-scheme wording and set Release grades to 'Later, after manual review', because Gemini drafts contain errors.
  5. Use 'Suggest questions' once for two extra items, then edit them; never regenerate the form, since regeneration replaces it with no undo.
Student workflow
  1. Answer each item, then write which assessment objective you think it was testing.
  2. For every wrong answer, quote the mark-scheme phrase from the feedback and rewrite your sentence to meet it.
  3. Bring your two weakest AO3 items to the next lesson with a redrafted judgement.
Copy and paste
Using the attached examiner report and mark-scheme extract, write a ten-question multiple-choice quiz for Year 13 A-level History on [topic and specification point]. Each question must test the specific weakness the examiner report names, not factual recall. Every wrong option must be a plausible error candidates actually make, such as describing rather than evaluating, or asserting significance without stating a criterion. Include an answer key, one point per question, and for each option a feedback sentence in mark-scheme language. Use British spelling. Include no student names.
The three routes
A → A*

Prompt Gemini from the highest-band descriptors and the report's comments on the strongest scripts, so items discriminate between sound and perceptive judgement. Follow the quiz with a timed paragraph that must build judgement through explicitly stated criteria.

B → A*

Ask for items spread across every topic the report covers, not one, so gaps are diagnosed systematically. Add a model full-mark paragraph as the correct-answer feedback, and repeat the quiz cumulatively each fortnight to force spaced retrieval.

C → A*

Prompt for six items only, on chronology and on the difference between describing, explaining and evaluating, keeping the success rate high. Put the sentence-stem scaffold into the feedback text and re-sit the same quiz weekly until it is secure.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyslexia, ask Gemini for short single-clause option text, check the readability yourself, and add a teacher-read audio version in Classroom; the analytical demand is untouched.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create a form with one long-answer question asking for a sixty-word thesis plus the criterion for judgement; keep 'Collect email addresses' off so responses stay anonymous.
  2. Add response validation of minimum two hundred characters with the custom error 'A thesis needs a claim and a criterion, so keep writing'.
  3. With twenty to thirty responses in, open Responses, choose 'Summarize responses' on that question and 'Show theme percentages'; delete artefact themes and add any you can see yourself.
  4. Read four or five actual responses inside each theme, because the summary is a draft and is not saved anywhere.
  5. Teach the next lesson from the weakest theme, modelling a thesis that repairs it, then re-run the form on a new question a fortnight later.
Student workflow
  1. Write the thesis in sixty words: a claim, a criterion, and no plot summary.
  2. When the themes are displayed, identify which one is yours and argue whether it is the strongest reading.
  3. Redraft your thesis against the modelled one and use it to open a timed essay.
Copy and paste
Form question (paste): 'In no more than sixty words, state the thesis you would argue for this question and name the criterion on which you will judge. A thesis is a position someone could reasonably disagree with. Do not summarise the plot. Shape: the play presents ambition as [X] rather than [Y]; judged by [criterion], the stronger reading is [X], because [reason]. Your response is anonymous and will be grouped with the class so we can see the range of readings.'
The three routes
A → A*

Ask for the thesis plus the strongest counter-reading inside the same sixty words, so the themes reveal whether the evaluation is genuine or formulaic. Teach into the theme that concedes nothing, and require a named critical position in the redraft.

B → A*

Run the task twice on the same question a fortnight apart to check whether the modelled thesis structure transferred. Themes will cluster on description, so the lesson explicitly models the move from AO1 description into AO2 and AO3 argument.

C → A*

Shorten to thirty words and a single claim, with the sentence stem given inside the question text. Aim for most students producing a recognisable claim, and repeat weekly on familiar extracts before moving to unseen questions.

SEND adaptation. A student with slow processing speed can dictate the thesis using voice typing in Docs and paste it in; the sixty-word discipline and the critical demand are unchanged.

Teacher workflow
  1. Write two anchor questions yourself on a known artist, one on formal analysis and one on context shaping meaning, both at full A* demand.
  2. Once the form holds two questions use 'Suggest questions' for two to four variants; it is English-only and ignores quiz settings, so set points and keys yourself.

Student workflow
  1. Analyse the unfamiliar work using the same analytical move you practised on the known artist.
  2. Name the contextual factor and explain how it changes the reading, not merely that it existed.
  3. Carry your strongest sentence into your sketchbook annotation in your own words, citing the source.
Copy and paste
Anchor question (paste and edit): 'Look at the image. In one hundred and twenty words, analyse how [the artist] uses [one formal element] to direct the viewer, then explain how one contextual factor, patronage, technology, politics or the exhibition context, changes what the work means. Do not describe the subject matter. Use specification vocabulary: composition, tonal range, materiality, picture plane, provenance. End with a one-sentence judgement on whether the context or the formal handling does more of the work.'

A → A*

Keep only unfamiliar artists and require the closing judgement to name its criterion explicitly. Use the variants as a weekly ten-minute transfer drill, and tie each one to a live decision in the personal investigation so the analysis has consequences.

B → A*

Alternate a known artist with an unfamiliar one so the transfer is supported rather than assumed. Give a full-mark exemplar paragraph as correct-answer feedback on the formal-analysis item, and repeat the analytical move across four artists before removing the model.

C → A*

Reduce to sixty words and one formal element, with a sentence-stem scaffold inside the question text. Build vocabulary with auto-marked terminology items first, reaching a high success rate before the analytical paragraph is asked for again.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create a form with one long-answer question holding a seventy-word English paragraph to translate; keep 'Collect email addresses' off so responses stay anonymous.
  2. Add validation of minimum three hundred characters and set automatic closing by date, so the set closes before the lesson you plan from.
  3. On the Responses tab choose 'Summarize responses' with theme percentages; non-English summarising is unconfirmed, so check themes against ten real responses (check availability).
  4. Delete artefact themes, add any you can see yourself, and rename every surviving theme as a grammatical error rather than a topic.
  5. Write next week's multiple-choice distractors from the top three themes, so every wrong option is an error this class actually made.
Student workflow
  1. Translate the paragraph in fifteen minutes, no dictionary, typing your accents.
  2. Next lesson, identify which of the class's three commonest errors was yours.
  3. Correct your own version against the rule, not against a model translation.
Copy and paste
Question text (paste): 'Translate the paragraph into Spanish. Fifteen minutes, no dictionary, type your accents. Write the whole paragraph even if one sentence defeats you.' Theme-naming rule for the teacher (keep in your notes): 'Rename every theme Gemini offers as the grammar it breaks: present indicative after a subjunctive trigger; adjective agreement in the plural; false friend, realizar for realise. A theme named after a topic is useless. Check ten real responses against each theme before planning from it.'
The three routes
A → A*

Use a paragraph with three embedded subjunctive triggers and mark precision only. Ask each student to predict the class's commonest error before the themes are shown, which makes their own miscalibration visible and worth a conversation.

B → A*

Re-run the same paragraph type fortnightly and use 'Refresh with latest responses' to see whether a theme is actually shrinking. Teach directly into the largest theme rather than covering all of them thinly each time.

C → A*

Shorten the passage to three sentences and supply the verbs in the infinitive. Use the themes to choose the single structure to drill for a fortnight, then translate the full paragraph and compare the themes.

SEND adaptation. A student with dyslexia may be over-represented in a spelling theme: separate spelling from grammar when naming themes, so teaching targets structure rather than orthography.
Rosenshine

  • 4 Provide models. The next lesson models the correct structure against the class's own commonest error, not a generic one.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Themes are re-measured fortnightly to show whether an error pattern is genuinely shrinking.
SAMR · Modification

Reading thirty translations for patterns is possible by hand but rarely done; thematic grouping makes error-led item writing a fortnightly routine instead of an ambition.

TPACK · PCK

Naming a theme as a grammatical error and converting it into a distractor is subject teaching knowledge; Gemini only clusters the text.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 3: translation precision decides the AQA Spanish A*. Evidence 2: feedback is strong, though clustering only informs planning. Dose 1: fortnightly and licence-limited. Cost and risk 0: Gemini is eighteen-plus and teacher-only, summaries are unsaved, and non-English support is unconfirmed.

EEF feedback; AQA Spanish examiner reports on accuracy in translation into the language.

5Draft a weekly currency check from your own slidesGemini drafts recall items from the teacher's Slides of this term's political developments, and the checked bank runs as a weekly cumulative review with automatic closing, keeping current examples genuinely current.Politics5AugmentationTPK1310Medium effort

A* lever Genuinely current examples and precise use of core political ideas and their thinkers, rather than the textbook cases every Edexcel candidate cites.

Board Politics, Pearson Edexcel (9PL0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Politics (Is…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Keep one Slides deck a fortnight of 2026 developments: named cases, dates, figures and the thinker each one illustrates, with no pupil data anywhere in it.
  2. In a new form use 'Help me create', referencing that deck, and ask for twelve short-answer and multiple-choice recall items with answer keys and points.
  3. Check every key against your deck and the specification, rewriting any item whose answer is a generality rather than a named case, date or thinker.
  4. Add last fortnight's six best items so each form is cumulative, and set automatic closing by date the evening before the lesson.
  5. Attach in Classroom with grade importing on, release grades immediately, and reteach the two cases the class could not name.
Student workflow
  1. Answer the twelve items from memory in eight minutes, with no notes.
  2. Add any case you could not name to your comparative examples grid.
  3. Bring one 2026 example of your own and defend its significance next lesson.
Copy and paste
Gemini prompt (paste, then check every key): 'Using the attached Slides deck only, write twelve recall questions for A-level Politics: eight multiple choice and four short answer, with answer keys and one point each. Every answer must be a named case, date, figure, institution or thinker taken from the deck, never a general statement. Include two items asking which core political idea a case illustrates. Do not invent examples that are not in the deck, and do not use anything dated after it.'
The three routes
A → A*

Add four items asking which UK case and which US case illustrate the same theoretical approach, so recall is stored comparatively. Require a one-line significance judgement, marked by hand, rather than the name of the case alone.

B → A*

Weight the cumulative half of the form more heavily and cycle each case three times across six weeks. Add one item a week asking which thinker the case supports, since idea-to-thinker recall is usually the gap.

C → A*

Keep the bank to six items and put a case list on screen for the first three weeks. Build the comparative grid together in class before any of it is asked for from memory.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, keep the form to one section, eight items and a stated time, and let the cumulative half be attempted separately later the same day.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. A short cumulative form opens the week and keeps this term's named cases in active recall.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Last fortnight's items return inside each new form, so review is built in rather than promised.
  • 3 Ask questions. Twelve items question every student on cases they would otherwise only read about.
SAMR · Augmentation

The same low-stakes recall quiz, but drafted from the teacher's own deck in minutes and auto-marked, which is what makes a weekly cumulative habit survivable.

TPACK · TPK

Spaced retrieval is general pedagogy that the tool makes cheap enough to run weekly; the Politics content comes from the teacher's own deck.

Impact 5 of 10

Proximity 2: current examples support the judgement that earns the A* but do not make it. Evidence 2: retrieval and spaced practice are strong, and the AI adds only speed. Dose 1: weekly but licence-limited. Cost and risk 0: every generated key must be checked.

EEF retrieval and spaced practice; Edexcel Politics examiner reports on use of contemporary examples.

Research: Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Spaced practice and distributed l… Strong Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Risks Gemini invents plausible cases, so check every key against the deck and let nothing generated reach students unchecked. Education Plus, eighteen-plus, teacher-only; the fallback is writing six items yourself from the same deck.

Success measure Students cite 2026 examples unprompted in essays, and named-case recall rises in weekly scores.

Gemini in Classroom

Teacher-facing AI for planning, differentiation and diagnosis. · 4 sub-tools · 20 examples

Availability. Included in Education Fundamentals, Standard and Plus since June 2025. Teachers must be verified teachers marked 18+ in Admin console age-based settings, with the 'Gemini in Classroom' service on for their organisational unit. Students of all ages can see the Gemini tab from 10 August 2026 (default On; admins can switch it off per OU). Gems need 'Gemini and Gems sharing' enabled; Notebooks need Gemini Notebook enabled. Feedback on written work and AI-suggested YouTube questions need Education Plus or Teaching & Learning.

Generate a quiz or questions from a text

From the Gemini tab, generates questions or a quiz on a topic, or 'text-dependent' questions from a Google Drive file or pasted passage (for example an unseen extract or source), targeting the comprehension and reasoning skills the teacher selects. Suited to exit tickets, retrieval quizzes and exam-style short answers.

Options. Inputs: topic, or Drive file / pasted text. Choose the skills students should demonstrate and a grade (year) level; refine in the follow-up chat (for example 'rewrite as 4-mark AO2 questions'). Export to a Google Form (self-marking quiz) or Google Doc, or use 'Add to class' to create an assignment with the file attached. Web only for text-dependent questions; topic quiz also in the Android and iOS Classroom apps.

Constraints. Number and type of questions and mark allocations are not documented; unconfirmed, check in the tool. No built-in UK exam board specifications; assessment objectives or mark schemes must be pasted. Outputs need checking for factual accuracy before assigning.

1Turn misconception distractors into a self-marking weekly FormGemini drafts multiple-choice retrieval questions whose wrong options are known chemistry misconceptions; the Form marks instantly, so students see which misconception they hold and reattempt without waiting a week.SEND: slow processing speed in Chemistry9AugmentationPCK167Low effort

A* lever Multi-step calculation accuracy with correct units and significant figures, where one misconception costs the top band.

Board Chemistry, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Chemistry 7405 (components 7405/1, 7405/2, 7405…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In the Gemini tab generate a quiz on the topic, pasting the specification points and the three misconceptions from the examiner report you want tested.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'make every wrong option a specific named misconception and show full working for each correct answer'; then check every answer yourself.
  3. Export to a Google Form as a self-marking quiz, add feedback text per wrong option naming the misconception, and allow unlimited attempts.
  4. 'Add to class' each Monday, keeping the previous three topics inside every Form so review is cumulative rather than only the last lesson.
Student workflow
  1. Attempt the Form untimed, writing full working on paper before choosing any option.
  2. Read the feedback on a wrong option and name that misconception in your own words in the error log.
  3. Reattempt the same item type in next week's cumulative section, checking the working rather than the answer.
Copy and paste
Write twelve multiple-choice retrieval questions on [topic] for a Year 13 A-level chemistry class, using the specification points I have pasted. Each question must need at least two steps of calculation, and every incorrect option must be a specific named misconception rather than a random number, including unit-conversion and significant-figure errors. After each question give the correct answer with full working, and one sentence naming the misconception behind each distractor. Do not simplify the calculations.
The three routes
A → A*

Set only the two-step and three-step items, and require the student to judge units and significant figures correct or incorrect before submitting. Every slip goes into a personal checking routine sheet, one line each, reviewed immediately before the next timed paper.

B → A*

Use all twelve with worked solutions released after the first attempt, so each wrong option is followed by a fully worked model. Spread the same twelve across three weeks to build spaced recall of the whole topic, not the last lesson.

C → A*

Start with six single-step items and aim for eighty per cent correct before two-step items appear. Pre-teach the unit conversion in a five-minute daily review and keep the Form open all week, so success comes before speed.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: let the student dictate the error-log line instead of writing it, and print the Form as a Doc so the whole question set can be read on paper first.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. The cumulative section reviews the previous three topics before any new content is tested.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Instant per-option feedback tells teacher and student which misconception is actually held.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Unlimited untimed attempts and staged difficulty keep success high without lowering demand.
SAMR · Augmentation

The same retrieval quiz, but misconception-specific instant feedback and unlimited untimed attempts change the feedback loop from weekly to immediate.

TPACK · PCK

The distractors come from the teacher's knowledge of chemistry misconceptions and examiner reports; the tool only scales them into a marked Form.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: multi-step accuracy and significant figures decide the last marks. Evidence 3: retrieval practice plus immediate feedback, both strong EEF strands. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, cumulative. Low cost and risk 1: every generated answer and unit needs checking. Total 9.

EEF retrieval and spaced practice, plus feedback; examiner reports name unit and significant-figure slips yearly.

Research: Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Spaced practice and distributed l… Strong Formative assessment and feedback… Strong

Risks Gemini miscalculates, so verify every answer and distractor against the specification. No pupil data in prompts. Under-18 tab access is admin-controlled: agree the OU setting with the DPO. Fallback: teacher-written Form from past-paper stems.

Success measure Named misconceptions disappear from class error logs and calculation marks on mock papers rise.

2Build a hardest-item ladder from an unseen sourceGemini writes text-dependent questions on an unseen source, which the teacher reorders into a difficulty ladder ending in AO3 judgement, so every student meets the item that separates A from A*.History8ModificationPCK459Medium effort

A* lever Sustained AO3 judgement on an unseen source under time, rather than description of its content.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In the class Gemini tab choose text-dependent questions, paste the unseen source with its provenance line, and set the skills to inference and evaluation.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'rewrite as six questions rising from comprehension to a twenty-mark judgement on utility, using the AO2 and AO3 wording I pasted'.
  3. Check every question against the source and the mark scheme, delete any that invent detail, then export to a Doc.
  4. 'Add to class' as a material; in the lesson model rung one aloud, then set rungs two to five for guided practice in pairs.
  5. Keep the final judgement question for independent practice and mark it against the AO3 descriptors only.
Student workflow
  1. Answer the ladder in order, writing from the source and its provenance, not from memory.
  2. Compare inference answers with a partner and mark where the evidence stops supporting the claim.
  3. Write the final judgement in twenty minutes, then self-check against the AO3 descriptor strip.
Copy and paste
Here is an unseen historical source with its provenance. Write six text-dependent questions on it that rise in demand: two on comprehension of content, two on inference from wording and tone, one on the limitations of the provenance, and one twenty-mark question asking how far the source is useful to a historian studying [topic]. Use only what the source says. Number them and state which assessment objective each targets, using the mark-scheme wording I am pasting. Do not answer the questions.
The three routes
A → A*

Give only the top two rungs. Students write the utility judgement in fifteen minutes, then compare their criteria with the top band and rewrite the conclusion so criteria are stated explicitly rather than implied. Finish by discussing which generated questions were weak, and why.

B → A*

Use all six rungs weekly across different source types. The comprehension rungs are answered orally for speed, then a modelled full-mark answer to the inference rung is studied before students attempt it, so evaluation is practised with the structure visible.

C → A*

Run the ladder over two lessons with a sentence-starter strip for each rung, and a success criterion of four correct inferences before any judgement is attempted. Remove one scaffold each fortnight and log which rung is now independent.

SEND adaptation. For a student with a visual impairment, export the ladder to a Doc for screen-reader use and allow oral answers to rungs one and two; the source stays at full complexity.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The teacher models rung one aloud, showing how provenance wording becomes a defensible inference.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Rungs two to five are attempted in pairs while the teacher checks how evidence is used.
  • 9 Independent practice. The twenty-mark judgement is written alone under timed conditions.
SAMR · Modification

The source task is redesigned as a graded ladder of items no teacher could write for every new source weekly; the reading and the judgement stay the student's.

TPACK · PCK

The gain comes from the teacher's mark-scheme knowledge setting the rung order and rejecting weak items; Gemini only supplies drafts.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: aims straight at AO3 judgement on unseen sources. Evidence 2: modelling and guided practice with mark-scheme feedback. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, any source. Low cost and risk 1: every generated question must be checked against the source. Total 8.

EEF feedback and metacognition strands; examiner reports repeatedly cite weak judgement on source utility.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong Intelligent tutoring systems Strong Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Risks Gemini can invent source detail, so check each question against the original. Paste no pupil data. The Gemini tab is now on by default for under-18s: confirm the OU setting with the DPO. Fallback: a teacher-written ladder from past papers.

Success measure Source-question AO3 marks rise a band across the mock series and fewer scripts stop at description.

3Make students mark-scheme the AI's complexity questionsGemini generates hard questions on algorithmic complexity; students write the mark scheme before answering, then mark peers with it, so assessment-objective wording becomes theirs rather than the teacher's.Computer Science7ModificationTPACK3610Medium effort

A* lever Justifying design and efficiency choices in the precise technical language the mark scheme actually rewards.

Board Computer Science, OCR (H446 - OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Computer Science, specif…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste the specification section on complexity and data structures into the Gemini tab and generate eight extended questions demanding justification, not recall.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'remove all mark allocations and model answers'; check each question is answerable from the specification, then export to a Doc.
  3. 'Add to class' the question Doc with the board's command-word list, and ask pairs to write a four-mark scheme for two questions each.
  4. Collect the schemes, compare two against the real past-paper scheme on the board, and name the wording differences that lose marks.
Student workflow
  1. Write a four-mark scheme for your two questions, deciding what earns each mark.
  2. Answer a different pair's question, then mark their answer using their scheme.
  3. Revise your scheme after seeing the real one, and say which mark you had been giving away.
Copy and paste
Using the A-level computer science specification section I have pasted, write eight extended written questions on algorithmic complexity, data structures and theory of computation. Each question must require a justified choice or a comparison, not the recall of a definition, and must be answerable from this specification alone. Use the board's command words. Do not include mark allocations, mark schemes or model answers, and do not answer the questions: the students will be writing the mark schemes themselves.
The three routes
A → A*

Give the two hardest questions only, and require the scheme to distinguish a five-mark from a seven-mark answer, including what makes a justification perceptive rather than adequate. Students then answer under timed conditions and mark blind against the real scheme.

B → A*

Provide one completed exemplar mark scheme as a model before students write theirs, and limit each pair to one question so the AO2 and AO3 split can be taught explicitly. Repeat fortnightly across different specification sections.

C → A*

Supply a mark-scheme frame with the command word and the number of marks already filled in. Students decide only what each mark is for, on questions from a topic taught last week, so the success rate is high and the routine becomes familiar.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, split the task across two lessons with one question each and a visible timer; the justification demand and the peer marking stay the same.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Writing the scheme forces students to ask what each mark is actually awarded for.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Peer marking with their own scheme exposes misreadings of the command words.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Fortnightly repetition across specification sections cumulatively covers the hardest written-paper items.
SAMR · Modification

The task changes from answering questions to authoring the criteria for them, which is only practical because a checked question bank appears in minutes.

TPACK · TPACK

Technology supplies the items, the pedagogy is criteria-writing and peer assessment, and the content is complexity theory; all three are needed.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: justification wording is the discriminator on the hardest items. Evidence 2: metacognition and peer assessment, less direct than feedback. Dose 1: fortnightly rather than weekly. Low cost and risk 1: every question must be checked against the specification. Total 7.

EEF metacognition and self-regulation, peer tutoring at KS5; examiner reports on unjustified answers.

Research: Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Exemplar deconstruction and makin… Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong

Success measure Students use command-word language unprompted and justification marks on the hardest paper items rise.

4Bank unpredictable Spanish follow-ups for the research project defenceGemini turns a student's anonymised research-project outline into forty unscripted follow-up questions in Spanish. Cold-called in pairs, students defend a position they cannot pre-learn, which is exactly what the AQA speaking exam rewards.Spanish7ModificationPCK3910Low effort

A* lever Spontaneity in the AQA speaking test: defending the individual research project under unpredictable follow-up questions rather than reciting a rehearsed script.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Retype one student's research-project outline without their name into the Gemini tab and ask for forty follow-up questions in Spanish at Year 13 level.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'half the questions must demand an opinion justified with a subjunctive or a conditional, and none may be answerable in one clause'.
  3. Check every question for idiom and register, delete the eight weakest, export to a Doc and 'Add to class' as a speaking resource.
  4. In class, pairs draw questions at random and answer for ninety seconds each with no notes; you circulate listening for tense sequence and pronoun placement.
  5. Repeat weekly with a fresh bank per student outline, keeping the same bank in reserve for a cold second attempt three weeks later.
Student workflow
  1. Answer a drawn question for ninety seconds in Spanish with no notes and no pause to translate.
  2. Your partner logs one accuracy slip and one place where you retold rather than argued.
  3. Re-answer the same question immediately, fixing both, then take a new question.
Copy and paste
I teach AQA A-level Spanish. The text below is an anonymised outline of a student's individual research project. Write forty follow-up questions in Spanish, at the level of the Year 13 speaking test, that a demanding examiner might ask about it. At least half must require an opinion justified with a subjunctive or conditional, and none may be answerable in a single clause. Do not write model answers, do not give vocabulary help, and do not repeat a question in different words. Number them and group them under the themes they probe.
The three routes
A → A*

Draw two questions at once and require an answer that links them, then a third that contradicts the position just taken. The student must concede ground in Spanish without losing fluency, which is the move that separates a confident A candidate from an A* one.

B → A*

Issue the themed groups a week ahead so preparation is by theme, never by question, and supply five high-utility structures to rehearse until automatic. In the lesson, questions are drawn only from those themes, so recall is fast enough to leave working memory free for the argument.

C → A*

Shorten answers to forty-five seconds and allow one written prompt card of connectives only, no content. Start with ten questions rather than forty, all on one theme, and remove the card once three answers run clean. Success is answering without translating from English, not sophistication.

SEND adaptation. For a student with a stammer or high speaking anxiety, let them answer to a recording alone first, then to a partner; the ninety seconds and the no-notes rule stay.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every student answers unscripted questions for ninety seconds, not the two who volunteer.
  • 9 Independent practice. Answers are given without notes, and the second attempt follows immediately with the slip named.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The same bank returns cold three weeks later to test durability, not familiarity.
SAMR · Modification

A bank of forty unpredictable questions per student outline is not something a teacher writes by hand, so the task becomes unscripted defence rather than rehearsed presentation.

TPACK · PCK

The value comes from knowing that the speaking mark is decided by unpredictability, so the generated questions are shaped to defeat rehearsal.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: spontaneity in the speaking test is a direct A* discriminator. Evidence 2: retrieval practice and peer feedback. Dose 1: one class, weekly, needs lesson time. Low cost and risk 1: Spanish questions need a teacher's ear before use. Total 7.

EEF oral language and peer tutoring strands; AQA examiner reports on rehearsed, inflexible speaking answers.

Research: Intelligent tutoring systems Strong Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed Screen versus paper reading Strong

Success measure Speaking mocks show fewer rehearsed answers and more justified opinions using the subjunctive under follow-up pressure.

5Let AI questions expose the missing links in analysisAn anonymised student paragraph becomes the text Gemini questions. Every question the AI must ask marks a link the student left implicit, so the rewrite builds the four-link chain examiners reward.Economics6ModificationTPACK369Medium effort

A* lever Chains of reasoning at least four links long, with each step stated rather than assumed, in extract-based analysis.

Board Economics, AQA (board not confirmed by LAET - AQA form) (7136 - AQA A-level Economics (spec version 1.3, 29 June 202…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Retype one anonymised paragraph of student analysis, with the extract it answers, into the Gemini tab and choose text-dependent questions (web only).
  2. Set the skills to inference and causal reasoning, then ask in the chat: 'ask only questions whose answers are missing from the paragraph'.
  3. Check each question is genuinely unanswered from the text, drop any that invent data, and export the survivors to a Doc with the paragraph.
  4. 'Add to class' as a diagnostic, and require the rewrite to answer every question inside the paragraph, with the diagram doing analytical work.
  5. Repeat fortnightly with a paragraph from a different student, always anonymised, until the class stops producing two-link chains.
Student workflow
  1. Read the questions before your paragraph and predict which of them you already answer.
  2. Rewrite so every question is answered in the chain, naming magnitude, time frame or elasticity.
  3. Label your diagram so it carries a step of the reasoning, not a decoration.
Copy and paste
Below is an A-level Economics extract and one anonymised student paragraph answering it. Generate twelve text-dependent questions on the paragraph, aimed at Year 13, that probe the causal chain: ask only about links the paragraph assumes rather than states, and about magnitude, time frame and elasticity where the paragraph is silent. Use only the extract's own data; invent no figures. Do not rewrite the paragraph, do not supply the answers, and do not comment on the student. Order the questions from the earliest missing link to the last.
The three routes
A → A*

Use a paragraph that is already strong, so the only unanswered questions concern magnitude and time frame. The rewrite must reach a judgement on which effect dominates and why, with the diagram shifted to show the weaker second-round effect.

B → A*

Number the links in a modelled four-link chain first, then show which numbered link each question attacks. Students rebuild their paragraph link by link against the model before the model is withdrawn, and repeat on a second extract the same week.

C → A*

Limit the bank to four questions and give a chain frame with connectives supplied: 'which causes', 'which in turn', 'so that'. Accept a three-link chain that is fully stated over a four-link chain with gaps, and withdraw the frame after three successes.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, issue the questions four at a time with a timer per question; the full chain is still expected by the end of the lesson.
Rosenshine

  • 3 Ask questions. Twelve probing questions per paragraph replace one teacher comment on the margin.
  • 9 Independent practice. Students rewrite alone, with the question list as the only support.

The student's own paragraph becomes the text being interrogated, a diagnostic reading of their reasoning that a margin comment cannot produce at this density.

TPACK · TPACK

Question generation, the economics of causal chains and the teacher's knowledge of where students stop reasoning are all needed for the questions to land.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: four-link chains sit just below the evaluation that decides A*. Evidence 2: feedback and metacognition. Dose 1: fortnightly, one paragraph at a time. Low cost and risk 1: questions must be checked for invented data. Total 6.

EEF feedback and metacognition strands; examiner reports on undeveloped analysis and decorative diagrams.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Create a rubric (from the assignment or a pasted mark scheme)

Drafts a Classroom-ready rubric with criteria and performance levels. From August 2026 the Rubrics section of the assignment page can generate one from the assignment itself; the Gemini tab can draft one from pasted assessment objectives or a mark scheme; and existing rubric files or images from Drive or the device can be converted into Classroom rubrics.

Options. Inputs: assignment title and instructions (assignment-page route), or a description of skills, year group and number of performance levels (Gemini tab route). Review and edit criteria and level descriptors before adding. Gemini-tab drafts export to Sheets or Docs and can then be imported; assignment-page rubrics attach directly and are used for marking in Classroom.

Constraints. Rubric generation is limited to users over 18. File or image conversion is English only. Whether the assignment-page generator reads attached files or learning standards is not documented (unconfirmed). Level descriptors are generic unless the teacher supplies the board's AO wording.

Teacher workflow
  1. In the Gemini tab paste the board's AO1 to AO3 wording for the essay and ask for a four-level rubric in that language.
  2. Edit every descriptor so the top level uses the board's own words, export to Sheets, then import it into the assignment's Rubrics section.
  3. Attach three anonymised exemplar essays, one top band, one middle, one on the boundary, with all names and marks removed.
  4. Students mark all three in Classroom; reveal the real marks and run a five-minute discussion of every disagreement.
  5. Set the same rubric on the next assignment so students mark their own draft against it before submitting.
Student workflow
  1. Mark each anonymised exemplar against the rubric, writing one sentence per criterion to justify the level.
  2. Compare your marks with the revealed marks and name the criterion you misjudged.
  3. Mark your own draft with the same rubric and rewrite the weakest criterion before submitting.
Copy and paste
I am pasting the assessment objectives for an A-level English literature essay. Draft a four-level rubric for a Year 13 class with one criterion per assessment objective, plus one for terminology and one for the handling of critical and contextual material. Use the wording of the objectives I pasted for the top level, and make the difference between adjacent levels concrete and observable rather than a matter of degree. Do not invent assessment objectives or mark totals.
The three routes
A → A*

Use only the boundary and top-band exemplars. Students must state the two criteria that separate them, rewrite one paragraph of the boundary essay so it crosses into the top level, then defend that rewrite against the rubric wording.

B → A*

Mark all three exemplars, but supply a completed rubric for the first as a worked example. Work on the evaluation criterion alone for three weeks, so the move from describing to judging is practised with the descriptor visible rather than guessed.

C → A*

Reduce to two criteria, structure and evaluation, on a short extract-based answer. Students highlight where in the exemplar each level is evidenced before assigning any level, and repeat weekly until agreement with the teacher's mark is routine.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, share the rubric a lesson early and set one exemplar rather than three; the criteria and the judgement demanded stay identical.
Rosenshine

Draft a four-level rubric for an A-level mathematics proof assignment with these criteria: correct and consistent notation; logical completeness with no unjustified steps; justification of each step by a named result or definition; and a clearly stated conclusion. A → A*

B → A*

Mark one criterion at a time over four weeks, starting with notation, with a fully worked exemplar for each. Students keep a list of results they are allowed to quote, so justification becomes citing a named result rather than guessing.

C → A*

Teacher workflow
  1. In the Gemini tab paste your board's written-exam criteria for director, performer and designer and ask for a four-level rubric in that wording (teacher must be 18+).
  2. Follow-up chat: 'make the top level about coherence between intention and choice, not about effort or confidence'; then export to Sheets and import to the assignment.
  3. Check every descriptor against the board's wording, cutting any criterion Gemini invented, then print the rubric as a single-page rehearsal-room sheet.
  4. During the run-through two peers score against one criterion each and must quote the moment; the performer answers orally before anything is written.

Student workflow

  3. Write the evaluation using the rubric's wording for the choices you actually made.
Copy and paste
I teach A-level Drama. Below are my board's assessment criteria for the written examination, answered as director, performer and designer. Draft a four-level rubric for Year 13 using the board's own wording wherever possible. The top level must describe coherence between a stated conceptual intention and every practical choice, and precision of theatrical vocabulary; it must not reward effort, confidence or enjoyment. Keep each descriptor to one sentence a student can hold in mind during a rehearsal. Add nothing that is not in the criteria I pasted, and list any criterion you could not cover.
The three routes
A → A*

Withhold the rubric until after the run-through and ask the performer to predict which criterion the peers scored lowest. Disagreement between prediction and score is the coaching point, and the next run must change one design choice to serve the intention.

B → A*

Model the scoring first: the teacher scores a recorded professional extract aloud against each criterion while students annotate. Peers then score only two criteria, and every judgement must be tied to a quoted moment, until all four criteria are used unaided.

C → A*

Reduce the rubric to one criterion, intention and choice, with a two-level split of met or not met and a sentence stem for the evidence. Add a second criterion only when the first is scored consistently by three different peers.

SEND adaptation. A second adaptation: for a student with a visual impairment, supply the rubric as a large-print card and an audio reading, and allow scoring from the sound and speech of the run.

I teach AQA A-level French. Below is the board's marking criteria for the Paper 2 literature essay. Draft a five-level rubric for Year 13 with separate criteria for analytical argument, use of evidence from the text, and accuracy and range of language. Use AQA's own wording where you can. The lower levels must name plot retelling and translated English idiom as faults; the upper levels must require complex structures used accurately. Write the descriptors in English so students can self-mark, add nothing beyond the criteria pasted, and flag anything you could not match.
The three routes
A → A*

Require the prediction to be band and mark, with a named reason the essay is not one level higher. The teacher replies only to that reason, so the conversation is about the ceiling rather than the whole essay, and the gap closes to within two marks.

B → A*

Self-marking is done first on two anonymised essays of known level so the rubric is understood before it is turned on their own work. Predictions then cover one criterion a week until all three are used, with the teacher's levels shown alongside.

C → A*

Use a three-level version of the rubric and ask only whether each criterion is met, not which band. Pair the prediction with a checklist of five high-utility structures the essay must contain, and count them together before the essay is submitted.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyslexia, allow the self-mark to be recorded as audio against each criterion; the justification is still required, only the writing of it is removed.

Re-level text and create a vocabulary list

Re-level text rewrites a passage to a chosen reading level, usable to simplify for support or to raise complexity for stretch. Create a vocabulary list produces topic- and level-specific word lists giving each word's grammatical category, definition and example sentence. Translate text (100+ languages) sits alongside for EAL pupils.

Options. Inputs: pasted text plus a target reading level (Drive file input unconfirmed); topic and grade level for vocabulary. Use the follow-up chat to demand a more academic register, subject terminology or tiered (Tier 2/Tier 3) lists. Outputs can be exported to Docs and assigned with 'Add to class'.

Constraints. Reading levels are expressed as US grade levels, not UK year groups or exam tiers; map them manually. Re-levelled literary or source text may alter quotations, so check against the original before use. Vocabulary definitions need checking against subject conventions.

Teacher workflow

  2. Follow-up chat: 'give each term its grammatical category, a definition in the conventions of Western tonal harmony, and an example sentence about this work'.
  3. Check every definition against the board's glossary and the score, correct any term used loosely, then export to a Doc.
  4. Play eight short extracts; students write the term and a bar reference, then verify each against the score.
  5. Reuse the list in weekly review, adding four terms a fortnight so the list becomes cumulative.

Copy and paste
Create a Tier 3 vocabulary list of the harmonic, textural and stylistic terms a Year 13 A-level music student needs in order to analyse [set work]. For each term give its grammatical category, a definition consistent with the conventions of Western tonal harmony, and an example sentence referring to a specific feature of this work. Exclude general musical vocabulary a GCSE student would already use, and do not invent features of the work that I have not described to you.
The three routes
A → A*

Use unfamiliar extracts by the same composer so the terminology must transfer, and require a judgement sentence: which device carries the stylistic argument here? Mark the precision of the term and the accuracy of the bar reference equally.

B → A*

Work through the set work in order with the score visible, four terms a week, each modelled in a full analytical sentence before students write their own. Weekly cumulative dictation covers every term met so far.

C → A*

Start with eight terms and clearly contrasting extracts, aiming for a high success rate before extracts become subtle. Pair each term with a short audio cue the class agrees on, and review the cues daily.

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste the textbook paragraph on the argument into Re-level text and set a much higher reading level, roughly first-year undergraduate.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'use precise philosophical terminology, mark the premises and conclusion explicitly, and add nothing that is not in my paragraph'.
  3. Check the harder version for inserted claims or misused terms, then place both versions side by side in one Doc and 'Add to class'.
  4. In the lesson ask which version states the argument more precisely and why, collecting the moves students name on the board.
  5. Set one of the students' own paragraphs from last week to be re-levelled upward by hand using those moves.

  1. Read both versions and list three changes that make the harder version more precise.
  2. Identify the premises and conclusion in each, and say which version is easier to attack.

Copy and paste
Re-level the philosophy paragraph I have pasted to a first-year undergraduate reading level. Use precise philosophical terminology, state each premise and the conclusion explicitly, and keep the logical structure of my paragraph exactly as it is. Do not add examples, objections or claims that are not already present, and do not remove any step of the argument. Then list, in three bullets, the specific changes you made to raise the register, so that students can name those moves themselves.
The three routes
A → A*

Add an objection-and-reply sentence pair to the harder version and ask students to judge whether the reply succeeds. The register work then feeds a timed paragraph in which the thesis is defended against the strongest objection.

B → A*

Work on one move at a time, starting with signposting premises, with both versions annotated by the teacher first. Students apply that single move to three of their own paragraphs before the next move is introduced.

C → A*

Use a three-sentence argument rather than a paragraph, and supply a bank of connective phrases for premises and conclusions. Success is whether the premises are identifiable, not how sophisticated the prose sounds.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, issue the two versions a lesson early and require only two named moves; the upward rewrite is still expected.

First, from the historical source I have pasted, create a vocabulary list of the Tier 3 terms a Year 12 student may not know. For each, give the grammatical category, a definition in the sense the source uses, and an example sentence from the period.
