The three routes
A → A*

Withhold the paraphrase and give only the vocabulary list, then ask the student to re-level the source upward into the register of a historiographical article and justify each word choice. Decoding support remains; the analytical demand rises.

B → A*

Give the paraphrase and the list, then require a comparison: which two words in the original carry weight that the paraphrase loses? This teaches that the wording, not the gist, is what earns the AO2 marks.

C → A*

Give the paraphrase, the list and a modelled sentence-level annotation of the first two lines of the original. Withdraw the paraphrase after four weeks, keeping the vocabulary list as the only remaining support.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Risks Re-levelled text silently changes quotations, dates and claims, so check every line and never issue the paraphrase as the source. Keep pupil details out of prompts. Fallback: a teacher-written glossary and paraphrase.

Success measure The student annotates the unabridged source independently and AO2 marks match the class average.

4Back-translate a harder French article into FrenchGemini raises a French article's complexity, lists the structures it now uses, then translates it into English. Students translate back into French and compare with the French version, so accuracy is self-evident.French7ModificationTCK149Medium effort

A* lever Accuracy of complex structures under pressure in the AQA translation into French: subjunctive, tense sequence, agreement and pronoun placement, produced rather than recognised.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste a 150-word French news article into Re-level text and set a higher reading level, roughly US grade 12 or first-year undergraduate.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'keep the facts unchanged but use a subjunctive, a pluperfect and two object pronouns', then create a vocabulary list of those structures.
  3. Read the harder French closely and correct any clumsy idiom yourself, then use Translate text to produce the English version.
  4. 'Add to class' a Doc holding only the English and the structure list; keep the French version back for the comparison lesson.
  5. Release the French only after submission, and collect the three structures the class most often avoided for next week's starter.
Student workflow
  1. Translate the English into French in twenty minutes, using every structure on the list at least once.
  2. Compare your version with the French original and mark each difference as error or valid alternative.
  3. Rewrite the three sentences you avoided, in the structure the list names.
Copy and paste
Below is a French news article. First, rewrite it in French at a higher reading level, roughly first-year undergraduate, keeping every fact and the same length: use at least one subjunctive, one pluperfect, two object pronouns and one relative clause with 'dont'. Do not add information. Second, list those structures with a grammatical category, a definition and the sentence from your version that uses it. Third, translate your French version into natural English for students to translate back. Label the three outputs clearly and change no proper nouns or figures.
The three routes
A → A*

Withhold the structure list and shorten the time to fifteen minutes, so the structures must be chosen as well as produced. After comparison, the student explains why the original's choice is better than their valid alternative, which is register judgement rather than accuracy.

B → A*

Do it in halves: translate the first half with the structure list open and the French original's opening sentence given as a model, then the second half unaided. Add a weekly five-minute retrieval starter on the same structures until they are automatic.

C → A*

Use a sixty-word text and only two target structures, with the French original's verbs supplied in the infinitive. Accept a version that is accurate before one that is ambitious, and remove the verb support once two texts are error-free.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyspraxia, accept the back-translation typed or dictated, and mark only the French; handwriting speed must not decide a translation mark.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The withheld French version is a full model answer, revealed only after independent production.
  • 9 Independent practice. Students produce French under time with no dictionary and no partner.
  • 1 Daily review. The avoided structures become the next week's five-minute starter.
SAMR · Modification

Re-levelling plus translation manufactures a matched French-English pair with a known correct answer, so a translation task becomes self-marking against a model.

TPACK · TCK

The tool controls the lexical and grammatical difficulty of target-language text, which in languages is the content itself rather than a delivery choice.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: translation into French and structural accuracy decide the AQA A*. Evidence 2: retrieval practice and immediate self-marking feedback. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, one article. Low cost and risk 0: machine French needs a teacher who reads it closely. Total 7.

EEF feedback and retrieval practice strands; AQA examiner reports on translation accuracy and anglicised idiom.

Research: Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Risks Re-levelled or translated French can be unidiomatic or drop a nuance, so read both versions before issuing. Never re-level a set-text quotation. Reading levels are US grades, so map them. Fallback: use a past-paper translation with its official answer.

Success measure Translation scores rise and the subjunctive and pronoun placement appear unprompted in timed essays.

5Fade a re-levelled case study back to full demandThe same OCR case-study source appears three times across three weeks, each version harder, ending at the untouched original with the same 20-mark question. The scaffold fades on a schedule; demand never drops.Geography6AugmentationTPK7810Low effort

A* lever Command of case-study detail with real figures and places, and evaluation of a model's limits, sustained in a substantiated 20-mark judgement.

Board Geography, OCR (H481 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Geography (fir…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Paste the original journal or report extract into Re-level text twice, at roughly US grade 9 and grade 11, keeping the original as week three's text.
  2. Follow-up chat: 'keep every figure, place name and qualification exactly as written'; then check both versions against the original for lost data.
  3. Create a vocabulary list of the extract's Tier 3 terms and statistical tests, with category, definition and example sentence, and issue it in week one only.
  4. Set the same 20-mark question all three weeks via 'Add to class', and mark only for figures used and model limits evaluated.
  5. Give the top group the original in week one and a journal-level re-level as their stretch text, so fading runs upward too.
Student workflow
  1. Answer the 20-mark question from the week's version, citing at least four figures with places.
  2. Each week, add what the harder version lets you say that the easier one did not.
  3. In week three, answer from the original with no vocabulary list and no notes.
Copy and paste
Below is an extract I use for an A-level Geography case study. Produce two easier versions of it, at US grade 9 and grade 11 reading levels, and label them. Keep every figure, percentage, date, place name and hedging word exactly as written, including any statement of a model's limits: simplify sentence structure and general vocabulary only. Do not summarise, do not omit a sentence, and do not round a number. Then list, beneath each version, any technical term you replaced, so I can decide whether the replacement is acceptable in geography.
The three routes
A → A*

Start at the original and add a second, contradictory source re-levelled to the same demand. The judgement must now weigh two sources, and the synoptic link to the physical strand is required in the final paragraph rather than optional.

B → A*

Run all three weeks as written, with a modelled paragraph in week one showing one figure carrying one evaluative point. Cumulative review: week four uses a different case study and the same question form, with no re-levelled version at all.

C → A*

Spend two weeks on the grade 9 version and require only four correctly cited figures and one named limit of the model. Move to the grade 11 version when those are secure, and reach the original by the end of the half term.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, keep the vocabulary list for all three weeks and give the text a lesson early; the original and the question do not change.
Rosenshine

  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Week one is pitched so the case study can be used successfully at once.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The same question returns three times, each time with less support.

The same source is simply produced at three demands; the pedagogy of fading is old, but building the three versions by hand rarely happens.

TPACK · TPK

Fading a scaffold on a schedule is a general pedagogical move; the tool makes the intermediate texts cheap enough to plan it.

Proximity 2: case-study detail and model limits matter, but the 20-mark judgement needs more than access. Evidence 2: scaffolding and spaced review. Dose 1: one source over three weeks. Low cost and risk 1: re-levelling can drop figures. Total 6.

EEF scaffolding and spaced practice evidence; OCR examiner reports on vague, figure-free case-study answers.

Research: Worked examples, fading and the e… Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Working memory, ADHD, dyslexia, a… Mixed

Risks Re-levelling can round figures, drop hedges or lose a place name, which would teach the wrong case study: diff every version against the original. Never issue a re-levelled version as the exam text. Fallback: use the board's own graded resources.

Success measure By week three, answers from the original cite four figures and name a model's limits unaided.

Gemini Notebook and Gems attached to Classwork (teacher-led AI)

Teachers create a Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM, up to 50 sources) or a Gem (custom Gemini persona, up to 10 sources) from Classwork > Create, or attach one to an assignment or material. Students then chat with an AI grounded in the teacher's chosen materials, such as mark schemes, exemplar A* essays and specification extracts.

Options. Sources: Drive files, external links and previously published class materials. Gems take custom instructions (for example 'act as an OCR examiner; question, never write the essay'), shaped by LearnLM pedagogy. Notebooks give students chat plus teacher-made studio items (audio overviews, study guides). Attached items appear as a Class learning resource or inside the assignment and are shared automatically.

Constraints. Requires Gemini Notebook and 'Gemini and Gems sharing' enabled by admin; students need the Student role and an OU with Gemini on. Students cannot add or edit sources or generate studio items. Teacher visibility of student chat transcripts was reported by Google at BETT 2026 but not verified here (unconfirmed).

1Attach an examiner Gem that questions but never writesA Gem grounded in the mark scheme and anonymised A* exemplars interrogates each student's thesis, so everyone meets the Socratic pressure a teacher can apply to only a few students a lesson.English Literature9ModificationTPACK356Medium effort

A* lever A thesis sustained under pressure, with judgement built through explicit criteria rather than asserted.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Classwork > Create make a Gem with up to ten sources: the mark scheme, three anonymised A* exemplars and the extract.
  2. Set instructions: 'Act as an A-level examiner, ask one question at a time about the thesis and evidence, and never write or rewrite the student's prose'.
  3. Test it yourself with a weak thesis and a strong one, tightening the instructions until it refuses to draft any sentences.
  4. Attach the Gem to the essay assignment so it appears for students, and require the chat to happen before the essay is written.
  5. Read three chats at random (transcript visibility unconfirmed) and reteach the question students answered worst.
Student workflow
  1. Type your thesis in one sentence and answer the Gem's questions without asking it to write.
  2. Record the two questions you could not answer, and find the evidence before writing.
  3. Write the essay from your own plan, then return to be questioned on your conclusion.
Copy and paste
You are an A-level English literature examiner using only the mark scheme and exemplars provided. A Year 13 student will give you a thesis about the set text. Ask exactly one question at a time that presses on their argument: the precision of the claim, the quality of the evidence, the alternative reading they have ignored, or the criteria behind their judgement. Never write, draft, rewrite or improve their sentences, never supply quotations, and never give a mark. If asked to write, refuse and ask another question.
The three routes
A → A*

Restrict the Gem to alternative readings and the criteria behind the judgement. Students log every question they cannot answer and must resolve it from the text itself, not from the Gem, before writing the timed essay.

B → A*

Restrict the chat to evidence quality: for each claim, which quotation, and why that one? A modelled transcript is studied first so students can see what a strong answer to the Gem looks like.

C → A*

Begin with three fixed questions the Gem always asks about a single paragraph, alongside a planning frame. Add a fourth question only once the first three are answered fluently, building over a term rather than a fortnight.

SEND adaptation. For a student with autism, publish the Gem's question types in advance so the interaction is predictable; the argumentative demand is unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every student is questioned on their own thesis, not just the three the teacher reaches.
  • 5 Guide student practice. The Gem guides planning while all the writing stays the student's own work.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The questions students log as unanswerable show the teacher what to reteach.
SAMR · Modification

Essay planning becomes a one-to-one viva that every student sits before writing, a redesign of the task rather than a faster version of it.

TPACK · TPACK

Subject criteria in the sources, Socratic questioning as pedagogy and the Gem's grounding must all work together for the questions to be worth answering.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: a thesis defended under questioning is the A to A* move. Evidence 3: feedback and metacognition at KS5. Dose 2: whole class, every essay. Low cost and risk 1: offloading if the Gem drafts prose, plus admin enablement. Total 9.

EEF feedback and metacognition strands; examiner reports on asserted, unevaluated judgements.

Research: Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Exemplar deconstruction and makin… Moderate

Risks Offloading is the main risk: test that the Gem refuses to draft prose. Anonymise exemplars. Needs Gemini and Gems sharing plus Gemini on for the student OU; transcript visibility is unconfirmed. Fallback: teacher-written question cards.

Success measure Essay plans state their criteria explicitly and evaluation marks rise across two assessment points.

2Build a Notebook of worked methods students must citeA Notebook of past-paper worked solutions and practical methods answers only with citations, so students hunt the method pattern across many questions instead of one answer, and justify the route they choose.Physics8ModificationTCK489High effort

A* lever Transfer of multi-step method to unfamiliar contexts, holding units and significant figures under time.

Board Physics, OCR Physics A (H556) (H556 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Physics A (spe…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Classwork > Create make a Gemini Notebook with up to fifty sources: mark schemes, worked solutions, required-practical methods and examiner reports.
  2. Make studio items for students: an audio overview of the topic's method families and a study guide of the commonest errors.
  3. Attach the Notebook to the topic material so it appears as a class learning resource and is shared automatically.
  4. Set the rule in writing: ask the Notebook for the method pattern and the citation, never for tonight's answer.
  5. Next lesson, give an unfamiliar-context question with no Notebook access and compare success with last term.
Student workflow
  1. Ask the Notebook which method family a question belongs to, then read the cited source.
  2. Attempt the unfamiliar question alone, writing the method name before any numbers.
  3. Check units and significant figures against the cited mark scheme, then log the error type.
Copy and paste
Which method family does this type of question belong to, and which sources in this notebook use the same method? For each source you name, quote the step where the method is set up and state the assumption that step depends on. Do not solve my question and do not give any numerical answer. Then list the two errors the examiner reports most often associate with this method, each with its citation.
The three routes
A → A*

Use only unfamiliar-context and synoptic questions. Students must name two candidate method families and justify their choice from the cited sources before calculating, then explain why the rejected route fails.

B → A*

Take one method family a week, with the audio overview as pre-reading and two worked examples faded from full solution to bare prompt. The Notebook is then used to find a third example of the same family.

C → A*

Restrict to one topic and three method families, with a printed decision tree for choosing between them. Students verify each step against the cited mark scheme so the success rate stays high while the tree is faded.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, use the audio overview for revision and cap each Notebook session at ten minutes against a written question list agreed beforehand.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. Fifty cited worked solutions model whole method families, not one board example.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. The decision tree and the cited set-up step scaffold method selection, then fade.
  • 9 Independent practice. The unfamiliar question is attempted with no Notebook access at all.
SAMR · Modification

Students interrogate a corpus of fifty worked methods for a pattern instead of asking the teacher for the next step; that corpus cannot be searched on paper.

TPACK · TCK

The Notebook represents physics method as a searchable, cited corpus, turning method selection into subject content students can examine.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: method transfer to unfamiliar contexts is where A* marks sit. Evidence 2: worked examples and scaffold fading. Dose 2: whole topic, every student. Low cost and risk 1: real offloading risk unless the no-answers rule is policed. Total 8.

EEF metacognition and self-regulation; worked-example research; examiner reports on method choice.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Success measure More students name a method before calculating, and unfamiliar-context question scores rise.

3Rehearse the seminar privately before speaking in itA Notebook of the set readings and the seminar's published questions lets a student rehearse and test positions privately, so the seminar demands the same argument rather than improvisation under social load.SEND: autism in Philosophy7ModificationTPK578Medium effort

A* lever Defending a thesis against objections in real time, the discussion that becomes top-band written evaluation.

Board Philosophy and Religion (Religious Studies), Edexcel (Pearson) (9RS0 — Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Religious St…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create a Notebook with the set readings, the seminar's four published questions and a page of standard objections and replies.
  2. Attach it to the seminar material a week early so every student can prepare, and make the study guide studio item available.
  3. Publish the seminar protocol: who speaks when, for how long, and the sentence stems used to object and to concede.
  4. In the seminar, ask this student for the position they tested and the objection they could not yet answer.
Student workflow
  1. Ask the Notebook for the strongest objection to your position and check it against the reading.
  2. Write your position and one prepared reply on a card before the seminar.
  3. In the seminar, state the position, then name the objection you could not answer.
Copy and paste
Using only the readings in this notebook, state the strongest objection to the position I am about to defend, and cite the source it comes from. Then ask me one question about my reply. Do not write my argument for me, do not give me a conclusion, and do not tell me which position is correct. If my reply misses the objection, say which part of it is left unanswered and cite the reading again.
The three routes
A → A*

Require two objections from different readings and a reply that concedes something before it rebuts. The seminar then opens with this student stating the strongest objection to their own position, which is the top-band move.

B → A*

Prepare one objection with the reply stem supplied, checking the citation against the reading before the seminar. The teacher models the same exchange aloud first so the structure of a reply is visible.

C → A*

Use one published question, one objection and a two-sentence reply frame. Success is speaking once with a cited reason; the number of exchanges grows across a term rather than within a lesson.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: allow the prepared card to be read verbatim and agree a signal for passing a turn; the argumentative content demanded stays identical.
Rosenshine
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. Private rehearsal and sentence stems scaffold live argument without reducing what must be argued.
  • 5 Guide student practice. The Notebook questions the reply before the seminar does, with every source cited.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Preparation makes a successful first contribution likely, which builds willingness to argue.
SAMR · Modification

Seminar preparation becomes a rehearsed dialogue with the readings, redesigning who can take part fully without changing what a contribution must contain.

TPACK · TPK

The tool delivers an access strategy, private rehearsal against sources, that would work in any discussion-based subject.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 2: oral defence feeds written evaluation rather than being assessed itself. Evidence 2: scaffolding and oral rehearsal. Dose 1: one seminar cycle, targeted rather than whole class. Low cost and risk 2: sources are teacher-curated and answers cited. Total 7.

EEF oral language interventions and metacognition; access arrangements practice on prepared contributions.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong

Risks The Notebook may misattribute an objection, so citations need checking. Needs Gemini Notebook enabled for the student OU, and students cannot add sources. No pupil data in sources. Fallback: a printed objections-and-replies sheet.

Success measure The student contributes in every seminar with a cited reason, and written evaluation marks follow.

4Replace textbook examples with a monthly current-affairs NotebookA Gemini Notebook of thirty sources the teacher refreshes monthly holds this term's real politics. Every essay plan must replace a textbook example with a cited 2026 one, paired across the UK and USA.Politics7ModificationTPACK139High effort

A* lever Genuinely current examples rather than textbook ones, used comparatively across the UK and USA to support an evaluative judgement on an institution's significance.

Board Politics, Pearson Edexcel (9PL0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Politics (Is…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Classwork > Create make a Gemini Notebook with thirty sources: this term's news analysis links, Supreme Court opinion extracts, Hansard pages and party documents.
  2. Pair sources deliberately: for each UK item add the closest US equivalent, so comparison is possible inside the Notebook rather than across lessons.
  3. Make the studio items yourself, a study guide per theme, since students cannot; attach the Notebook to the essay assignment as a class learning resource.
  4. Require every essay plan to cite the Notebook source behind each example, and reject any example that appears in the textbook.
  5. Refresh ten sources each month and retire the stalest; check Gemini's summaries against the source before teaching from them.
Student workflow
  1. Find two paired examples, one UK and one US, and cite the Notebook source for each.
  2. Ask the Notebook what the sources disagree about, then decide which reading you defend.
  3. Write the judgement paragraph yourself, naming the theoretical approach it rests on.
Copy and paste
Use only the class Notebook. Find me two events from this academic year, one in the UK and one in the USA, that bear on the significance of the Supreme Court. For each, quote the source and give its date, and say which of the sources in this Notebook disagree about what the event shows. Do not use examples from outside the Notebook, do not summarise a textbook, and do not write my paragraph or offer a judgement: list the evidence and the disagreement only.
The three routes
A → A*

Require the pairing to be defended: why is this the right US comparator, and where does the analogy break? The judgement must rank the two systems on the institution's significance, using one theoretical approach explicitly, in a timed forty-minute essay.

B → A*

Give a modelled example pair with the citation and the analytical point written out, then require one new pair a week on a different theme. A cumulative Sheet of the class's examples is reviewed every Friday so recall becomes fast.

C → A*

Restrict the Notebook to six sources on one institution and ask for one UK example only, with a sentence stem for its significance. Add the US comparator once the UK example is used accurately twice without prompting.

SEND adaptation. For a student with ADHD, publish a six-source themed sub-Notebook per essay so the search space is small; the requirement to cite a current example is unchanged.
Rosenshine

  • 3 Ask questions. Students interrogate the sources for disagreement instead of receiving a list of examples.
  • 9 Independent practice. The judgement paragraph is written without the Notebook open.
SAMR · Modification

A teacher-curated, monthly-refreshed corpus students can question turns example-hunting into source work, which no textbook or handout could support at this currency.

TPACK · TPACK

Curating current sources, knowing what Edexcel counts as comparative analysis, and grounding the AI in those sources are all required together.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: current, comparative examples are the Edexcel A* discriminator. Evidence 2: retrieval and teacher-grounded feedback. Dose 1: whole class but monthly curation. Low cost and risk 1: summaries can misread a source and admin enablement is needed. Total 7.

EEF retrieval practice and homework at KS5; Edexcel examiner reports on dated, textbook-bound examples.

Success measure Essays cite examples from this academic year, paired UK and US, with sources named rather than vague references.

5Debate the set film with a Spanish-only GemA Gem grounded in the set film's scenes and AQA's essay criteria argues back in Spanish, refuses plot retelling and never writes prose to copy, so students build a thesis while thinking in Spanish.Spanish6ModificationTPACK359Medium effort

A* lever Analytical argument about the AQA set film rather than plot retelling, produced in Spanish without translating an English thought first.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. From Classwork > Create make a Gem with ten sources: AQA's essay criteria, your scene-analysis notes and three anonymised strong paragraphs in Spanish.
  2. Instruct it: 'respond only in Spanish, demand a thesis, ask one follow-up per turn, and never write a sentence the student could copy'.
  3. Test it yourself for ten turns, checking it neither drifts into English nor invents scenes, then attach it to the essay assignment.
  4. Set a twelve-turn conversation as the homework before the essay, and ask students to bring the thesis it failed to shake.
  5. Open the next lesson by testing three of those theses yourself in Spanish, so the Gem's pressure is followed by a teacher's.
Student workflow
  1. Argue a thesis about the film in Spanish for twelve turns, never asking for translations.
  2. Log the follow-up you could not answer and the structure you reached for and lacked.
  3. Write the essay paragraph from your own notes, with the Gem closed.
Copy and paste
You are an AQA A-level Spanish examiner discussing the set film with a Year 13 student. Respond only in Spanish, at the level of the sources provided. Demand a thesis in the student's first reply and challenge it every turn with one follow-up question. If the student retells the plot, ask what it proves. Never write a full sentence the student could copy into an essay, never translate into English, and never supply vocabulary unless asked to define one word in Spanish. Correct only by re-asking the question so the student self-repairs. Refer only to my sources.
The three routes
A → A*

Add an instruction that the Gem must take the opposing critical reading and hold it. The student's task is to concede one point and still defend the thesis, in Spanish, then bring both positions into the essay's conclusion as an evaluative judgement.

B → A*

Publish five thesis statements in Spanish to choose from, so the conversation starts from a defensible claim. Six turns rather than twelve, twice a week, with a list of ten high-utility structures the student must use at least once each.

C → A*

Allow the Gem to accept one-sentence answers and to define words in Spanish on request, and set four turns on a single scene. Success is four turns with no English and no plot retelling, before the length is raised.

SEND adaptation. For a student with an autism diagnosis who finds unpredictable oral work costly, the typed Gem is the rehearsal; the same thesis is then defended aloud to one partner, not the class.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every student faces twelve targeted follow-ups in Spanish, not one class question.
  • 5 Guide student practice. The Gem corrects by re-asking, so the student repairs their own Spanish.
  • 9 Independent practice. The essay paragraph is written with the Gem closed and no copyable text.
SAMR · Modification

A grounded persona that argues in Spanish and refuses to supply language gives every student the interrogation a teacher can manage with only a few.

TPACK · TPACK

The Gem's instructions encode AQA's essay demand, the pedagogy of Socratic questioning and the language itself as the medium of thought.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: typed argument in Spanish helps the essay more than the speaking test. Evidence 2: feedback and questioning. Dose 1: homework, needs admin enablement. Low cost and risk 1: the Gem may model imperfect Spanish. Total 6.

EEF feedback and metacognition strands; AQA examiner reports on essays that narrate the set film.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong

Risks The Gem can model flawed Spanish or invent scenes, so test it before attaching and tell students to flag oddities. Offloading risk if it writes prose: the instruction forbids it. Needs Gems sharing enabled. Fallback: paired teacher-led questioning in Spanish.

Success measure Essays open with a thesis and argue it, and fewer paragraphs read as translated English.

Classroom Resources

Reusable material that accumulates across a department. · 3 sub-tools · 15 examples

Availability. Practice sets and video activities: help articles say Education Plus or Teaching and Learning Upgrade only (the public editions page is ambiguous; check your own Resources menu); YouTube must be turned on by the admin; AI-suggested video questions need a teacher designated 18+. Gemini Notebook and Gems: all editions, but the admin must enable Gemini Notebook and/or Gemini for pupils (age-based settings; an under-18 OU can be switched off); usage analytics need Google AI Pro for Education. Gemini tab and Classroom app in Gemini: 18+ educators.

Practice sets (Resources > New practice set)

Build auto-marked, question-by-question drills (retrieval, exam technique, timed data response) in the Resources area, attach them to assignments, and read class insights per problem or per pupil to target reteaching before the next essay or paper.

Options. Create in Resources or inside an assignment (Attach > Practice sets); import questions from Google Forms (file-upload, grid and date/time questions not supported); short-answer, single-select and multi-select questions may suggest an answer; questions set to "Auto" are auto-graded; More > Make a copy; More > Share link > "Allow teachers to access via link", recipient clicks "Make a copy" into "My practice sets"; Class insights offer "All students" and "Problem number" views.

Constraints. Education Plus or Teaching and Learning Upgrade. An assigned practice set cannot be edited (copy it instead). Sharing works only with verified teachers in the same Workspace domain and creates a copy, not a live shared set. Scores must be entered into the gradebook manually. Hint or video-help features: unconfirmed.

Board Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9MA0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Mathematics,…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New practice set, build ten items lifted from past papers, weighted to the final part-marks of modelling and proof questions.
  2. Set every short-answer and single-select question to Auto so it auto-marks; check each suggested answer against the mark scheme before saving.
  3. Attach to an assignment from Classwork; never edit an assigned set - use More > Make a copy for next week's version.
  4. After the deadline open Review work > Class insights, Problem number view, and list the three items with lowest success.
  5. Teach a ten-minute worked example on the weakest item next lesson, then reissue those three items inside the following week's copy.
Student workflow
  1. Complete the set in 25 timed minutes, writing full method on paper before entering each answer.
  2. Read the auto-mark immediately; redo any wrong item from scratch rather than repairing the line that failed.
  3. Log the error type - algebraic slip, misread, method - in a personal error ledger.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description: 'This set is ten of the hardest part-marks from recent papers. Work on paper, 25 minutes, no calculator on items 1-4. Enter an answer only when your method is complete. If an item is marked wrong, start it again on a clean line - do not repair the old attempt. Then write one line in your error ledger: item number, error type (algebra, misread, method, arithmetic), and the checking step that would have caught it. Bring the ledger to Thursday's lesson.'
The three routes
A → A*

Same ten items, no scaffolds, 25 minutes. Feedback focuses on error type rather than content: pupils classify each slip and rehearse one checking routine - substitute back, sense-check magnitude, check units. Insights should show near-full success, so target the single item the class still loses.

B → A*

Twelve items: six cumulative retrieval items from earlier topics, six of this week's hardest. Worked examples precede the hard six and are faded over three weeks. Insights identify topic gaps, so the reteach is content and structure, not only checking routines.

C → A*

Eight items in a small-step ladder from a secure foundation in algebraic fluency to one exam-standard part. Aim for 80% success. Scaffolds - a method prompt inside the question stem - are removed a fortnight later using More > Make a copy.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed, issue the same ten items with the timer removed and the set split across two sittings; the demand and the mark scheme stay identical.
Rosenshine

  • 6 Check for understanding. Problem-number insights check the whole class item by item, not just the pupils who volunteer.
  • 9 Independent practice. Timed solo completion on paper, with auto-marking closing the correction loop in the same session.

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New practice set, build twenty calculation items across moles, Kc, pH and titration, each requiring units and three significant figures.
  2. Set questions to Auto; where a unit must be typed, check the suggested short answer accepts every correct form before saving.

Student workflow

  2. Where auto-marking rejects your answer, decide whether the chemistry or the rounding failed before retrying.
  3. Rework the two items you lost in the same session, from the given data upward.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description: 'Twenty calculations. Carry units through every line of working and give final answers to three significant figures unless the question says otherwise. Enter only the final value. If an item is marked wrong, decide first whether the chemistry failed or the rounding failed, then rework the whole item from the data - do not patch your old line. The three routes
A → A*

Twenty items at full paper demand, no unit prompts, thirty minutes. Feedback centres on rounding discipline and order-of-magnitude checking, since the chemistry is usually secure; insights should isolate one or two stubborn item types, such as Kc with a changing volume.

B → A*

Split into two sets of ten across a fortnight, each opening with four retrieval items on mole ratios. A worked example precedes each new type and is withdrawn in the second set, so technique becomes consistent rather than occasional.

C → A*

Ten items beginning with single-step mole calculations and building to a two-step titration. Unit prompts stay in the stems for six weeks and the success target is 80%. A later copy removes the prompts once the ledger shows no unit errors.

SEND adaptation. For a visual impairment, supply the item text as a large-print or screen-reader-friendly sheet for working, with answers still entered and auto-marked on screen.

Board Computer Science, OCR (H446 - OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Computer Science, specif…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources, build three five-item practice sets on time complexity, hashing and tree traversal, each completable in eight minutes.
  2. Use single-select for the complexity class and short-answer for the justifying phrase; check every suggested answer against the specification's wording.
  3. Attach one set to a Monday, Wednesday and Friday assignment; make copies rather than editing an assigned set.
  4. Read Problem number insights after each set and open the next lesson with the one justification the class worded loosely.
Student workflow
  1. Answer five items in one sitting of eight minutes, without pausing to look anything up.
  2. Where a justification is marked wrong, rewrite it in the specification's own vocabulary before moving on.
  3. On Friday, retry the two items you missed earlier in the week from memory.
Copy and paste
Paste into each assignment description: 'Five items, eight minutes, one sitting - close every other tab first. Give the complexity class and then one sentence of justification using the specification's vocabulary: comparisons, elements, worst case, amortised. If an answer is marked wrong, rewrite the whole justification rather than adding words to it. On Friday you will meet the two items you missed again, unseen, so make the correction stick now.'
The three routes
A → A*

Same five items, but the justification must name the worst case and the dominant operation. Feedback targets loose phrasing - 'it is faster' becomes a comparison count - because the complexity classes themselves are already secure.

B → A*

Six items per set, the first two retrieval items on definitions from earlier in the specification. A fully worded model justification sits above the new items for a fortnight, then is removed from the next copy.

C → A*

Four items per set, starting from counting operations inside a loop before any Big-O notation appears. A sentence frame for the justification stays in the stem, removed only when three consecutive sets are fully correct.

SEND adaptation. A second adaptation: fix each burst to the same timetable slot and accept a typed rather than handwritten error note, so the routine does not depend on recall.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New practice set, import your department's Google Form of translation and grammar items; file-upload, grid and date questions will not transfer.
  2. Set each short-answer item to Auto, then check the suggested answer accepts every correct variant and decide whether an unaccented form counts as wrong.
  3. Attach to a Monday assignment, then open Review work > Class insights, All students view, and note the one structure each pupil is still losing.
  4. Give every pupil that single structure as their week's target and rebuild it into next week's copy (More > Make a copy) as four interleaved items.
Student workflow
  1. Translate each sentence in Spanish before typing, saying the verb ending aloud; no dictionary and no English draft first.
  2. When an item is marked wrong, retype the whole sentence rather than the word that failed.
  3. Add your named structure to your phrase book and use it in this week's essay paragraph.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description: 'Twenty sentences, twenty minutes, no dictionary. Think in Spanish: if you catch yourself translating an English sentence in your head, stop and start again from the Spanish verb. Accents count, so type them. When an item is marked wrong, retype the whole sentence correctly rather than patching one word, then say it aloud twice. Before you submit, write down the structure you had to think hardest about. That is your target this week, and it must appear in Friday's essay paragraph.'
The three routes
A → A*

Twenty items at essay demand: the subjunctive after expressions of doubt, sequence of tenses in reported speech, and se constructions. No dictionary, twenty minutes. Feedback targets idiom rather than accuracy, which is largely secure, so the goal is Spanish that was never English first.

B → A*

Twelve items: four cumulative retrieval items on tenses from earlier units and eight on this week's structure. A worked model translation sits in the assignment description for a fortnight, then is withdrawn from the next copy so the structure becomes automatic rather than copied.

C → A*

Eight items in a ladder from a single clause with a regular present-tense verb to one subordinate clause taking the subjunctive. Aim for eighty per cent success, keep the trigger phrase inside the stem for six weeks, and remove it in a later copy.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed, remove the timer and split the twenty items across two sittings; the structures, the no-dictionary rule and the marking standard stay identical.

5Drill method selection with multi-select items, not the arithmeticMulti-select items ask which opening lines are valid for long Core Pure questions, de Moivre or binomial, reduction formula or substitution, so route choice is drilled fifteen times without fifteen full solutions.Further Mathematics6ModificationPCK4610Medium effort

A* lever Choosing an efficient route at the start of a long Edexcel Core Pure question; A* candidates commit to a workable method, A candidates lose minutes restarting.

Board Further Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9FM0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Further Math…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New practice set, write fifteen multi-select items, each a Core Pure question stem with five candidate opening lines, some valid but wasteful.
  2. Mark every genuinely valid line correct, set the items to Auto, and check each suggested answer against the specification before saving.
  3. Attach as a ten-minute starter: no calculator, no working, only the decision, and say in the stem that valid includes wasteful.
  4. Read the insights for items where the class chose a valid but wasteful line, then time two routes against each other on the board next lesson.
  5. Add three items each half-term, drawn from the anonymised Year 13 mock questions that cost the most time, using More > Make a copy.
Student workflow
  1. Select every opening line that would reach an answer, then star the one you would actually use.
  2. Where a line you rejected was valid, work two lines of it and see why it survives.
  3. In the next timed paper, write your chosen method before any algebra and stay with it.
Copy and paste
Paste into the assignment description: 'Ten minutes, no calculator, no working. For each stem, select every opening line that would actually reach the answer, including the ones you would never choose, then star the single line you would use under exam pressure. A line can be valid and still be a bad idea: your star is a judgement about time, not about correctness. If you select a line you cannot justify, you are guessing. Bring your three starred choices you are least sure about to the lesson.'
The three routes
A → A*

Fifteen items, two of them cases where every offered line is valid and the judgement is purely about time. Feedback compares route cost in minutes, since both routes reach the answer and the marginal marks are lost to restarts rather than to ignorance of method.

B → A*

Ten items on one topic at a time, complex loci then matrices, with a fully worked comparison of two routes in the description for a fortnight, then withdrawn. Insights show which topics still produce guessing rather than choice, and those topics are retaught before the next copy.

C → A*

Six items offering only three candidate lines, two of them clearly invalid, on topics already taught. Aim for eighty per cent success and require a one-line reason for each rejection; the written reasons are dropped once choices are consistently right across two sets.

SEND adaptation. For dyspraxia affecting written output, this drill removes handwriting from method practice entirely; supply the stems on paper as well so the screen is not the only place to read them.
Rosenshine

  • 6 Check for understanding. Every pupil commits to a route on every item, and insights show where wasteful lines were preferred.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The set is reissued as a copy before each mock, mixing topics from across both Core Pure papers.

TPACK · PCK

Dose 1: one class, a starter each fortnight. Cost and risk 1: licence-gated, and item writing takes a careful hour.

EEF: feedback and worked examples; examiner reports note abandoned methods on long Core Pure questions.

Video activities (Resources > New video activity; interactive questions for YouTube videos)

Turn an explainer, lecture or examiner-walkthrough YouTube video into a checkpointed activity with embedded questions so pupils cannot watch passively; class insights show which checkpoint each pupil missed, exposing misconceptions before an A* essay or problem set.

Options. Menu > Resources > New video activity, or Classwork > Create > Assignment > Attach > YouTube; search or paste a URL; add multiple-choice, checkbox or open-ended questions at timestamps; "AI generated suggested questions" appear (spark icon) for certain English-language videos; Class insights via Review work > Class insights, per question or per pupil, with correct, correct-after-retries and incorrect markers.

Constraints. Education Plus or Teaching and Learning Upgrade; YouTube must be turned on by the admin; AI-suggested questions need a teacher designated 18+. Once attached, an activity cannot be edited (create a new one). Scores are entered manually into the gradebook. Sharing or copying an activity between teachers: unconfirmed (not documented).

1Checkpoint a critic's lecture to build AO3 argumentA filmed lecture on the set text becomes a checkpointed activity: at each timestamp pupils turn the critic's claim into a line of argument about the text, not a quotation to drop in.English Literature9ModificationPCK346Medium effort

A* lever Assured AO3 use: critical readings handled as contested positions the essay evaluates, rather than name-dropped, which separates A* from competent A.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Menu > Resources > New video activity; paste the URL of a vetted lecture on the set text and watch it through, noting four claim moments.
  2. Add an open-ended question at each timestamp: state the critic's claim in one sentence, then the textual evidence that resists it.
  3. Check any AI-suggested questions if the spark icon appears; keep only those demanding evaluation and rewrite the rest yourself.
  4. Attach to an assignment, then read Review work > Class insights per question to find the checkpoint where paraphrase replaced evaluation.
  5. Keep the activity in Resources and reissue it next year; build a new one rather than editing an attached activity.
Student workflow
  1. Watch to each checkpoint and answer before the video continues; no skipping ahead.
  2. Write the critic's claim in your own words, then one moment in the text that resists it.
  3. In the next lesson, use two checkpoints as the counter-argument in a timed paragraph.
Copy and paste
Paste as the open-ended question at each checkpoint: 'In one sentence, what is the critic claiming? Now quote or name one moment in the text that does not fit that claim. Finally, write the sentence you would use in an essay that holds both together - it must contain a judgement, not a summary. Do not reuse the critic's wording; if you cannot say it differently, you have not understood it yet.'
The three routes
A → A*

Two critics whose readings conflict, one activity each, in the same week. The checkpoint asks which reading the text supports and on what criteria, so evaluation stops being formulaic and becomes a judgement built from evidence.

B → A*

One lecture with six shorter checkpoints, the first two asking only for the claim. A modelled sentence pairing claim with counter-evidence sits in the assignment description for a fortnight before being withdrawn.

C → A*

A ten-minute extract rather than a full lecture, with a glossary of critical terms in the description and multiple-choice checkpoints identifying the claim before any open-ended ones. Open writing begins at the third activity.

SEND adaptation. For dyslexia, spoken delivery already removes a reading load; allow checkpoint answers to be dictated and keep captions on so critical terminology can be checked visually.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. A checkpoint question every few minutes replaces passive watching, and every pupil answers, not only the confident.
  • 4 Provide models. The critic models expert reading; the checkpoint makes pupils convert that modelling into their own argument.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Per-question insights show exactly which claim the class paraphrased instead of evaluating.

TPACK · PCK

EEF: feedback and metacognition strong at KS5; examiner reports criticise decorative critical quotation.

Board Music, AQA (7272 (AQA A-level Music)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Find a full performance of the set work on YouTube; in Resources > New video activity paste the URL and log every modulation and cadence timestamp.
  2. Place a multiple-choice question two seconds after each event: the correct cadence plus three plausible distractors drawn from common misidentifications.
  3. Add one open-ended checkpoint asking how the shift serves the text or the drama at that moment.
  4. After the deadline read per-question insights; events with most 'correct after retries' become the focus of the next aural starter.
Student workflow

  2. Where you were wrong, replay the bar and say aloud what you actually heard.
  3. In the next lesson, identify the same event types in an unheard extract.
Copy and paste
Paste as the open-ended checkpoint: 'You have just heard a harmonic shift. Name it precisely - the chord, the cadence or the key it moves to - and give the bar or the words it lands on. Then, in two sentences, explain what the shift does dramatically at this point in the work. Use the vocabulary of the specification, not impressions: unsettling only counts once you have said what is happening harmonically.'
The three routes
A → A*

Distractors are near-misses, an imperfect against an interrupted cadence, and the open checkpoint demands a link between harmony and word-setting. The aim is speed and certainty, since recognition is already largely reliable.

B → A*

Half the checkpoints identify the event from three options and half ask for the name unaided. A one-page harmonic reference stays in the assignment description for three weeks, then is withdrawn.

C → A*

Six checkpoints only, all multiple choice, on perfect and imperfect cadences within a single movement, with the score extract attached. Unaided naming begins once insights show consistent success across two activities.

SEND adaptation. For a visual impairment the aural checkpoints already carry the content; supply the score extract in an accessible enlarged format and allow spoken answers to the open checkpoint.

Board Physics, OCR Physics A (H556) (H556 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Physics A (spe…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New video activity paste a filmed required practical - determining the Young modulus, for example - and note each procedural decision.
  2. Add an open-ended checkpoint at each: which measurement dominates the uncertainty here, and what would you change?
  3. Add checkbox checkpoints where several improvements are defensible, so pupils must select and then justify.
  4. Read per-question insights and reteach the one decision point where answers were generic rather than quantitative.
  5. Keep the activity in Resources as the department's standard pre-lab; sharing activities between teachers is undocumented (check availability).
Student workflow
  1. At each checkpoint, name the dominant uncertainty with a rough percentage before continuing.
  2. Propose one change and state quantitatively what it would improve.
  3. Carry your two best improvements into the real practical the next day.
Copy and paste
Paste as the open-ended checkpoint: 'Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the measurement just taken, showing the resolution you assumed. Which single measurement dominates the overall uncertainty in this experiment? Name one change to the procedure or apparatus that would reduce it, and say roughly by how much. Repeat and average is not an answer unless you state which random error it addresses and why that error is the limiting one here.'
The three routes
A → A*

No prompts and no options: every checkpoint is open, and the final one asks pupils to redesign the experiment to halve the dominant uncertainty, justifying the trade-off between resolution and range.

B → A*

Checkbox checkpoints precede the open ones, so a judgement is recognised before it must be produced. A worked percentage-uncertainty calculation sits in the assignment description for the first three activities, then is withdrawn once the arithmetic is reliable.

C → A*

A shorter video with a resolution-and-uncertainty recap in the description, multiple-choice checkpoints on which instrument limits precision, and one open question at the end. Percentage estimation is introduced after four weeks.

SEND adaptation. For dyspraxia affecting written output, the video rehearses the procedure before the lab so attention in the practical goes to measurement; allow dictated checkpoint answers.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The filmed practical models expert technique, including the decisions a live demonstration usually hides.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. Checkbox options scaffold evaluation before the same judgement is asked open-ended.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Insights per checkpoint show whether evaluation was quantitative or generic across the class.
SAMR · Augmentation

The same pre-lab video, but pupils cannot watch passively and the teacher sees who understood which decision before the practical rather than after it.

TPACK · TPACK

Physics content on uncertainty, the pedagogy of checkpointed questioning and the tool's timestamping combine to place a question at the exact procedural moment.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 2: evaluation marks matter but are a minority of the paper. Evidence 2: feedback and questioning. Dose 2: whole class before each required practical, reusable. Cost and risk 1: licence and YouTube needed, and a filmed practical must be vetted.

EEF feedback; examiner reports note generic evaluation answers as a common A-grade limit.

Research: Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Mastery learning and high success… Moderate

Risks Licence-gated with YouTube enabled by the admin; AI-suggested questions need an 18+ teacher, so write your own. The video must match the board's apparatus. Fallback: play it in class with a paper checkpoint sheet.

Success measure Evaluation questions in the next mock draw quantitative answers, and write-ups name dominant uncertainties.

4Transcribe the clause you just heard at natural speedAn authentic francophone news clip becomes checkpointed dictation: pupils transcribe the clause they have just heard, then answer in French. Insights separate pupils who cannot decode from pupils who cannot infer.French7ModificationTPACK136Medium effort

A* lever Listening at natural speed with regional accents, where AQA Paper 1 marks are lost to decoding rather than comprehension, and answers must themselves be written in French.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Menu > Resources > New video activity; paste a two-minute report from a francophone broadcaster's official channel, choosing an accent other than metropolitan Parisian.
  2. At four points add an open-ended checkpoint: write the exact clause you have just heard, then answer the comprehension question in French.
  3. Write those four yourself; AI-suggested questions need a teacher designated 18+ and rarely pitch at natural listening speed.
  4. Read Review work > Class insights per question: a wrong transcription means decoding, a correct transcription with a wrong answer means inference.
  5. Keep the clip in Resources for the next cohort; an attached activity cannot be edited, so build a new one for a new clip.
Student workflow
  1. Write the clause exactly as heard, accents included, before the video continues; one replay only.
  2. Answer in French using a structure from the clip rather than your own English thought.
  3. Mark your transcription against mine: missed liaison, missed verb ending, or word simply unknown.
Copy and paste
Paste as the open-ended checkpoint: 'Write down the clause you have just heard, word for word, with accents. You may replay once only. Then answer this question in French in one full sentence, using a structure you heard in the clip rather than one you would have written in English. Finally, mark your own transcription against the version I release and write one letter beside it: L if you missed a liaison, T if you missed a verb ending, V if the word was simply unknown to you.'
The three routes
A → A*

Four clips a fortnight, each with a different accent, Quebecois, Marseillais, Senegalese, and no replay allowed. Feedback targets idiom carried from the clip into the next essay, since comprehension is already sound and the remaining gap is spontaneity and register.

B → A*

One clip with six shorter checkpoints, the first two transcribing a five-word phrase only. A full transcript is released after the activity for a fortnight and then withheld, so decoding is trained rather than merely confirmed afterwards.

C → A*

A ninety-second clip with captions on for three weeks, multiple-choice comprehension checkpoints before any transcription, and answers accepted in English at first. Transcription of short phrases begins once insights show reliable gist across two consecutive activities.

SEND adaptation. For a hearing impairment, keep captions and a printed transcript so the inference demand survives while the decoding barrier goes; assess transcription only through arrangements agreed with the exams officer.
Rosenshine
  • 6 Check for understanding. Every pupil commits a transcription and an answer at each checkpoint, so decoding failures surface individually.
  • 3 Ask questions. A question every thirty seconds keeps listening active at natural speed instead of passive.
  • 1 Daily review. The words nobody decoded open the next lesson as a two-minute oral retrieval starter.
SAMR · Modification

Listening homework becomes individually diagnosed: the tool separates decoding from inference at the exact second the speech occurred, which one class playback cannot do.

TPACK · TPACK

French at authentic speed, the pedagogy of checkpointed dictation and the tool's timestamping fuse; remove any one and it is a comprehension worksheet again.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: listening at natural speed with answers in French is a direct AQA discriminator. Evidence 3: feedback, retrieval and questioning. Dose 1: one class, fortnightly, one clip at a time. Cost and risk 0: licence, YouTube enablement and vetting every clip cost teacher time.

EEF feedback and retrieval practice; dictation is long established for decoding accuracy in modern languages.

Research: Intelligent tutoring systems Strong Multimedia and video learning (Ma… Strong Assistive technology and access a… Moderate

Risks Needs Education Plus or Teaching and Learning Upgrade with YouTube enabled by the admin; AI-suggested questions need an 18+ teacher, so write your own. Use official broadcaster channels only. Fallback: your own recorded bulletin, unlisted, with a paper checkpoint sheet.

Success measure Paper 1 listening marks rise and French answers reuse structures from the clips rather than translated English.

5Pause before the reveal and direct the moment yourselfA staged extract from a theatre company's own channel stops just before each key moment; pupils commit their own directorial and design choice, then watch what the production did and defend or revise their concept.Drama6ModificationTPK345Medium effort

A* lever A directorial intention sustained coherently through every practical and written choice, and live-theatre analysis recalled from memory in specific detail under exam conditions.

Board Drama (AQA option - board not confirmed by LAET), AQA (7262 (AQA A-level Drama and Theatre)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. In Resources > New video activity, paste an extract from a theatre company's own YouTube channel, licensed footage only, and note four decision moments.
  2. Place an open-ended checkpoint one second before each: state your staging, lighting or vocal choice here, and the intention it serves.
  3. Add one checkbox checkpoint after the reveal, listing four defensible readings of the production's choice, so pupils must choose and then justify.
  4. Read per-question insights for the checkpoint where intentions were described rather than chosen, and rehearse that moment physically next lesson.
  5. Where no licensed footage exists, film your own staged walkthrough of the moment and upload it unlisted to the school channel.
Student workflow
  1. Before the reveal, write your choice and its intention in one sentence each, in precise theatrical vocabulary.
  2. Watch the production's choice and decide whether it serves your intention better than yours did.
  3. Log the moment in your live-theatre notes with two specific details you could quote in the exam.
Copy and paste
Paste as the open-ended checkpoint: 'Do not play on. You are directing this moment. Write one sentence naming your choice, whether blocking, lighting state, pace, vocal quality or design, and one sentence naming the intention it serves for the audience. Use precise theatrical vocabulary, not adjectives. When the production's choice appears, decide whether it serves your intention better than yours did, and say why in one sentence. Keep all three sentences in your live-theatre notes; you cannot look this clip up in the exam.'
The three routes
A → A*

Two extracts of the same scene from different productions, checkpointed identically. The judgement is which staging realises the concept more fully and against what criteria, so evaluation becomes comparative rather than appreciative, and the written answer gains a sustained line of argument.

B → A*

One extract with six checkpoints, the first two naming only the choice the production has already made before any prediction is asked. A modelled intention sentence sits in the assignment description for a fortnight and is then withdrawn as intentions become independent.

C → A*

A two-minute extract with a vocabulary list in the description, multiple-choice checkpoints identifying the choice that was made, and one prediction checkpoint at the end. Prediction moves earlier in the clip once insights show the vocabulary is secure.

SEND adaptation. For autism, the fixed checkpoint structure suits and writing precedes speaking; state explicitly that there is no single correct staging, which the checkbox readings make visible.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The production models expert choice, but only after the pupil has committed one, so modelling follows the attempt.
  • 3 Ask questions. Every pupil answers as director at every decision moment, not only those who speak up in rehearsal.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Checkbox readings after the reveal guide evaluation before the same judgement is demanded unaided.
SAMR · Modification

The recording stops being something to watch and becomes a rehearsal decision each pupil must make and then test against a professional company's choice.

TPACK · TPK

The move is prediction before reveal, which would work in any subject; Drama simply supplies content where an expert's decision is visible on screen seconds later.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: directorial coherence is the Drama A* discriminator, though the written paper also rewards recalled detail. Evidence 2: modelling, questioning and feedback. Dose 1: one class, one set-text moment at a time. Cost and risk 1: licence, YouTube access and finding legitimate footage.

EEF feedback and metacognition; prediction before feedback is well evidenced for retention.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong

Risks Licence-gated with YouTube enabled; use only footage a company publishes itself, since commercial recordings are rarely licensed for classroom streaming. If none exists, film your own walkthrough. An attached activity cannot be edited, so proof it first.

Success measure Written-paper answers name specific staging with an intention, and live-theatre notes carry quotable detail.

Teacher-led Gemini Notebook and Gems (Class learning tools)

Create a notebook or Gem grounded only in your chosen sources (A* exemplars, mark schemes, examiner reports, class notes) and attach it as a class learning tool, so pupils can interrogate the standard, self-quiz and hear audio overviews, while you see who opened it and who started a conversation.

Options. Classwork > Create > Gemini Notebook or Gem; "Select existing" to reuse across classes or "Create new"; tick class materials to import as sources; Notebook up to 50 sources (Drive files and links) with studio items such as audio overview or notes; Gem up to 10 Drive sources with templates Study partner, Quiz me, Brainstorm partner, Real-world connector; "Opened by" engagement on the Classwork page; co-teachers get access automatically; class copies re-use the same notebook.

Constraints. All editions, but the admin must enable Gemini Notebook and/or Gemini for the pupils' OU; pupils on personal accounts cannot open them; access ends when a pupil leaves the class. Usage analytics need a Google AI Pro for Education licence. A copied class re-uses, not duplicates, the notebook, so edits affect every class. Lives on Classwork, not the Resources menu.

1Ground a notebook in A-star scripts and examiner reportsA notebook whose only sources are the mark scheme, three examiner reports and four anonymised A* scripts lets pupils interrogate the standard themselves and name what makes a judgement top-band.History9ModificationPCK4610Medium effort

A* lever A sustained, criteria-based judgement across the whole essay rather than a concluding assertion - the top-band descriptor most A-grade essays never reach.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Classwork > Create > Gemini Notebook; upload the specification, mark scheme, three examiner reports and four anonymised A* scripts with names and marks removed.
  2. Add the class's own model paragraphs by ticking class materials to import them as sources, keeping the total well under fifty.
  3. Generate an audio overview of the top-band descriptors, listen to it and check it against the mark scheme before pupils see it.
  4. Attach as a class learning tool; reuse it next year with Select existing, adding that summer's examiner report.
  5. Use 'Opened by' on the Classwork page to see who engaged, and follow up in a lesson rather than by message.
Student workflow
  1. Ask the notebook which phrases in the mark scheme distinguish the top band, then find them in the exemplar scripts.
  2. Write your own paragraph, then ask which descriptor it does not yet meet, with the source cited.
  3. Rewrite the paragraph yourself; the notebook may not draft it for you.
Copy and paste
Paste as the pupil task: 'Using only the sources in this notebook, answer three questions and cite the source each time. First, which exact wording in the mark scheme separates the top band from the one below? Second, find two sentences in the exemplar scripts that do that work, and say how. Third, paste your own paragraph and ask which descriptor it does not yet meet. Do not ask the notebook to write or improve your paragraph - the rewrite is yours, and I will see both versions.'
The three routes
A → A*

Sources are two A* and two strong-A scripts on the same question. The task is to locate the difference, state it as a criterion, then apply that criterion to their own last essay and rewrite one paragraph.

B → A*

Sources add a full-mark answer annotated paragraph by paragraph. Pupils rebuild the structure from the annotation before writing, and the annotation is removed from the reused notebook in the spring term.

C → A*

A smaller notebook: the mark scheme, one exemplar and a single examiner report. Questions are given as a fixed list, and the first task is to summarise one paragraph's function before any judgement work begins.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed, the audio overview lets a pupil meet the descriptors twice at their own pace; extend the reading window rather than shortening the source list.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. Anonymised A* scripts and the mark scheme are the models; pupils extract the criteria rather than being told them.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Pupils test their own paragraph against a named descriptor and must cite the source that judged it.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The notebook stays open all year, so descriptors are revisited before every timed essay.
SAMR · Modification

The exemplar folder becomes interrogable: a pupil can ask why a sentence is top-band and get an answer anchored to the mark scheme, which a printed pack cannot do.

TPACK · PCK

Mark-scheme literacy and the choice of which scripts contrast usefully drive the gain; grounding merely keeps answers inside those sources.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: judgement is the History A* discriminator. Evidence 3: feedback, metacognition and modelling. Dose 2: whole class, all year, reused annually. Cost and risk 1: admin must enable Gemini for the pupils' OU and outputs still need checking.

EEF: metacognition and self-regulation, and feedback, are the strongest KS5 levers.

Research: Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Screen versus paper reading Strong Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong

Risks Anonymise every script: no names or marks in sources under UK GDPR, and confirm the school's Gemini position with the DPO. Admin must enable Gemini for under-18s. Outputs can be wrong, so check the audio overview. Rewrites stay the pupil's own.

Success measure Pupils name the descriptor they are targeting, and top-band judgement marks rise across timed essays.

2Build a Gem that attacks your argument reconstructionsA Gem grounded in the set texts and mark scheme takes the Study partner template and one instruction: raise the strongest objection to whatever the pupil argues, and never write the reply.Philosophy8ModificationTPACK359Medium effort

A* lever Defending a thesis against the strongest objection with logical precision - the evaluative move that separates A* from accurate exposition.

Board Philosophy and Religion (Religious Studies), Edexcel (Pearson) (9RS0 — Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Religious St…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Classwork > Create > Gem; choose the Study partner template and attach up to ten Drive sources: set-text extracts, the mark scheme and your objection bank.
  2. Write instructions telling it to respond only with objections and clarifying questions, never a reply, a paragraph or an essay plan.
  3. Test it with a deliberately weak argument, checking the objections are sound and sourced, before attaching it as a class learning tool.
  4. Reuse it across Year 12 and Year 13 with Select existing, remembering that editing the Gem changes it for every class.
Student workflow
  1. State your thesis and reconstruct your argument in numbered premises.
  2. Take the Gem's objection, decide whether it hits a premise or the inference, and answer it yourself in writing.
  3. Repeat until an objection survives, then bring that one to the seminar.
Copy and paste
Paste as the Gem's instructions: 'You are a demanding A-level Philosophy interlocutor working from the attached specification and texts. When the student gives an argument, restate it in numbered premises, then raise the single strongest objection, citing the attached source where relevant. Never write the student's reply, paragraph, plan or essay, and never say whether the argument succeeds. If the student asks you to write for them, refuse and ask a sharper question instead. If a premise is unclear, ask which reading they intend before objecting.'
The three routes
A → A*

Objections are drawn from the named philosophers on the specification, so replies must engage a real position. The pupil must also state which premise they would abandon - precision about commitments, not only defence.

B → A*

Instructions add a first step: the Gem checks the reconstruction is valid before objecting, so exposition is secured before evaluation. That check is removed from a second Gem once reconstructions are consistently sound.

C → A*

A narrower Gem on one topic with two texts. It asks for premises one at a time and offers a sentence frame for the reply, withdrawn after a term once the pupil can state a premise unaided.

SEND adaptation. For autism, the Gem's predictable one-objection-per-turn structure suits; agree in advance that it will never judge whether the argument succeeds, which the seminar does openly.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every turn is a question or an objection, so the pupil argues continuously rather than reading about argument.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Guided practice at scale: each pupil meets an objection pitched at their own argument and answers it in writing.
  • 9 Independent practice. The reply is always the pupil's own text; the Gem is barred from drafting it.
SAMR · Modification

Socratic pressure, previously available only in the few seminar minutes each pupil gets, becomes available to every pupil for every argument they write.

TPACK · TPACK

Philosophical content in the sources, the pedagogy of guided practice and the Gem's instruction limits fuse; weaken one and it becomes an essay generator.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: objection-handling is the Philosophy A* discriminator. Evidence 2: guided practice and feedback, with offloading a live risk. Dose 2: every pupil, every essay, reused across classes. Cost and risk 1: admin enablement, and instructions must be policed.

EEF feedback and metacognition; dialogic questioning is well evidenced at KS5.

Research: Screen versus paper reading Strong Rosenshine's Principles of Instru… Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong

Success measure Essays contain a named objection and a reasoned reply, and seminar contributions become more precise.
