  1. Take one unfamiliar data extract from a past paper and model a four-link chain on the board, numbering each link and naming its mechanism.
  2. Post the Guided Learning link with the rule: your own numbered chain is typed into the first message, or Gemini has nothing to question.
  3. Require the paper chain sheet rather than the chat: links numbered, weakest link circled, evaluation naming magnitude, time frame and elasticity.
  4. Tally the circled weakest links across the class and reteach the mechanism most often missing in the next lesson's daily review.
Student workflow
  1. Write your chain on paper first, numbering each link and naming its mechanism, before opening Guided Learning.
  2. Answer Gemini's question on each link; add a link only when you can state its mechanism.
  3. Circle the weakest link yourself and justify that choice by magnitude, time frame or elasticity.
  4. Rewrite the chain unaided against a different extract the following lesson.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level Economics tutor in Guided Learning mode. Below is a data extract and my own numbered chain of reasoning. Do not write a better chain and do not give me the answer. Take my links one at a time and ask me what mechanism makes that link follow, and what would have to be true for it to fail. If a link is missing, ask a question that makes me notice the gap rather than filling it. Finally, ask which link is weakest and make me justify that by magnitude, time frame or elasticity.
The three routes
A → A*

The chain is usually complete, so attack the evaluation. Gemini must ask for a quantified magnitude and a time frame for every judgement and reject any however that is not weighed against the main effect. Re-time the whole answer to twenty-five minutes.

B → A*

Provide a worked four-link chain as a model, then fade it: the model stays visible in week one, only the link headings by week three, nothing by week five. Add a weekly cumulative retrieval starter on diagram shifts and elasticity definitions.

C → A*

Start at two links with a high success rate, using a printed chain template carrying mechanism prompts. Add one link a fortnight. Every session opens by re-explaining last week's chain aloud, so the habit of stating a mechanism forms before length grows.

SEND adaptation. For a student with slow processing speed, let the chain be built across two shorter sessions and dictated before writing; the four-link requirement and the evaluation demand do not change.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. The teacher's board-modelled four-link chain is the standard the student's own chain is questioned against.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Gemini questions each link as the student builds it, so practice is guided rather than marked afterwards.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Chains are rewritten against a fresh extract each week, cumulatively across taught topics.
SAMR · Augmentation

The same extract and chain task, but every student is questioned link by link at the moment of writing instead of receiving comments days later.

TPACK · PCK

The move depends on knowing how Economics answers fail: chains that stop at two links, and evaluation that lists points rather than weighing them.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: chain length and weighed evaluation are the discriminators. Evidence 2: feedback strong, though quality depends on the prompt. Dose 2: weekly, whole class. Low cost and risk 1: Gemini may assert wrong economics, so chains are checked on paper.

EEF: feedback high impact; metacognitive self-questioning strong at KS5.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed Rosenshine's Principles of Instru… Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong

Risks Gemini can state incorrect economic mechanisms and will write the chain if asked loosely; the paper-first rule and the teacher's tally contain both. Under-18s get the youth experience and the thinking model is 18+; school accounts only. Fallback: teacher-written link-by-link question cards.

Success measure Mean chain length rises and evaluation paragraphs weigh magnitude and time frame in the next mock.

6Photograph your working and be questioned, not correctedStudents photograph their statistical working, such as Spearman's rank for the OCR Geography investigation, into Guided Learning, which withholds the answer and questions each step, so the error is found by the student.Core Maths8ModificationTPK356Low effort

A* lever Serves A* in OCR Geography and Biology: data-skills and statistics questions where method choice and arithmetic accuracy, not knowledge, cost the top band.

Teacher workflow
  1. Open gemini.google.com, click Add files, More tools, Guided Learning, and rehearse one Spearman's rank question yourself to see where it hints too readily.
  2. Post a dedicated Guided Learning link in Classroom with the copy prompt as the opening line pupils paste before their photograph.
  3. Set the rule in class: photograph the working, never the question alone, so the conversation is about the method rather than the answer.
  4. Collect the three questions pupils reported being stuck on and teach those steps from the front the following week.
Student workflow
  1. Photograph your own working, paste the opening line, and ask for a check of one step only.
  2. Say what you think is wrong before it tells you; then repair the step yourself.
  3. Redo the whole calculation on paper from the start, unaided, and compare the two answers.
  4. Write one line in your Geography notes on when this test is the right choice.
Copy and paste
I am a Year 12 Core Maths student. I will upload a photograph of my own working on a statistics question. Do not give me the answer, do not do the arithmetic and do not tell me which line is wrong. Ask me one question at a time about the step you think I should check, starting with whether the test I chose suits the data. If I ask for the answer, ask me a question instead. When I have found the error myself, ask me to state the rule I broke in one sentence.
The three routes
A → A*

The A-to-A* OCR Geography candidate can already run the test, so the conversation moves to justification: why this test and not another, what the significance level means for the NEA conclusion, and what the critical value does not tell them. No hints allowed.

B → A*

The B-to-A* Geography candidate has patchy method recall, so the student first asks for a model of the next step, works it, then asks for the step after that unaided. Every session revisits one test from a fortnight earlier as well as the new one.

C → A*

The C-to-A* Geography candidate works on one ranking or one percentage change per session, with the formula visible and the numbers small enough to check mentally. Keep sessions to ten minutes, insist on a written first attempt before any question, and stage significance testing until the spring.

SEND adaptation. A student with dyspraxia photographs working written in large squares, or types it instead; the barrier removed is legible handwriting, not the statistical reasoning being assessed.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Each turn is a question about one step, so the student does the diagnosing.
  • 5 Guide student practice. Guided prompts sit between modelling and independent work: the student attempts, is questioned, then repairs.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The closing demand to state the rule broken in one sentence checks understanding, not the answer.
SAMR · Modification

One-to-one questioning on a student's own working, previously possible only while the teacher stood at the desk, now runs for every student at home; the task becomes diagnosis rather than correction.

TPACK · TPK

Guided Learning supplies a general pedagogical move, withholding the answer and questioning a step, that transfers to any calculation; Core Maths content is the vehicle.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 2: quantitative accuracy decides A* in OCR Geography and Biology, but the gain is one subject away. Evidence 3: metacognition, self-regulation and feedback are strongly evidenced. Dose 2: any homework, whole class, no licence. Cost and risk 1: the model can still reveal answers when pushed.

EEF metacognition and self-regulation; LearnLM's active-learning design withholds answers and prompts self-explanation.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Digital technology as a delivery… Moderate

Risks Gemini can be wrong on method choice and can be pushed into giving the answer, which is offloading: require the unaided paper redo. Thinking model is 18+. Chats are Vault-searchable, so tell pupils and upload only their own working.

Success measure Method-choice marks rise in Geography data-skills questions, and fewer NEA statistical tests are the wrong test.

Concept explanation with diagrams, videos and quiz checks

Gemini automatically adds images and diagrams to learning responses and embeds relevant YouTube videos, then can check understanding with quiz questions. Pupils can ask for a diagram of a mechanism, request a video on a topic, or paste a YouTube lecture link and have Gemini build notes or questions from it.

Options. Prompts: 'Explain X with a diagram', 'Show me a video on X', 'Make study notes from this YouTube link', then 'Quiz me on that'. Works inside Guided Learning or ordinary chat. Videos appear only when Gemini Apps Activity is on. Diagrams are generated or sourced images rather than exam-board figures; ask for the labelled version and compare with the textbook.

Constraints. YouTube embedding needs Gemini Apps Activity on, which school admins may disable (LAET setting unconfirmed). Music and video generation are 18+; image generation for under-18s is unconfirmed, but learning diagrams carry no stated age limit. 'Comprehension checks' are quiz prompts, not a separate switch. Verify diagrams against the specification.

1Sketch the mechanism from memory, then hunt your errorsStudents draw a mechanism unaided, then ask Guided Learning for a labelled diagram and quiz questions, marking their own sketch against both and recording the specific labels they missed.Science (Biology)8AugmentationTCK146Low effort

A* lever Precise definitions and accurate mechanism detail under unfamiliar-context questions, where vague labelling costs the top band.

Board Biology, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Biology 7402 (components 7402/1, 7402/2, 7402/3…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Name the mechanism and the specification point - for example synaptic transmission - and require a memory sketch first, on paper, no notes.
  2. Post the Guided Learning link and the prompt: 'Explain synaptic transmission with a labelled diagram', then 'Quiz me on that'.
  3. Tell students the diagram is generated, not an exam-board figure; they must confirm each label against the textbook page you cite.
  4. Collect the missed-label lists, tally them and reteach the two labels most often missing in the next daily review.
Student workflow
  1. Draw the mechanism from memory in five minutes, no notes open.
  2. Request a labelled diagram, then mark your sketch in a different colour.
  3. Answer Gemini's quiz questions in writing before reading any explanation.
  4. List the labels you missed and check two against the textbook.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level Biology tutor in Guided Learning mode. I have already drawn this mechanism from memory. Explain it with a labelled diagram, then quiz me on it with five questions, one at a time. Wait for my written answer before telling me anything. After each answer, tell me only whether it is right and which precise term I should have used. Do not give me a summary I could copy. At the end, list the labels I got wrong, and which are worth checking in a textbook because you may be inaccurate.
The three routes
A → A*

Sketch from memory in three minutes, then apply: ask for an unfamiliar context - a named toxin or mutation - and predict the effect at each labelled step before Gemini comments. Precision of terminology is the only feedback focus.

B → A*

Cover the specification systematically: one mechanism a week from a teacher-set list, each with a memory sketch, diagram comparison and quiz, and a monthly cumulative quiz across all mechanisms sketched so far.

C → A*

Break the mechanism into three chunks and sketch one at a time, with a partly labelled outline supplied. The success rate stays high; the outline is withdrawn once two consecutive sketches are complete. Quiz questions stay multiple choice at first.

SEND adaptation. For a visually impaired student, ask for the mechanism as an ordered verbal description and build a tactile or large-print label set; the recall demand is unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. The memory sketch is a retrieval starter that shows what is already secure.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Quiz answers written before any explanation reveal gaps rather than hiding them.
  • 4 Provide models. The labelled diagram is a model to compare against, checked on the teacher's cited page.
SAMR · Augmentation

Sketch-and-compare is an existing paper routine; the tool supplies the comparison diagram and questions instantly for every student.

TPACK · TCK

The tool represents the content itself - a mechanism made visual and labelled - which is what makes the comparison possible.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: terminological precision in mechanisms is a top-band discriminator. Evidence 2: retrieval practice and feedback. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, no cost. Low cost and risk 1: generated diagrams can be wrong, so labels are checked against a cited textbook page.

EEF retrieval and spaced practice; feedback strand.

2Annotate the set work by ear before Gemini names itStudents annotate a set-work extract by ear from a YouTube performance, then use Guided Learning to interrogate their terminology, and must justify every harmonic label they keep or change.Music7ModificationTCK3610Medium effort

A* lever Aural precision and harmonic analysis expressed in accurate terminology - the gap between hearing a change and naming it correctly.

Board Music, AQA (7272 (AQA A-level Music)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Choose a public performance of the set-work extract on YouTube and time-stamp four moments you want heard.
  2. Students annotate a blank score by ear first; only then paste the link into Guided Learning with the opening message.
  3. Require the annotated score, not the chat, with changed labels circled and a one-line reason for each change.
  4. Play the extract in class and compare two students' justified labels; correct any term Gemini used loosely.
Student workflow
  1. Annotate the four time-stamped moments by ear on the blank score.
  2. Paste the link and ask Gemini to question, not tell, your labels.
  3. Circle any label you change and write why you changed it.
  4. Play the extract again and check the change is audible to you.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level Music tutor in Guided Learning mode. Here is a YouTube link to the extract and my own aural annotations at four time-stamps. Do not give me the correct analysis. For each of my labels, ask me one question about what I heard that led to it - bass movement, quality of the chord, cadence. If my label is wrong, point to the feature I should listen for again, without naming the chord. At the end, list which of my terms were imprecise rather than wrong.
The three routes
A → A*

Unfamiliar repertoire: an unheard work in the same style, annotated cold, then defended. Feedback focuses on precision - inversion figures, cadence type, modulation destination - and on writing the analysis in examiner vocabulary within timed conditions.

B → A*

Two time-stamps only, with a chord-quality checklist and a modelled annotation from the teacher. Weekly aural dictation of the same extract until labels are stable, plus monthly review of terminology across all set works studied.

C → A*

Begin with hearing the difference between two chords played in class, then one time-stamp with the chord options given. The scaffolds are the options list and a keyboard; both are withdrawn once the student names changes unaided.

SEND adaptation. A student with slow auditory processing keeps the score-with-timings and unlimited replays; the number of moments falls but the depth of justification required stays the same.
Rosenshine

  • 6 Check for understanding. Circled changes with reasons show whether the correction was understood or copied.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Terminology is revisited across all set works each month.
SAMR · Modification

Ear-training with instant questioning on a student's own annotations is not a task a single teacher could run for thirty students at once.

TPACK · TCK

Sound is transformed into named harmonic content, the specific representation music analysis is assessed on.

Proximity 3: accurate harmonic terminology is the A* aural discriminator. Evidence 2: feedback and retrieval. Dose 1: one extract a week, needs teacher time-stamping. Low cost and risk 1: Gemini's aural claims can be wrong, so labels are rechecked in class.

EEF feedback strand; no music-specific AI evidence base.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

3Interrogate a technique on video, then test it physicallyStudents find a technique in a video and contextual images through Guided Learning, write a comparison with their own work, then make a physical trial; the sketchbook, not the chat, is the evidence.Art6AugmentationTPK49Medium effort

Board Art & Design (Art, Craft and Design), Pearson Edexcel (9AD0 (Advanced GCE in Art and Design - Art, Craft and Desig…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Name the technique and two artists; state plainly that no AI image or text may enter the portfolio (JCQ).
  2. Post the Guided Learning link with prompts: 'Show me a video on this technique' and 'Ask me what to look for'.
  3. Require a sketchbook double page: what they observed, one question Gemini asked them, and a physical trial.
  4. Review the double pages in a ten-minute tutorial and agree the next refinement step with the student.
Student workflow
  1. Watch the suggested video and note what the artist actually does differently.
  2. Answer Gemini's questions about your own piece in your sketchbook, in writing.
  3. Make a physical trial of the technique and photograph both attempts.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level Art tutor in Guided Learning mode. I am working on a personal investigation and I need to understand a technique, not have work made for me. Show me a video on it and one or two contextual images, then ask me questions about what I can see and how it differs from my own piece, which I will describe. Do not generate artwork, write my annotation, or tell me what to make next. Ask me what I will try physically and why, and challenge my reason once.
The three routes
A → A*

Push contextual depth: the student compares two artists' handling of the same problem and argues which serves their own intention, then makes two trials and selects one with written reasons. Annotation is assessed for critical judgement.

B → A*

Coverage and habit: one technique a fortnight from a teacher-set list, each with a modelled sketchbook page, so the journey is documented consistently rather than assembled in a rush before the deadline.

C → A*

One technique, broken into three physical trials with a written prompt sheet for each. A high success rate matters more than range; the prompt sheet is removed once the student annotates a trial unaided.

SEND adaptation. A student with ADHD benefits from a single time-boxed question set and an immediate physical trial in the same session, so the dialogue does not replace making.
Rosenshine

  • 9 Independent practice. The physical trial and its annotation are made unaided in the sketchbook.
SAMR · Augmentation

Contextual research and video demonstration already happen; the tool finds them faster and adds questioning, but the making is unchanged.

TPACK · TPK

Questioning before making is a general pedagogical move; the tool supplies it rather than any art-specific representation.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: refinement matters but the portfolio mark rests on making. Evidence 2: feedback and metacognition. Dose 1: fortnightly tutorials. Low cost and risk 1: JCQ risk is real, contained by a no-AI-content rule and sketchbook evidence.

EEF metacognition strand; JCQ non-exam assessment guidance.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed

Risks JCQ: no AI-generated image or text may appear in the portfolio; the sketchbook trial is the evidence of authorship. Image generation for under-18s is unconfirmed (check availability). Fallback: a teacher-curated video playlist and question sheet.

Success measure Sketchbooks show dated trials with reasons, and contextual annotation moves from description to judgement.

4Diagnose why your French structure failed, then rebuild itFrom their own marked translation, students ask Guided Learning for a decision diagram of the trigger they missed, write the rule themselves, then face French quiz items forcing production of that structure.French9AugmentationTCK126Medium effort

A* lever Accuracy of complex structures in the AQA translation into French under time: subjunctive triggers, tense sequence, agreement and pronoun placement.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Mark the translation yourself and code errors by structure rather than by sentence: subjunctive trigger, tense sequence after si, agreement, pronoun order.
  2. Students paste their own coded errors into Guided Learning and ask for a labelled decision diagram of one trigger only.
  3. Require that diagram checked against the textbook page you name; generated grammar diagrams are not exam-board material.
  4. Require the rule written in the student's own words, then: quiz me in French on that rule, with ten new sentences to produce.
  5. Collect rule cards and cause logs, then reteach the trigger most often misdiagnosed in the next lesson's daily review.
Student workflow
  1. Sort your own marked errors by structure before opening Guided Learning; name the trigger you think you missed.
  2. Ask for a decision diagram of that trigger, then write the rule in your own words.
  3. Produce ten French quiz sentences using the structure: no dictionary, no copying the diagram's examples.
  4. Log why you chose the wrong form and what your version actually meant.
Copy and paste
Tu es mon professeur de français de niveau A. Voici mes erreurs corrigées, classées par structure. Ne réécris pas mes phrases. Explique-moi d'abord le déclencheur avec un schéma clair et étiqueté, puis demande-moi de formuler la règle avec mes propres mots. Ensuite, pose-moi dix phrases à traduire en français qui obligent à utiliser cette structure, une à la fois, sans donner la réponse avant ma tentative. Quand je me trompe, dis-moi ce que ma version signifie réellement et demande-moi pourquoi je l'ai choisie.
The three routes
A → A*

Accuracy is mostly there, so target the remaining precision slips: quiz sentences must combine two structures at once, for example a subjunctive inside reported speech, and be produced under a two-minute timer with the diagram closed.

B → A*

Diagnose systematically, one trigger a week across a term, each revisited in the following week's starter. The labelled diagram stays visible while producing sentences in week one, then is withdrawn, and the rule is rewritten from memory before each quiz.

C → A*

Begin with one high-utility structure and eight easy sentences for a success rate above eighty per cent. Verb tables and the diagram stay on the desk, withdrawn after two unaided successes. Five minutes of weekly retrieval keeps the structure automatic rather than relearned.

SEND adaptation. For a student with dyslexia, accept the rule recorded aloud rather than written and enlarge the diagram; the ten production sentences and the no-dictionary rule stay exactly as they are.
Rosenshine
  • 2 Present new material in small steps. One trigger at a time, represented as a decision diagram before any production is attempted.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Ten production sentences and the cause log reveal whether the rule is understood or merely copied.
  • 1 Daily review. The most misdiagnosed trigger becomes the next lesson's starter for the whole class.

Board Geography, OCR (H481 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Geography (fir…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Name the OCR model and the case study and give students the figures table they must use; no figures come from Gemini.
  2. Post the Guided Learning link with the prompt: explain the model with a labelled diagram, then ask me where my figures do not fit.
  3. Require an annotated diagram on paper: three figures that fit, two that do not, and one human consequence of the mismatch.
  4. Add: quiz me on which statistical test suits this data and why, with the choice justified in writing before any explanation is read.
  5. Mark ten annotated diagrams against the specification wording and reteach the limitation the class most often misses.
Student workflow
  1. Request the labelled diagram, then write down the two assumptions the model depends on.
  2. Enter your case-study figures and state in writing where the model fails.
  3. Write one consequence for the people who live there before asking Gemini anything further.
  4. Justify your statistical test choice in writing, then check the explanation against the specification.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level Geography tutor in Guided Learning mode. Explain this model with a labelled diagram and tell me the assumptions it depends on. Do not evaluate it for me. I will then give you real figures from my case study: ask me questions that make me notice where the model does not fit, one at a time, and make me say what that mismatch means for the people who live there. Afterwards quiz me on which statistical test suits my data, but ask for my choice and my reason before you say anything.
The three routes
A → A*

Push synopticity and precision: the mismatch must be expressed with figures and units and a named place, and a second model that handles the anomaly better is judged in one paragraph against stated criteria under exam timing.

B → A*

Cover the specification systematically, one model a week, with the teacher's assumptions list supplied in week one and withdrawn by week four. Each session opens with cumulative retrieval of earlier models' limits and their case-study figures.

C → A*

Use one familiar case study and two figures only, with a printed sentence frame for stating a limit. The success rate stays high and the frame goes after two unaided uses. Statistical tests arrive as a single decision question each week.

SEND adaptation. For a student with a visual impairment, ask for the diagram described in words as well as drawn and supply the figures table as accessible text; the evaluation and test choice are unchanged.

The task is redesigned: instead of learning a model and evaluating it much later, students stress-test it against their own figures inside one lesson.

TPACK · TCK

Custom practice quizzes, flashcards and study guides

Generates unlimited custom quizzes on any topic or from uploaded notes and past papers, with hints, explanations for right and wrong answers and a summary of weak areas; also builds flashcards and study guides. In the Classroom Gemini tab, pupils pick a class and assignment so quizzes and flashcards draw on the teacher's materials.

Options. Ask for multiple-choice or open-ended questions, a question count, a difficulty or a named specification topic; upload notes, a mark scheme or a chapter; in Classroom use the Learn with Gemini starter prompts; sync NotebookLM notebooks for flashcards, study guides, infographics and audio overviews. Teachers can post NotebookLM notebooks to Classroom; assigning Gems to pupils was announced but is unconfirmed.

Constraints. OpenStax (@OpenStax) practice content is US-only, English-only, 18+ and not for school accounts. Quizzes and flashcards for all ages are confirmed via the Classroom Gemini tab since 10 August 2026; in the standalone app under-18 quiz generation was 'expanding' from June 2025 (assumed live). Study notebooks (diagnostic quiz, adaptive plan) are not yet on school accounts.

1Run a weekly cumulative quiz across the whole specificationGemini builds a cumulative quiz from teacher-uploaded set-text notes and past questions; the weak-area summary becomes flashcards the student writes themselves, and quotations are recalled unaided.English Literature9AugmentationTPK1710Low effort

A* lever Retrieval strength across every text and critical position, so no paper is the weak one that costs the A*.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload your own anonymised topic notes and a list of past questions per text; no pupil names or marks.
  2. In the Classroom Gemini tab, post starter prompts tied to the unit; ask for ten open-ended questions, mixed texts, hardest first.
  3. Require quotations written from memory on paper, then the weak-area summary pasted into a shared retrieval log.
  4. Read the logs weekly and reteach the two positions or texts that recur, using your own exemplar paragraph.
Student workflow
  1. Answer every question in writing before asking for any explanation.
  2. Write each quotation from memory; mark yourself against the text afterwards.
  3. Turn your weak areas into flashcards you write in your own words.
  4. Repeat last week's weakest three questions before starting this week's quiz.
Copy and paste
You are my A-level English Literature tutor in Guided Learning mode. Using the notes and question list I have uploaded, give me ten open-ended questions across all the texts I have studied, hardest first, one at a time. I will answer in writing, from memory, including quotations. Do not show me the answer or a model paragraph before I answer. After each answer, tell me what a top-band response would have added, in one sentence. At the end, summarise my three weakest areas as topics, not as answers.
The three routes
A → A*

Questions target critical positions and comparative judgement, not plot. Answers are timed single paragraphs, marked against the top band, and the weak-area summary decides which examiner-report comment the student reads that week.

B → A*

Board Further Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9FM0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Further Math…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Open Guided Learning from the Gemini text box: Add files, More tools, Guided Learning, then upload your two topic lists and last term's past-paper questions.
  2. Ask for twelve unlabelled items at raised difficulty, six from each qualification, drawn only from the uploaded topics, and check every item against the specification before issuing.
  3. Issue it as a forty-five-minute Friday block with the qualification labels removed, and require a triage line at the top of each answer.
  4. Collect the triage lines, not the answers, count the items mis-triaged, and reteach the two boundaries the class cannot see.
Student workflow
  1. Before any algebra, write for each item whether Mathematics methods suffice or Further Mathematics machinery is needed, and name the method.
  2. Solve in the order you judge cheapest, keep the clock visible, and stop at forty-five minutes wherever you are.

Copy and paste
I am a Year 13 student taking Edexcel Mathematics and Further Mathematics together. Using only the two topic lists and past-paper questions I have uploaded, write twelve practice items at the hardest difficulty these papers reach, six from each qualification, as one mixed list with no labels and no answers. Do not tell me which qualification an item belongs to. When I have attempted them, ask me one question at a time about the ones I got wrong, and give hints only, never a full solution.
The three routes
A → A*

Twelve items from the low-facility tail, timed at the real mark-per-minute rate. The triage line must also predict which two items will take longest, and comparing that prediction with the outturn is the coaching conversation rather than the score itself.

B → A*

Eight items, two topics a fortnight, with the triage step modelled first by the teacher on two worked examples. Guided Learning may explain the boundary between the two qualifications explicitly. The block runs at thirty minutes and grows to forty-five across a term.

C → A*

Six items, labelled by qualification for the first month so triage is confirmation rather than judgement, and two of them already started. Aim for a high success rate; remove the labels one topic at a time, and only after two clean sets.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed, cut the block to eight items at the same difficulty and grant the agreed extra time, so the interleaving demand is met without a pace penalty.

NotebookLM (Gemini Notebook)

A grounded knowledge base built from teacher-curated sources. · 9 sub-tools · 48 examples

Timing constraint: student access to NotebookLM has not been released yet. Teachers can build and check notebooks now, but anything that needs a student to open one has to wait until access lands. Plan it for later in the programme.

Availability. Core Workspace service, on by default for Education Fundamentals, Standard and Plus; AI Pro for Education add-on raises limits (reported April 2026 Education Plus/Teaching and Learning expansion: unconfirmed). Available to Education users of all ages with stricter under-18 policies, but several outputs are 18+. Admins can turn NotebookLM off per OU. Classroom integration (Classwork, Create, Attach, NotebookLM, pulling class materials; since Sept 2025) needs Gemini, NotebookLM and Gemini in Classroom On.

Audio Overview

Generates a downloadable spoken overview of selected sources. The default 'Deep Dive' is a two-host conversation; other formats give a short single-speaker summary, a constructive critique of a piece of work such as an essay, or a two-host debate. Interactive mode lets the listener join and question the hosts.

Options. Formats: Deep Dive (default), Brief (single speaker, under two minutes), Critique, Debate. Length: Shorter / Default / Longer (English only). Language: 80+ output languages. Focus prompt to target topics or set expertise level. Interactive mode ('Join', English only). Choose which sources to include. Share link (requires notebook sharing), share notebook, or download the audio file. Counts against compute-based daily limits (standard tier for Education without add-on).

Constraints. No age gate stated on the help page. A 'Lecture' format reported by press: unconfirmed. Interactive mode and length controls are English only. Public link sharing disabled for Education accounts. Generation takes several minutes.

Board Physics, OCR Physics A (H556) (H556 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Physics A (spe…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build one notebook per module from the specification, your own lesson notes and the required-practical sheets; add no pupil data of any kind.
  2. Generate an Audio Overview per topic with format Brief, length Shorter, and a focus prompt naming the definitions, units and equations only.
  3. Listen, check every equation and unit against the specification, then download the audio files and post them to the Classroom topic.
  4. Open each lesson with a three-question written retrieval quiz on that topic, marked in class against your own answer key.
Student workflow
  1. Replay the Brief audio the night before and again on the way into the lesson.
  2. Write the definitions, units and equations from memory before the audio is available to check.
  3. Mark your own quiz, then log which unit or significant-figure error recurred.
Copy and paste
Produce a single-speaker recap of under two minutes on [topic] using only the sources in this notebook. Cover only the definitions, quantities, units and equations the A-level specification requires for this topic. State each equation in words and then in symbols, and say the SI unit of every quantity. Do not add worked examples, analogies or exam technique. Speak slowly and leave a short pause between items. Do not mention any student, school or teacher name.
The three routes
A → A*

Set the focus prompt to the rarely examined definitions and derived units only, since the common ones are secure. Pair each audio with one hardest-item calculation from a past paper, done in five minutes with units and significant figures checked.

B → A*

Generate a Brief for every topic in the module and schedule them across a six-week spaced cycle, so knowledge gaps surface. Students keep a self-quizzing log naming the topic, the error type and the fix they will apply.

C → A*

Break each topic into two shorter Briefs and pair them with a partly completed definitions sheet. Students fill three blanks, not twelve, and repeat the same audio weekly until they score full marks twice running.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation: a student with dyspraxia dictates the retrieval answers using Docs voice typing, so handwriting speed does not mask secure recall; the questions themselves stay unmodified.

  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Narrow audios and three-question quizzes keep success high enough to build recall fluency.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Briefs recirculate on a spaced cycle across the whole module.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 2: secure recall frees capacity for the hardest items. Evidence 3: retrieval and spaced practice are EEF's strongest. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, reusable for years. Cost and risk 2: short, narrow audio is quick to verify. Total 9.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Create a notebook holding the specification, the assessment-objective grid, the relevant examiner report and one anonymised A-grade essay you have retyped without names.
  2. In Studio choose Audio Overview, format Critique, length Default, with a focus prompt directing the critique at the AO3 top band only.
  3. Listen first and check every claim against the mark scheme; discard the audio if the hosts invent descriptors or misread the AO weighting.
  4. Play the critique in lesson, pausing after each criticism so students locate the evidence in their printed copy of the essay.

  1. Read the anonymised essay silently and rank its three weakest paragraphs before hearing any critique.
  2. Annotate each criticism you agree with; write one sentence rejecting any criticism you think is wrong.
  3. Redraft the weakest paragraph to the AO3 top band, then swap and mark against the descriptor.
Copy and paste
Critique the attached anonymised A-level English Literature essay using only the specification, assessment-objective grid and examiner report in this notebook. Judge it against the top band for AO3 evaluation and AO2 analysis of language, form and structure. For each weakness, quote the exact phrase from the essay and name the descriptor it fails to meet. Do not rewrite the essay and do not invent criteria. Finish by naming the two changes that would most raise the mark, and state the band the essay currently sits in.
The three routes
A → A*

Use an essay already awarded a high A and focus the critique on AO3 alone, so students hear the difference between a judgement asserted and one built through explicit criteria. They redraft the conclusion only, in a timed eight minutes.

B → A*

Use a mid-B essay and widen the focus prompt to AO1 and AO2, so terminology and quotation selection are covered. Give students the descriptor grid and a sentence-stem bank, and rebuild two paragraphs across a fortnight.

C → A*

Critique a single paragraph rather than a whole essay, at length Shorter. Pair the audio with a teacher-written model of that paragraph. Students fix one named feature, such as embedding quotation, and repeat it weekly.

SEND adaptation. A student with dyslexia keeps the downloaded audio plus the essay printed in a sans-serif face at 14 point, so criticism arrives by ear while evidence stays visible; the redraft demand is unchanged.

A* lever A* history builds a sustained, criteria-led judgement between interpretations; A-grade answers narrate both sides and then assert a bare preference.

Board History, AQA (7042 — AQA A-level History) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a notebook holding two contrasting secondary extracts, the relevant source booklet and the AO3 interpretations mark scheme; school-owned material only.
  2. Select those sources, choose Audio Overview, format Debate, length Longer, with a focus prompt naming the enquiry question and the two positions.
  3. Check the audio for invented quotations or dates against the extracts, and regenerate with a tighter focus prompt if either host drifts.
  4. Give students a two-column criteria grid before playing, then play the debate once without pausing.
Student workflow
  1. Score each host live against the criteria: use of evidence, handling of counter-argument, precision of claim.
  2. Identify the strongest point the weaker host made, and the weakest point the stronger host made.
  3. Write a 400-word judgement that reaches a verdict by criteria, quoting the extracts, not the audio.
Copy and paste
Debate this enquiry question using only the sources in this notebook: [paste enquiry question]. Host one argues [position A]; host two argues [position B]. Each host must quote only from the extracts provided, name the historian, and respond directly to the other's strongest point rather than restating their own case. Do not invent evidence, dates or quotations. Keep the register of an A-level history seminar, using terms such as interpretation, provenance and weight of evidence. End without resolving the question, so the listener must reach the verdict.
The three routes
A → A*

Withhold the criteria grid and require students to generate the criteria themselves before listening, then defend their choice. The judgement is written in twenty-five minutes under examination conditions and marked against the AO3 top band only.

B → A*

Supply the criteria grid with one worked example, and pause the debate at each turn to check understanding. Students first rebuild each host's argument in three bullets, then write the judgement with a paragraph-structure scaffold.

C → A*

Use a Shorter debate on one narrow disagreement. Give a teacher-written model judgement to imitate and a sentence-stem bank. Students complete a comparison table before writing two paragraphs, with the stems removed after four weeks.

SEND adaptation. A student with ADHD receives the debate as two downloaded halves with a tick-box scoring sheet, so attention is anchored to a task; the written judgement stays full length.
Rosenshine

  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. The criteria grid scaffolds the move from describing interpretations to weighing them.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Rotate the enquiry question so earlier topics resurface in later debates.

The tool redesigns the seminar: two positions are argued aloud at length, which one teacher cannot stage alone, and students take the arbiter's role rather than a side.

TPACK · TCK

The audio represents historiographical disagreement as live argument, transforming static extracts into the contested interpretation the specification actually assesses.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: criteria-led judgement is the AO3 discriminator. Evidence 2: oral rehearsal and peer scoring are solid but less evidenced than feedback. Dose 1: once a unit. Cost and risk 1: invented quotations and dates must be checked. Total 7.

EEF oral language and metacognition strands; examiner reports on judgement as the A* feature.

Teacher workflow

  2. In Studio open Audio Overview, set output language to Spanish, keep format Deep Dive, and add a focus prompt naming the theme and an educated adult register.
  3. Length control and Interactive mode are English only, so accept the default length; whether a regional accent can be requested is undocumented (check availability).
  4. Listen right through against your own sources, checking register and any invented statistics, then download the audio and post it in Classroom with no transcript.
Student workflow

  2. Listen again, noting five complex structures you could not have produced yourself: subjunctive, pronoun placement, tense sequence.
  3. Write a ninety-word reply in Spanish arguing against one claim, reusing three of those structures.
Copy and paste
Habla en español de España, en registro culto de adulto, sobre el tema indicado en el mundo hispanohablante, usando solamente las fuentes de este cuaderno. Presenta dos posturas opuestas, cada una con argumentos desarrollados y datos citados de las fuentes. No inventes cifras ni ejemplos. Emplea estructuras complejas: subjuntivo, oraciones concesivas, pronombres de objeto. No traduzcas al inglés y no expliques el vocabulario. Habla a velocidad natural, sin simplificar, y termina con dos preguntas dirigidas al oyente.
The three routes
A → A*

Use sources on an unfamiliar sub-theme and set a demanding focus prompt: two opposed positions with cited data and concessive structures. Students write the ninety-word rebuttal in eight timed minutes, then mark each other only on accuracy of complex structures and precision of idiom.

B → A*

Choose one familiar theme, generate weekly so the same high-utility structures recur, and issue a printed bank of five target structures beforehand. Students transcribe two sentences verbatim before replying, so accuracy is checked against what they actually heard rather than what they assumed.

C → A*

Pause the audio every thirty seconds against a printed gapped summary in Spanish, and replay twice. The written reply drops to forty words and one target structure, repeated weekly until it is produced unprompted, after which the gapped summary is withdrawn.

SEND adaptation. A student with an auditory processing difficulty replays the downloaded file on headphones one sentence at a time; the listening load is staged but the Spanish reply and structure demand stay identical.

5Join Interactive audio to interrogate study methodologyInteractive mode lets a student with ADHD break into the hosts' conversation with their own methodological questions, so attention is held by participation while the AO3 elaboration demand stays exactly as examiners set it.SEND: ADHD in Psychology6ModificationTPACK369High effort

A* lever AQA Psychology A* turns on research methods and AO3 evaluation elaborated to a consequence for the theory, not a list of labelled criticisms.

Board Psychology, AQA (7182 - AQA A-level Psychology (first teaching 2015)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a notebook with the AQA specification's research-methods section, two study summaries you have written yourself, and the mark scheme for sixteen-mark questions.
  2. Generate an Audio Overview with a focus prompt on the study's design, sampling and controls, then use Join to test whether the hosts answer methodological questions accurately.
  3. Give each student three question stems to ask live: sampling bias, control of extraneous variables, and what the flaw means for the theory's validity.
  4. Interactive mode is English only and needs the notebook shared with edit access; check every live answer against your own summaries before students accept it.
Student workflow
  1. Write three methodological questions before listening; you may not ask a question you have not written down.
  2. Join the audio, ask your questions aloud, and record each answer in one sentence.
  3. Convert your best answer into a full AO3 paragraph naming the consequence for the theory.
Copy and paste
Using only the sources in this notebook, discuss the methodology of the study I name: sampling method, experimental design, controls and measurement. For every criticism you raise, state what it means for the validity of the theory the study supports, not simply that it is a limitation. Use the exact terminology in the specification: independent measures, standardisation, demand characteristics, ecological validity. Give figures only where a source supplies them, and say so when a source does not. Do not evaluate the study's ethics unless I ask, and do not write the evaluation paragraph for me.
The three routes
A → A*

Students interrogate a study they already know well and must push the hosts to a consequence for the theory. Any answer stopping at a label such as lacking ecological validity is rejected in writing, with the student supplying the missing link themselves in two sentences.

B → A*

Pre-teach the three question stems, then run the same study twice a fortnight apart so procedure and figures become automatic. Students keep a running AO3 bank of one elaborated paragraph per study, checked fortnightly against the sixteen-mark mark scheme rather than against each other.

C → A*

Give two of the three questions ready-made and model the third aloud. Students complete a sentence frame linking flaw to consequence, then read it back to a partner. Add one unaided question each fortnight until all three questions are genuinely theirs.

SEND adaptation. Second adaptation for the same student: agree a fixed turn order so waiting is predictable, and allow recorded answers to be typed rather than handwritten; the AO3 paragraph demand is unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every student asks their own methodological questions aloud, so the questioning rate per pupil rises sharply.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Written answers to their own questions reveal whether a criticism has been linked to a consequence.
  • 9 Independent practice. The elaborated AO3 paragraph is written alone, from their own notes, against the sixteen-mark descriptors.
SAMR · Modification

The task changes from listening to a recap into conducting a live methodological interrogation, so the student sets the agenda instead of receiving one.

TPACK · TPACK

Cost and risk 0: answers arrive unverified, English only, and every pupil needs edit access. Total 6.

A* lever Analytical argument about the set text rather than plot retelling, in the formal register the mark scheme expects: the gap that fluency hides in community languages.

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a notebook from four or five Italian-language sources on the set text: a published critical essay, the author's preface, a review, and your own scene notes.
  2. In Studio choose Audio Overview, format Debate, output language Italian, and a focus prompt naming the question, for example the narrator's reliability.
  3. Listen before sharing and note two claims the hosts get wrong; set those as the pupil's checking task rather than removing them.
  4. Share the notebook with the Italian group as Viewer and attach it to Classwork; viewers cannot generate, so the audio must be teacher-made.
Student workflow
  1. Listen once, then list in Italian the two critics' claims and the evidence each uses.
  2. Check the two claims the teacher flagged against the text itself and say which host is wrong.
  3. Write your own paragraph taking a third position, borrowing the critics' connectives, not their opinions.
  4. Reuse five phrases of academic register from the audio in your next timed essay.
Copy and paste
Focus this debate on one question only: is the narrator of the set text reliable? Give each host a clear position and make them disagree about the evidence, not about taste. Quote short passages from my sources and say which source each claim comes from. Use the formal register of Italian literary criticism, define each critical term the first time it is used, and address a Year 13 A-level audience who speak Italian at home but have not studied literary analysis. Do not summarise the plot.
The three routes
A → A*

The A-to-A* pupil already analyses, so generate two debates on the same question from different source sets and ask which argument is better and why, with a written judgement. Then have them write the third host's script and defend it aloud.

B → A*

The B-to-A* pupil retells plot, so pair the debate with the source extracts and mark where each host moves from event to interpretation. Supply a list of the connectives used and require three of them in the next paragraph; drop the list after a month.

C → A*

The C-to-A* pupil needs shorter input, so generate a Brief single-speaker overview of under two minutes on one scene, replayed across the week, before any debate. Ask for one sentence of interpretation at a time, and build to a paragraph over a fortnight.

SEND adaptation. A pupil with a specific learning difficulty listens to the downloaded audio at reduced speed in a media player while following the printed Italian extracts, so listening and reading support each other.
Rosenshine

  • 1 Daily review. A downloaded ten-minute audio can be replayed on the commute across the week.
  • 3 Ask questions. Pupils answer a set question in Italian after each listening rather than listening passively.

Listening comprehension becomes a model of academic argument in Italian, generated from department sources on the actual set text; the task is redesigned, not merely made more convenient.

Video Overview

Generates a narrated video from the sources. 'Explainer' is a structured slide-style walkthrough with visuals; 'Short' is a roughly 60-second portrait video on key concepts; 'Cinematic' is an immersive animated narrative. Can be steered to a topic, downloaded, or shared with the notebook.

Options. Formats: Explainer, Short (~60 s, Nano Banana 2 Lite), Cinematic (English only). Visual styles (18+, Explainer only): Auto-select, Classic, Whiteboard, Watercolor, Retro Print, Heritage, Paper-craft, Kawaii, Anime, or a custom description. Language: 60+ for Explainer and Short. Optional steering prompt (suggested or custom topics). Playback speed, full screen, download file, share link. Mobile app has fewer options.

Constraints. Cinematic is 18+ and needs an AI Pro/Ultra/Expanded for Education add-on. Visual styles are 18+, so under-18 pupils get Classic. Whether under-18s can generate Explainer/Short is not explicitly stated: unconfirmed. Generation can exceed 30 minutes. Public sharing disabled for Education.

Copy and paste
Make a sixty-second recap of [topic] for an A-level computer science student, using only the sources in this notebook. A → A*

B → A*

Cover every topic on a spaced six-week cycle so gaps surface, and pair each Short with a partly worked definition table. Students complete the table, then answer one past-paper part on that topic under timed conditions.

C → A*

Use two Shorts per topic, the first on the underlying idea and the second on terminology, with a glossary card supplied. Students match terms to definitions to a high success rate before meeting any exam wording.

A* lever A* maths is won in the last ten to fifteen per cent of marks: multi-step modelling and proof items where method choice and accuracy decide the grade.

Board Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9MA0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Mathematics,…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload to a notebook the specification, the formula booklet, your own worked solutions and the published mark schemes for three hardest past-paper questions.
  2. Generate a Video Overview, format Explainer, with a steering prompt naming one question and asking for method choice and justification, not the numerical answer.
  3. Watch it through and check every line against your worked solution; generation can exceed thirty minutes, so prepare a week ahead.
  4. Set the question cold for fifteen minutes, collect scripts, then release the checked video in Classroom for self-diagnosis.
Student workflow
  1. Attempt the question cold, showing every line, before the video is released.
  2. Watch at reduced playback speed and mark the first line where your method diverged.
  3. Write the decision you should have made and why, then redo it from that line.
  4. Add the error to your personal error log and retest it in next week's starter.
Copy and paste
Explain the method for question [number] in the sources in this notebook, for an A-level mathematics student who has already attempted it. Do not state the final answer. Work through the decisions: why this method rather than an alternative, where the modelling assumption enters, which line most candidates get wrong, and what the mark scheme awards at each stage. Use correct notation and name the theorems used. Stop before the final line of arithmetic and tell the viewer to complete it themselves.
The three routes
A → A*

Use only the final parts of the hardest questions and steer the prompt at error elimination and checking routines. Students must predict the mark scheme's allocation before watching, then justify their own method in writing against it.

B → A*

Steer the prompt to a full worked example with every algebraic step named, then fade: the second video omits the middle steps. Students complete two structurally similar questions before attempting the unfamiliar-context version.

C → A*

Steer the prompt to the prerequisite skill, such as rearranging or index laws, before the exam item itself. Students complete four short, high-success questions with the video paused after each step, then attempt one exam part.

SEND adaptation. A student with dyspraxia affecting written output records a spoken method commentary in Classroom instead of a written error log; the algebra is still worked by hand.

Teacher workflow

  2. Generate a Video Overview, format Explainer, steering prompt: set out the premises and conclusion of [argument], then the strongest objection.

Using only the sources in this notebook, set out [named argument] as numbered premises leading to a conclusion, in the wording the A-level specification uses. A → A*

  1. Collect four French-language articles on a research-project theme, for example la loi de 1905, into a notebook with the AQA speaking mark scheme.
  2. Generate a Video Overview, format Explainer, output language French, with a steering prompt naming the theme and requiring two opposed positions and no English.

Copy and paste
Explique en français, sans une seule phrase en anglais, le thème indiqué en te servant uniquement des sources de ce cahier. Présente deux positions opposées, chacune avec deux arguments et un exemple précis tiré des sources. N'invente aucune donnée et ne cite aucun chiffre absent des sources. Utilise des connecteurs logiques et le subjonctif là où la langue l'exige. Termine par trois questions difficiles qu'un examinateur pourrait poser à un candidat qui défendrait l'une de ces positions. A → A*

A → A*

B → A*

C → A*

Cut the deck to a four-paragraph exemplar and revise slides into plain-language statements of what each paragraph does. Students fill a structure grid, then write two paragraphs to a high success rate before a whole essay.

Using only the sources in this notebook, build a detailed slide deck on required practical [number and title] for A-level chemistry. One slide per stage: purpose, apparatus and quantities, method, principal sources of uncertainty, how each affects the result, how percentage uncertainty is calculated here, and how the procedure could be improved. Prompt for a Short deck on one practical in plain language, and supply a completed uncertainty calculation to imitate. Students repeat that calculation type across four practicals until accurate twice running.

C → A*

Reports (study guide, briefing doc, FAQ, timeline, custom report)

Produces written syntheses of the sources. 'Document' reports use templates or formats suggested from the content (Google names Study Guide, Briefing Doc, Blog Post; FAQ and Timeline appear in older lists) or a custom prompt. 'Interactive' reports (Learning Overview template) embed suggested Studio artefacts such as quizzes or audio.

Options. Studio, Reports, then Document or Interactive. Templates plus dynamically suggested formats (for example glossary, character analysis) based on the sources. Edit a template's settings before generating; 'Generate now' or 'Generate later'. Custom report via prompt. Share an individual report link (recipient needs notebook access) or the notebook. Third-party guides describe export to Google Docs.

Constraints. Interactive reports web only; 'some content' 18+. Current help page names only Learning Overview and generic templates, so FAQ, Timeline and Table of Contents as presets: unconfirmed. Export to Google Docs: unconfirmed on the help page. Google notes reports may contain inaccuracies.

Teacher workflow

  2. In Studio choose Reports, then Document, then a custom report, and paste the prompt asking for named errors with marks lost and the fix.

Using only the examiner reports, mark schemes and specification in this notebook, list the errors A-level candidates actually make on [topic]. For each: state the error in one sentence, name the question type where it appears, say how many marks it typically costs, quote the examiner report's own wording, and give one checking routine a candidate can apply in under thirty seconds. The three routes
A → A*

Restrict the report to the final parts of questions and to precision errors such as notation, domain and exact form. Students build a personal checking routine and are timed on whether it costs under two minutes per paper.

C → A*

Limit the report to the five commonest errors on foundational skills such as algebraic manipulation. Supply a worked correction for each and drill one error type per week until it disappears twice running.

Teacher workflow
  1. Curate this year's sources yourself: Hansard extracts, Supreme Court judgment summaries and Congressional research briefings, plus the Edexcel specification and comparative theory pages.
  2. Choose Reports, then Document, then the Briefing Doc template, edited for A-level and prompted to list only what the sources evidence, with dates.
  3. Verify every date, name and outcome against the source and delete any example the sources do not support, because reports can contain inaccuracies.
  4. Issue the briefing only after students have written from memory, so it corrects and updates rather than supplies their examples.
Student workflow
  1. Write your best current UK and USA example for the institution from memory, with dates.
  2. Read the briefing and mark every example of yours that is out of date or wrong.
  3. Rewrite one paragraph reaching a comparative judgement, naming the theoretical approach you are using.
Copy and paste
Using only the sources in this notebook, produce a briefing document on the institution I name for A-level Politics. For the UK and the USA separately, list the events of the last two years that the sources evidence, each with its date, the actors involved and the outcome. Then list the points of comparison the sources support, labelled structural, rational or cultural. Include no example the sources do not contain, and do not write the evaluative judgement: leave that to the student.
The three routes
A → A*

These students hold examples but recycle textbook ones. Require every paragraph of the next essay to use a briefing example and to label its comparative approach, with the judgement built from the significance of the difference rather than asserted in a final sentence.

B → A*

Issue one briefing a fortnight across the institutions, with a cumulative examples grid students complete from memory before reading. Model one full comparative paragraph aloud, then fade to a sentence frame naming approach, evidence and judgement before removing it.

C → A*

Reduce the briefing to four events on a timeline and give a two-column grid to complete. Students write one comparison sentence per row before attempting a paragraph, and the frames are removed once dates and outcomes are secure.

SEND adaptation. A student with an autism spectrum condition benefits from the briefing's fixed order of events, dates and outcomes, which makes implicit comparisons explicit; the evaluative judgement remains entirely theirs to build.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. A two-minute written recall of dates and outcomes opens each lesson before the briefing is reopened.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. A cumulative examples grid is revisited monthly, so current examples are retained across both papers.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Marking their own out-of-date examples reveals who is still relying on the textbook.
SAMR · Augmentation

The teacher still curates and verifies every source; the report only synthesises them into a briefing far faster than writing one by hand.

TPACK · PCK

Knowing that examiners reward current examples and comparative approaches drives the task; the report only organises sources the teacher selected.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 2: currency of examples supports evaluative judgement rather than being it. Evidence 2: retrieval before reading and cumulative review are strong EEF strands. Dose 1: fortnightly, one class, with curation time. Cost and risk 1: every date must be verified. Total 6.

EEF retrieval and spaced practice strand; Edexcel examiner reports on the recycling of dated examples.

Success measure Essays cite examples from the last two years and label the comparative approach explicitly.

Flashcards

Generates a deck of question-and-answer cards from the sources for self-testing. Learners flip cards, mark 'Got it' or 'Missed it', shuffle, delete cards and press 'Explain' for a cited explanation. Progress is saved between sessions; the deck can be downloaded as CSV.

Options. Quantity: Fewer / Standard / More. Difficulty: Easy / Medium / Hard. Prompt for topic, outline, audience, style or focus. Source selection. Explain button with citations. Progress saved; Got it / Missed it; shuffle; delete items. CSV download. Web and mobile.

Constraints. Available to all ages (Workspace Updates, March 2026). Needs edit access to generate, so viewers use teacher-generated decks. Language option not documented. CSV download blocked with Play Books sources.

Board Mathematics, Pearson Edexcel (9MA0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Mathematics,…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload to Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM) the Edexcel specification, your worked-solution booklets and the last three examiner reports; no pupil names or marks.
  2. Studio, Flashcards. Quantity More, Difficulty Hard, prompt: 'Cards on method steps and standard results for Year 13 pure mathematics.'
  3. Share the notebook as Viewer; pupils flip cards and press Explain, marking Got it or Missed it across the fortnight.
  4. Download the deck CSV, ask pupils to report their Missed-it card numbers, and tally the ten most-missed cards.
  5. Open Monday with a five-question daily review on those ten, then reteach the single worst method at the board.
Student workflow
  1. Work each card answer on paper first, then flip; only then mark Got it or Missed it.
  2. Press Explain on any missed card and write the cited method step into your error log.
  3. Report your three most-missed card numbers to your teacher before Friday.
Copy and paste
Generate flashcards for Year 13 A-level Mathematics pupils working towards A*. Cover only method steps, standard results and conditions of use for the topics named in the uploaded specification. Each front must ask for a precise statement or a single method step, not a multi-part question. Each back must state the result exactly as the mark scheme words it, including conditions and ranges. Prioritise topics the uploaded examiner reports name as poorly answered. Use British mathematical notation. Do not include worked numerical examples.
The three routes
A → A*

Set Difficulty Hard and restrict sources to the examiner reports and your hardest-item booklet, so the deck holds only results these pupils misapply under time. Require each error-log entry to name the exam step lost, and cap flipping at eight seconds a card.

B → A*

Set Difficulty Medium and include the whole specification, so the deck diagnoses which topics are genuinely insecure rather than merely slow. Run the deck twice, four days apart, keep the Missed-it list visible, and pair each stubborn card with a teacher worked example before independent practice.

C → A*

Build a separate small deck, Quantity Fewer and Difficulty Easy, on algebraic prerequisites only, so the success rate stays high. Ten cards a night for a fortnight, teacher-checked, before adding any Year 13 content; add further cards in small blocks as each block is secured.

SEND adaptation. For dyspraxia affecting written output, allow the answer to be spoken to a partner or dictated rather than written before flipping; the recall demand and the eight-second cap stay unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 1 Daily review. Monday's five-question opener is built from the pupils' own most-missed cards, not the teacher's guess.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Re-running the deck each fortnight makes cumulative review of the whole specification routine.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The Missed-it tally gives a class-level check before the next topic is taught.
SAMR · Augmentation

The same retrieval task as paper flashcards, but generation is instant from the specification and the CSV plus Missed-it data makes the class-level pattern visible.

TPACK · TPK

The tool supplies the retrieval-and-review mechanism; the subject content comes entirely from the teacher's own specification and worked solutions.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: recall fluency feeds accuracy on the hardest items. Evidence 3: retrieval and spaced practice plus feedback. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, one deck. Low cost and risk 1: the teacher must check every card against the specification.

EEF: retrieval and spaced practice, and feedback, both strong at KS5.

Research: Generative AI tutoring and chatbo… Mixed Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Spaced practice and distributed l… Strong

Generate hard flashcards for Year 13 A-level Music pupils aiming for A*. Use only the uploaded set-work scores, glossary and analysis notes. Each front should name a bar or section and ask which harmonic, tonal, textural or rhythmic device operates there and what its effect is. A → A*

C → A*

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload to Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM) the AQA Spanish specification, your grammar-in-context booklet and six authentic articles the department licenses; no pupil work.
  2. Studio, Flashcards. Quantity More, Difficulty Hard, prompt: 'Front, a Spanish sentence with one gap only the subjunctive, correct tense or pronoun fits; back, the full sentence.'
  3. Check every card against the grammar booklet, delete any card that accepts two answers, then share the notebook as Viewer so pupils use your checked deck.
  4. Run it as a paired starter with shuffle on: one pupil reads the front, the partner says the whole sentence aloud inside five seconds.
  5. Fortnightly, dictate ten of the same sentences for written translation and compare that accuracy with the spoken rounds.
Student workflow
  1. Say the complete sentence aloud, not just the missing word, inside five seconds; then flip.
  2. Mark Got it only if your ending, agreement and pronoun position were all correct.
  3. Press Explain on a missed card and write the rule, in Spanish, in your structure log.
  4. Reuse two of the drilled structures unprompted in your next essay paragraph.
Copy and paste
Generate flashcards for Year 13 AQA Spanish pupils working towards A*. Use only the uploaded specification, grammar booklet and articles. Each front is one authentic Spanish sentence with a single gap that only a correct subjunctive, tense sequence, agreement or pronoun position can fill; keep the sentence in Spanish with no English. Each back gives the complete sentence and names the structure in Spanish. Draw contexts from the uploaded articles, not invented topics. Avoid single-word vocabulary items and memorised set phrases. Every card must require a grammatical decision, not recognition.
The three routes
A → A*

Keep Difficulty Hard and restrict sources to the articles and your idiom bank, so cards demand idiom and register rather than textbook phrasing. Cut the clock to four seconds, and require each pupil to log one structure they still translate from English rather than think in Spanish.

B → A*

Set Difficulty Medium and include the whole grammar booklet, so the deck diagnoses which tense and agreement families are genuinely insecure. Run the deck twice a week, keep the missed families visible on the board, and model one full-mark sentence before pupils practise that family independently.

C → A*

Build a separate small deck, Quantity Fewer and Difficulty Easy, on present and preterite endings and adjective agreement only, so the success rate stays high. Ten cards a night spoken to a partner, before any subjunctive card is added; add the next family only once the previous one is secure.

SEND adaptation. For a pupil with a stammer or speech anxiety, allow the sentence to be typed inside the same five seconds rather than spoken aloud; the production demand and the structure log stay identical.

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload the AQA Psychology specification, your study summaries with procedures and figures, the sixteen-mark mark scheme and two examiner reports; no pupil data.

  3. Check every figure and sample size against your summaries, delete cards the sources do not support, then share the notebook as Viewer.

  1. Answer the front from memory with the figures, then flip and correct your numbers.
  2. Write a three-link chain from the card: claim, evidence, consequence for the theory.

Copy and paste
Generate flashcards for Year 13 AQA Psychology pupils working towards A*. Use only the uploaded specification, study summaries and mark scheme. Each front asks for one precise element of a named study: sample, procedure, a control, or an exact finding with its figure. Each back states it exactly as the uploaded summary does, including numbers and units. Include cards on research methods and the mathematical content: levels of measurement, choice of statistical test, significance and calculation steps. Do not write evaluation on the backs; evaluation is the pupils' work. Use British spelling.
The three routes
A → A*

Keep Difficulty Hard and restrict sources to the examiner reports and the sixteen-mark mark scheme, so cards target the studies these pupils cite loosely. Require four links rather than three, with the final link naming what the finding costs the theory, and mark only that final link.

B → A*

Set Difficulty Medium across the whole specification, so the deck finds which topics are insecure before evaluation is attempted. Model a full three-link chain at the board, then fade: give the claim and evidence and ask only for the consequence, until pupils supply all three unaided.

C → A*

Use Quantity Fewer and Difficulty Easy on research-methods vocabulary and one core study per topic, so success stays high. Chains start at two links with a sentence stem supplied; add the third link and remove the stem once the AO1 figures are reliably recalled.

SEND adaptation. For a pupil with a working-memory difficulty, allow the chain to be dictated to a partner or recorded rather than written, and keep the card visible while the third link is composed.

A* lever A conceptually coherent directorial intention sustained through every practical and written choice, in precise theatrical vocabulary, rather than a list of unconnected staging ideas.

Board Drama (AQA option - board not confirmed by LAET), AQA (7262 (AQA A-level Drama and Theatre)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Upload the set text, your board's written-paper mark scheme, the practitioner texts the department holds and your own staging notes; no pupil work.
  2. Studio, Infographic. Orientation Landscape, Detail Standard, Style Instructional, prompt: 'One page showing a Brechtian concept and every design and performance choice it implies.'
  3. Regenerate with a naturalistic concept prompt for the second page, then check both against the practitioner texts; staff generate because Infographic is 18+.
  4. Print both PNGs at A3 for the rehearsal room with a blank third column headed 'the moment in the text that justifies this choice'.
  5. Pupils defend one concept in a timed written answer, marked only against the mark scheme's descriptor for coherence.
Student workflow
  1. For each choice on both pages, name the moment in the text that justifies it.
  2. Mark any choice neither concept requires, and say why it is merely decorative.
  3. Choose one concept and defend it in twenty-five minutes, using precise theatrical vocabulary.
  4. Rewrite your weakest paragraph so every choice follows from your stated concept.
Copy and paste
Create a single-page infographic for Year 13 A-level Drama pupils working towards A*. Using only the uploaded set text, practitioner texts and mark scheme, show one named directorial concept for this play and the choices it implies: staging form, lighting, sound, set, costume, proxemics, and vocal and physical choices for two key moments. Label each choice with the concept's logic in one clause, using precise theatrical vocabulary. Cite the act and scene for every moment. Do not invent practitioner claims or production history the sources do not contain.
The three routes
A → A*

Prompt for two concepts that are close rather than opposed, so the distinction turns on detail. Require pupils to defend a concept against the strongest objection drawn from the rival page, and mark only whether every choice follows from their stated intention.

B → A*

Keep the two concepts sharply contrasted and add a column of the mark scheme's coherence wording beside them. Model one fully justified choice aloud, then fade: pupils justify three choices with the text open before writing the defence unaided.

C → A*

Use Detail Concise and one concept only, with three choices and the act and scene printed beside each. Pupils match choice to moment using sentence stems, build to six choices over a term, and write the defence only once matching is reliable.

SEND adaptation. For a pupil with autism, the two pages make implicit staging conventions explicit; add a column naming the audience effect each choice is meant to produce, so nothing is left to inference.

Teacher workflow

  1. Verify every method and condition on the page against the formula booklet and textbook.
  2. Annotate each claim as correct, imprecise or wrong, citing the page that decides it.
  3. Rewrite the three weakest conditions precisely, as you would state them in a proof.
  4. Compare with the teacher's key and log any claim you accepted without checking.
Copy and paste
Create a single-page infographic for Year 13 Edexcel Further Mathematics pupils working towards A*. Using only the uploaded specification, formula booklet and worked solutions, map the standard methods for complex numbers and matrices: for each method give its name, when it applies, the condition that must hold, and one line of the method. Group the methods by the type of question they answer.
