A* lever Sustained AO2 precision and AO3 evaluation across every paper, evidenced by whether the redraft actually moved the mark the feedback targeted.

Board English Literature, OCR (H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a template site with one page per assessment: two embedded Docs side by side, a collapsible 'What I changed and why', and an embedded Sheets chart.
  2. Share the template read-only so pupils can use More > Make a copy of the entire site; there is no force-copy link for Sites, so copying needs source access.
  3. On each pupil's copy, untick 'Editors can publish, change permissions, and add new people' and publish Restricted to that pupil and the teacher only.
  4. Leave feedback as comments in the embedded draft Doc, since Sites has no comments, and name one assessment objective per essay.
  5. Every half term, open two journals in lesson with the pupil's permission and model what a precise 'what I changed' entry looks like.
Student workflow
  1. Before reading feedback, predict your own band against the descriptors and write it on the page.
  2. Redraft in the second Doc, then write three sentences naming what changed and which assessment objective it served.
  3. Add the new mark to the Sheet and check whether the targeted objective actually moved.
Copy and paste
Paste into the collapsible group on every journal page: 'Before you open my comments, write the band you think this draft earns and the descriptor phrase that justifies it. Then redraft in the right-hand document. Finally write three sentences: what I changed, which assessment objective it serves, and how I know it is better. Add the new mark to the chart. If the objective I targeted did not move, say what you will try instead next time.'
The three routes
A → A*

Feedback targets AO2 precision and AO3 evaluation only. The pupil predicts their band before reading comments, so calibration against the descriptors becomes the point of the exercise, and the chart is read for unevenness across papers rather than for an average.

B → A*

Name one assessment objective per essay and embed a full-mark model of the same question as a third Doc, so the structure is visible while redrafting. Weekly paragraph redrafts rather than whole essays, until describing turns reliably into evaluating.

C → A*

Redraft one paragraph, not the essay, with a frame the teacher supplies. The chart tracks a single objective so progress is visible. The teacher writes the first 'what I changed' entry alongside the pupil, then hands it over across the term.

SEND adaptation. For dyslexia, let the reflection be recorded as an unlisted screencast embedded on the page rather than typed, and keep the two Docs in a dyslexia-friendly font and generous line spacing.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. A full-mark answer sits beside the pupil's own draft, so the target structure is visible while redrafting.
  • 6 Check for understanding. Band prediction before feedback shows the teacher whether the pupil can read the mark scheme.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The marks chart is read half-termly for uneven papers, which is what costs the A*.
SAMR · Augmentation

Redrafting is unchanged, but juxtaposing draft and redraft with a two-year marks chart makes improvement, and its absence, visible in a way a paper folder does not.

TPACK · TPACK

Mark-scheme literacy, self-regulated redrafting and the site's side-by-side structure combine; the chart only means something because the assessment objectives define the columns.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 3: uneven papers and formulaic evaluation are the A to A* problem. Evidence 3: feedback plus metacognition and self-regulation are the strongest KS5 strands. Dose 2: every assessment, whole class. Cost and risk 1: pupil work is personal data and journals need setting up.

EEF feedback and metacognition and self-regulation strands.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Screen versus paper reading Strong

Risks Pupil work is personal data: publish Restricted to pupil and teacher, never publicly, and untick editor publishing rights. Journals die with the account unless copied out. Keep AI out of drafting; feedback and revision only.

Success measure By the second mock, redraft targets are stated in assessment-objective terms and paper-to-paper variation narrows.

2Order the portfolio by refinement decision, not artworkThe journal has one page per decision the artist made, each holding the work before, the experiment, the work after, and eighty words on the reference that caused the change.Art8ModificationTCK4810Medium effort

A* lever A coherent journey of refinement with critical and contextual reasoning made explicit - the difference between a complete portfolio and an A* personal investigation.

Board Art & Design (Art, Craft and Design), Pearson Edexcel (9AD0 (Advanced GCE in Art and Design - Art, Craft and Desig…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a template site with pages named 'Decision 1 to 8: what I changed and why', each with image blocks, a collapsible 'Evidence' group and an embedded Doc.
  2. Share the template read-only so pupils copy the entire site; check 'Allow users to create new sites' is on for the sixth-form organisational unit.
  3. On each copy, publish Restricted to pupil and teacher, untick editor publishing rights, and remind pupils that under-18 accounts must not publish publicly.
  4. Half-termly, display two anonymised decision pages and model reasoning that is critical and contextual rather than a description of what was done.
  5. Record in the pupil's Doc that all portfolio content is their own work, as JCQ non-exam assessment rules require.
Student workflow
  1. Photograph the work before and after each experiment and place both on the decision page.
  2. Write eighty words naming the artist reference, the problem it solved and the alternative you rejected.
  3. At half term, reread your decision pages and write the line of enquiry they add up to.
Copy and paste
Paste into each decision page: 'A decision page is not a diary entry. Put the work before and the work after at the top. Then answer in eighty words: what was the problem, which artist or work showed you a way to solve it, what did you change, and what did you deliberately not do? At half term, read all your decision pages in order and write two sentences naming the line of enquiry they add up to.'
The three routes
A → A*

Every decision page must name a critical or contextual reference and the alternative rejected, so reasoning moves from description to evaluation. At half term the pupil writes the line of enquiry and then tests it by removing one page's claim and checking the journey still holds.

B → A*

The teacher supplies the eight decision prompts and a stem bank for the eighty words. Two pages a half term are checked, and at least two must show a change caused by an artist reference rather than by convenience, closing the contextual gap deliberately.

C → A*

Four decision pages a year. Photographs go up first, then forty words dictated and typed, using a three-question frame. The teacher completes one page fully with the pupil as the model, and the frame stays until the second year.

SEND adaptation. For dyspraxia affecting written output, accept the eighty words as voice-typed in the embedded Doc and let image sequencing carry the argument, keeping the reasoning demand identical.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. Anonymised decision pages shown half-termly define what critical reasoning looks like in this portfolio.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. The four-question frame turns 'reflect on your work' into an answerable set of questions.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The half-termly reread of all decision pages forces the journey to be seen as a whole.
SAMR · Modification

The portfolio is restructured around decisions rather than chronology, and two years of change sit on one navigable site, which a date-ordered sketchbook cannot show.

TPACK · TCK

The site represents the investigation as a sequence of decisions, making refinement itself visible, and refinement is precisely the Art content being assessed.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: the personal investigation journey is the A* discriminator in Art. Evidence 2: metacognition and self-regulation are strong. Dose 2: every pupil, across two years. Cost and risk 1: pupil images are personal data and JCQ authenticity must be documented.

EEF metacognition and self-regulation; examiner emphasis on sustained investigation.

Research: Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong

Risks Images of pupil work are personal data: Restricted publishing only, never public, and no pupil names on exemplar pages. JCQ forbids AI-produced portfolio content, so keep AI out entirely and record authorship.

Success measure By the spring, pupils can state their line of enquiry unprompted and cite the decision page that set it.

A* lever Justified design decisions with complexity reasoning in the NEA, plus the auditable development trail that evidences the work as genuinely the pupil's own.

Board Computer Science, OCR (H446 - OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Computer Science, specif…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a template site with an iteration page pattern: objective, embedded Doc of the test table, screenshots of evidence, and a collapsible 'Why this design, not that one'.
  2. Share read-only so pupils copy the whole site; publish each copy Restricted to pupil and teacher, with editor publishing rights unticked.
  3. Fortnightly, comment in the embedded Doc rather than on the site, since Sites has no comments, and question one justification per iteration.
  4. Remind pupils in writing that the submitted NEA report is the assessed document and that AI may not produce any content submitted as their own.
  5. Use version history on the site to show the trail if authenticity is ever questioned (check board requirements for the final submission format).
Student workflow
  1. Before coding an iteration, write the objective and the tests that will prove it works.
  2. After coding, add the evidence and justify the data structure or algorithm chosen against one rejected alternative.
  3. At each milestone, reread earlier iterations and note which justification you would now argue differently.
Copy and paste
Paste into each iteration page: 'Write the objective and the tests before you write code. After coding, paste the evidence, then answer: which data structure or algorithm did you choose, what was the alternative, and why is yours better for this input size? Use complexity terms precisely. This site is your development record, in your own words - AI may help you plan or revise your understanding, but nothing AI writes may appear in what you submit.'
The three routes
A → A*

Each iteration page must justify a data structure or algorithm choice with explicit complexity reasoning and a rejected alternative, and one milestone page must argue why an earlier justification was wrong, which is the evaluative writing the top band rewards.

B → A*

The teacher supplies the iteration pattern with prompts and checks two pages a fortnight. Theory vocabulary is pre-taught from the page headings, so the write-up doubles as spaced revision of complexity, data structures and testing terminology across the whole specification.

C → A*

Three large iterations rather than eight, with objectives agreed with the teacher and test tables pre-filled with the test types. Justifications start as a two-sentence frame; screenshots and captions come first so early success is guaranteed.

SEND adaptation. For autism, keep every iteration page identical in layout and order so the routine is predictable, and state the completion criteria for a page explicitly at the top.
Rosenshine
  • 2 Present new material in small steps. One iteration per page, each with a single objective, breaks a year-long project into completable units.
  • 3 Ask questions. The teacher questions one justification per iteration in the embedded Doc, so reasoning is probed fortnightly.
  • 9 Independent practice. The pupil writes objectives and tests before coding, so the design thinking stays theirs.
SAMR · Modification

The write-up becomes an ongoing, navigable record produced during development rather than a retrospective document assembled at the end, which changes how design reasoning is captured.

TPACK · PCK

The page pattern encodes what NEA mark schemes reward - justification, testing, evaluation - so subject-specific assessment knowledge drives the structure the site merely hosts.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: NEA justification marks are where A* projects separate. Evidence 2: self-explanation and feedback are well supported. Dose 1: one cohort, one project, not weekly across the class. Cost and risk 1: JCQ authenticity and teacher checking time.

EEF feedback strand; examiner reports on NEA justification and evaluation.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong

Risks JCQ: AI must not produce any submitted NEA content, so the site records the pupil's own reasoning and the teacher signs authenticity. Publish Restricted; keep code and credentials out of screenshots.

Success measure At moderation, every iteration page carries a justification and a rejected alternative, with no retrofitted write-ups.

4Turn the Geography investigation into a defensible decision trailThe journal carries one page per investigation stage, each pairing the decision made with the alternative rejected and the statistical test chosen. Spoken notes are allowed, so reasoning is captured while the fieldwork memory is fresh.SEND: dyspraxia affecting written output in Geography7ModificationTPACK468Medium effort

Board Geography, OCR (H481 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Geography (fir…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a template site with six pages: question, methodology and its justification, data collection, statistical test and result, conclusion, evaluation of limits.
  2. On each page place a prompt Doc, the pupil's spoken note as an inserted Drive file (playback inside Sites: check availability), and a Sheets chart of their own data.
  3. Pupils take a copy via More > Make a copy; publish each Restricted to that pupil and you, with editor publishing rights unticked.
  4. Read the methodology page before data collection and ask one question: what result would have made you reject your hypothesis?
  5. Keep JCQ rules explicit on the home page: planning and feedback may be discussed, but every submitted word is the pupil's own.
Student workflow
  1. Within a day of fieldwork, record a two-minute spoken note on why you sampled that way.
  2. Write the decision page yourself from your own recording, naming the alternative you rejected.
  3. Before the conclusion page, state plainly what your data cannot show.
Copy and paste
Paste on each stage page: 'State the decision you made. Name one alternative you rejected, and why. Say what this choice does to the reliability of your data. If a statistical test belongs here, name it, say why it fits this data, and state what result would have made you reject your hypothesis. Finally, one sentence: what would a critical reader still doubt? Record this aloud first if writing is slow, then write it up yourself; the submitted words must be yours.'
The three routes
A → A*

The pupil argues the limits of their own method, and the evaluation page must reach a judgement about confidence rather than list problems. The teacher asks one unpredictable follow-up per page, as the investigation defence will.

B → A*

Model a completed stage page from an anonymised past investigation, then fade it. Weekly checkpoints, because drift is the usual cause of a thin write-up, and explicit practice of the statistical test on supplied data before the pupil's own.

C → A*

Two pages at a time, with sentence frames for the methodology justification and the statistical test taught first on a worked class dataset. The teacher co-writes the first evaluation, then withdraws. A realistic calendar staged across two terms.

SEND adaptation. A second adaptation: give a printed page-order map and a fixed weekly writing slot, because dyspraxia often carries organisational load. The analytical demand of every page is untouched.
Rosenshine
  • 4 Provide models. An anonymised completed stage page shows what a justified methodology decision reads like before the pupil writes one.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. Spoken capture and sentence frames carry the writing load while the pupil still does the geographical reasoning.
  • 6 Check for understanding. The teacher reads the methodology page before fieldwork, so a flawed sampling plan is caught early.
SAMR · Modification

The write-up becomes a staged, auditable trail of decisions rather than one document produced at the end, and spoken capture removes the handwriting bottleneck without reducing the reasoning.

TPACK · TPACK

5Build the French research project as a defence fileOne page per sub-question of the AQA individual research project: French sources, the pupil's argument, and a growing bank of self-recorded answers to unpredictable follow-ups, showing the move from script to spontaneity.French6ModificationTPACK139Medium effort

A* lever The AQA speaking test turns on defending the individual research project under unpredictable follow-up questions, in accurate French, without reciting a prepared script.

Board French, AQA (7652 (AQA A-level French)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a template site: a home page for the research question, then one page per sub-question with an embedded Doc of French sources and the pupil's argument in French.
  2. Add a collapsible group per page, 'Questions que je n'attendais pas', where the pupil logs each new follow-up and inserts their recorded answer from Drive (playback: check availability).
  3. Pupils copy the template; publish each Restricted to that pupil and you. Feedback lives as comments in the embedded Doc, since Sites has none.
  4. Each fortnight, ask two unscripted follow-ups in French, unrehearsed, and require the pupil to log the question they handled worst.
  5. Audit the argument pages for retelling: every source summary must serve a claim, not narrate the source.
Student workflow
  1. Summarise each French source in French, never in English, then argue rather than retell.
  2. Log every follow-up you were not ready for, and record a better answer the same day.
  3. Re-record one older answer each week without reading your notes or this page.
Copy and paste
Paste into the collapsible group on every sub-question page: 'Note la question que tu n'attendais pas, mot pour mot. Enregistre ta reponse, sans lire tes notes, en deux minutes maximum. Puis ecris en francais: quelle structure complexe as-tu utilisee, et quelle erreur as-tu entendue en te reecoutant? Une semaine plus tard, reenregistre la meme reponse sans regarder cette page, et dis si elle est plus precise ou seulement plus longue.'
The three routes
A → A*

Follow-ups are deliberately hostile: the pupil must concede a point and still defend the thesis. Recordings are timed and unscripted, because rehearsed fluency collapses under a question the pupil has never met before.

B → A*

The teacher records a model answer in French for one sub-question, and the pupil logs six high-utility structures to reuse. Fortnightly follow-ups stay on the same page until recall is automatic, then move on.

C → A*

Two sub-questions only, with a bank of likely questions visible and a structure list on the page. The pupil answers from bullet points, never a script, and the bullets shrink month by month across Year 12.

SEND adaptation. For a stammer or high speaking anxiety, let the first recording be made alone at home, and keep the log rather than the live performance as the artefact discussed in lessons.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Fortnightly unscripted follow-ups in French are the check, and the questions that defeat the pupil become the log.
  • 1 Daily review. Re-recording an older answer each week returns high-utility structures until they are automatic under pressure.
  • 9 Independent practice. The pupil records alone, from notes they wrote, with no script and a two-minute limit.
SAMR · Modification

Speaking practice becomes a cumulative, re-recordable record of spontaneity across two years, which a classroom conversation leaves no trace of; the site is where the comparison happens.

TPACK · TPACK

Knowledge of the AQA speaking format, the retrieval routine of re-recording, and the site's audio and log structure are genuinely fused here.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 3: defending the research project is where A* speaking marks are won. Evidence 2: retrieval and self-regulation, less direct than teacher feedback. Dose 1: fortnightly, individual. Cost and risk 0: audio is personal data and recording time competes with lessons.

EEF metacognition and self-regulation; oral rehearsal evidence thinner.

Research: Formative assessment and feedback… Strong Metacognition and self-regulated… Strong Cognitive offloading, AI reliance… Moderate

Risks Voice recordings identify pupils: keep them in school Drive, publish Restricted, delete at course end. Audio playback inside Sites needs checking. No AI-generated French may be submitted as the pupil's own speech.

Success measure By the second term, unscripted answers hold accurate complex structures and the unexpected-question log shrinks.

Embedded guided pathway with checks (Forms quizzes, Docs, YouTube, NotebookLM and Gem links)

A sequenced page per topic: teach (YouTube or embedded Slides), check (embedded Forms quiz, auto-marked), apply (Docs task), extend (buttons to a shared NotebookLM notebook built from department sources, or a Gemini Gem), so A* routes are explicit and pupils self-check before writing an essay.

Options. Insert > Forms: quiz mode with auto-grading and feedback; responses land in Forms or Sheets, not Sites; Forms 'Help me create' with Gemini drafts a quiz from a prompt (July 2026 launch). Insert > YouTube and Slides. Button elements linking to a NotebookLM notebook (share within the domain; premium tier adds chat-only sharing that hides sources) and to a Gem share link. Collapsible groups per step; site search indexes embedded Docs, Slides and PDF text.

Constraints. Forms results are not visible in Sites; teachers check in Forms. NotebookLM must be admin-enabled; under-18 pupils get a guarded experience and some features are 18+; personal class notebooks in Classroom are 18+ higher education only. Sharing a Gem with under-18 accounts: unconfirmed. YouTube embeds depend on the school's YouTube restrictions for pupils. Model outputs need teacher checking.

1Add a rolling mixed-quiz page for monthly reviewThe pathway ends on a review page whose embedded Forms quiz mixes items from every topic taught so far, auto-marked with feedback naming the misconception, refreshed on a six-week cycle.Science (Chemistry)9AugmentationTPK1710Low effort

A* lever Multi-step calculation accuracy with units and significant figures across the whole specification, so no single paper collapses and costs the A*.

Board Chemistry, AQA and OCR compared - LAET's board not specified (AQA A-level Chemistry 7405 (components 7405/1, 7405/2, 7405…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Add a 'Cumulative review' page at the end of the pathway and embed one Form set to quiz mode with auto-grading and answer feedback.
  2. Write feedback text for every wrong answer that names the misconception and the rule, for example 'moles before mass' or 'significant figures follow the least precise datum'.
  3. Use Forms 'Help me create' with Gemini to draft items from a pasted specification extract, then check and correct every key against the mark scheme.
  4. Rebuild the item mix every six weeks so each topic reappears at least twice; results are checked in Forms or Sheets, never in Sites.
  5. Reteach on Monday only the two items with the lowest facility, using the pathway's teach page for that topic.
Student workflow
  1. Do the cumulative quiz closed book on the same day each week, showing working on paper.
  2. Read the feedback on every wrong answer and write the rule it names into your notes.
  3. Return to the pathway's teach page for any topic you scored below half on.
Copy and paste
Paste into the Form's description: 'Closed book, ten minutes, working on paper. This quiz covers everything taught this year, not this week - that is the point. For each wrong answer, read the feedback, write the rule it names into your notes, and redo the calculation with units and significant figures shown. If you get an item right but guessed, mark it as a guess; I would rather know now than in June.'
The three routes
A → A*

Weight the mix towards unfamiliar-context multi-step calculations and required-practical evaluation. Pupils must submit working, and the teacher reviews only items below seventy per cent facility, so time goes to the precision slips rather than to secure content.

B → A*

Run a rolling six-week cycle covering the whole specification so gaps surface systematically, with feedback text that names the misconception and links to a worked example. Two quizzes a week until the weakest three topics stop appearing in the low-facility list.

C → A*

Four items only, the same topics twice before anything new is added, and an eighty per cent success target before the mix widens. Feedback gives the rule and the first step; a worked example page sits beside the quiz all term.

SEND adaptation. For slow processing speed, remove the ten-minute cap on this formative quiz and allow the calculation steps to be typed into the Form rather than handwritten; the demand stays identical.
Rosenshine
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. A cumulative mix rather than a topic test, refreshed every six weeks so nothing taught is left unreviewed.
  • 1 Daily review. Monday reteaching starts from the two lowest-facility items, so review is driven by data not guesswork.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Item mix is tuned so most pupils clear eighty per cent, keeping the quiz diagnostic rather than demoralising.
SAMR · Augmentation

It is still a cumulative quiz, but auto-marking with misconception-naming feedback at the end of the pathway gives immediate, specific correction at no marking cost.

TPACK · TPK

Spaced cumulative retrieval is a general pedagogical move; the Form's auto-grading and feedback fields make it sustainable weekly whatever the subject.

Impact 9 of 10

Proximity 2: precision across all papers rather than one discriminator item. Evidence 3: retrieval and spaced practice plus feedback are the strongest strands. Dose 2: weekly, whole class, auto-marked. Cost and risk 2: one Form to maintain, no pupil data beyond school accounts.

EEF retrieval and spaced practice; feedback strand.

Research: Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Spaced practice and distributed l… Strong Studying erroneous worked example… Weak

Risks Gemini-drafted items can be wrong, so check every key against the specification before publishing. Responses are personal data: keep the Form inside the domain and report scores without naming pupils publicly.

Success measure In six weeks the low-facility list shortens and calculation marks in mocks stop varying by topic.

Board Music, AQA (7272 (AQA A-level Music)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Make one page per set-work section: embedded Slides of the score extract, a YouTube performance, and an embedded Form in quiz mode with auto-grading.
  2. In the quiz's answer feedback, put the link to the next page, so the apply step is reached only after the aural check is correct.
  3. Use Forms 'Help me create' to draft terminology items from a specification extract, then correct every key against the score yourself.
  4. Keep steps in collapsible groups labelled teach, check, apply, extend, with an extend button to a shared NotebookLM notebook of department analysis notes.

Student workflow
  1. Listen to the extract twice with the score open before opening the check.
  2. Answer the aural check; read the feedback and follow its link only when the answer is right.
  3. On the apply page, write the analysis with bar references and the correct terminology.
Copy and paste
Paste at the top of each set-work page: 'Work in order: listen, check, apply. Listen twice with the score open before you open the check - if you cannot hear it, playing it a third time is the work, not a failure. The check tells you when you are ready and gives you the link to the apply step. In the apply step, every claim needs a bar reference and the correct term.'
The three routes
A → A*

The gate item uses an extract they have not heard, and the apply step demands the harmonic device named and justified with bar references. Extend links to the notebook of department analysis notes for a comparison with a second work in the same style.

B → A*

The gate item tests terminology with feedback that defines the term, and two attempts are allowed. The apply step supplies a full-mark model of one paragraph of analysis, and the teacher reteaches the two weakest items before the next section is unlocked.

C → A*

Recognition with the score visible, three items only, and a high success rate by design. The apply step is a sentence frame naming the feature, the bar and the effect; frames narrow once two sections are secure.

SEND adaptation. For a visual impairment, ensure the score extract is embedded as an accessible Doc or PDF that reads at high magnification, and allow spoken answers to the aural check recorded for the teacher.

  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Gate items are pitched so most pupils pass on a second attempt after relistening.

3Send pupils to a sourced notebook for objectionsThe pathway's extend step buttons through to a domain-shared NotebookLM notebook of teacher-curated primary texts, where pupils hunt an objection to the argument they have just reconstructed, then reply.Philosophy7ModificationTCK349Medium effort

A* lever Reconstructing and evaluating arguments with logical precision, handling objections and replies, and defending a thesis - the top-band demand in A-level Philosophy.

Board Philosophy and Religion (Religious Studies), Edexcel (Pearson) (9RS0 — Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Religious St…) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Build the notebook first from teacher-curated set texts and department commentaries held in Drive, and share it within the domain; add no pupil data.
  2. On the topic page, sequence teach (embedded Slides), check (Form in quiz mode on the argument's premises) and extend (a button to the notebook).
  3. Write the extend task in an embedded Doc: reconstruct the argument in premise-conclusion form, find an objection in the sources, quote it, then reply.
  4. Require the pupil to cite the source the notebook points to and read that passage in the original before using it.
  5. Check two reconstructions per class in the lesson and correct any objection the model has misattributed before it spreads.
Student workflow
  1. Reconstruct the argument in numbered premises and a conclusion before opening the notebook.
  2. Use the notebook to locate an objection, then read the cited passage in the original text.
  3. Write the objection in premise-conclusion form and a reply that defends or amends your thesis.
Copy and paste
Paste into the extend task Doc: 'First, without the notebook, write the argument as numbered premises and a conclusion. Then use the notebook to find one objection to a named premise. Quote it, note which source it came from, and read that passage in the original before you use it. Finally write the objection in premise-conclusion form and your reply. The notebook can find the objection; only you can decide whether it succeeds - say why.'
The three routes
A → A*

The pupil must find an objection not taught in class and write a reply that defends the thesis with logical precision, then state the strongest remaining worry. Evaluation becomes argued rather than formulaic, which is the A to A* move in Philosophy.

B → A*

The objection is named for them. They reconstruct it in premise-conclusion form from the notebook's cited passage, then reply using a supplied structure: concede, distinguish, defend. One argument a week until reconstruction is reliable across the specification.

C → A*

Use a teacher-made objections handout instead of the notebook, since the under-18 experience is guarded and some features are 18+. Premise-conclusion frames, one objection a fortnight, and the reply modelled fully before independent attempts.

SEND adaptation. For ADHD, put the extend task in three timed chunks on the page - reconstruct, find, reply - each with its own completion criterion, so the open-ended hunt has visible edges.
Rosenshine
  • 3 Ask questions. Every extend task ends in a question the pupil must answer in their own argument, not in a summary.
  • 9 Independent practice. Reconstruction happens before the notebook opens, so the logical work is done by the pupil.
  • 4 Provide models. A modelled concede-distinguish-defend reply sits on the page for pupils who need the structure.
SAMR · Modification

The task is redesigned: pupils must find and answer an objection in curated primary sources, work that previously depended on whichever objections the teacher chose to supply.

TPACK · TCK

The notebook turns a body of set texts into something queryable by argument and premise, which changes how philosophical content can be interrogated.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: objections and replies are the top-band discriminator. Evidence 2: self-explanation and peer-style dialogue are supported. Dose 1: weekly for one class, needing teacher checking each time. Cost and risk 1: hallucination and misattribution risk plus age-gated features.

EEF metacognition strand; examiner reports on evaluative argument.

Research: Cognitive offloading, AI reliance… Moderate Working memory, ADHD, dyslexia, a… Mixed Screen versus paper reading Strong

Risks NotebookLM output can misattribute, so pupils read the original passage and the teacher checks in lesson. Under-18 pupils get a guarded experience and some features are 18+; the C-route handout is the fallback. No pupil data in sources.

Success measure Within a term, essays contain an objection and reply the class was never taught.

4Give each assessment objective its own pathway pageThe topic pathway splits into three pages, recall, application to an unfamiliar scenario and elaborated evaluation, each with its own auto-marked Forms check, so pupils see that consequences, not more description, earn the sixteen-mark marks.Psychology7ModificationTPACK267High effort

A* lever AQA Psychology A* rests on AO3 evaluation developed to a consequence for the theory, and on the research methods and mathematical content.

Board Psychology, AQA (7182 - AQA A-level Psychology (first teaching 2015)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. For each topic make three pathway pages titled AO1, AO2 and AO3, each with an embedded Slides summary, a Form in quiz mode and a Doc task.
  2. AO1 items test procedures and figures of named studies; AO2 gives an unfamiliar scenario; AO3 items ask which consequence follows for the theory, with feedback naming why.
  3. Use Forms 'Help me create' to draft AO1 items from your own notes, then check every item against the specification before you publish the page.
  4. Add a fourth page for research methods and maths: an embedded Sheet of raw data and a quiz on choosing and justifying the statistical test.
  5. Check responses in Forms, not Sites, and reteach the AO3 items with the lowest facility.
Student workflow
  1. Take the AO1 check until you score full marks; knowledge must be automatic, not effortful.
  2. Apply the theory to the unfamiliar scenario before you read any evaluation.
  3. For each AO3 point, write the consequence for the theory, not just the criticism.
Copy and paste
Paste as the AO3 page instruction: 'A criticism is worth little until you say what follows from it. For each of the three studies on this page write the evaluation point, the evidence for it, and then the consequence: what it means for the theory's validity, its generalisability, or its use in practice. If you cannot write the consequence, the point is description. Finish with one sentence saying which of the three does most damage to the theory, and why.'
The three routes
A → A*

Only the AO3 and methods pages are used, with items drawn from the lowest-facility questions in past papers. Pupils write consequences under timed conditions, since unevenness across papers, not missing knowledge, is what costs them the A*.

B → A*

All three pages in order, weekly, with the AO1 quiz repeated until automatic and a full-mark sixteen-mark answer modelled on the AO3 page. The teacher fades that model paragraph by paragraph over a term.

C → A*

AO1 and AO2 pages only for the first term, with short quizzes and a high success rate. AO3 arrives as a two-sentence frame: point, then consequence. The maths page uses one test on class data before any exam item.

SEND adaptation. For autism, keep the page order and quiz format identical across every topic, and state explicitly that the AO3 page asks for judgement rather than more facts; the demand is unchanged.
Rosenshine
  • 2 Present new material in small steps. One assessment objective per page, so recall, application and evaluation are practised separately before being combined.
  • 6 Check for understanding. An auto-marked Form on each page, with feedback naming the misconception, before the pupil moves on.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. The AO1 check is repeated to full marks, so application and evaluation rest on secure knowledge.
SAMR · Modification

Splitting one topic into three assessment-objective pages, each with its own auto-marked check, redesigns revision around what is actually assessed rather than around content coverage.

TPACK · TPACK

Assessment-objective knowledge sets the structure, the Forms checks supply retrieval and feedback, and the pathway makes the description-evaluation distinction visible.

Impact 7 of 10

Proximity 3: AO3 elaboration and the methods maths separate A from A*. Evidence 3: retrieval practice and feedback are the strongest strands. Dose 1: one pathway per topic, whole class. Cost and risk 0: quiz writing is heavy and AI-drafted items need checking.

EEF feedback and retrieval practice strands.

Research: Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Comment-only marking versus grades Moderate Intelligent tutoring systems Strong

Risks Gemini-drafted quiz items can misstate a study's procedure or figures: check each against the specification. Forms responses hold pupil data, so keep them in the domain and never publish scores on the site.

Success measure Within six weeks, AO3 paragraphs end in a consequence and sixteen-mark scores rise faster than AO1 scores.

5Rebuild the translation check from the class's own errorsEach half term the pathway's check is rebuilt from an anonymised log of the class's actual translation errors, with an embedded chart showing which error types are falling and which are not.Spanish6AugmentationPCK6710Medium effort

A* lever The translation into Spanish is decided by recurring accuracy errors, mood, tense sequence, agreement and pronoun placement, under time, not by breadth of vocabulary.

Board Spanish, AQA (7692 (AQA A-level Spanish)) · what the top band demands

Teacher workflow
  1. Keep a Sheet of error types from marked translations with no names: one row per error, tagged mood, tense sequence, agreement or pronoun placement.
  2. Embed the Sheets chart of error frequency on the pathway's first page so the class sees its own profile, and update it after each assessment.
  3. Build the check page's Form in quiz mode from the top four error types only, with answer feedback naming the rule and giving a correct model sentence.
  4. Rebuild the Form each half term from the new log, and retire item types whose frequency has fallen below a threshold you set and state.
Student workflow
  1. Read the class error chart and name the type you personally lose most marks to.
  2. Take the check, then rewrite each wrong sentence correctly from memory rather than copying the feedback.
  3. Add your own errors to your row of the log, using the error type words.
Copy and paste
Paste above the embedded chart: 'This chart shows our class's real translation errors, not a textbook list. Name the type you lose most marks to. Take the check below. For every sentence you got wrong, close the feedback and rewrite the sentence correctly from memory, then explain the rule in one line in Spanish. Add the error type to your own row of the log. At the end of the half term, say which type you have moved, and what evidence you have.'
The three routes
A → A*

Items are drawn only from errors the pupil still makes, attempted under time pressure with a word limit. The chart is read for one thing: whether the targeted error type has actually fallen, not whether accuracy feels better.

B → A*

Four error types at a time, revisited weekly with the model sentence visible, then hidden. The teacher translates one sentence aloud, thinking the mood choice through, before pupils attempt the set alone.

C → A*

Two error types only, with the rule and a model sentence on the page and a high success rate as the aim. Sentences are short and the verb is given. Types are added, never swapped, so nothing is lost.

SEND adaptation. For dyslexia, let the error type be chosen from a list rather than written out, and keep model sentences in a dyslexia-friendly font; rewriting from memory stays as it is.
Rosenshine
  • 6 Check for understanding. The auto-marked check reports which error types persist, and feedback names the rule rather than only the answer.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. The half-termly rebuild returns the class's live errors, so old weaknesses are revisited rather than assumed fixed.
  • 7 Obtain a high success rate. Only four error types at a time, with a model sentence, keeps accuracy high enough to build fluency.
SAMR · Augmentation

The translation drill is unchanged, but auto-marking and a live error chart let the check be rebuilt from the class's own data instead of a published exercise book.

TPACK · PCK

The driver is knowing which accuracy errors actually cost marks in AQA translation; Forms and the chart only make that knowledge visible and testable.

Impact 6 of 10

Proximity 3: translation accuracy is a direct A* discriminator. Evidence 2: feedback and retrieval, weakened by self-reported logging. Dose 1: half-termly rebuild, whole class. Cost and risk 0: maintaining the log and rewriting the Form is real teacher time.

EEF feedback strand; retrieval and spaced practice.

Research: Retrieval practice and the testin… Strong Spaced practice and distributed l… Strong Intelligent tutoring systems Strong

Risks The error log must carry error types only, never names or marks. Forms responses stay inside the domain. Do not let pupils paste translations into AI tools; rewriting from memory is the whole point.

Success measure By the next assessment, the top two error types fall in frequency on the class chart.

6Publish a self-study pathway for untaught Turkish candidatesA domain-restricted Site sequences teach, check, apply and extend for each Turkish paper, so a candidate with no timetabled lesson has an explicit route and self-marks before the fortnightly meeting.Turkish8AugmentationTPACK2810High effort

A* lever Translation conventions and exam technique, not fluency: candidates who speak Turkish at home still lose marks to over-translation, register slips and untaught essay structure.

Teacher workflow
  1. Build a Site with one page per paper and a collapsible group per step: teach, check, apply, extend; publish Restricted with the Turkish candidates as published viewers.
  2. Teach: embed a Doc of ten worked translation pairs showing the convention and the over-translation to avoid, plus your board's mark scheme extract.
  3. Check: insert an auto-marked Forms quiz per step with per-answer feedback naming the convention breached; results land in Forms, so read them there.
  4. Extend: add a button to the examiner-feedback Gem and share the Drive folder with the same group before publishing, or embedded files will not open.
  5. Tick Request public search engines not to display my site, and use Review changes before publishing when a colleague edits.
Student workflow
  1. Work one page a week in order: read the worked pairs, take the check quiz, then attempt the apply task unaided.
  2. Note every convention the feedback names and translate the same passage again from scratch.
  3. Bring the two conventions you keep breaching to the fortnightly meeting with your own examples.
Copy and paste
Apply task, translation into Turkish. Translate the passage in the Doc above. Before you submit, check each of these and write yes or no beside it: every tense sequence matches the English, no phrase has been expanded into an explanation, the register stays formal throughout, idioms are rendered by a Turkish idiom rather than word for word, and proper nouns are left untouched. Then translate the passage a second time without looking at your first attempt, and list the differences. Bring the list, not the translation, to the meeting.
The three routes
A → A*

The A-to-A* candidate needs the last marks in translation and essay, so the check quizzes use only disputed renderings where two options are defensible and the feedback explains which the mark scheme credits. The extend step becomes a timed unseen passage every week.

B → A*

The B-to-A* candidate has uneven technique, so every page opens with a fully worked example, the check quiz repeats the conventions from two pages earlier, and the apply task is half-scaffolded with the first two sentences modelled before fading.

C → A*

The C-to-A* candidate needs the route staged over two years, so each page covers one convention, the apply task is three sentences rather than a passage, and a Forms self-assessment scale records confidence. Add the essay pages only in Year 13, once translation is secure.

SEND adaptation. For a pupil with ADHD, keep one step visible per collapsible group and put the week's single task in a button at the top, so the route never looks like a wall of text.
Rosenshine
  • 2 Present new material in small steps. Each page is one convention, taught, checked and applied before the next is opened.
  • 8 Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks. Worked translation pairs and a self-check list scaffold a task nobody is timetabled to teach.
  • 10 Weekly and monthly review. Check quizzes revisit conventions from earlier pages, so the whole route is cycled.
SAMR · Augmentation

A paper booklet could hold the same sequence; the functional gains are instant self-marking, searchable embedded documents and a route that updates for every candidate at once.

TPACK · TPACK

Translation conventions (content), the teach-check-apply sequence (pedagogy) and a restricted site with auto-marked checks (technology) together stand in for lessons nobody is timetabled to teach.

Impact 8 of 10

Proximity 3: translation conventions and essay technique are precisely where these candidates lose the A*. Evidence 2: homework and self-regulation at KS5 are solid, a website alone is only an enabler. Dose 2: every week, every community-language candidate. Cost and risk 1: the build is a term's work.

EEF homework at KS5 and self-regulation; structured sequences with checks outperform undirected independent study.

Research: Homework and independent study at… Mixed Cognitive offloading, AI reliance… Moderate Working memory, ADHD, dyslexia, a… Mixed

Risks Publish Restricted to named viewers; never name pupils on exemplar pages. Examiner reports are board copyright, so link rather than re-host. Embedded files need the same group on the Drive folder. Gem sharing with under-18 accounts is unconfirmed; verify first.

Success measure Every community-language candidate completes a check weekly, and translation marks stop trailing their speaking grades.

A* by subject and exam board

What each board actually rewards at the top, from its own specifications, mark schemes and examiners’ reports. Band descriptors are paraphrased, never reproduced, because those documents are copyright.

How the A* is awarded. In reformed linear A-levels only grades A and E are judgemental, set by the awarding committee from scripts plus statistics. B, C and D are arithmetic, evenly spaced between them. A* is a separate statistical boundary set at subject level so the A* standard is carried forward from the previous year. No arithmetic rule, no fixed percentage.

Exceptions. A* is not awarded at AS. In unitised A-levels (legacy and International A-levels) it still needs grade A overall plus at least 90% of the maximum uniform mark on the aggregate of A-level units. For Project qualifications including the EPQ, A* is itself a judgemental boundary.

How high the bar actually sits

The published boundaries span 70.2% to 94.0%. A single cohort-wide percentage target is therefore wrong in nearly every department.

English Literature

OCR · H472 — OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in English Literature

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
H472/01 Drama and poetry pre-1900 (Shakespeare passage + essay; comparative drama/poetry essay); closed text2 hours 30 minutes6040%
H472/02 Comparative and contextual study (unseen prose close reading 30 marks; comparative essay 30 marks); closed text2 hours 30 minutes6040%
H472/03 Literature post-1900 (non-exam assessment, two tasks, internally marked, OCR moderated)not applicable (coursework)4020%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Informed, personal, creative response; concepts, terminology, accurate coherent expression20% (01: 10%, 02: 5%, 03: 5%)
AO2Analyse how meanings are shaped by language, form and structure30% (01: 7.5%, 02: 15%, 03: 7.5%)
AO3Significance and influence of the contexts of writing and reception25% (01: 10%, 02: 12.5%, 03: 2.5%)
AO4Explore connections across literary texts12.5% (01: 5%, 02: 5%, 03: 2.5%)
AO5Explore texts informed by different interpretations and changing critical views12.5% (01: 7.5%, 02: 2.5%, 03: 2.5%)
What the top band demands
  • Level 6 AO2: discussion of language, form, structure and dramatic effect is fully developed and detailed throughout; analytical method described as 'excellent' and effective without lapse.
  • Quotation and reference are handled critically and blended into the argument, not appended as illustration after a point has already been asserted.
  • Level 6 AO1: understanding of text and question is detailed and sustained; argument is well structured, coherent and developed continuously; expression fluent, accurate, in register.
  • Level 6 AO5: judgement is itself informed by other interpretations and by how critical views of the text have changed over time, not merely aware of them.
  • Level 6 AO3: contextual significance and influence are understood in consistent detail and used inside the argument rather than bolted on as background.
  • Level 6 AO4: exploration of connections between texts is purposeful, detailed and consistent, driving the comparison rather than noting resemblance.
What separates it from the band below
  • The load-bearing word is 'consistently'. Level 6 demands excellence sustained across the whole answer; Level 5 accepts quality that is 'good' and 'secure' but intermittent.
  • Level 5 says 'good' and 'developed'; Level 6 says 'excellent' and 'well-developed... consistently detailed'. Degree and constancy both change, in OCR's wording.
  • AO5: Level 5 recognises and explores interpretations; Level 6 lets them shape the judgement. Listing critics cannot reach Level 6.
  • AO2: Level 5 quotation is 'generally critically addressed'; Level 6 is 'blended into discussion'. Integration, not quantity of textual reference, moves the band.
  • Marking is holistic, positive and best-fit across the AO strands for that question; a weak dominant-AO strand caps the whole mark.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Summer 2025: GCSE habits persist — feature spotting of devices and formulaic structures, and complex literary terms deployed for their own sake.
  • Critical views, performance examples and contextual material were listed or 'bolted on' rather than treated as organic parts of the argument.
  • Paper 2: time split unevenly, with the comparative essay often twice as long; contextual reference attached to every analytical point in the unseen.
  • Comparative essays crammed in many texts, contexts and critics, becoming long and disjointed; examiners note longest essays are rarely the best.
  • Unseen passages answered without an overview read: over-long on the opening, thin on later material; 'oxymoron' and 'unreliable narrator' commonly misused.
Surprises from another board
  • Both written papers are closed text; no annotated copies and no extracts of set texts in the examination room.
  • AO2 is the largest AO at 30% but the Paper 2 comparative essay is AO3-dominant, not AO2-dominant.
  • Coursework titles and text combinations must be pre-approved by OCR through an online tool, not chosen freely in school.

Non-exam assessment H472/03, 40 marks, 20%, about 3000 words. Task 1 close reading or re-creative writing with commentary; Task 2 comparative essay. Three post-1900 texts (prose, poetry, drama), one from 2000 or later; OCR must approve texts and titles by 31 January.

Boundaries June 2026 (OCR published): overall A* 188/200 = 94%, A 178 = 89%, on the scale weighting papers 01 and 02 to 80 marks each. Notional raw A*: 55/60, 58/60, 37/40. June 2025 A* was 187/200.

History

AQA · 7042 — AQA A-level History

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 1 Breadth study: Section A one compulsory interpretations question (30); Section B two essays from three (2 x 25)2 hours 30 minutes8040%
Component 2 Depth study: Section A one compulsory primary-source question (30); Section B two essays from three (2 x 25)2 hours 30 minutes8040%
Component 3 Historical investigation (non-exam assessment, teacher-marked, AQA-moderated)not applicable (3500-4500 words)4020%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge deployed to analyse, evaluate and make substantiated judgements using second-order concepts60% (C1 25%, C2 25%, C3 10%)
AO2Analyse and evaluate primary or contemporary source material within its historical context20% (C2 15%, C3 5%; none in C1)
AO3Analyse and evaluate different interpretations of the past in context20% (C1 15%, C3 5%; none in C2)
What the top band demands
  • L5 essays (AO1): the full demands of the question are met, the answer is fully analytical with a balanced argument, and the judgement is well substantiated.
  • L5 essays: supporting material is 'well-selected, specific and precise', showing very good grasp of key features, issues and the relevant historical concepts.
  • L5 interpretations (AO3, C1): all three extracts' arguments understood, with strong contextual knowledge used to evaluate how convincing each is; evaluation 'well-supported and convincing'.
  • L5 sources (AO2, C2): all three sources weighed on content and provenance together, against context, for the exact purpose named, ending in a substantiated judgement.
  • Marking is best-fit and positive: the level comes from overall quality, the mark within it from how far the answer reaches into the level above.
What separates it from the band below
  • Judgement is the hinge: at L4 it 'may be partial or limited in substantiation'; at L5 it is well substantiated and grows out of the argument.
  • L4 answers are 'analytical in style'; L5 answers are 'fully analytical'. Comment attached to narrative is L4; argument that controls the material is L5.
  • L4 evidence is 'clear and specific'; L5 evidence is 'well-selected... and precise'. Selection and precision, not volume of detail, move the band.
  • On source and extract questions L4 may show 'minor limitations of depth and breadth'; L5 handles all three fully and convincingly with no imbalance.
  • Descriptive source answers that ignore historical context are capped at Level 2 whatever their factual range.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025 (7042/1G): the strongest answers covered the full chronological range; many strong candidates confined themselves to one part of the period.
  • Evidence was recalled but not made to work — little explanation of why an example mattered or how it supported the overall argument.
  • Component 1 extract question: some still discussed provenance, tone or utility, which is not credited there; others paraphrased or accepted arguments uncritically.
  • Counter-arguments were named but not developed, for example asserting that Liberal division automatically benefited the Conservatives.
  • NEA 2025: some centres treated the investigation as historiography, emphasising AO3 at AO1's expense; 'stepping stones' coverage left gaps in the period.
Surprises from another board
  • Component 1 assesses interpretations only and Component 2 primary sources only; the two skills never appear in the same paper.
  • AO1 is 60% of the A-level, so the four Section B essays, not the source questions, decide the grade.
  • Components 1 and 2 must pair a British with a non-British option, and all three components together must span 200 years.

Non-exam assessment Component 3, 40 marks, 20%, 3500-4500 words, 4500 absolute. A student's own question set in a context of about 100 years (80-120 allowed), not duplicating Components 1 or 2. Question Approval Form due each October. AO1 is half the marks.

Boundaries June 2026 (AQA published, max 200): subject A* boundaries vary by option pairing from 153 to 168, that is 76.5% to 84%; most option codes fall at 159-162, about 80%. Grade A sits roughly 23-24 marks lower.

Philosophy and Religion (Religious Studies)

Edexcel (Pearson) · 9RS0 — Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Religious Studies, Issue 4 (September 2025)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1 Philosophy of Religion (9RS0/01): Section A two structured questions (20); Section B anthology extract two-part question (30); Section C extended essay (30)2 hours8033.33%
Paper 2 Religion and Ethics (9RS0/02): same three-section structure2 hours8033.33%
Paper 3 New Testament Studies (9RS0/03): same three-section structure2 hours8033.33%
Paper 4 Study of Religion (9RS0/4A-4F: Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism); students take three papers from the four2 hours8033.33%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge and understanding of religion and belief, including thought, influence, similarity and difference40% overall; 13.33% per paper
AO2Analyse and evaluate aspects of and approaches to religion and belief60% overall; 20% per paper
What the top band demands
  • Level 5 AO1: a wide range of knowledge, specialist language and terminology is carefully chosen and used accurately and, in Pearson's word, 'sustained' throughout the answer.
  • Level 5 AO2: the candidate 'critically' deconstructs the issue, producing coherent and logical chains of reasoning rather than a sequence of reported views.
  • Level 5 AO2: connections are made between the full range of elements the question raises, leaving no strand of the question untouched.
  • Level 5 AO2: judgements are coherent and reasoned across that full range and fully supported by a comprehensive appraisal of the evidence.
  • On AO2 questions, an answer showing only AO1 achievement cannot be credited beyond the top of Level 1, however extensive the knowledge.
What separates it from the band below
  • Coverage is the boundary: Level 4 connects and judges 'many but not all' elements of the question; Level 5 covers the full range of them.
  • Level 4 'deconstructs'; Level 5 'critically deconstructs'. The evaluation must interrogate the reasoning, not just separate the positions out.
  • Level 4 appraises 'some evidence'; Level 5 offers a 'comprehensive appraisal'. Partial weighing of evidence holds an otherwise strong essay at Level 4.
  • Level 4 terminology is accurate in most places; Level 5 accuracy is sustained throughout, so late lapses in precision cost the top band.
  • Levels are best-fit and the mark bands are wide (17-20 of 20, 25-30 of 30), so the top band is reachable without perfection but not with gaps.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025 Paper 1: a one-size-fits-all essay template was applied to 'explore', 'assess' and 'evaluate' alike, ignoring command words and AO splits.
  • Candidates answered a remembered general question rather than the precise wording, for example assessing cosmological arguments generally instead of the Kalam focus.
  • Less commonly taught areas were underprepared — process theology, and religious language topics such as bliks and language games.
  • Anthology questions were answered from topic knowledge rather than the printed extract; examiners stress working directly with the text.
  • June 2025 Paper 2: applied ethics answers needed wider scholarship; philosophical terms such as a priori and contingency were used without explanation.
Surprises from another board
  • AO2 is 60% of the qualification: evaluation, not content coverage, carries the A-level.
  • Students take three papers from four; Paper 3 New Testament Studies and Paper 4B Christianity are a forbidden combination.
  • Every paper has an anthology extract question, and the relevant extract is printed in the paper itself.

Boundaries June 2026 (Pearson published, max 240 = three papers of 80): A level A* 212-214 depending on the paper combination, that is about 88-89%; A is 188-194. Notional per-paper A* is 69-72 out of 80.

French

AQA · 7652 (AQA A-level French)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Listening, reading and writing (incl. summaries and two translations)2h 30m10050% (scaled x2 to 200)
Paper 2: Writing - two essays of about 300 words on set text(s) and/or film2h8020% (scaling x1)
Paper 3: Speaking (NEA) - stimulus-card discussion plus individual research project21-23 min incl. 5 min preparation6030% (scaled x2 to 120)
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Understand and respond in speech and writing to spoken language, including face-to-face interaction20% (Paper 1 12.5, Paper 3 7.5)
AO2Understand and respond in speech and writing to written language from varied sources30% (Paper 1 27.5, Paper 3 2.5)
AO3Manipulate the language accurately in speech and writing, using a range of lexis and structure30% (10 in each of Papers 1, 2, 3)
AO4Show knowledge of, and respond critically and analytically to, the culture and society studied20% (Paper 2 10, Paper 3 10)
What the top band demands
  • Speaking AO1 (9-10 of 10 in the IRP discussion): fluent throughout, ideas and opinions nearly always developed without prompting, engaging very well and answering nearly all questions appropriately.
  • Speaking AO3 (9-10): wide vocabulary and complex language plus good command of idiom; grammar highly accurate with only occasional minor errors; very good pronunciation and intonation.
  • Speaking AO4 (9-10 in discussion, 5 of 5 for the 2-minute presentation): thorough knowledge of the researched area and a very good critical and analytical response.
  • Essay AO4 (17-20 of 20): described as an excellent critical and analytical response; knowledge consistently accurate and detailed, every view evidenced from the work, excellent evaluation of themes and contexts.
  • Essay AO3 (17-20): mainly accurate with occasional minor errors only, a consistently secure grasp of grammar, complex language manipulated accurately, wide vocabulary suited to the task.
  • Translations: full marks need every element of the passage rendered with no omission or paraphrase; into the target language, spelling and gender errors are not tolerated.
What separates it from the band below
  • Rehearsed IRP answers can score top-band AO4 yet cap AO1: stage-managed exchanges with no spontaneity are the single biggest brake on high speaking marks.
  • On the stimulus card AO2 carries as many marks as AO4, yet describing the photographs earns nothing; only the printed text counts, and two student questions are compulsory.
  • Essays are won by selecting evidence relevant to the question, not by knowledge; narrating plot and deploying pre-learnt quotations depress AO4.
  • Pre-learnt complex phrases delivered inaccurately score lower under AO3 than simpler language handled securely.
  • In the summary tasks AO3 rewards manipulation, so lifting wording straight from the source cannot be credited.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2023 Paper 3 report: stage-managed question-and-answer with little or no spontaneity stopped many strong candidates reaching high AO1 marks.
  • Presentations spent signposting what would follow, or listing and evaluating sources, earned nothing; only knowledge of the topic is rewarded.
  • Teacher-examiners who accepted a brief first answer on the card left AO2 in the limited bands; supplementary questions were needed.
  • Paper 2 2023: many arrived with a ready-made essay; learnt quotations were used because learnt, not because relevant, and marred responses.
  • Recurrent AO3 faults: verb plus infinitive, subjunctive, pronouns, numbers, faux amis, anglicisms and invented words.
Surprises from another board
  • Teachers conduct the speaking test but do not mark it; an AQA examiner marks the recording.
  • Record-form headings phrased as questions that reappear in the test can be reported as malpractice.
  • Questions the student asks after the six-minute card cut-off do not count, so the AO2 cap still applies.

Non-exam assessment Paper 3 speaking is the NEA: conducted by a trained teacher-examiner or visiting examiner, recorded unedited and uploaded, then marked by an AQA examiner. Signed candidate record form; minimum two research sources, at least one online; no dictionary.

Boundaries June 2026 (AQA, published 13 Aug 2026), max scaled 400: A* 362 = 90.5%, A 329 = 82.3%. Notional components: Paper 1 93/100, Paper 2 70/80, Paper 3 54/60.

What separates it from the band below

  • June 2023 Paper 3 report: pre-learnt responses to familiar questions hurt AO1; a genuinely spontaneous conversation is required.

  • Students who pre-learnt over-complex phrases they could not deliver accurately lost AO3 marks they would have kept with simpler language.

  • Performance is marked on four grids: ambition of project 5, technical control 15, expressive control 15, performance quality 15. Full ambition marks need repertoire averaging above grade 7 plus real expressive variety.
  • Top technical and expressive bands need fluent, secure playing with few pitch or rhythm errors, mature tone across the range, and the student's own interpretation rather than only what is printed.
  • Performance quality at the top is assured and engaging, inhabiting the style with real flair; repertoire that offers little expressive scope puts the top band out of reach.
  • Composition 1 at 21-25 is called an authoritative composition: imaginative use of the brief fundamentally informs the piece, with a commanding structure going beyond a standard form.
  • Composition 2 at 21-25 needs sustained mastery of technical control, contrasting ideas genuinely developed, and musical elements used with flair and strong creative purpose.
  • Supporting documentation is separately described in the grid: the top level is music communicated fluently on paper with a comprehensive score or commanding aural guide, plus a 150-word programme note.
What separates it from the band below
  • Section B analysis of Area of study 1 set works is consistently the weakest section; harmonic and tonal analysis with the score in front of candidates is where marks go.
  • Chorales reward modulation, varied cadences with suspensions and passing sevenths, singable spacing and quaver enrichment; consecutives and unresolved dissonances cap the mark.
  • Free compositions that stay diatonic, keep one texture or repeat a short progression block the upper bands for ideas, contrast, development and structure.
  • Repertoire choice sets the ceiling both ways: easy programmes cap ambition, while over-ambitious ones cost technical control.
  • Section C essays need specific, well-chosen repertoire evidence answering the question, not general description of instrumentation.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2023 performance report: several students fell short of the 10-minute minimum by a minute or more and a marking penalty was applied.
  • Ensembles larger than eight players could not be assessed at all; the student's part must be undoubted and audible to the examiner.
  • Composition brief infringements persisted - omitting a required instrument or altering given material - and in most cases reduced the mark.
  • Briefs that set an occasion (pop concert, art gallery, embassy) were often ignored, producing music unplayable live or wrong in atmosphere.
  • Appraising: Section B analysis remained the weakest area, with analysis of harmonic progression rarely found.
Surprises from another board
  • Teachers do not mark the NEA at all; AQA marks both performance and composition externally.
  • Scaling is uneven: performance x2.1, composition x1.5, appraising x1, so a performance raw mark is worth more than double.
  • Video files are not accepted, even for composition written to picture.

Non-exam assessment Performance and composition are NEA, externally marked by AQA. Recorded under teacher supervision between 1 March and the deadline; single final recording; signed candidate record form; score, lead sheet or aural guide plus a 150-word programme note per composition.

Boundaries June 2026 (AQA, published 13 Aug 2026), max scaled 300: A* 247 = 82.3%, A 223 = 74.3%. Notional components: written 89/120, performance 46/50, composition 41/50.

Art & Design (Art, Craft and Design)

Pearson Edexcel · 9AD0 (Advanced GCE in Art and Design - Art, Craft and Design; spec Issue 6, June 2024)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 1: Personal Investigation (supporting studies, practical work, personal study) - internally marked, externally moderatedcoursework across the course9060%
Component 2: Externally Set Assignment - preparatory period from 1 February plus supervised period of sustained focus15 hours, in at most five sessions across three consecutive weeks7240%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Develop ideas through sustained, focused investigations informed by contextual sources, with critical understanding25%
AO2Explore and select resources, media, materials, techniques and processes, reviewing and refining as work develops25%
AO3Record ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions, reflecting critically on progress25%
AO4Present a personal and meaningful response that realises intentions and makes connections between elements25%
What the top band demands
  • Each AO is marked out of 18 in six three-mark levels, Level 6 (16-18) being labelled exceptional ability. Component 2 is 4 x 18; Component 1 adds 18 for the personal study.
  • AO1 at Level 6 needs investigation that is sustained, focused and thoroughly informed by contextual sources - the escalator runs partially informed, informed, thoroughly informed, so sources must visibly drive the work.
  • AO2 at Level 6 rewards exploration and selection appropriate to intentions plus exceptional reviewing and refining; breadth of media for its own sake is not credited.
  • AO4 at Level 6 needs a personal and meaningful response that realises the student's stated intentions - the board's own word for the top level is exceptional, not merely accomplished.
  • Sustained in practice means continuous self-driven enquiry across the course, with sketchbooks actively recording, experimenting, developing and reviewing, not a run of discrete teacher-set projects.
  • Personal in practice means the student's own direction and voice; 2025 reports contrast this against pastiches of other artists with superficial analysis.
What separates it from the band below
  • The personal study (minimum 1000 words, own bibliography) is marked on its own criterion out of 18, about 12% of the qualification; Level 6 needs complex ideas expressed with authority.
  • The personal-study grid stacks: Level 6 main-grid descriptions apply as well as the written-communication strand, so marking it on writing quality alone misapplies it.
  • Scale is not a proxy for quality; 2025 feedback said scale and complexity were not necessarily indicators of success, and smaller works often showed better refinement.
  • Art, Craft and Design requires at least two disciplines from different endorsed titles in Component 1; a single-discipline Component 2 is standardised against that endorsed title's cohort.
  • Teacher-led courses running beyond the first term of Year 12 achieved less; letting students work independently early is named the most successful strategy.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Summer 2025 Component 1: weak sketchbooks were decorative and passive - unfocused description, biographical padding, gathered-image collages, meandering intent statements.
  • Heavy reliance on AI-generated text produced bland, generic personal studies lacking personal voice that were easily distinguishable from the student's own annotation.
  • Personal studies failed through unwieldy titles, no link to the student's own practical work, or long description of their projects adding no critical value.
  • Summer 2025 Component 2 (theme Union): weaker responses took the obvious reading without developing a personal viewpoint.
  • The board states A* candidates have effectively demonstrated full marks, and warns centres not to inflate marks to protect a student's position.
Surprises from another board
  • The components are marked out of 90 and 72 but weighted 60/40, so Component 1 raw marks are scaled up to a 180-mark subject total.
  • AO1-AO4 cover practical work and annotation only; the 1000-word study is marked on its separate criterion, not double-marked.
  • Moderation is a physical visit with all sampled work displayed, and internet access must be disabled, not merely discouraged.

Non-exam assessment Both components are NEA. Student and teacher sign the Art and Design Authentication Sheet. The 15 hours are unaided under exam conditions with internet disabled; preparatory work is labelled and stored securely; teachers clarify but never supply solutions.

Boundaries June 2026 (Pearson), subject max 180: A* 141 = 78.3%, A 129 = 71.7%. June 2025: A* 141 = 78.3%, A 128 = 71.1%. Notional 2026: Component 1 A* 72/90 = 80%, Component 2 A* 55/72 = 76.4%.

Drama (AQA option - board not confirmed by LAET)

AQA · 7262 (AQA A-level Drama and Theatre)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 1: Drama and Theatre, open-book written exam (Section A set play from List A 25; Section B three-part question on a List B extract 30; Section C live production seen 25)3h8040%
Component 2: Creating Original Drama (devising) - NEA, centre-marked and AQA-moderated; working notebook 40 plus devised performance 20; influenced by one prescribed practitionercoursework; duo 5-10 min, group of 3-6 up to 30 min6030%
Component 3: Making Theatre - NEA marked by an AQA examiner; performance of Extract 3 in a practitioner's style 40 plus reflective report on all three extracts 20coursework; report max 3000 words6030%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Create and develop ideas to communicate meaning, connecting dramatic theory and practice20% (all in Component 2)
AO2Apply theatrical skills to realise artistic intentions in live performance30% (Component 2 10, Component 3 20)
AO3Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of how drama and theatre is developed and performed30% (all in Component 1)
AO4Analyse and evaluate their own work and the work of others20% (Component 1 10, Component 3 10)
What the top band demands
  • Written paper top marks require answers pinned to the precise demand of the chosen question; List A answers need at least two of the performer, designer and director perspectives, List B all three.
  • Section C demands explicit, developed reference to the total dramatic effectiveness of the production seen; asserting the phrase without explaining how it was achieved earns nothing.
  • Design answers in Section B must be the student's own ideas, supported by neatly drawn labelled sketches, on any aspect - set, costume, make-up, props or accessories.
  • Devising: a top-band working notebook shows a rationale of genuine personal engagement, research and specific individual aims in sympathy with the chosen practitioner's methods.
  • The individual Statement of Dramatic Intentions is assessed in the fourth strand of the devised performance mark, so it must be individual and specific about the intended audience effect.
  • Making Theatre: the highest bands need a personal interpretation exceptionally appropriate to the play as a whole, which a continuous extract supports and an abridgement of the play cannot.
What separates it from the band below
  • Directorial and design intention is assessed by role perspective in the written paper, and in the practicals through the chosen specialism, the notebook and the statement of intentions.
  • Only one student per design or directing specialism is allowed in a group, and costume designers may dress only one performer in one costume.
  • Time and extract rules bite: duos must run 5-10 minutes, key extracts must be continuous and at least ten minutes if performed in full, and wording must not be altered.
  • Word limits are absolute - the reflective report caps at 3000 words including quotations, and anything beyond is not credited.
  • Section A and B plays may not be the same play used for Section C, so the live production must be chosen deliberately.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2023 devising report: over-generous centre marking was the main cause of moderation changes - work that was good was placed in bands reserved for excellent or exceptional.
  • Whole cohorts offered identical design ideas with identical sketches in Section B; teachers should not impose a corporate design vision.
  • Many students omitted total dramatic effectiveness in Section C, or asserted it without explaining how, which held their marks down.
  • Making Theatre: abridging a whole play instead of performing a continuous extract self-penalised students out of the higher bands.
  • Recurrent vocabulary faults: opening and closing proxemics, and gait attributed to seated or still characters, attracted no credit.
Surprises from another board
  • Component 2 is centre-marked but Component 3 is marked by an AQA examiner, so the two practicals are moderated differently.
  • Non-examinees are allowed in devising only when the cohort is one student, and never in Component 3.
  • AQA warns against relying on social-media teacher groups and directs queries to the assigned NEA adviser.

Non-exam assessment Components 2 and 3 are NEA. Student and teacher sign a candidate record form; supervision must allow authentication; teachers may clarify the task, not supply content, and give no guidance during assessed performance. Recordings are single fixed-camera; USBs encrypted.

Boundaries June 2026 (AQA, published 13 Aug 2026), max 200: A* 157 = 78.5%, A 142 = 71.0%. Notional: written 56/80, internal practical 53/60, external practical 49/60.
