Drama (Pearson Edexcel option - board not confirmed by LAET)

Pearson Edexcel · 9DR0 (Advanced GCE in Drama and Theatre; spec Issue 6, August 2025)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 1: Devising (9DR0/01) - NEA, internally assessed and externally moderated; portfolio 60 (AO1 40, AO4 20) plus devised performance or design realisation 20 (AO2)coursework; portfolio 2500-3000 words or 12-14 min8040% (scaled x1.5 to 120)
Component 2: Text in Performance (9DR0/02) - NEA, externally assessed by visiting examiner or recording; group 36 plus monologue or duologue 24, all AO2monologue 2-3 min, duologue 5-6 min, group from 6 min6020% (scaling x1)
Component 3: Theatre Makers in Practice (9DR0/03) written exam - Section A live theatre evaluation 20 (AO4), Section B page to stage 36 (AO3), Section C interpreting a text 24 (AO3)2h 30m8040% (scaled x1.5 to 120)
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Create and develop ideas to communicate meaning, connecting dramatic theory and practice20% (all in Component 1)
AO2Apply theatrical skills to realise artistic intentions in live performance30% (Component 1 10, Component 2 20)
AO3Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of how drama and theatre is developed and performed30% (all in Component 3)
AO4Analyse and evaluate their own work and the work of others20% (Component 1 10, Component 3 10)
What the top band demands
  • Grids run Level 1 to Level 5, the top level being labelled Sophisticated. Portfolio AO1 Level 5 (17-20) needs accomplished use of research, contexts and live theatre informing perceptive decisions.
  • Portfolio AO1 second strand at Level 5 needs sophisticated knowledge of the chosen practitioner and perceptive connections when applying their methods to the student's own practice.
  • Portfolio AO4 Level 5 (17-20) needs accomplished analysis of the student's personal contribution and perceptive evaluation, with analysis and evaluation fully balanced.
  • Section C Level 5 (20-24) rewards a perceptive director's concept connected to the text, practitioner method applied to the specific element named, and research into original performance conditions feeding the concept.
  • Section B designer answer at Level 5 (16-18) needs sophisticated interpretation of the unseen extract and perceptive understanding of how theatrical elements communicate meaning.
  • Component 2 top-band design work is integral to the creative process, developed across rehearsals and clearly tied to genre, style and the playwright's intentions.
What separates it from the band below
  • There is no director route in the NEA, yet every candidate writes as a director in Section C for 24 of the paper's 80 marks.
  • Section B has no choice: one answer as a performer and one as a designer, on an unseen extract, and the text may not be taken in.
  • Only Section C allows a clean copy of the text in the exam room; Section A forbids musicals and scores zero for writing about a Section B or C text.
  • Component 2 is externally examined while Component 1 is teacher-marked - the opposite pairing to AQA, so internal standardisation matters most on devising.
  • Timing is mechanical: under-length work is penalised proportionally after marking, and examiners simply stop marking at the maximum time.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Summer 2025 Component 1: centre marking at the top was lenient, with work given Level 5 really sitting at Level 4 - repeated from the previous year.
  • Portfolios well short of the word limit lacked the depth needed for upper levels, and continuous prose instead of the six set statements drifted into description.
  • Component 3 Section A: over-reliance on the 500 words of notes produced hurried prepared essays that addressed the given statement only in passing.
  • Section B: failure to embed whole-text examples restricted work to the lower levels, flagged as worse this series; long biographical introductions wasted time.
  • Section C: original performance conditions stayed an add-on, and thin practitioner knowledge produced a repeated handful of methods rather than a framework.
Surprises from another board
  • Three different texts and two different practitioners are required across the qualification, and choices must be submitted to Pearson.
  • The live performance statement deadline moved to 1 May in Issue 6, effective from September 2025.
  • The Component 1 duologue option is new: first teaching September 2025, first assessment 2027.

Non-exam assessment Components 1 and 2 are NEA. The portfolio needs sufficient direct supervision; teachers may not write any of it; feedback is one draft, once, and extra feedback must be recorded on the authentication sheet both sign. Performances are recorded unedited.

Boundaries June 2026 (Pearson), max scaled 300: A* 264 = 88.0%, A 242 = 80.7%. June 2025: A* 267 = 89.0%, A 243 = 81.0%. Notional raw 2026: Paper 01 70/80, Paper 02 54/60, Paper 03 70/80.

Mathematics

Pearson Edexcel · 9MA0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Mathematics, Specification Issue 4, February 2020

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Pure Mathematics 1 (9MA0/01)2 hours10033.33%
Paper 2: Pure Mathematics 2 (9MA0/02)2 hours10033.33%
Paper 3: Statistics and Mechanics (9MA0/03), Section A Statistics and Section B Mechanics2 hours10033.33%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Use and apply standard techniques: select and carry out routine procedures, recall facts and definitions48-52% of the A level; 16.00-17.33% on each of the three papers
AO2Reason, interpret and communicate: rigorous argument and proof, deduction, validity, explanation, correct notation23-27% of the A level; 8.66-10% on Papers 1 and 2, 5.66-7.00% on Paper 3
AO3Solve problems and model: translate contexts, interpret and evaluate solutions, build, use and refine models23-27% of the A level; 6.33-7.67% on Papers 1 and 2, 10.33-11.67% on Paper 3
What the top band demands
  • Three mark types. M marks reward knowing a method and attempting it. A marks are accuracy marks awarded only if the relevant M marks were earned. B marks are unconditional accuracy marks.
  • Because A marks sit downstream of M marks, one early arithmetic slip in a long question typically leaves the M marks intact but forfeits every A mark after it, losing roughly half the available credit.
  • Follow-through (ft) lets a later mark stand on an earlier wrong value, but marks tagged cao (correct answer only) or cso (correct solution only) need an error-free answer or an error-free solution respectively.
  • Working earns credit. Quote a learnt formula first and small substitution slips still score the method mark; if the formula is not quoted the mark comes only by implication from flawless working.
  • Where a calculator warning or a printed answer appears, full working is required; where an exact answer or surd form is asked for, resorting to rounded decimals normally loses marks.
  • Misreads that do not simplify the question cost two A or B marks in the affected part; isw means correct work followed by wrong statements is ignored, so do not spoil a right answer.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO2 plus AO3 are 46-54% of the A level. Edexcel tags every mark in the mark scheme with an AO code (1.1b, 2.1, 3.1a), so top-band loss is directly auditable.
  • Conclusions that answer the question actually asked: hypothesis tests, proofs and modelling comments repeatedly lose the final mark for a vague or absent conclusion.
  • Distinguishing a limitation of a model from a limitation on a value; examiners flagged this specific confusion in Summer 2025.
  • Paper 3 is the AO3-heavy paper (10.33-11.67%), combining contextual modelling, mechanics assumptions and the prescribed large data set.
  • Calculator discipline: knowing when technology is permitted but working must still be shown, and when exact form is compulsory.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Paper 1, Summer 2025: clear conclusions matching the question were needed at 2(b), 4(b) and 10(b); learners confused the limitation of a model with a limitation on a value.
  • Paper 1, Summer 2025: inverse-function coordinate work (reflecting in y = x) produced very few correct responses and successfully discriminated between stronger and weaker learners.
  • Paper 2, Summer 2025: overreliance on calculator technology, with a routine cubic factorisation causing unnecessary difficulty and many learners confusing factorising with solving.
  • Paper 2, Summer 2025: full working is required to solve quadratic or higher-order equations where calculator warnings are present, for example 8(c) and 15(a).
  • Paper 1, Summer 2025: demand ramped up sharply between 6(c) and 8; time was not an issue, so the losses were understanding and communication, not pace.
Surprises from another board
  • Paper 3 statistics assumes familiarity with Pearson's prescribed large data set; questions are deliberately designed to advantage learners who studied it.
  • Each mark in the published mark scheme carries an AO strand code, so departments can audit AO2 and AO3 loss question by question.
  • Calculators are permitted on all three papers and the Mathematical Formulae and Statistical Tables booklet is provided.

Boundaries June 2026: A* 254/300 = 84.7%, A 210 = 70.0%. June 2025: A* 258/300 = 86.0%, A 214 = 71.3%. The A*-to-A gap was 44 marks in both series.

Further Mathematics

Pearson Edexcel · 9FM0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Further Mathematics, Specification Issue 4, June 2023

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Core Pure Mathematics 1 (9FM0/01) - mandatory1 hour 30 minutes7525%
Paper 2: Core Pure Mathematics 2 (9FM0/02) - mandatory1 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 1 paper 3A: Further Pure Mathematics 11 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 1 paper 3B: Further Statistics 11 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 1 paper 3C: Further Mechanics 11 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 1 paper 3D: Decision Mathematics 11 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 2 paper 4A: Further Pure Mathematics 2 (only with 3A)1 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 2 paper 4B: Further Statistics 2 (only with 3B)1 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 2 paper 4C: Further Mechanics 2 (only with 3C)1 hour 30 minutes7525%
Option 2 paper 4D: Decision Mathematics 2 (only with 3D)1 hour 30 minutes7525%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Use and apply standard techniques: select and carry out routine procedures, recall facts and definitions48-52% of the A level; 11.67-13.00% on every paper in every route
AO2Reason, interpret and communicate: rigorous argument and proof, deduction, validity, explanation, correct notationAt least 15% overall; per paper 3.00-4.33% (Further Mechanics 1) up to 8.33-9.67% (Further Pure 2)
AO3Solve problems and model: translate contexts, interpret and evaluate solutions, build, use and refine modelsAt least 15% overall; per paper 3.00-4.33% (Further Pure 2, Decision 1) up to 8.67-10.00% (Further Mechanics 1)
What the top band demands
  • Same mark mechanics as 9MA0: M marks for attempting a method, A marks conditional on the relevant M marks, B marks unconditional. Seventy-five marks in ninety minutes leaves little recovery time.
  • Where a question names a method, only that method earns credit. Summer 2025 examiners flagged learners who ignored the required method of differences, or who did not use the result they had been given.
  • Printed and show-that answers require enough detail to warrant every mark. Circular reasoning that assumes the general result in order to verify a particular case is not creditworthy proof.
  • Completeness marks are lost routinely: not giving all four complex roots, not writing y equals, not stating a conclusion at the end of a proof or a test.
  • Cancelling a factor without considering the zero case, for example dividing by sinh x, loses the B mark. Reaching an expression for e to the x is not reaching x equals ln.
  • Calculator use must not replace mathematical communication. Storing values and writing arrow-A notation instead of setting out the algebra was criticised in Further Mechanics 1.
What separates it from the band below
  • Route choice moves the assessment load: Further Mechanics 1 carries 8.67-10.00% AO3, while Further Pure 2 and Decision 1 carry only 3.00-4.33%, with AO2 running the opposite way.
  • Route choice moves the A* threshold by 13 marks out of 300 in June 2026 and 25 in June 2025, a measurable strategic decision.
  • Rigour and signposting on Core Pure: examiners saw work with no explicit indication of what was being attempted, and minimal conclusions that did not secure the final mark.
  • Flexibility of representation, especially in Further Mechanics, where the strongest learners work fluently in both vectors and magnitude-and-direction rather than converting to a preferred form.
  • The genuinely hard end of each paper sits in the last three or four questions; Core Pure 1 2025 named questions 7 to 10 as the most demanding.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Core Pure 1, Summer 2025: marks lost unnecessarily by not finding all four complex numbers, not writing y equals, and giving no conclusion at question 9(i)(b).
  • Core Pure 2, Summer 2025: question 1 responses lacked rigorous structure, many gave minimal or no acceptable conclusion, and there was a tendency to circular reasoning.
  • Further Mechanics 1, Summer 2025: the most successful learners work with vectors and with magnitudes and directions; those lacking that flexibility err while converting the information.
  • Further Pure 1, Summer 2025: a sign error trebled an integral instead of dividing it and went unnoticed, which examiners described as weak number sense.
  • Decision 1, Summer 2025: the paper was accessible on questions 1 to 4, with the simplex and linear programming questions 5 and 7 differentiating the most able.
Surprises from another board
  • Only ten legal option pairs exist: any two Option 1 papers, or a matched Option 1 with Option 2 pair such as 3A with 4A.
  • Each route is awarded on its own boundaries, and a student may sit extra optional papers, with the combination producing the best grade used.
  • AO2 and AO3 are floors, at least 15% each, not the 23-27% ranges used in 9MA0, so AO1 dominance varies by route.

Boundaries June 2026 A* out of 300 by route: 3D+4D 262 (87.3%) lowest to 3A+3B 275 (91.7%) highest. June 2025 ranged from 3D+4D 241 (80.3%) to 3A+3C 266 (88.7%).

Computer Science

OCR · H446 - OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Computer Science, specification version 2.6, 2023 (first teaching 2015)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 01: Computer systems (H446/01), written paper, no calculators2 hours 30 minutes14040%
Component 02: Algorithms and programming (H446/02), written paper, Sections A and B, no calculators, synoptic2 hours 30 minutes14040%
Component 03 (moderated upload) or 04 (moderated postal): Programming project, non-exam assessment, synopticnot timed - internally assessed, OCR moderated7020%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of principles and concepts: abstraction, logic, algorithms, data representation35% of the A level; 21% on component 01, 15% on component 02, 0% on the project
AO2Apply knowledge and understanding of principles and concepts, including analysing problems in computational terms30% of the A level; 9% on component 01, 18% on component 02, 3% on the project
AO3Design, program and evaluate systems that solve problems, making reasoned judgements and presenting conclusions35% of the A level; 10% on component 01, 7% on component 02, 17% on the project
What the top band demands
  • Starred extended-response questions are marked in three bands. The top band needs accurate description, explicit application to the given scenario, and a justified conclusion; knowledge alone caps a response in the middle band.
  • Section B of H446/02 is a single scenario with largely higher-tariff questions. Fluency in object-oriented programming, including instantiating classes and writing methods for a scenario, is the gate to it.
  • Big O work must go beyond stating time and space complexity: examiners wanted explicit links to the scenario data, for instance noticing the data was already ordered before recommending binary search.
  • Data structures are assessed as application, not recall. Stacks, trees, graphs and linked lists must be traced, modified and debugged, with AO1 knowledge alone scoring poorly.
  • Answers may be written in any pseudocode style whose meaning a competent programmer could reasonably infer, and minor syntax slips are not penalised; clarity of algorithmic logic is what is marked.
  • The project's notional A* boundary is 63 of 70 marks (90.0%), far above either written paper, so an A* candidate is effectively expected to reach near-full marks on the NEA.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO3 is 35% of the A level and 17 of its 20 percentage points sit in the programming project, so the NEA, not the exams, is where A* candidates separate.
  • H446/02 carries the heaviest AO2 load at 18%, rewarding applied computational thinking and code manipulation rather than recall of definitions.
  • Precision of terminology: examiners reported that vague definitions and generic answers not applied to the context were the main mark-losers on component 01.
  • Comparison questions require both sides plus a judgement; giving only one side was a named weakness in Summer 2025.
  • Practical programming experience underpins everything, since both papers are written but assume extensive hands-on object-oriented and data-structure work.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • H446/02, Summer 2025: strong candidates interpreted, modified, debugged and wrote pseudocode and showed clear object-oriented understanding; weaker ones showed AO1 knowledge of stacks and linked lists but little AO2 application.
  • H446/02, Summer 2025: most described linear and binary search with Big O complexities, but fewer linked explicitly to the scenario, so most landed top Level 2 or bottom Level 3.
  • H446/02, Summer 2025: on bubble sort, fewer candidates reached full marks; the temporary variable for swapping and the swap-flag optimisation were far less frequently cited.
  • H446/01, Summer 2025: definitions were at times not clearly expressed and key terms not used; generic responses not applied to the context cost marks.
  • H446/01, Summer 2025: weaker extended responses showed only basic knowledge, and comparison questions often received only one side of the comparison.
Surprises from another board
  • JCQ (revision two, 30 April 2025): unacknowledged AI use is malpractice; even acknowledged AI use earns no marks where criteria were not independently met.
  • OCR (blog updated 4 February 2026) permits AI for ideas, debugging prompts and reflection, never worked solutions; AI can never be sole marker.
  • No on-screen practical programming exam, and no Turing machines, regular expressions or Backus-Naur form, unlike AQA. Calculators are banned.

Non-exam assessment Programming project, 70 marks, 20%, internally marked on best-fit bands and OCR moderated: Analysis 10 (AO2.2), Design 15 (AO3.1), Developing the coded solution 25 (AO3.2, iterative development 15 plus testing to inform development 10), Evaluation 20 (AO3.3).

Boundaries June 2026 overall: A* 289/350 = 82.6%, A 254 = 72.6%. Notional components: 01 112/140 (80.0%), 02 114/140 (81.4%), project 63/70 (90.0%). June 2025 overall A* was 291/350 (83.1%).

Physics

OCR Physics A (H556) · H556 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Physics A (specification version 3.0, 2026; first assessment June 2017). Total qualification time 360 hours.

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
H556/01 Modelling physics - modules 1, 2, 3, 5; Section A 15 multiple-choice marks, Section B 85 marks2 hours 15 minutes10037% of the A level
H556/02 Exploring physics - modules 1, 2, 4, 6; Section A 15 multiple-choice marks, Section B 85 marks2 hours 15 minutes10037% of the A level
H556/03 Unified physics - all modules 1-6, fully synoptic, no multiple choice1 hour 30 minutes7026% of the A level
H556/04 Practical Endorsement in physics - non-exam assessment, teacher assessedcarried out across the two-year course0reported separately; 0% of the A level grade
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of scientific ideas, processes, techniques and procedures.31-34% overall; 13-14% from each of 01 and 02, 5-6% from 03 (shares of the whole A level)
AO2Apply that knowledge in theoretical and practical contexts and when handling qualitative and quantitative data.40-43% overall; 15-16% from each of 01 and 02, 10-11% from 03
AO3Analyse, interpret and evaluate information, ideas and evidence; judge, conclude, refine practical design.25-28% overall; 8-9% from each of 01 and 02, 9-10% from 03 - so more than a third of AO3 sits in the 70-mark synoptic paper
What the top band demands
  • Maths: at least 40% of written marks must be Level 2 or above. OCR excludes simple substitution and GCSE-style structured maths; it counts choosing the equation or data, multi-area problem solving and logarithmic work.
  • Significant figures and working: an answer below 2 sf is penalised once per paper; extra figures are not penalised. C marks need visible working or a correct route, B marks need the specific point stated.
  • Extended response: two levels-marked questions per written paper, 6 marks each. Level 3 needs a valid conclusion with sound, detailed reasoning plus a "well-developed line of reasoning", clear and logically structured (OCR mark scheme).
  • Unfamiliar contexts: H556/03 weights AO2 and AO3 hardest and any question may cross topics. Generic recall that ignores the given scenario is capped low; examiners say deciding what to leave out matters too.
  • Practical writing: planning and evaluation answers need named instruments, stated measurements, controlled variables and an explicit graph, with the gradient or intercept tied to the quantity being found.
  • Precision of language: exact definitions of key terms, correct SI prefixes, correct units in every stage, and clean separation of precision, resolution and accuracy.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO3 is 25-28% of the marks, and roughly 9-10 percentage points of it sit in H556/03 alone - a 70-mark paper decides most of the analysis and evaluation grade.
  • The 40% Level 2 maths floor is the highest of the three sciences, four times biology's 10%, and it is met by questions that require choice of route, not substitution.
  • The two 6-mark levels questions per paper (about 12% of the written total) reward structure and completeness; strong candidates lose them by answering only part of the prompt.
  • Stretch and challenge questions are written specifically to differentiate the most able; OCR says they "support the awarding of A* grade at A level".
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Summer 2025, H556/01: weaker candidates re-used answers from previous mark schemes without adapting them to an unfamiliar context, and did not address every requirement of a levels question.
  • Summer 2025, H556/01: strong performance depended on showing each step in "show that" questions, naming instruments, and using the Data, Formulae and Relationships booklet carefully.
  • Summer 2025, H556/02: candidates could not reliably distinguish precision, resolution and accuracy, drew poor lines of best fit through a false origin, and used too narrow a range for gradients.
  • Summer 2025, H556/03: candidates handled mathematical questions more confidently than descriptive ones; generic descriptions that ignored the question's context failed, alongside SI prefix errors and haphazard working.
  • Summer 2025, H556/01 and /03: disorganised presentation of thinking, trigonometry errors, and failure to rearrange formulae were recurring causes of lost marks among otherwise able candidates.
Surprises from another board
  • OCR publishes no percentage for practical marks in its papers; AQA states at least 15% for its sciences, the boards' common DfE-derived figure.
  • The significant-figure penalty is applied once per paper, not per question - so one habit costs one mark, not many.
  • OCR's AO table gives shares of the whole A level; AQA's gives shares of each paper. The two tables are not directly comparable.

Non-exam assessment H556/04 Practical Endorsement is teacher assessed against the common CPAC over at least 12 activities (PAG1-PAG12); Pass or Not Classified appears on the certificate and never affects the grade. Module 1.1 skills are assessed indirectly in all three papers.

Boundaries June 2025 (OCR, published 14 August 2025): A* 206/270 = 76.3%, A 179 = 66.3%, E 69 = 25.6%. June 2024: A* 207/270 = 76.7%. The Practical Endorsement is excluded from the 270.

AOAssessesWeight
AO1Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of scientific ideas, processes, techniques and procedures.Ofqual band 30-35%. AQA 30-35% overall (P1 44-48%, P2 23-27%, P3 28-32% of each paper). OCR 31-34% (01 13-14%, 02 13-14%, 03 5-6% of the A level).
AO2Apply knowledge in theoretical and practical contexts and when handling qualitative and quantitative data.Ofqual band 40-45%. AQA 40-45% overall (P1 30-34%, P2 52-56%, P3 35-39% of each paper). OCR 40-43% (01 15-16%, 02 15-16%, 03 10-11% of the A level).
AO3Analyse, interpret and evaluate information, ideas and evidence; judge, conclude, refine practical design.Ofqual band 25-30%. AQA 25-30% overall, highest in Paper 3 at 31-35% of that paper. OCR 25-28%, with 9-10 of those points in the 70-mark Unified biology paper.
What the top band demands
  • Maths is only 10% of marks at Level 2 or above, but it is where able candidates lose most: statistics, logarithmic scales, standard form, rounding, magnification, rates, and AQA's 15-mark critical analysis.
  • AQA's 25-mark essay is levels-marked. Its top band (21-25, "Extended Abstract") needs a holistic answer linking several topics to the theme, no significant errors, and for top marks reading beyond the specification.
  • OCR has no essay. Its extended response is 6-mark Level of Response questions, two in each of papers 01 and 02, where Level 3 needs every strand of the question answered with linked, structured reasoning.
  • Precision of terminology decides marks on both boards: cells versus tissues (sieve tube element, not phloem), structure explicitly tied to function, and on AQA abbreviations only where the specification itself abbreviates them.
  • Unfamiliar contexts: both boards reward answers that use the table headings, axes and stem data given, and reject rehearsed evaluation phrases such as "no stats test" where they do not apply.
  • Units, significant figures and consistency with the supplied data: means, relative values and extrapolations must be consistent with the figures printed in the question.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO3 is a quarter to nearly a third of the marks and concentrates in Paper 3 on both boards (AQA 31-35% of that paper; OCR's Unified biology 9-10 points).
  • AQA's essay alone is 25 of 260 marks - 9.6% of the A level - and only about 3% of candidates reached its top band in June 2023.
  • Marks are lost to imprecise expression and GCSE-depth answers rather than missing knowledge; examiners on both boards report this as the main ceiling on strong candidates.
  • Transferring practical understanding to unfamiliar apparatus, indicators or statistical tests, instead of reciting a rehearsed required practical.
  • Time control: AQA examiners link over-long essays to unattempted questions elsewhere on Paper 3.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • AQA June 2023, 7402/3: rote evaluation phrases appeared regardless of relevance, stem information was ignored, and "probability", "chance" and "significant" were misused; maths questions had the highest non-attempt rate.
  • AQA June 2023, 7402/3: essays were unusually long, only 3% reached the extended-abstract band and 0.05% scored 25; added introductions and conclusions earned nothing and cost time.
  • AQA June 2023, 7402/1 and /2: recall was substituted for context, sometimes at GCSE depth; unspecified abbreviations such as DCT and PCr were rejected, and imprecise terminology blocked marking points.
  • OCR Summer 2025, H420/01: candidates could state a null hypothesis but chose the wrong t-test and degrees of freedom; practical knowledge did not transfer to a hydrogen carbonate indicator task.
  • OCR Summer 2025, H420/03: weaker answers lacked depth on practical questions, mishandled extrapolation and choice of units, and could not use the images and data supplied in the paper.
Surprises from another board
  • AQA prints AO percentages per paper; OCR prints them as shares of the whole A level. Side by side, both get misread.
  • Only AQA has the 25-mark synoptic essay and a 15-mark comprehension; only OCR has 15 multiple-choice marks in each of papers 01 and 02.
  • AQA's total is 260 scaled marks with x1 scaling factors; OCR's is 270 raw marks summed, so per-mark value differs between the boards.

Non-exam assessment Practical Endorsement is teacher assessed against the common CPAC across at least 12 activities, giving Pass or Not Classified on the certificate; it never affects the grade. AQA states at least 15% of written marks assess practical work.

Boundaries June 2025: AQA 7402 A* 192/260 = 73.8% (A 165 = 63.5%); OCR H420 A* 187/270 = 69.3% (A 161 = 59.6%). OCR's A* was also 187/270 in June 2024. The endorsement is excluded from both totals.

AOAssessesWeight
AO1Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of scientific ideas, processes, techniques and procedures.Ofqual band 30-35%. AQA 30% overall (P1 30%, P2 30%, P3 32% of each paper). OCR 31-34% (01 13-14%, 02 13-14%, 03 5-6% of the A level).
AO2Apply knowledge in theoretical and practical contexts and when handling qualitative and quantitative data.Ofqual band 40-45%. AQA 45% overall (P1 48%, P2 48%, P3 34% of each paper). OCR 40-44% (01 15-16%, 02 15-16%, 03 10-12% of the A level).
AO3Analyse, interpret and evaluate information, ideas and evidence; judge, conclude, refine practical design.Ofqual band 25-30%. AQA 25% overall but 34% of Paper 3 - the same as AO2 there. OCR 25-28%, with 9-10 points in the 70-mark Unified chemistry paper.
What the top band demands
  • Maths: 20% of marks must be Level 2 or above - double biology, half physics. It lands on moles and titrations, pH and Ka, Kc and Kp, Born-Haber, rate equations and percentage yield.
  • Setting out calculations is marked, not just the answer. Unstructured working with unlabelled numbers scattered across the page loses the intermediate marks even when the final value is right - OCR's most repeated criticism.
  • Significant figures and units: answers must be given to the number of figures the question specifies, with correct unit conversions (g to mg, cm3 to dm3) shown rather than assumed.
  • Extended response is levels-marked. OCR has two levels questions in each of H432/01 and H432/02; AQA has one on Paper 3. Level 3 needs a sequence of clear, precise, linked points covering the indicative content.
  • Definitions must be exact and distinguished: transition metal complex versus transition metal, monodentate ligand, nucleophile; electron configurations of the ion, not just of the atom; cis/trans assignment, not just a drawing.
  • Unfamiliar contexts: writing equations for unseen reactions from information supplied, using clues planted in the stem, and interpreting a novel titration or spectrum is where AO2 and AO3 marks sit.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO3 is 25-28% and concentrates in Paper 3 on both boards - 34% of AQA's Paper 3, and OCR's Unified chemistry is explicitly the application-heavy component.
  • OCR Chemistry A's A* boundary has sat at 90% of the total in both 2024 and 2025, so a handful of significant-figure, unit or presentation slips costs the grade outright.
  • Clear, labelled, staged calculation layout - OCR has flagged the same unstructured mole-calculation fault in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports.
  • Explaining rather than describing: naming a shape or trend without the bonding or structure reason, and drawing apparatus without the critical labelled detail, both cap strong candidates.
  • Applying method knowledge to novel apparatus and novel reactions instead of reproducing a rehearsed required practical.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • OCR Summer 2025, H432/01: weaker candidates did not set calculations out clearly or give answers to the specified number of significant figures, and could not apply learning to unfamiliar situations.
  • OCR Summer 2025, H432/01: common failures were ion electron configurations, the labelled standard electrode potential diagram, buffer mass calculations and describing buffer action.
  • OCR Summer 2025, H432/03: unstructured mole calculations with unlabelled numbers scattered across the page, explicitly noted as the same issue reported in 2023 and 2024.
  • OCR Summer 2025, H432/03: candidates could not write equations for unfamiliar reactions from supplied information, or use the clues placed within the questions.
  • AQA June 2023, 7405/3: the commonest causes of lost marks were lack of precision in describing calculation steps and loose chemical terminology; few reached Level 3 on the levels question.
Surprises from another board
  • OCR Chemistry A's A* has sat at 243/270 (90.0%) in both June 2024 and June 2025 - about ten percentage points above AQA's.
  • AQA puts 30 multiple-choice marks in Paper 3; OCR puts 15 in each of papers 01 and 02 and none in Paper 03.
  • AQA's AO figures are shares of each paper, OCR's of the whole A level, so the tables look more different than they are.

Non-exam assessment Practical Endorsement is teacher assessed against the common CPAC across at least 12 activities, giving Pass or Not Classified on the certificate; it never affects the grade. AQA states at least 15% of written marks assess practical work.

Boundaries June 2025: AQA 7405 A* 239/300 = 79.7% (A 197 = 65.7%); OCR H432 A* 243/270 = 90.0% (A 213 = 78.9%). OCR's A* was also 243/270 in June 2024. The endorsement is excluded from both totals.

OCR · H481 - Cambridge OCR Level 3 Advanced GCE in Geography (first teaching 2016; spec version 2.1)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Physical systems (H481/01)1 hour 30 minutes6622%
Human interactions (H481/02)1 hour 30 minutes6622%
Geographical debates (H481/03) - includes synoptic assessment2 hours 30 minutes10836%
Investigative geography (H481/04 or 05) - non-exam assessment, includes synoptic assessmentno timed assessment; 3,000-4,000 word report6020%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge and understanding of places, environments, concepts, processes, interactions and change at varied scales34% overall (01: 10, 02: 10, 03: 14, NEA: 0)
AO2Apply that understanding in new contexts to interpret, analyse and evaluate geographical information and issues38% overall (01: 9, 02: 9, 03: 20, NEA: 0)
AO3Use quantitative, qualitative and fieldwork skills to investigate, analyse evidence, build arguments and conclude28% overall (01: 3, 02: 3, 03: 2, NEA: 20)
What the top band demands
  • The 33-mark essays on Paper 3 need a planned, balanced argument that answers the exact command word, weighs named factors against one another, and ends in a substantiated judgement rather than a summary.
  • Place-specific detail is written into the levelled mark schemes. Naming a scheme or location is not enough: candidates must say what it does and then judge its effect.
  • The 12-mark synoptic questions require an explicit, process-level bridge from an Option topic to compulsory Component 01 or 02 content - a named transfer, not a vague gesture at links.
  • Top answers quantify. Examiners recommend a handful of well-chosen current figures to give a discussion authority, and want interpretation of statistics rather than only correct calculation.
  • The 16-mark starred responses must substantiate evaluation - scale, permanence, reversibility, ease of implementation, prior success - and must address both named elements of a two-part question.
  • The independent investigation needs a question pinned to one specification bullet, justified sampling, hypothesis-led statistics shown in the main body, and a hedged conclusion tested against its own evaluation.
What separates it from the band below
  • Synopticity is concentrated in Geographical debates, 36% of the A level, through 12-mark synoptic questions and 33-mark essays. Cross-component transfer is the scarce skill.
  • AO3 is 28% of the qualification and 20 of those percentage points sit in the NEA alone, making coursework the largest single skills block.
  • Statistical interpretation, not calculation. Examiners report candidates run Spearman's rank or standard deviation competently then cannot explain what the result shows.
  • Centres must certify at least four days of fieldwork across the A level course; the independent investigation may itself contribute to those four days.
  • Required quantitative skills are named: mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, standard deviation, chi-squared, Spearman's rank, Mann-Whitney U, t-test, lines of best fit, sampling and measurement error.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • Summer 2025: pre-learned case studies were dumped into the 33-mark essays, with some candidates effectively rewriting the question to justify the material they had memorised.
  • Paper 2 answers repeatedly reached only the first AO2 idea, ranking players by influence, instead of showing players interacting and operating across scales.
  • Paper 1: able candidates asserted that one factor mattered more without substantiating it, and many answered only half of a two-part question.
  • NEA moderators found statistical tests run with no stated hypothesis, no data and no working, and Spearman's rank applied to fewer than ten paired values.
  • NEA marking was more often generous than severe: over-long, poorly referenced reports were still awarded upper Level 3 by centres.
Surprises from another board
  • Paper 1's 2025 A* notional boundary was 45/66 while Paper 2's was 53/66; component boundaries are illustrative and the grade rests on the 300-mark total.
  • Sand dune succession sits outside the specification; moderators say rule such NEA titles out at proposal stage, not after the fieldwork.
  • Geographical debates is 36% of the A level, more than either short paper, yet carries only 2 percentage points of AO3.

Non-exam assessment Investigative geography (04/05): independent 3,000-4,000 word report, 60 marks, 20%, six marked sections, internally assessed and OCR-moderated. Teachers may guide on title and proposal only - no model answers, templates, or provisional marks shared.

Boundaries June 2025, H481 all options, 300-mark total: A* 239 (79.7%), A 210 (70.0%), E 95 (31.7%). Notional components: 45/66, 53/66, 87/108, 54/60.

Politics

Pearson Edexcel · 9PL0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Politics (Issue 1, March 2017)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Component 1: UK Politics and Core Political Ideas (9PL0/01)2 hours8433 1/3%
Component 2: UK Government and Non-core Political Ideas (9PL0/02)2 hours8433 1/3%
Component 3: Comparative Politics - USA (9PL0/3A) or Global (9PL0/3B)2 hours8433 1/3%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge and understanding of political institutions, processes, concepts, theories and issues35% overall (C1 11.1, C2 11.1, C3 12.7)
AO2Analyse politics and political information, including parallels, connections, similarities and differences35% overall (C1 11.1, C2 11.1, C3 12.7)
AO3Evaluate political information, construct arguments, make substantiated judgements and draw conclusions30% overall (C1 11.1, C2 11.1, C3 7.9)
What the top band demands
  • The 30-mark source answers must pair naturally competing arguments taken from the source and evaluate within each pair; handling one whole side then the other caps AO2 and AO3.
  • Ignoring the source costs more than copying it: answers argued from own knowledge alone can earn AO1 but no AO2 or AO3 marks at all.
  • The 24-mark ideas answers must be thematic, use named thinkers to establish divisions between strands, and treat each strand as internally nuanced rather than monolithic.
  • Component 3 Section B requires at least one comparative theory integrated into the analysis of both countries. A label bolted on at the start or end stays at Level 3.
  • Conclusions must answer the question, justify why that judgement follows, and place it in the current political situation. A restatement of paragraph themes is a summary, not a conclusion.
  • Judgements must be argued towards, not announced. Examiners treat a conclusion that surprises the reader as evidence that AO3 was never developed.
What separates it from the band below
  • Component 3 is AO1 and AO2 heavy at 12.7% each and AO3 light at 7.9%, so comparative analysis rather than evaluation wins the USA or Global paper.
  • Currency of examples is rewarded to the exam date. June 2025 credited the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling on the meaning of sex under the Equality Act.
  • Named thinkers appear in nearly every script now, so mere compliance no longer differentiates; using a thinker to establish a division between strands does.
  • Theory integration is a hard cap. On Global, an answer referring to only one named comparative theory cannot exceed Level 1.
  • The USA option uses rational, cultural and structural approaches; the Global option uses realism, liberalism, anarchy, security dilemma and complex interdependence.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025: introductions had become sharper but conclusions were weaker, often working as summaries rather than as judgements.
  • Ideas answers were most often the short or incomplete ones, and pre-prepared essays were submitted in place of answers to the question actually set.
  • Divisions were drawn too starkly: Third Way socialism described as wholly individualistic, classical liberals as simply anti-democratic.
  • Using a different theme as the evaluation of the current theme was flagged as not evaluation at all.
  • Accuracy errors cost strong candidates: a UK 'Bill of Rights', Dobbs placed before Obergefell, and justices labelled Republican or Democrat.
Surprises from another board
  • Component 3 carries only 7.9% AO3. The comparative paper rewards analysis far more than evaluation, the reverse of the usual assumption.
  • The 12-mark questions need no introduction or conclusion; examiners say this essay furniture earns nothing and wastes time.
  • Nothing restricts a comparative topic to one direction, so similarities and differences must both be prepared for every topic.

Boundaries June 2025, 9PL0, 252-mark subject total: A* 177 (70.2%) for both 01+02+3A and 01+02+3B; A 157 (3A) or 158 (3B); E 66 or 68. Notional papers: 56, 61, 60, 60 out of 84.

Psychology

AQA · 7182 - AQA A-level Psychology (first teaching 2015)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Introductory Topics in Psychology (7182/1) - four 24-mark sections2 hours9633.3%
Paper 2: Psychology in Context (7182/2) - Sections A and B 24 marks each, Section C Research Methods 48 marks2 hours9633.3%
Paper 3: Issues and Options in Psychology (7182/3) - compulsory Issues and Debates plus three options, 24 marks each2 hours9633.3%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of scientific ideas, processes, techniques and procedures30-33% overall (P1 11-14, P2 7-10, P3 9-12)
AO2Apply knowledge and understanding to novel scenarios, including practical, theoretical and mathematical contexts30-33% overall (P1 6-9, P2 16-19, P3 5-8)
AO3Analyse, interpret and evaluate scientific information, ideas and evidence, making judgements and drawing conclusions36-38% overall (P1 12-14, P2 7-9, P3 15-17)
What the top band demands
  • AO3 is the largest objective at 36-38%, so top-band scripts spend their words on elaborated evaluation with counterargument rather than on additional description.
  • The 16-mark extended responses split 6 marks AO1 to 10 marks AO3. Top-band AO3 links each point explicitly to the question and evidences it with named studies carrying identifying detail.
  • Application is stem-dependent. Quoting the scenario without elaborating on it earns nothing, and a 16-marker with high-level content but no application is capped at 12 of 16.
  • Research methods answers must justify choices in context, reasoning from level of measurement and experimental design together, rather than reciting the features of a test.
  • Operationalisation is marked mark by mark: hypotheses lose marks for a vague dependent variable, and graphs lose marks for axes that are unlabelled or unoperationalised.
  • Paper 3 extended answers must engage the interactionist or integrative logic of a model, not treat its components as two separate mini-essays.
What separates it from the band below
  • At least 25-30% of the A level assesses research methods and at least 10% is Level 2 mathematics or above - roughly a third of the qualification.
  • Paper 2 Section C is 48 marks of compulsory research methods, half of that paper, so Paper 2 is where research-methods teaching is actually cashed in.
  • Formulaic PEEL is explicitly named as insufficient for the highest marks; what lifts AO3 is counterargument and elaboration tied to the specific question.
  • Paper 3 carries the heaviest AO3 load at 15-17% of the whole qualification, and low-scoring scripts are those stuck in the lower levels of the 8- and 16-mark schemes.
  • Paper 2 carries AO2 at 16-19% against 5-8% on Paper 3, so novel-scenario application is disproportionately a Paper 2 skill.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025: detailed knowledge sat alongside limited evaluation; students were told to keep description concise so as to leave time for thorough evaluation.
  • Pre-learned answers were diagnosed directly: many justified a non-directional hypothesis by claiming there was no prior research when the stem gave conflicting evidence.
  • Many read p<0.01 as a 1% probability of results being due to chance rather than less than 1%.
  • Peer review and science-as-a-discipline drew the most non-attempts; falsifiability was often explained wrongly and paradigm shifts attributed to a single study.
  • Paper 3 diathesis-stress answers treated diathesis and stress as two separate essays, missing the interactionist point, and some used too little material for 16 marks.
Surprises from another board
  • AO1 is only 30-33% of the A level. AO3 is the biggest objective, yet revision is usually organised around content recall.
  • The inferential statistics, sign test, distributions and probability notation are examinable arithmetic, and 2025 showed significance notation itself misread.
  • Notional component A* boundaries differed by only two marks across the three papers, but only the 288-mark total decides the grade.

Boundaries June 2025, AQA A-level Psychology 7182, 288-mark total: A* 222 (77.1%), A 198 (68.8%), B 163, C 128, D 94, E 60 (20.8%). Notional components: 75/96, 74/96, 73/96.

Economics

AQA (board not confirmed by LAET - AQA form) · 7136 - AQA A-level Economics (spec version 1.3, 29 June 2022)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Markets and market failure (7136/1) - Section A data response 40 marks, Section B essay 40 marks2 hours8033.3%
Paper 2: National and international economy (7136/2) - Section A data response 40 marks, Section B essay 40 marks2 hours8033.3%
Paper 3: Economic principles and issues (7136/3) - Section A multiple choice 30 marks, Section B case study 50 marks2 hours8033.3%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge of terms, concepts, theories and models of how economic agents behave and respond20-23% overall (P1 5-8, P2 5-8, P3 7-10)
AO2Apply knowledge and understanding to economic contexts to show how agents are affected and respond26-29% overall (P1 7-10, P2 7-10, P3 9-12)
AO3Analyse issues within economics, showing understanding of their impact on economic agents26-29% overall (P1 9-11, P2 9-11, P3 6-9)
AO4Evaluate economic arguments using qualitative and quantitative evidence to support informed judgements22-25% overall (P1 7-10, P2 7-10, P3 5-8)
What the top band demands
  • Papers 1 and 2 are two 40-mark halves: one data-response context and one two-part essay. The 25-mark essay part is where Level 5 is won or lost.
  • Level 5 responses judge the likely effectiveness of each policy or argument as they go, then reach a final judgement supported by both theoretical analysis and data from the extracts.
  • Diagrams must do analytical work. Examiners credit diagrams that generate developed chains of reasoning, not diagrams bolted on beside the prose.
  • On Paper 3's case study the level awarded depends partly on effective use of the numerical data: calculating and quoting percentage changes rather than misquoting raw figures.
  • Four-mark data questions require the evidence and then an explanation of how that evidence supports the stated proposition - not one without the other.
  • Marking is holistic within levels of response, so a response strong in analysis but weak in evaluation cannot reach the top level.
What separates it from the band below
  • Quantitative skills are guaranteed at a minimum of 20% of overall A-level marks - 15% at AS - and may be assessed across any assessment objective.
  • Paper 3's 30 multiple-choice marks assess AO1, AO2 and AO3 and quantitative skills but never AO4, so all of that paper's evaluation sits in the 50-mark case study.
  • AO1 is the smallest objective at 20-23%, so roughly three quarters of the marks are application, analysis and evaluation.
  • AO4 is 22-25% but is concentrated in the highest-tariff questions, so weak evaluation costs disproportionately at the top of the range.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025 Paper 1: over 45% of students scored zero on a two-mark calculation, finding the change in India's rice exports rather than in its share of world exports.
  • Paper 3 multiple choice had a mean facility just under 50%, with eight questions at 30% or below and only one above 80%.
  • Paper 3: students quoted extract data inaccurately; those who calculated percentage changes were far better placed to support a judgement.
  • Judgements were frequently stated without support, and low-level responses made little use of the extracts at all.
  • Paper 1: diagrams were usually drawn accurately but incomplete use of them led to simplistic analysis and inadequate evaluation of a maximum price policy.
Surprises from another board
  • Paper 3 contains no essay at all: 30 marks of multiple choice plus one 50-mark case study.
  • Quantitative skills are assessed inside the multiple-choice section, so mathematics cannot be dodged by question choice.
  • Component marks are scaled to the 33.3% weightings before boundaries are applied, giving a 240-mark subject total rather than 240 raw marks taken directly.

Boundaries June 2025, AQA A-level Economics 7136, 240-mark scaled total: A* 177 (73.8%), A 153 (63.8%), B 130, C 107, D 84, E 61 (25.4%). Notional components: 61/80, 60/80, 56/80.

Economics

Pearson Edexcel (board not confirmed by LAET - Economics A form) · 9EC0 - Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Economics A (Issue 2, October 2016)

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Paper 1: Markets and business behaviour (9EC0/01) - Section A multiple choice and short answer, Section B data response, Section C one extended open response from two2 hours10035%
Paper 2: The national and global economy (9EC0/02) - same three-section structure2 hours10035%
Paper 3: Microeconomics and macroeconomics (9EC0/03) - two data response questions, each with a choice of extended open response2 hours10030%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Knowledge of terms, concepts, theories and models of how economic agents behave and respond22-24%
AO2Apply knowledge and understanding to economic contexts to show how agents are affected and respond22-24%
AO3Analyse issues within economics, showing understanding of their impact on economic agents26-28%
AO4Evaluate economic arguments using qualitative and quantitative evidence to make informed judgements26-28%
What the top band demands
  • Extended answers are marked on two separate ladders - KAA covering AO1 to AO3, and EV covering AO4 alone - so strong analysis cannot compensate for weak evaluation.
  • Evaluation must show critical distance: a judgement on the significance, value or extent of the argument, not a summary of the points already made.
  • One thoroughly developed evaluation point can secure all the EV marks on a 10-mark question. Depth beats breadth in the evaluation strand.
  • Effects cannot be used to evaluate a cause; examiners treat that move as answering a different question from the one set.
  • Chains of reasoning need secure, explicit links at every step, and diagrams must be accurate and actually used to derive the argument.
  • Evaluation must be sustained through the whole answer, since Level 3 EV requires sustained critical distance rather than a single strong paragraph.
What separates it from the band below
  • At least 20% of the marks assess quantitative skills, and Section A of Papers 1 and 2 mixes multiple choice with calculation.
  • AO3 and AO4 are the two largest objectives at 26-28% each, so analysis and evaluation together exceed half the qualification.
  • Evaluation allocations vary sharply by tariff: about two marks on an 8-mark examine, four on a 10-mark, six on a 15-mark and nine on a 25-mark question.
  • Because Papers 1 and 2 are weighted 35% and Paper 3 only 30%, the subject total is 335 scaled marks, not 300.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2025 Paper 3: evaluation was the weakest area, with answers summarising or merely concluding instead of reaching a judgement with critical distance.
  • Many candidates offered stock, pre-formulated answers, and discussed policy responses to inflation rather than the effects of inflation itself.
  • Every step in the chain of reasoning must be spelt out; examiners repeatedly found connections assumed rather than explained.
  • Paper 1: on 8-mark examine questions evaluation was often not attempted, or the same point was offered twice as though it were two.
  • Paper 1 Section A continues to highlight the need to practise quantitative skills, with common errors in a change-in-supernormal-profit calculation.
Surprises from another board
  • The 2025 A* boundary was about 86% of the scaled total, among the highest of any A level, so near-perfect performance is required.
  • AO1 is only 22-24%, so the knowledge that dominates most revision earns under a quarter of the marks.
  • Paper 3 is the lowest-weighted paper at 30% yet draws on all four themes, making it the most synoptic of the three.

Boundaries June 2025, 9EC0, 335-mark scaled subject total: A* 287 (85.7%), A 262 (78.2%), B 227, C 192, D 158, E 124 (37.0%). Notional papers: A* 87, 85 and 85 out of 100.

Extended Project Qualification

AQA · 7993 - AQA Level 3 Extended Project Qualification (specification version 1.4); graded A* to E

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Extended Project (7993) - single component: Production Log and Assessment Record, project product with written report, and live presentation; internally assessed, AQA-moderatedNo timed examination; about 120 guided learning hours, roughly 30 taught skills and 90 independent50100%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Manage: identify, design, plan and carry out a project, applying skills, strategies and methods20% (top mark band 7-10 of 10 marks)
AO2Use resources: research, critically select, organise and use information; analyse data and show links and complexities20% (top mark band 7-10 of 10 marks)
AO3Develop and realise: use skills including new technologies and problem-solving to decide critically and achieve outcomes40% (top mark band 14-20 of 20 marks)
AO4Review: evaluate all aspects and own learning, and present evidenced outcomes and conclusions appropriately20% (top mark band 7-10 of 10 marks)
What the top band demands
  • AQA's A* descriptor asks for an effective design and thorough plan, a highly organised approach, excellent independent working, and clear evidence of responding very effectively to guidance.
  • A wide range of resources used critically, data analysed effectively and findings applied, with clear links between sources and project themes and the complexities of the topic fully explored.
  • Problems and issues identified, fully explored and addressed, and skills including new technologies used to achieve high-quality outcomes that fully realise the project's intentions.
  • Full, in-depth evaluation showing a high level of insight into how the project was conducted and into the limitations of the resources available.
  • Outcomes and conclusions presented clearly in an appropriate format with excellent supporting evidence, plus deep and extensive subject knowledge shown in answers to questions.
  • Shortcomings in one aspect may be balanced by stronger performance elsewhere, because the award depends on how far the assessment objectives are met overall.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO3 alone is 40% of the marks, so the gap between A and A* is usually decision-making and the quality of realisation, not the polish of the prose.
  • High AO1 marks require evidence of project management in the Production Log, not essay planning; monitoring that is merely quantitative does not reach the top band.
  • Top AO2 marks need genuine critical source evaluation - whether to use a source at all - rather than a completed usefulness table.
  • AO4 covers both the review and the presentation, so a superficial presentation record or a summary-and-thanks review caps the grade.
  • Genuine student autonomy over planning tools, report structure, presentation format and evidence submitted is what generates AO1 and AO3 evidence.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2023 (AQA's most recent published EPQ report found): some centres treated the EPQ as a long essay, using the Production Log to plan paragraphs rather than manage a project.
  • Centre templates, generic objectives and exemplar projects suppressed the autonomy AO1 and AO3 credit; one student copied an exemplar's structure outright.
  • 'To what extent' titles were widely recommended but few students set criteria for measuring extent, producing description and vague conclusions.
  • Referencing was a major weakness: inconsistent methods, bibliographies that were lists of URLs, and some reports with no references at all.
  • Over-marking was common - near-full AO1 marks for sparse logs, high AO2 marks with little critical source evaluation, and inflated AO4 for brief reviews.
Surprises from another board
  • The A* boundary was 45 of 50 - 90% - in both June 2024 and November 2025. It barely moves, unlike an A-level boundary.
  • AQA's awarding committee scrutinises work at E and A* for the EPQ, so its A* is a judgemental boundary, not a statistical one.
  • Dual accreditation is a real risk: overlap with a student's A-level content can invalidate the project, and Year 11 entries concerned moderators.

Non-exam assessment Entirely non-exam: Production Log and Assessment Record, a project product with a written report (about 5,000 words, or a minimum of 1,000 alongside an artefact), and a live presentation to a non-specialist audience with questioning.

Boundaries AQA EPQ 7993, 50 raw marks: A* 45 (90%), A 40 (80%), B 35 (70%), C 30 (60%), D 25 (50%), E 21 (42%) in both the June 2024 and November 2025 series.

Extended Project Qualification

Pearson Edexcel · Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Extended Project (cash-in ZPJ30), taken through one unit: P301 Dissertation, P302 Investigation/Field Study, P303 Performance or P304 Artefact; graded A* to E

ComponentTimeMarksWeighting
Extended Project - one unit from Dissertation, Investigation/Field Study, Performance or Artefact; internally assessed by the centre and subject to Pearson quality assuranceNo timed examination; project plus presentation54100%
AOAssessesWeight
AO1Manage: identify, design, plan and carry out the project, applying a range of skills and methods17% (9 of 54 marks)
AO2Use resources: research, critically select, organise and use information; analyse data and show links22% (12 of 54 marks)
AO3Develop and realise: use skills and problem-solving to take decisions critically and achieve planned outcomes44% (24 of 54 marks)
AO4Review: evaluate the project and own learning, and present evidenced outcomes and conclusions17% (9 of 54 marks)
What the top band demands
  • AO3 is 44% of the marks, so the decisions taken and the quality of the realised outcome dominate the grade far more than the write-up does.
  • Assessment is best fit across three bands per objective, then a mark chosen within the band, so band 3 performance must be consistent across all the evidence.
  • AO4 includes the presentation: a succinct summary of the project's main features delivered to an audience, followed by questions, and assessable only once.
  • A tightly specified initial brief - style, medium, purpose, materials, user group - lets a candidate plan, research, develop and evaluate against the same criteria throughout.
  • Referencing and a bibliography form part of the AO2 evidence, so inconsistent referencing reduces that objective directly.
  • Centre marks are moderated against the national standard and adjusted where they vary from it, so internal generosity does not survive.
What separates it from the band below
  • AO1 and AO4 are only 9 marks each, so the swing marks are the 24 for Develop and Realise and the 12 for Use Resources.
  • The raw unit total is 54 but results are reported as points out of 28, so raw boundaries move between series while the reported scale does not.
  • The presentation may be given for assessment only once, so rehearsal and feedback must happen before the assessed delivery.
  • The unit chosen changes what counts as evidence: an artefact candidate who submits a dissertation-style literature review weakens AO3.
Why strong candidates miss it
  • June 2022, Unit P304 Artefact (the most recent Pearson EPQ moderators' report located publicly): AO3 was the objective most likely to be assessed leniently by centres.
  • Some candidates over-evidenced AO2 at the expense of the time needed to develop and realise the artefact, which is where 44% of the marks sit.
  • Brief plans and non-reflective activity logs gave weaker AO1 evidence; stronger logs were detailed, reflective and commented on how the process was managed.
  • Inconsistent in-text referencing or a missing bibliography reduced AO2 evidence, because the bibliography forms part of that objective.
  • More recent Pearson EPQ moderator feedback is distributed to centres through ResultsPlus and was not verified for 2024 or 2025.
Surprises from another board
  • Pearson weights AO3 at 44% and AO1 at 17%, against AQA's 40% and 20%, so the two EPQs are not interchangeable in teaching.
  • The June 2025 unit A* boundary was 50 of 54, about 93% - higher even than AQA's 90%.
  • Results are reported in points, not raw marks: the overall qualification maximum is 28 points, with A* at 24.

Non-exam assessment Entirely non-exam: one unit chosen from Dissertation, Investigation/Field Study, Performance or Artefact, evidenced by the project product, supporting materials and a presentation, internally assessed and moderated by Pearson.

Boundaries June 2025, Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Extended Project: unit raw A* 50/54 (92.6%), A 44 (81.5%), E 23 (42.6%), identical across all four units. Overall qualification in points, maximum 28: A* 24, A 20, E 4.

Sources. Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Extended Project specification · Pearson Edexcel Projects (Level 3) grade boundaries, June 2025 · Moderators' Report / Principal Moderator Feedback, Extended Project A… · JCQ, AI Use in Assessments (revision 2, April 2025)

Evidence base

These 188 examples are not 188 separate bets. They rest on 30 mechanisms, and those have been studied. What follows is what the research supports, how strongly, and where it breaks down.

Say these out loud in the sessions. The evidence does not support them.

  • Matching teaching or resources to a pupil's visual, auditory or kinaesthetic learning style raises attainment. Pashler et al. found virtually no studies with the design needed to support it. The one recent meta-analysis reporting a small effect (g = 0.31) found the required crossover interaction in only 26% of outcomes and advises against adoption.
  • Dual coding means giving visual learners pictures and verbal learners text. Dual coding is a claim about everyone's two processing channels, not about individual preferences. The evidence supports combining words with graphics for all learners and cutting redundancy; it does not support sorting pupils by modality.
  • Adding more images, animation, video or VR to a resource makes it more effective. Cromley and Chen found no significant effect for virtual reality and inconsistent effects for animation, games and simulations, with the largest gains coming from removing seductive detail. The EEF found classroom visuals frequently have no effect and are often harmful.
  • Interleaving is better than blocking, so mix everything up. Brunmair and Richter found blocking significantly better for word and vocabulary learning (g = -0.39) and no reliable interleaving effect for expository texts. Interleaving helps discrimination between confusable categories; it is not a general improvement.
  • Expanding the gaps between reviews is the optimal spacing schedule. In classroom research expanding inter-study intervals produced smaller or negative effects, and benefits diminished beyond three re-exposures. Cepeda et al. show the best gap depends on the retention interval, not on a fixed expanding pattern.
  • Quizzing beats any alternative use of the same lesson time. Yang et al. found the classroom testing advantage was g = 0.610 against a filler activity, g = 0.330 against restudy, but only g = 0.095 against other elaborative strategies. Against genuinely active alternatives the margin is very small.
  • Showing students a wrong answer teaches them the right one. The pooled effect of erroneous examples is only g = 0.136, and the single significant moderator is whether the error is explicitly explained. Barbieri et al. found correct examples outperformed incorrect ones in mathematics.
  • Bolting self-explanation prompts onto a worked example always improves it. In the mathematics worked-examples meta-analysis, conditions with self-explanation prompts were less effective than example conditions without them. Bisra et al. also found multiple-choice and metacognitive prompts had no detectable effect.
  • These techniques are established classroom practice, so applying them reliably raises results. The EEF's review concluded that practice in this area can only be said to be evidence-informed in a weak sense, that initial evidence of successful classroom application is mixed, and that the impact of cognitive-science-informed interventions remains uncertain.
  • Formative assessment reliably produces effect sizes of 0.4 to 0.7. That range summarises scattered individual studies, not a pooled analysis. Kingston and Nash's meta-analysis found a weighted mean of 0.20 (English 0.32, mathematics 0.17, science 0.09) from only 13 usable studies and said the higher claim is unsupported.
  • More feedback is always better, so more marking means more progress. Over a third of feedback interventions reduced performance in Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis. In the EEF-commissioned review, every individual Key Stage 4 study favoured the control group, pooling to g = -0.04 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.09).
  • Praise and encouragement in feedback raise attainment. Reinforcement and punishment feedback returned d = 0.24 against d = 0.99 for high-information feedback, and 86% of the negative feedback effects came from uninformative rewards or punishments. Praise added nothing to detailed comments in Lipnevich and Smith's experiment.
  • Giving a grade alongside comments is a sensible compromise. The grade crowds out the comment. Butler found grades plus comments as undermining as grades alone; the EEF marking review cites King's College evidence that pupils of all abilities acted on feedback less when a grade was attached.
  • Discrete study-skills or learning-to-learn sessions build metacognition. The EEF guidance states there is little evidence of benefit from teaching metacognitive approaches in separate thinking-skills sessions, because pupils do not transfer generic tips to specific tasks; self-regulation is context-dependent and must be taught within subjects.
  • Weaker students cannot judge their own work, as the Dunning-Kruger effect shows. The classic quartile-split pattern is mostly an artefact of the better-than-average effect plus regression to the mean, and reproduces from simulated data. With valid methods the ability to self-assess is roughly linear across the range.
  • Toolkit months-of-progress figures can be ranked against each other to choose a strategy. Standardised effect sizes shift with sample restriction, comparison group and how closely the test matches what was taught, so league tables may rank openness to design choices rather than impact. Kulik's local-versus-standardised test gap shows the same problem.
  • Teaching should be matched to students' learning styles (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic). Pashler et al. found almost no studies using the crossover design the hypothesis requires. Clinton-Lisell and Litzinger found g = 0.31 but the necessary crossover interaction in only 26% of outcomes, and only 5 of 21 studies were methodologically sound.
  • Meta-analysis shows generative AI has a large effect on learning performance (g = 0.87). That figure comes from Wang and Fan (2025), retracted on 22 April 2026 over discrepancies in the meta-analysis that undermined the editor's confidence in its validity; the authors did not respond. It had already been cited over 400 times.
  • AI tutors match or beat human tutors, delivering the legendary two-sigma effect. VanLehn tested this folklore and found it unsupported: human tutoring d = 0.79, intelligent tutoring d = 0.76, not 2.0 and 1.0. Kestin's large effect came from one session, one topic, immediate post-test only.
  • Keep videos under six minutes because short videos improve learning. Guo et al. measured watch time and whether students attempted post-video problems across 6.9 million MOOC viewing sessions. It is an engagement finding with no attainment outcome, and it says nothing about comprehension or retention.
  • Working memory or brain-training apps will help able students with poor working memory learn more. Melby-Lervag et al. found improvements only on tasks resembling the training, with no convincing far transfer to ability, decoding, reading comprehension or arithmetic. Cortese et al. found ADHD gains collapsed once outcomes were blinded.
  • Universal Design for Learning is grounded in neuroscience and the brain's three learning networks. Boysen's analysis of the sources CAST itself cites found they provided little evidence for UDL claims, mostly offered no learner choice and did not measure learning, and none concerned brain function. The neuroscientific framing is presentational, not evidential.
  • If students are more engaged with a digital tool, they are learning more. EEF identifies poor implementation, not low engagement, as the main reason technology underdelivers, and insists the pedagogy carries the effect. Altamura et al. found frequent digital leisure reading barely relates to comprehension (r = .055) despite high engagement.
  • AI feedback improved the students' work, so it improved their learning. Fan et al. found the ChatGPT group made the largest essay-score gains yet showed no significant advantage in knowledge gain or transfer. Bastani et al. found practice gains reversed into a 17% deficit on the later unaided exam.
  • NotebookLM Audio Overviews, Gemini Gems and Google Vids are evidence-based learning tools. No randomised trial of any of these products exists. Evidence is indirect and mixed: listening matches reading overall (g = 0.07) but is worse for inferential comprehension, and Stanford found only 20 of 800+ AI-in-education papers give strong causal evidence.
  • Using ChatGPT for planning raises pupil attainment, as the EEF trial showed. The EEF trial measured teacher workload, not pupil outcomes. Teachers saved 25.3 minutes per week (69% of comparison time) with no evidence of a difference in resource quality from a blind expert panel. Attainment was never an outcome.

Where this bank is on weaker ground

  • Generative AI tutoring and chatbots Mixed — 47 examples. Kestin's tutor was expert prompt-engineered question by question, on one topic, in one session, with no delayed retention test. Bastani's harm disappeared under hint-only guardrails. Stanford's 2026 review found only 20 of 800+ AI-in-education papers give strong causal evidence.
  • Dual coding and Mayer's principles of multimedia learning Mixed — 20 examples. The EEF concluded, at low confidence, that visual aids frequently have no effect and can sometimes be harmful, and that diagrams in secondary maths and science are mostly helpful but frequently have no effect and are often harmful. Redundant narration plus on-screen text, decorative images and seductive detail all reduce learning.
  • Working memory, ADHD, dyslexia, autism and processing speed in a selective setting Mixed — 13 examples. The constructive side rests on EEF's recommendation 3 repertoire (explicit instruction, scaffolding, cognitive and metacognitive strategies, flexible grouping, technology) rather than on condition-specific trials, and EEF warns that searching for a magic bullet distracts from these. Twice-exceptional evidence is descriptive: Reis and Renzulli (2025) is interview and survey work, not causal.
  • Calibration, judgements of learning and overconfidence Mixed — 2 examples. Once the better-than-average effect and regression to the mean are modelled with polynomial or LOESS regression, the unskilled-and-unaware asymmetry largely disappears; quartile-split graphs reproduce from random data. So do not tell staff that weak students are uniquely blind to their own work.
  • Studying erroneous worked examples and error analysis Weak — 1 examples. The pooled effect is statistically significant but weak. The one significant moderator is the design of the error-explanation activity: self-explanation prompts or instructional explanations of the error are needed, and without them the benefit is negligible. Presenting an error without resolution risks the error being encoded.
  • Homework and independent study at Key Stage 5 Mixed — 1 examples. Cooper's experiments are few, short and design-flawed: trim-and-fill lowers d to 0.48, and assuming an intraclass correlation of .4 removes significance. Returns are curvilinear, with mathematics and science scores declining beyond 90-100 minutes a day. Homework with feedback and peer collaboration outperforms homework without.
  • Universal Design for Learning: evidence and critiques Mixed — 1 examples. Because UDL specifies principles not procedures, trials differ in what was actually done and rarely isolate components, so the pooled estimate may reflect good teaching generally. Studies are small, often uncontrolled and heavily US. Boysen et al. found 1% of CAST's cited sources are neuroscience and 75% of the guidelines cite none.

Those examples are not worthless. Their impact score leans on the A* discriminator they target and on your judgement rather than on a research base, and they are the first to drop if the programme shrinks.
