An example is attached to a mechanism when its text matches at least two of that mechanism’s keywords. That is a keyword match, not a judgement: check the mechanism really is what the example depends on before leaning on its effect size.

Core learning science

Retrieval practice and the testing effect

Strong

Being made to retrieve material from memory produces better later retention than restudying it. This is one of the few findings that survives the move from laboratory to real classrooms, including at high-school level.

Effect g = 0.50, CI [0.42, 0.58], 159 lab effect sizes (Rowland, 2014); g = 0.499 across 222 classroom studies and 48,478 students, with the high-school subgroup at g = 0.655 (Yang, Luo, Vadillo, Yu & Shanks, 2021)

Breaks down The advantage shrinks sharply against active comparisons: g = 0.330 versus restudy and only g = 0.095 versus other elaborative strategies (Yang et al., 2021). Feedback matters (g = 0.537 with, 0.374 without). Untested content gains less (g = 0.321). 18% of Rowland's effects favoured restudy. Classroom outcomes were mostly factual recall.

Age caveat Rowland's lab base was almost entirely undergraduates. Yang's high-school subgroup is reassuring, but virtually no studies use UK A-level essay or extended-response assessment.

Classroom rule Make students produce answers from memory, then give the correct answer. Recall beats recognition; feedback roughly doubles the gain.

Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432-1463.
Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2021). Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 147(4), 399-435.
Agarwal, P. K., Nunes, L. D., & Blunt, J. R. (2021). Retrieval practice consistently benefits student learning: A systematic review of applied research in schools and classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, 33(4), 1409-1453.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.

Spaced practice and distributed learning

Strong

Spreading the same study time across separated sessions produces better retention than massing it. The effect is robust in laboratories and holds, more modestly, in classrooms across primary, secondary and university.

Effect d = 0.54, CI [0.31, 0.77], 22 classroom studies and 31 effect sizes, n > 3,000 (Mawson & Kang, 2025); Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006) synthesised 839 assessments across 317 verbal-recall experiments

Breaks down Reading showed a negative effect (d = -0.11); primary settings produced the most negative effects; expanding inter-study intervals gave smaller or negative results; benefits diminished beyond three re-exposures (Mawson & Kang, 2025). The optimal gap depends on how distant the test is (Cepeda et al., 2006), so any fixed interval misfits most content.

Age caveat Mawson & Kang spans ages 6-17 plus university. The EEF's high-quality classroom studies were limited to maths, science and critical thinking, not A-level essay subjects.

Classroom rule Plan deliberate returns to earlier content across weeks. Match the gap to how far off the exam is; do not use expanding intervals.

Mawson, R. D., & Kang, S. H. K. (2025). The distributed practice effect on classroom learning: A meta-analytic review of applied research. Behavioral Sciences, 15(6), 771.
Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.

Interleaving of problem types

Mixed

Mixing problem types within a practice set helps learners discriminate between them and choose a method. It is the most conditional of the popular strategies and reverses outright for some material.

Effect Overall g = 0.42, CI [0.34, 0.50], 59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples; paintings g = 0.67, mathematical tasks g = 0.34 CI [0.11, 0.57], expository texts non-significant, words g = -0.39 CI [-0.64, -0.14] (Brunmair & Richter, 2019)

Breaks down Blocking beats interleaving for word and vocabulary learning (g = -0.39) and there is no reliable effect for expository texts (Brunmair & Richter, 2019). Gains require high between-category similarity and within-category variety. The EEF found 11 of 12 classroom studies were maths strategy-selection, ages 8-14, and stated generalisation beyond that is not possible.

Age caveat Classroom evidence is ages 8-14 and almost entirely maths; the EEF rated its own conclusion low confidence. There is no A-level evidence, and none for essay subjects.

Classroom rule Interleave problem types once a method is fluent, so students must decide which to use. Do not interleave new vocabulary or terminology.

Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029-1052.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.
Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4-58.

Worked examples, fading and the expertise-reversal effect

Strong

Studying a fully worked solution beats solving equivalent problems for learners who lack the relevant schema, and the advantage disappears then reverses as expertise grows, which is why support must be faded.

Effect g = 0.48 across 43 articles, 55 studies and 181 effect sizes in mathematics (Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste & Chawla, 2023). Expertise reversal: 60 studies, 5,924 participants; published abstract reports d = 0.505 favouring high assistance for low prior knowledge and d = -0.428 favouring low assistance for high prior knowledge (Tetzlaff et al., 2025)

Breaks down The same support that helps novices harms experts, so an unfaded worked example becomes a cost. Sweller et al. (2019) state cognitive load theory is only relevant for complex, high element-interactivity material. Barbieri et al. (2023) found adding self-explanation prompts made worked-example conditions worse in maths. Deans for Impact warn against procedural copying without reasoning.

Age caveat This is the best age match of the ten: the EEF rated worked examples moderate confidence with results concentrated in secondary-age students aged 11-18, though in maths and science rather than essay subjects.

Classroom rule Give full models to novices, then fade to partial then unaided. Judge fading by the student's knowledge, not the lesson plan.

Barbieri, C. A., Miller-Cotto, D., Clerjuste, S. N., & Chawla, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance. Educational Psychology Review, 35(1), 11.
Tetzlaff, L., Simonsmeier, B. A., Peters, S., & Brod, G. (2025). A cornerstone of adaptivity: A meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect. Learning and Instruction, 98. Study scale verified; the d values are taken from the published abstract, which I could not open directly.
Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261-292.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.

Self-explanation and elaborative interrogation

Moderate

Prompting learners to explain why something is true, or how a step works, improves learning across many tasks. The benefit is real but smaller for school-age students than for undergraduates, and several prompt types do nothing.

Effect Overall g = 0.55 from 69 effect sizes in 64 reports; by education level, high school g = 0.426 CI [0.247, 0.606] (k = 13) against undergraduate g = 0.611 (k = 42) (Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi & Winne, 2018)

Breaks down Multiple-choice prompts (g = 0.24), metacognitive prompts and essay-formatted outcomes were not statistically distinguishable from zero. The advantage over a teacher-supplied explanation is only g = 0.35. Barbieri et al. (2023) found self-explanation prompts reduced the worked-example benefit in maths. Dunlosky et al. note students with thin prior knowledge generate wrong explanations.

Age caveat The high-school estimate (g = 0.426) is reliably positive but clearly smaller than the undergraduate one, and essay-format outcomes showed no detectable effect at all.

Classroom rule Ask open why and how prompts on content students already part-know. Avoid multiple-choice or purely metacognitive prompts.

Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing self-explanation: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703-725.
Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4-58.
Barbieri, C. A., Miller-Cotto, D., Clerjuste, S. N., & Chawla, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance. Educational Psychology Review, 35(1), 11.

Studying erroneous worked examples and error analysis

Weak

Showing and dissecting a wrong solution produces a small average benefit, and only when the error is explicitly explained. On its own it is close to useless, and correct examples generally beat incorrect ones.

Effect g = 0.136 across 42 papers and 177 effect sizes comparing erroneous examples with correct examples or problem solving (Alemdag, Eichelmann & Narciss, 2025); Barbieri et al. (2023) found correct examples outperformed incorrect examples in mathematics

Breaks down The pooled effect is statistically significant but weak. The one significant moderator is the design of the error-explanation activity: self-explanation prompts or instructional explanations of the error are needed, and without them the benefit is negligible. Presenting an error without resolution risks the error being encoded.

Age caveat Example-based work sits largely in secondary algebra and geometry. There is no evidence base for error analysis on A-level essays, marked scripts or extended prose.

Classroom rule Never show a wrong answer without making students name the error and state the correct principle. Pair it with a correct example.

Alemdag, E., Eichelmann, A., & Narciss, S. (2025). A framework for learning from erroneous examples and meta-analysis of empirical research. Review of Educational Research (advance online publication).
Barbieri, C. A., Miller-Cotto, D., Clerjuste, S. N., & Chawla, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance. Educational Psychology Review, 35(1), 11.
Barbieri, C. A., & Booth, J. L. (2020). Mistakes on display: Incorrect examples refine equation solving and algebraic feature knowledge. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 34(4), 862-878.

Dual coding and Mayer's principles of multimedia learning

Mixed

Pairing words with a purposeful graphic helps, and the strongest reliable gains come from removing extraneous material rather than adding visuals. Classroom evidence for visuals is weak and includes frequent null and harmful results.

Effect Overall g = 0.37 across 92 articles, 181 studies and 591 effects, with a small decline in effect size per year; largest effects for removing seductive detail, modality, personalisation, the multimedia principle and sentence-level coherence; no significant effect for virtual reality (Cromley & Chen, 2025)

Breaks down The EEF concluded, at low confidence, that visual aids frequently have no effect and can sometimes be harmful, and that diagrams in secondary maths and science are mostly helpful but frequently have no effect and are often harmful. Redundant narration plus on-screen text, decorative images and seductive detail all reduce learning.

Age caveat Mayer's base is largely undergraduates on short multimedia lessons. EEF classroom evidence spans ages 7-18 but two-thirds was maths and science; diagram studies were almost all ages 12-16.

Classroom rule Cut decoration and duplicated text before adding graphics. Narrate a diagram rather than making students read and listen to the same words.

Cromley, J. G., & Chen, R. (2025). A meta-analysis of Richard Mayer's multimedia learning research: Searching for boundary conditions of design principles across multiple media types. Educational Research Review, 49, 100730.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.
Deans for Impact (2nd edn). The Science of Learning. Austin, TX: Deans for Impact.

Desirable difficulties: the generation effect and hypercorrection of confident errors

Moderate

Conditions that slow performance during study can improve retention. Generating an answer beats reading one, and confidently held errors are the easiest to correct once feedback arrives.

Effect Generation effect d = 0.40 from 445 effect sizes across 86 studies (Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott & McDaniel, 2007). For hypercorrection there is no reliable pooled estimate; it is a repeatedly replicated direction-of-effect finding (Butterfield & Metcalfe, 2001; Metcalfe & Finn, 2011)

Breaks down Bjork and Bjork (2020) are explicit: if the learner lacks the background knowledge or skills to respond successfully, desirable difficulties become undesirable difficulties, and the optimal level varies with prior learning. Rowland (2014) notes generation can reverse to a disadvantage. Hypercorrection studies show high-confidence errors can return after a week's delay.

Age caveat The hypercorrection literature rests on undergraduates answering general-knowledge questions, not sixth-formers on subject content. Bertsch's generation studies are overwhelmingly undergraduate word-list and paired-associate tasks.

Classroom rule Make students commit to an answer and rate their confidence before feedback. Only add difficulty where prerequisites are secure.

Bertsch, S., Pesta, B. J., Wiscott, R., & McDaniel, M. A. (2007). The generation effect: A meta-analytic review. Memory & Cognition, 35(2), 201-210.
Metcalfe, J., & Finn, B. (2011). People's hypercorrection of high-confidence errors: Did they know it all along? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 37(2), 437-448.
Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2020). Desirable difficulties in theory and practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 9(4), 475-479.

Cognitive load theory as the underlying account

Moderate

Cognitive load theory explains why several of these techniques work: novel material passes through a capacity-limited working memory, so instruction should cut load that is not about the content itself.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate for the theory itself; it is a framework. Its derived effects carry their own estimates, for example worked examples g = 0.48 (Barbieri et al., 2023) and the expertise reversal asymmetry (Tetzlaff et al., 2025). The EEF rated worked examples and scaffolds at moderate confidence

Breaks down Sweller et al. (2019) concede that cognitive load theory is only relevant for complex learning with high element interactivity, and that many of its experiments never measured load directly but inferred support from learning outcomes. Load measurement remains contested. The EEF found collaborative load-reduction variants gave some negative results at low confidence.

Age caveat The EEF's cognitive-load classroom evidence is concentrated in secondary-age students aged 11-18, the closest fit of the ten mechanisms, but almost entirely in maths and science.

Classroom rule Remove split attention and redundancy on genuinely complex material. Do not strip difficulty from simple tasks; load theory does not apply there.

Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261-292.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.
Deans for Impact (2nd edn). The Science of Learning. Austin, TX: Deans for Impact.

Practice testing and distributed practice as rated in Dunlosky et al. (2013)

Strong

Of ten study techniques reviewed, only practice testing and distributed practice earned a high utility rating, because they help learners of different ages and abilities across many materials and criterion tasks, including in real educational settings.

Effect Utility ratings rather than pooled effect sizes: high for practice testing and distributed practice; moderate for interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation; low for rereading, highlighting, summarisation, the keyword mnemonic and imagery for text (Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan & Willingham, 2013)

Breaks down The review deliberately produced no single meta-analytic estimate per technique, so the ratings are not effect sizes. A low rating often reflects thin evidence or heavy training demands rather than proven harm: summarisation can work once trained. The interleaving rating predates Brunmair and Richter's finding that it reverses for some material.

Age caveat Dunlosky et al. flag that much of the evidence came from college students on laboratory materials, and that younger learners need training before summarisation or elaborative interrogation pays off.

Classroom rule Teach students to self-test and space their revision. Actively discourage rereading and highlighting as their main method.

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4-58.
Dunlosky, J. (2013). Strengthening the student toolbox: Study strategies to boost learning. American Educator, 37(3), 12-21.
Perry, T., Lea, R., Jorgensen, C. R., Cordingley, P., Shapiro, K., & Youdell, D. (2021). Cognitive Science in the Classroom: Evidence and Practice Review. London: Education Endowment Foundation.

Feedback, assessment and self-regulation

Formative assessment and feedback quality

Strong

Feedback raises attainment on average, but the average hides a wide spread: over a third of feedback interventions lower performance. What separates the effective third is information about the task and the process that the learner is then required to act on.

Effect d = 0.41 across 607 effect sizes and 23,663 observations, with over 1/3 of interventions decreasing performance (Kluger & DeNisi 1996); d = 0.48 from 994 effects in 435 studies, high-information feedback d = 0.99 vs reinforcement/punishment d = 0.24 (Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie 2020); EEF-commissioned review of feedback-only trials g = 0.17, 95% CI 0.09-0.25 (Newman et al. 2021); EEF Toolkit +6 months, 155 studies.

Breaks down Heterogeneity is large and unexplained (I-squared 44%); the EEF review found individual studies where the feedback group did worse. Feedback that moves attention to the self, or that arrives with no time or requirement to act, can depress performance. The Toolkit's +6 months is a mixed-design synthesis, not a pooled trial estimate.

Age caveat Newman et al.'s 51 studies covered ages 4-17; only two included 16-year-olds and one a 17-year-old. No pooled evidence on A-level courses at all.

Classroom rule Say what to change in the work, not what the pupil is like, and give lesson time to make the change before moving on.

Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: a historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254-284.
Wisniewski, B., Zierer, K., & Hattie, J. (2020). The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 3087.
Newman, M., Kwan, I., Schucan Bird, K., & Hoo, H.-T. (2021). The impact of Feedback on student attainment: a systematic review. Education Endowment Foundation.
Education Endowment Foundation. Feedback. Teaching and Learning Toolkit (read via the Queen Rania Foundation mirror of the EEF Toolkit).

Comment-only marking versus grades

Moderate

Attaching a grade or mark to comments reliably weakens the comments: pupils read the score and act less on the advice. The mechanism is ego-involving versus task-involving evaluation. Direct A-level evidence is absent.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate. Butler (1988), 48 Israeli 11-year-olds from top and bottom quartiles: grades, and grades plus comments, had similar undermining effects on interest and performance relative to comments alone. Lipnevich & Smith (2009), N = 464 undergraduates: a tentative grade depressed essay improvement; detailed descriptive feedback alone was most effective, and praise added nothing.

Breaks down Effects differ by pupil. Butler found high achievers kept interest under grades when more grades were expected; the EEF marking review cites a longitudinal study where annual grades helped girls but held boys back. Withholding grades from students who need calibration against exam standards has not been tested.

Age caveat Butler's pupils were 11; Lipnevich & Smith's were US undergraduates. The King's College finding on grades suppressing engagement with comments is secondary-school, not post-16.

Classroom rule Give comments first and hold the grade back until pupils have responded; never hand over a mark and a target at the same moment.

Butler, R. (1988). Enhancing and undermining intrinsic motivation: the effects of task-involving and ego-involving evaluation on interest and performance. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 58(1), 1-14.
Lipnevich, A. A., & Smith, J. K. (2009). Effects of differential feedback on students' examination performance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 15(4), 319-333.
Elliott, V., Baird, J.-A., Hopfenbeck, T., Ingram, J., Thompson, I., Usher, N., Zantout, M., Richardson, J., & Coleman, R. (2016). A marked improvement? A review of the evidence on written marking. Education Endowment Foundation.
Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and Classroom Learning. Assessment in Education, 5(1), 7-74.

Metacognition and self-regulated learning

Strong

Teaching pupils to plan, monitor and evaluate their own work raises attainment, and the gains hold up at follow-up. It works when taught inside subject content by a teacher who models thinking; generic study-skills lessons do not transfer.

Effect EEF Toolkit +7 months from 246 studies, high security (secondary +7, primary +8). Hedges g = 0.50 at post-test rising to 0.63 at follow-up across 48 metacognitive strategy instruction interventions (de Boer et al. 2018). University self-regulated learning training g = 0.38 overall, academic performance g = 0.37, from 49 studies and 251 effects (Theobald 2021).

Breaks down Self-regulation is subject- and task-specific: strength in KS2 art planning does not imply strength in A-level essay planning. EEF notes many studies were not independently evaluated, which can inflate impact. The active ingredients are teacher modelling, metacognitive talk and appropriate challenge, not templates or reflection sheets.

Age caveat Toolkit figures span 5-16. Theobald (2021) covers university students, the nearest phase to KS5, and reports larger effects for older students and those with lower prior attainment.

Classroom rule Model your own thinking aloud on a real A-level task, then make pupils plan, check and revise on that same task, in that subject.

Education Endowment Foundation (2018). Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning. Guidance Report.
de Boer, H., Donker, A. S., Kostons, D. D. N. M., & van der Werf, G. P. C. (2018). Long-term effects of metacognitive strategy instruction on student academic performance: a meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 24, 98-115.
Theobald, M. (2021). Self-regulated learning training programs enhance university students' academic performance, self-regulated learning strategies, and motivation: a meta-analysis. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 66, 101976.
Education Endowment Foundation. Metacognition and self-regulation. Teaching and Learning Toolkit (read via the Queen Rania Foundation mirror).

Calibration, judgements of learning and overconfidence

Mixed

Students' confidence in their learning tracks their actual learning only weakly, and overconfidence makes them stop studying too early. Predict-then-check routines improve calibration. The familiar Dunning-Kruger curve is mostly a statistical artefact.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate for classroom calibration training. Self-assessed and objectively measured ability correlate about r = 0.28 in field data (N = 929), close to the meta-analytic r = 0.33, and the association is essentially linear (Gignac & Zajenkowski 2020). Dunlosky & Rawson (2012): overconfident judgements of learning predicted poorer learning and poorer long-term retention.

Breaks down Once the better-than-average effect and regression to the mean are modelled with polynomial or LOESS regression, the unskilled-and-unaware asymmetry largely disappears; quartile-split graphs reproduce from random data. So do not tell staff that weak students are uniquely blind to their own work.

Age caveat Calibration evidence is overwhelmingly undergraduate laboratory work on key-term definitions and short comprehension texts, not A-level essays, proofs or practicals.

Classroom rule Make pupils predict their mark before you release it, then show the gap; repeat until predictions match the mark scheme.

Gignac, G. E., & Zajenkowski, M. (2020). The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data. Intelligence, 80, 101449.
Dunlosky, J., & Rawson, K. A. (2012). Overconfidence produces underachievement: inaccurate self evaluations undermine students' learning and retention. Learning and Instruction, 22(4), 271-280.
Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18(2), 119-144.

Self-assessment and peer assessment with rubrics

Strong

Structured self- and peer-assessment raise attainment, roughly as much as each other and at least as much as teacher assessment, provided pupils have explicit criteria and act on what they find. Rubrics add a further small-to-moderate gain.

Effect Hedges g = 0.585 (self-assessment), 0.606 (peer), 0.448 (combined), from 175 studies, 626 effects, 19,383 participants (Yan et al. 2022); self versus peer difference g = -0.065, i.e. none. Peer assessment g = 0.31 vs no assessment and 0.28 vs teacher assessment, 54 studies (Double, McGrane & Hopfenbeck 2020). Rubrics on academic performance g = 0.45, k = 21 (Panadero et al. 2023).

Breaks down Effects shrink with study quality: Yan et al. report g = 0.246 in moderate-quality studies against 0.699 in weak ones, funnel plots suggest inflation, and repeated-measures designs give roughly triple the effect of controlled comparisons. Peer assessment depends on training and on criteria pupils can actually apply.

Age caveat Samples run from primary to university. Double et al. found peer-assessment effects stable across age groups, but no pooled estimate exists specifically for 16-18 year olds on A-level courses.

Classroom rule Train pupils on the criteria with real scripts first, then let them assess; require them to revise their own work afterwards.

Yan, Z., Lao, H., Panadero, E., Fernandez-Castilla, B., Yang, L., & Yang, M. (2022). Effects of self-assessment and peer-assessment interventions on academic performance: a meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 37, 100484.
Double, K. S., McGrane, J. A., & Hopfenbeck, T. N. (2020). The impact of peer assessment on academic performance: a meta-analysis of control group studies. Educational Psychology Review, 32(2), 481-509.
Panadero, E., Jonsson, A., Pinedo, L., & Fernandez-Castilla, B. (2023). Effects of rubrics on academic performance, self-regulated learning, and self-efficacy: a meta-analytic review. Educational Psychology Review, 35, 113.
Panadero, E., & Jonsson, A. (2013). The use of scoring rubrics for formative assessment purposes revisited: a review. Educational Research Review, 9, 129-144.

Exemplar deconstruction and making criteria explicit

Moderate

Assessment standards are largely tacit, so publishing criteria does not transmit them. Pupils acquire the standard by judging real work against the criteria and arguing about the judgements with the teacher and each other.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate: design variation prevented meta-analysis. To, Panadero & Carless (2021) reviewed 40 studies; of the 15 measuring performance, 10 improved, 4 showed no change, 1 declined. Rubric use overall g = 0.45 (Panadero et al. 2023). Sadler (1989) is a theoretical account, not a trial.

Breaks down Passive exposure to model answers does not work and can produce formulaic imitation; the gain comes from marking and discussing exemplars. Sadler argues reliance on teachers' guild knowledge keeps the standard inaccessible; O'Donovan, Price and Rust argue explicit articulation alone must fall short of conveying standards.

Age caveat The exemplar and assessment-literacy literature is almost entirely higher education, much of it UK undergraduate business and nursing courses. Sadler's three conditions are conceptual, not age-specific evidence.

Classroom rule Give pupils two real scripts of different quality, make them mark and rank both against the mark scheme, then defend the ranking.

Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18(2), 119-144.
To, J., Panadero, E., & Carless, D. (2021). A systematic review of the educational uses and effects of exemplars. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 47(8), 1167-1182.
O'Donovan, B., Price, M., & Rust, C. (2004). Know what I mean? Enhancing student understanding of assessment standards and criteria. Teaching in Higher Education, 9(3), 325-335.
Panadero, E., & Jonsson, A. (2013). The use of scoring rubrics for formative assessment purposes revisited: a review. Educational Research Review, 9, 129-144.

Goal setting, implementation intentions and deliberate practice

Mixed

Specific difficult goals beat trying your best, and if-then plans naming when and where to act beat intentions alone. But a large university replication found no attainment effect, and deliberate practice explains little variance in education.

Effect Goal-setting meta-analyses give effect sizes of 0.42 to 0.80 (Locke & Latham 2002). Implementation intentions d = 0.65 across 94 independent tests (Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006). Deliberate practice explains 4% of performance variance in education (r = 0.21) against 26% in games (Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald 2014). Dobronyi, Oreopoulos & Petronijevic (2019), N approximately 1,400: no effect on GPA, credits or persistence.

Breaks down Goal effects require progress feedback, commitment, and the ability and knowledge to do the task; goals beyond current skill can reduce performance. The null replication was an online goal-setting task with reminders and was precise enough to detect a 7% standardised effect, so brief written goal exercises should not be expected to move grades.

Age caveat Locke and Latham's base is largely workplace and laboratory; Gollwitzer and Sheeran's is largely health behaviour. The null replication is first-year undergraduates. No A-level trial located.

Classroom rule Turn each target into a when-and-where plan tied to a specific task, and check the plan was executed, not just written.

Locke, E. A., & Latham, G. P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: a 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705-717.
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119.
Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608-1618.
Dobronyi, C. R., Oreopoulos, P., & Petronijevic, U. (2019). Goal setting, academic reminders, and college success: a large-scale field experiment. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 12(1), 38-66.

Mastery learning and high success rates

Moderate

Requiring mastery of a unit before moving on, with corrective teaching and retesting, raises examination scores and helps weaker students most. Gains are much larger on teacher-made tests than on standardised ones, and the approach costs time.

Effect d = 0.52 across 103 of 108 controlled evaluations (Kulik, Kulik & Bangert-Drowns 1990); Learning for Mastery 0.59, Personalised System of Instruction 0.48; less able students 0.61 against more able 0.40 (not significant). EEF Toolkit: +5 months overall, secondary +3, primary +8. Rosenshine (2012) puts the optimal success rate at about 80%.

Breaks down Effects are trivially small on nationally standardised tests while moderate on locally developed ones, which invites a teaching-to-the-test reading. Self-paced mastery reduced course completion in college classes (average h = -0.14 across 32 studies). Mastery consumes instructional time, and unmastered units must actually be retaught.

Age caveat Unusually good for post-16: much of Kulik's pool is college and high-school courses, so the evidence is closer to KS5 than most strands. The EEF secondary figure of +3 months is KS3-4.

Classroom rule Set a pass threshold per unit, reteach and retest the pupils who miss it, and aim for about 80% success in practice.

Kulik, C.-L. C., Kulik, J. A., & Bangert-Drowns, R. L. (1990). Effectiveness of mastery learning programs: a meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research, 60(2), 265-299.
Rosenshine, B. (2012). Principles of instruction: research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, 36(1), 12-19, 39.
Education Endowment Foundation. Mastery learning. Teaching and Learning Toolkit.

Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction

Moderate

Rosenshine's principles are a careful synthesis of cognitive science, classroom observation of high-gain teachers, and scaffolding research. They are a defensible design frame, but the paper is not a meta-analysis and reports no pooled effect size.

Effect No pooled estimate: Rosenshine (2012) gives none. The nearest quantified claim is an optimal success rate of about 80%, drawn from studies in which the most successful teachers' classes answered 82% of questions correctly against 73% for the least successful, in fourth-grade mathematics. Coe et al. (2014) reach similar conclusions from over 200 studies without assigning effect sizes to the set.

Breaks down The master-teacher evidence is correlational process-product observation, largely 1970s-80s US elementary and junior-high mathematics and reading. Rosenshine limits the principles to well-structured material and warns some may not fit tasks needing a creative or unique response. Coe et al. caution against reading observed teaching as causal.

Age caveat Almost none of the underpinning observation research is post-16. Applying the principles to A-level essay subjects and open-ended coursework is reasoned extension, not tested evidence.

Classroom rule Use the principles as a lesson design checklist for well-structured content, and say openly which A-level tasks they do not fit.

Rosenshine, B. (2012). Principles of instruction: research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, 36(1), 12-19, 39.
Coe, R., Aloisi, C., Higgins, S., & Major, L. E. (2014). What makes great teaching? Review of the underpinning research. Sutton Trust.
Rosenshine, B., & Stevens, R. (1986). Teaching functions. In M. C. Wittrock (Ed.), Handbook of Research on Teaching (3rd ed., pp. 376-391). Macmillan.

Homework and independent study at Key Stage 5

Mixed

Homework correlates with attainment much more strongly for older pupils than younger, but the causal evidence is thin, low-security and stops at 16. Quality, alignment with lessons and feedback matter more than quantity, and returns turn negative.

Effect Homework-achievement correlation r = .25 for Grades 7-12, .07 middle grades, near zero K-6; d = 0.60 (95% CI .38 to .82) across five small homework-versus-no-homework experiments (Cooper, Robinson & Patall 2006). EEF Toolkit: +5 months secondary, +3 primary, 43 studies, evidence security low. Fernandez-Alonso et al. (2015): about 60 minutes a day is reasonable.

Breaks down Cooper's experiments are few, short and design-flawed: trim-and-fill lowers d to 0.48, and assuming an intraclass correlation of .4 removes significance. Returns are curvilinear, with mathematics and science scores declining beyond 90-100 minutes a day. Homework with feedback and peer collaboration outperforms homework without.

Age caveat There is effectively no KS5 evidence. Cooper's high-school band is US Grades 7-12; the curvilinear study sampled 13-year-olds. A-level independent study is untested at this scale.

Classroom rule Set fewer, tighter tasks tied to the lesson, give feedback on them, and cap the load rather than raising it.

Cooper, H., Robinson, J. C., & Patall, E. A. (2006). Does homework improve academic achievement? A synthesis of research, 1987-2003. Review of Educational Research, 76(1), 1-62.
Education Endowment Foundation. Homework. Teaching and Learning Toolkit (read via the Queen Rania Foundation mirror).
Fernandez-Alonso, R., Suarez-Alvarez, J., & Muniz, J. (2015). Adolescents' homework performance in mathematics and science: personal factors and teaching practices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(4), 1075-1085.

Technology, AI and SEND

Digital technology as a delivery mechanism, not an intervention

Moderate

Technology lifts attainment only when it makes a named pedagogical mechanism work better: clearer modelling, more or better-quality practice, faster feedback. The EEF's own framing is that the question of how to use technology is not separate from how to teach.

Effect EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit, digital technology strand: +4 months' additional progress, moderate cost, 3/5 evidence security, with component reviews ranging from +2 months to over a year. The live EEF Toolkit page is Cloudflare-blocked so its citation url is empty and the figure was cross-checked against a secondary tabulation; the EEF guidance report itself was read in full.

Breaks down The effect sits in the pedagogy, not the device. EEF's own worked example found ABRA's content and teacher development mattered more than the delivery medium. Poor implementation is the main reason technology underdelivers. Adding technology to existing teaching outperforms substituting it for teaching.

Age caveat EEF states the guidance applies to all settings but that most research is on school-age and older learners. Almost nothing is A-level specific, and nothing covers Google tools at 16-18.

Classroom rule Name the teaching mechanism first, then ask whether the tool does it better than paper. If you cannot name it, do not use the tool.

Stringer, E., Lewin, C., & Coleman, R. (2019). Using Digital Technology to Improve Learning: Guidance Report. Education Endowment Foundation.
Education Endowment Foundation. Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Digital Technology strand. EEF.
Roy, P., Poet, H., Staunton, R., Aston, K., & Thomas, D. (2024). ChatGPT in Lesson Preparation: A Teacher Choices Trial. Evaluation Report. NFER for the Education Endowment Foundation.

Intelligent tutoring systems

Strong

Systems that track a student's steps and respond at step or sub-step level produce gains close to one-to-one human tutoring. This is the strongest technology-and-learning finding in education, and it predates generative AI entirely.

Effect VanLehn (2011): intelligent tutoring systems d = 0.76 versus no tutoring; adult human tutoring d = 0.79, so the two are near-equivalent, and the folklore figures of d = 1.0 and d = 2.0 were not supported. Kulik & Fletcher (2016): median d = 0.66 across 50 controlled evaluations, substantially smaller on standardised than on locally developed tests.

Breaks down Confined to well-structured domains with checkable steps: mathematics, physics, statistics, programming. Answer-only systems are weak; step and sub-step feedback carries the effect. Gains shrink markedly when the outcome test is not aligned to the tutor's objectives, which is the usual case in public examinations.

Age caveat Mostly US school-age and undergraduate STEM. No pooled estimate exists for A-level essay subjects or for 16-18 humanities and social sciences.

Classroom rule Reserve tutoring systems for procedural, step-checkable content, and assess on the exam's terms rather than the system's.

VanLehn, K. (2011). The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems. Educational Psychologist, 46(4), 197-221.
Kulik, J. A., & Fletcher, J. D. (2016). Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review. Review of Educational Research, 86(1), 42-78.
Weidlich, J., Gasevic, D., Drachsler, H., & Kirschner, P. A. (2025). ChatGPT in Education: An Effect in Search of a Cause. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.

Generative AI tutoring and chatbots

Mixed

Chatbots reliably raise performance while the student holds the tool, and much less reliably once it is removed. Guardrails, teacher-written hints and withheld answers separate the positive trials from the harmful ones. Pooled estimates are not yet trustworthy.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate: the most-cited meta-analysis (g = 0.867) was retracted in April 2026. Kestin et al. (2025) RCT, N = 194 Harvard undergraduates: d = 0.63 by regression, 0.73-1.3 by quantile regression, immediate post-test, in less time. Bastani et al. (2025) RCT, ~1,000 Turkish students grades 9-11: +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor) during assisted practice, but -17% on the later unassisted exam for GPT Base and no significant difference for the guardrailed GPT Tutor.

Breaks down Kestin's tutor was expert prompt-engineered question by question, on one topic, in one session, with no delayed retention test. Bastani's harm disappeared under hint-only guardrails. Stanford's 2026 review found only 20 of 800+ AI-in-education papers give strong causal evidence.

Age caveat Bastani is the closest fit and is secondary mathematics in Turkey, grades 9-11, not A-level. Kestin is undergraduate physics. Nothing exists on A-level essay subjects or UK sixth forms.

Classroom rule Deploy AI only where a teacher wrote the hints and answers are withheld, then reassess the same content with the tool switched off.

Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports, 15.
Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakci, O., & Mariman, R. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS, 122(26), e2422633122.
Fesler, L., Martinez Claeys, J. P., Agnew, C., & Loeb, S. (2026). The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review. Stanford SCALE Initiative.
Wang, J., & Fan, W. (2026). Retraction Note: The effect of ChatGPT on students' learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 13, 528.

Cognitive offloading, AI reliance and metacognition

Moderate

Offloading thinking to a tool improves the immediate product and can leave the learning undone. The distinctive risk with fluent AI output is metacognitive: students mistake the ease of reading a good answer for having understood it.

Effect Bastani et al. (2025): -17% on an unassisted exam after unguarded GPT-4 practice. Fan et al. (2025, N = 117 university writers): the ChatGPT group gained most on essay score but showed no significant advantage in knowledge gain or knowledge transfer. Gerlich (2025, N = 666) reports a significant negative correlation between AI use and critical thinking, mediated by offloading, but it is cross-sectional self-report with a published correction.

Breaks down Offloading is not inherently harmful; notes, calculators and glossaries are offloading. Risko and Gilbert's framework predicts costs when the aid is withdrawn and when metacognitive judgements of one's own ability are wrong. Any measure taken with the tool present will overstate learning.

Age caveat Bastani is secondary, grades 9-11; Fan is university second-language writers; Gerlich is a general adult sample. No cohort study of 16-18 year olds on A-level courses.

Classroom rule Judge any AI-supported task by a later unaided performance on the same content, never by the artefact produced with the tool.

Bastani, H., et al. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS, 122(26), e2422633122.
Fan, Y., Tang, L., Le, H., Shen, K., Tan, S., Zhao, Y., Shen, Y., Li, X., & Gasevic, D. (2025). Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance. British Journal of Educational Technology, 56(2).
Risko, E. F., & Gilbert, S. J. (2016). Cognitive Offloading. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 20(9), 676-688.
Gerlich, M. (2025). AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking. Societies, 15(1), 6. [Correction: Societies, 15(9), 252.]

Multimedia and video learning (Mayer's principles)

Strong

Video helps most when it is added to teaching rather than substituted for it, and when it is segmented, signalled and free of narration that duplicates on-screen text. Individual design principles are real but individually small.

Effect Noetel et al. (2021), 105 randomised trials, 7,776 students: adding video to existing teaching g = 0.80; swapping video for existing teaching g = 0.28. Rey et al. (2019) segmenting, 56 investigations: d = 0.32 retention, 0.36 transfer; system-paced 0.42 retention, learner-paced retention non-significant. Richter et al. (2016) signalling of text-picture relations: r = 0.17.

Breaks down Segmenting increases time on task (d = -0.92 on learning time) and in Rey's data helped high prior-knowledge learners more on retention; signalling helped low prior-knowledge learners most. Noetel et al.'s meta-meta-analysis of 29 reviews and 1,189 studies finds most single principles small, well below textbook medians.

Age caveat Overwhelmingly undergraduate and laboratory; Noetel et al. (2021) is explicitly higher education. Very little school-age evidence, and none on A-level subject content.

Classroom rule Add video alongside teaching, segment it, signal what matters, and never read aloud text already on screen.

Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2021). Video Improves Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research, 91(2), 204-236.
Rey, G. D., Beege, M., Nebel, S., Wirzberger, M., Schmitt, T. H., & Schneider, S. (2019). A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 389-419.
Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 92(3), 413-454.
Mayer, R. E. (2017). Using multimedia for e-learning. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 33(5), 403-423.

Learning by teaching and the protege effect

Moderate

Expecting to teach helps a little; actually generating the explanation helps more, and shows up mainly on delayed tests. The gain comes from constructing the explanation, not from the recording equipment.

Effect Kobayashi (2019) meta-analysis of 28 studies: preparing to teach g = 0.35; preparing plus actually teaching g = 0.56, with larger gains when students expected and engaged in interactive teaching than non-interactive teaching. Kobayashi (2024) meta-analysis confirms interactivity as the key moderator. Benefits held after a delay and on deep as well as surface measures.

Breaks down Reading a prepared script to camera adds little; answering questions or anticipating a learner's confusion is what works. Explainers need enough prior knowledge to generate rather than recite. Immediate post-tests often show no advantage, so the effect is easy to miss in a single lesson.

Age caveat Predominantly undergraduate laboratory studies on short science and psychology texts. Little at 16-18, and nothing on A-level essay construction or extended writing.

Classroom rule Make students generate the explanation and then field questions on it; do not let production values substitute for explaining.

Kobayashi, K. (2019). Learning by Preparing-to-Teach and Teaching: A Meta-Analysis. Japanese Psychological Research, 61(3), 192-203.
Kobayashi, K. (2024). Interactive Learning Effects of Preparing to Teach and Teaching: a Meta-Analytic Approach. Educational Psychology Review, 36.
Fiorella, L. (2023). Learning by Teaching. In In Their Own Words: What Scholars Want You to Know About Why and How to Apply the Science of Learning. Society for the Teaching of Psychology.

Universal Design for Learning: evidence and critiques

Mixed

UDL-labelled instruction is associated with moderate achievement gains, but UDL is a framework rather than a defined intervention, the trials are small and weakly controlled, and its neuroscientific framing does not hold up.

Effect King-Sears et al. (2023) meta-analysis, 20 studies and 50 effects: g = 0.43 overall, 0.48 for school-aged learners, 0.28 for adults. Capp (2017) meta-analysis of 18 pre-post studies reported UDL as effective, but with weak designs and no control in many studies. Boysen (2024) found the studies CAST cites for its own guidelines mostly did not offer learners choice and did not measure learning.

Breaks down Because UDL specifies principles not procedures, trials differ in what was actually done and rarely isolate components, so the pooled estimate may reflect good teaching generally. Studies are small, often uncontrolled and heavily US. Boysen et al. found 1% of CAST's cited sources are neuroscience and 75% of the guidelines cite none.

Age caveat Effects are pooled from pre-kindergarten to adult, with the school-aged subgroup mostly primary and middle school. No A-level or selective sixth-form evidence exists.

Classroom rule Use UDL to plan access routes such as captions, readable text and alternative outputs; do not claim that offering choice raises attainment.

King-Sears, M. E., Stefanidis, A., Evmenova, A., Rao, K., Mergen, R. L., & Owen, L. S. (2023). Achievement of learners receiving UDL instruction: A meta-analysis. Teaching and Teacher Education, 122, 103956.
Capp, M. J. (2017). The effectiveness of universal design for learning: a meta-analysis of literature between 2013 and 2016. International Journal of Inclusive Education, 21(8), 791-807.
Boysen, G. A. (2024). A critical analysis of the research evidence behind CAST's universal design for learning guidelines. Policy Futures in Education.

Assistive technology and access arrangements

Moderate

Text-to-speech and speech-to-text remove a decoding or transcription barrier so a student can show what they know. That changes the route in, not the thinking the task requires. Keep the construct; change the access.

Effect Wood et al. (2018) meta-analysis of 22 studies and 2,942 students with reading disabilities: text-to-speech and related read-aloud tools improved reading comprehension at g = 0.35 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.56). Sireci et al. (2005) review of 28 accommodation studies: extended time raised scores for all students but more for students with disabilities. Speech-to-text has no pooled estimate.

Breaks down The interaction hypothesis is the honest test: a legitimate arrangement should help the student who needs it more than one who does not. Read-aloud on a reading-comprehension assessment can change what is measured. Matre and Cameron found only eight peer-reviewed speech-to-text studies at secondary level, of which two were experimental.

Age caveat Wood et al. pool grade 3 to postsecondary. Matre and Cameron cover ages 12-18 but with very few controlled studies. UK access-arrangement evidence at 16-18 is thin and largely survey-based.

Classroom rule Ask what the task measures. Remove barriers to getting in and out; never remove the reasoning being assessed.

Wood, S. G., Moxley, J. H., Tighe, E. L., & Wagner, R. K. (2018). Does Use of Text-to-Speech and Related Read-Aloud Tools Improve Reading Comprehension for Students With Reading Disabilities? A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 51(1), 73-84.
Sireci, S. G., Scarpati, S. E., & Li, S. (2005). Test Accommodations for Students with Disabilities: An Analysis of the Interaction Hypothesis. Review of Educational Research, 75(4), 457-490.
Matre, M. E., & Cameron, D. L. (2022). A scoping review on the use of speech-to-text technology for adolescents with learning difficulties in secondary education. Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, 19(3).

Working memory, ADHD, dyslexia, autism and processing speed in a selective setting

Mixed

High ability masks difficulty: able students with ADHD, dyslexia, autism or slow processing often reach an acceptable standard while working far harder. What helps is reducing extraneous load and making structure explicit, not training memory or lowering demand.

Effect No reliable pooled estimate for this combination. The negative evidence is firm: Melby-Lervag et al. (2016), 87 publications and 145 comparisons, found no convincing far transfer from working-memory training to verbal or nonverbal ability, decoding, reading comprehension or arithmetic. Cortese et al. (2015), 16 RCTs and 759 children, found cognitive-training effects on ADHD symptoms fell to marginal or non-significant under probably-blinded measures.

Breaks down The constructive side rests on EEF's recommendation 3 repertoire (explicit instruction, scaffolding, cognitive and metacognitive strategies, flexible grouping, technology) rather than on condition-specific trials, and EEF warns that searching for a magic bullet distracts from these. Twice-exceptional evidence is descriptive: Reis and Renzulli (2025) is interview and survey work, not causal.

Age caveat EEF's SEND report covers 5-16 mainstream. Reis and Renzulli follow US high-school students with autism into selective colleges, the closest available analogue to a selective sixth form.

Classroom rule Cut extraneous load: chunk, dual-code, give structure in writing. Keep the subject's cognitive demand fully intact.

Education Endowment Foundation (2020). Special Educational Needs in Mainstream Schools: Guidance Report. EEF.
Melby-Lervag, M., Redick, T. S., & Hulme, C. (2016). Working Memory Training Does Not Improve Performance on Measures of Intelligence or Other Measures of Far Transfer: Evidence From a Meta-Analytic Review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 512-534.
Cortese, S., Ferrin, M., Brandeis, D., Buitelaar, J., Daley, D., Dittmann, R. W., et al. (2015). Cognitive Training for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Meta-Analysis of Clinical and Neuropsychological Outcomes From Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 54(3), 164-174.
Reis, S. M., & Renzulli, S. J. (2025). Research-Based Strength-Based Teaching and Support Strategies for Twice-Exceptional High School Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Behavioral Sciences, 15(6), 834.

Screen versus paper reading

Strong

Reading dense expository text on screen produces slightly worse comprehension than on paper, alongside overconfidence about how much was understood. The penalty is largest under time pressure and disappears for narrative text.

Effect Delgado et al. (2018) meta-analysis, 54 studies and 171,055 participants: paper advantage Hedges' g = -0.21, concentrated in expository text (g = -0.27) and absent for narrative (g = 0.01). Clinton (2019): g = -0.25 overall, -0.32 for expository text. Altamura et al. (2025), 40 effect sizes and 469,564 participants: leisure digital reading correlates with comprehension at only r = .055, against medium effects for print.

Breaks down This is not a property of pixels. Self-paced, single-purpose reading narrows the gap; time pressure and multitasking widen it, and calibration of one's own comprehension is worse on screen. Substituting listening for reading is neutral overall (g = 0.07) but worse for inferential comprehension (g = 0.36 favouring reading).

Age caveat Delgado and Clinton pool school through university. Altamura found negative associations at primary and middle school and positive ones later. Little 16-18 specific evidence and none on A-level set texts.

Classroom rule Keep first close reading of dense or examined text on paper; use screens for search, annotation and revisiting.

Delgado, P., Vargas, C., Ackerman, R., & Salmeron, L. (2018). Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension. Educational Research Review, 25, 23-38.
Clinton, V. (2019). Reading from paper compared to screens: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Research in Reading, 42(2), 288-325.
Altamura, L., Vargas, C., & Salmeron, L. (2025). Do New Forms of Reading Pay Off? A Meta-Analysis on the Relationship Between Leisure Digital Reading Habits and Text Comprehension. Review of Educational Research, 95(2).
Clinton-Lisell, V. (2022). Listening Ears or Reading Eyes: A Meta-Analysis of Reading and Listening Comprehension Comparisons. Review of Educational Research, 92(4), 543-582.

How to read this

Impact /10Proximity to an A* discriminator (0–3) + evidence strength (0–3) + dose and scalability (0–2) + low cost and risk (0–2). The four sub-scores are stated in each rationale, so you can disagree with one rather than with the number.
SAMRSubstitution is the same task with no functional change. Augmentation is a functional improvement. Modification means the task is significantly redesigned. Redefinition was previously inconceivable. Most good ideas are Augmentation or Modification, and the labels here are not inflated.
TPACKThe dominant intersection. TPK: the tool enables a pedagogical move. TCK: the tool represents subject content. PCK: subject-specific teaching knowledge drives it. TPACK: all three fused.
Rosenshine1 Daily review · 2 Small steps · 3 Ask questions · 4 Provide models · 5 Guide practice · 6 Check for understanding · 7 High success rate · 8 Scaffolds · 9 Independent practice · 10 Weekly and monthly review
EffortTeacher set-up and ongoing time. Low means you could run it next week.

The three routes

A → A*

Knowledge is secure. Marks go on the hardest items, precision slips, uneven papers, formulaic evaluation and timing. Attack exemplar deconstruction, calibration, hardest-item practice and checking routines.

B → A*

Topic gaps, partial assessment-objective coverage, inconsistent technique, recall too slow. Attack systematic diagnosis, spaced retrieval across the whole specification and weekly cumulative review.

C → A*

Significant gaps, weak foundations, poor habits, lower self-efficacy. Attack with a high success rate, small steps, scaffolds later removed and explicit study routines, staged over two years.

SEND

SEND here means a high-attaining student whose access to the demand is obstructed, not a student working below the standard. Adaptations remove the barrier and leave the thinking intact, because reducing cognitive demand forfeits the A*. Every example carries an adaptation; 30 are built around a need from the start.

Running the sessions

There is no fixed week-by-week schedule here: you decide what runs when. The tools are presented in a suggested order that moves from features every teacher already has, to teacher-facing AI, to student-facing AI, to the production tools. Nothing stops you reordering it.

One hard constraint. Timing constraint: student access to NotebookLM has not been released yet. Teachers can build and check notebooks now, but anything that needs a student to open one has to wait until access lands. Plan it for later in the programme.

Run each session the way you want staff to teach: review last session’s commitment and the evidence they brought, model one example live with real subject materials, guided practice with their own specification and mark scheme, independent planning of the classroom step including which route they will run and which student with SEND it must work for, a check for understanding, then a written commitment.

Guardrails

  • Data protection. No pupil names, marks or personal data in NotebookLM sources, Gem instructions, prompts or Vids scripts. School Workspace accounts only. SEND status is special category data and never enters a prompt or a shared resource.
  • Academic integrity. For non-exam assessment, including the Computer Science project, Art portfolio and Music composition, AI may support planning, feedback and revision but must not produce submitted content.
  • Cognitive offloading. The student must do the thinking. Scaffolds are temporary and every example that starts with a generated structure names when it is withdrawn.
  • Age gates. Several 2026 features are 18+ or need a paid licence, and Year 12 contains under-18s. Each example’s risks line names the gate and its fallback. Ask the Workspace admin to confirm each service is on for the right organisational unit before you introduce it.

How this was built

Tool capabilities were verified against Google’s own documentation on 17 September 2026. Exam-board criteria came from specifications, mark schemes, examiners’ reports and published grade boundaries. The research base was compiled from meta-analyses and Education Endowment Foundation reviews. The examples were written from those verified notes, then checked mechanically for completeness, word limits, Rosenshine number and name agreement, and that each impact score equals the four sub-scores in its own rationale. They were not independently verified by a second pass.
